APEX-M

The Sellers Guide · Microsoft Platform Edition
Volume I · Commercial
Pursuing Microsoft Revenue in Industry Accounts

A field guide for Deloitte Microsoft-practice sellers, Global Practice Leaders, and co-selling account teams. Position APEX-M–accelerated Services — the productized 38-Service catalog Deloitte's Microsoft practice delivers — to drive Fabric, Copilot, Foundry, Microsoft Agent Framework, and Purview revenue at your industry's anchor accounts. Clients buy Services with KPI envelopes; APEX-M is the framework that builds them faster on the Microsoft Platform. Part of the APEX-M Trilogy — paired with the Services Guide (Volume II) and the Deployment Guide (Volume III).

About this edition

APEX-M is the Microsoft Platform edition of the APEX framework — the canonical edition Deloitte Microsoft Technology & Services Practice (DMTSP) uses to deliver Services on Microsoft Fabric · Microsoft Foundry · Microsoft Agent Framework · Microsoft 365 Copilot · Microsoft Purview · Microsoft Entra.

Two sister editions are on the roadmap for clients whose architectural commitments lead with a different hyperscaler: APEX-G (Google Cloud Platform · Vertex AI · BigQuery · Gemini) and APEX-A (Amazon Web Services · Bedrock · SageMaker · Q). Each will ship its own Sellers Guide, Services Guide, and Deployment Guide trilogy.

This book — Professional APEX-M: The Sellers Guide — assumes a Microsoft-anchored pursuit. The four-Microsoft-pillar arguments in Part II, the Industry Playbooks in Part III, and the 38-Service catalog throughout all land on the Microsoft Platform.

How to Use This Book

What APEX Is — read this first

APEX is a framework that accelerates the building of services and agents on the Microsoft Platform. It is the architectural substrate Deloitte's Microsoft practice uses internally to deliver Services faster, more consistently, and with more rigorous governance. APEX is not a product and is not sold to clients. What clients buy are Services — productized envelopes with KPI commitments, scope, persona model, and two-contract Independence-compliant commercial structure. The 38-Service catalog this book repeatedly references (RC-E2E-03 · HLS-E2E-04 · TMT-TEL-RAA-04 · etc.) is the catalog of Services the framework can build; each individual Service is the contractable unit.

What this means for sellers: when this book talks about "positioning APEX" at an anchor account, read "positioning the APEX-accelerated Service that fits the account's pursuit." When it talks about "selling APEX," read "winning a Service engagement that Deloitte will deliver using the APEX framework on the Microsoft Platform." The two-contract model (client ↔ Microsoft for platform · client ↔ Deloitte for the Service-delivery engagement) makes the Service the contractable unit, not the framework. Sellers position Services that APEX accelerates · GPLs prioritize Service pursuits · ECIF flows through the Microsoft contract for the platform consumption that the Service runs on. APEX is the means; the Service is what the client signs for.

Professional APEX: The Sellers Guide is a Wrox-style field book for sellers pursuing APEX-accelerated Service opportunities in named industry accounts. It is not the architect's reference — that book is the Services Guide (Volume II of the trilogy). This book is what you open before a client meeting, during a pursuit, or when the GPL asks "what's the play at Walmart?".

The book is organised around three seller questions:

  • "What am I selling, and why does it move Microsoft revenue?" → Parts I and II.
  • "What do I say in this industry / to this specific client?" → Parts III and IV. Open Part III for the industry play; open Part IV for the named-account play; use both.
  • "What do I do next in my pursuit cycle?" → Part V and the Appendices.
Independence Reminder

This book contains publicly-observable strategic signals on named accounts. It does not represent that Deloitte is currently engaged with any named account, nor does it disclose confidential client information. All account narratives are framed as hypotheses to validate in discovery.

This edition: APEX-M

This is the APEX-M Sellers Guide — the Microsoft Platform edition. The framework you'll see described as "APEX" throughout is APEX-M unless the text explicitly names a different edition. APEX-M is what Deloitte Microsoft Technology & Services Practice (DMTSP) ships today on Microsoft Fabric · Microsoft Foundry · Microsoft Agent Framework · Microsoft 365 Copilot · Microsoft Purview · Microsoft Entra. Sister editions APEX-G (GCP) and APEX-A (AWS) are on the roadmap; see Ch 0A for the full family framing and when to pick which.

What APEX stands for

APEX — Agent-based Platform for EXecution.

APEX is Deloitte's internal delivery accelerator for agentic AI. APEX-M — the edition this book covers — is anchored to the Microsoft technology platform. The acronym encodes the core idea: a platform built specifically to turn reasoning agents into executable, governable, auditable business decisions at enterprise scale.

  • A — Agent-based
  • P — Platform
  • E — for
  • X — EXecution

APEX-M is a framework of methodology, semantic-model libraries, agent catalogs (authored in Microsoft Agent Framework), MCP tool libraries, HITL gate patterns, audit-row discipline, and Wave 1/2/3 playbooks — all anchored to the Microsoft Platform. APEX is Deloitte-internal — it is the accelerator that makes delivery fast, not a product the client buys. Clients contract Deloitte for Agentic AI Delivery Services; Deloitte uses APEX-M to deliver them on the Microsoft Platform. See §1.0 and Appendix Y for the complete positioning, and Ch 0A for the APEX-M / APEX-G / APEX-A family framing.

A note from the author

You are holding (or reading on a screen) the Deloitte sellers guide for Agentic AI Delivery Services. The guide exists because the window of opportunity for enterprise agentic AI is genuinely open and genuinely finite. Clients who move now with discipline will have agentic operations that compound for a decade. Clients who delay by eighteen months will have catching up to do. Clients who move without discipline — who skip Independence, skip HITL, skip audit-row attribution — will have failed deployments that harden the organization against future attempts. Sellers have a material role in whether enterprises end up in the first, second, or third category.

This is the guide I wish I had when I started delivering enterprise agentic AI on the Microsoft platform. It codifies what works and, just as importantly, what does not. The first discipline — established in §1.0 and restated throughout — is that Deloitte does not sell APEX. Clients buy Agentic AI Delivery Services from Deloitte; they buy the Microsoft platform from Microsoft; APEX is the internal delivery accelerator that lets us move faster than a ground-up build allows. Sellers who internalise this discipline carry credibility that sellers who blur it do not.

The second discipline is Independence. Deloitte is Microsoft external auditor. Every sentence about the Deloitte-Microsoft relationship is regulatorily material. The approved language ("technology platform relationship," "collaboration," never "partnership" or "alliance"), the approved funding paths (direct client, DCIF to client, ISV Marketplace, SI teaming — never ECIF direct to Deloitte), and the audit-client pre-clearance requirement are not stylistic preferences. They are what keep Deloitte audit practice credible.

The third discipline is client outcomes. Every agent decision writes an audit row that attributes measurable business outcome. No hand-waving. A CFO asking "what are we getting for this" should get a defensible dollar-per-decision answer. Chapter 1 §1.3 covers the three executive pains; Appendix S covers expected KPI ranges per Industry and Functional Area. The discipline is measurement, attribution, and honest range-commitment.

How to use the guide — reading paths by persona

First-time seller (never pursued an APEX engagement): Read linearly Parts I and II. Then read the Practice chapter for your pursuit (Ch 9–15). Then read Chapter 29 (Qualifying) and Chapter 30 (Discovery). Skim Appendix V to learn the cross-reference index so you can navigate the rest as questions come up. Total time: ~6 hours focused reading.

Experienced seller preparing a specific pursuit: Start with Appendix V (cross-reference index). Jump to the Practice deep-dive (§9.11, §10.10, §11.10, §12.10, §13.13, §14.9, §15.9 depending on industry). Read the relevant anchor-account playbook (Ch 16–28) if applicable. Open Appendix W (Discovery-to-SOW artifacts) to start drafting. Total time: ~90 minutes per pursuit.

Architect preparing a client workshop: Open §1.6 (canonical schema), §1.6A (industry standards), §2.2A (envelopes), §2.2B (value-delivery chain), §2.2C (oversight spectrum), §6.9 (orchestration), §6.10 (audit row — agent-side), §8.8 (audit — end-to-end), and the relevant Practice deep-dive. These ten sections cover the architect conversation end-to-end. Total time: ~3 hours.

Practice Leader: Reference deployments are canonical — Big Box Store §16.13, hospital §10.9, utility §11.9, plant §12.9A, airline §14.8. Use these in client business-case construction. Chapter 38 is the end-to-end pursuit walkthrough.

Pursuit QR (quality reviewer): Appendix V (cross-reference index), §1.5A (go/no-go cheat sheet), §C.9 (pricing objections), §X.8 (QR checklist), Independence content in Appendix E and §E.1–E.x.

Independence bright-line quick-reference

The single most-used reference card. Ten things never to say; ten compliance-safe substitutes.

Never saySay instead
"Deloitte partners with Microsoft""Deloitte has a technology platform relationship with Microsoft"
"Our joint venture with Microsoft""Deloitte delivers services on the Microsoft platform"
"Microsoft and Deloitte are aligned on pricing""Microsoft sets platform pricing; Deloitte sets services pricing independently"
"We can bundle Microsoft and Deloitte""You contract Microsoft platform separately from Deloitte services"
"Microsoft ECIF funds this work""Compliant funding paths are direct client, DCIF allocated to client, ISV Marketplace, SI teaming"
"APEX is a Microsoft-endorsed product""APEX is Deloitte's internal delivery accelerator, not a product offered to clients"
"We sell APEX""Clients contract Deloitte for Agentic AI Delivery Services; Deloitte uses APEX internally"
"Microsoft guarantees this outcome""Microsoft provides the platform; Deloitte is accountable for the delivery outcome"
"The audit committee approved this at all Deloitte audit clients""Audit Committee pre-clearance is engagement-specific and must be confirmed per pursuit"
"Microsoft promised ECIF""ECIF direct to Deloitte is prohibited by Independence rules regardless of who promises it"

When uncertain, route the language through the Deloitte Independence Office before external use.

Who contributed to this guide

This guide synthesizes learning from hundreds of Deloitte consultants across the DMTSP practice, industry practice leaders in RC / HLS / ER / AXLE / TMT / TH / ICE, the AXLE automotive framework team, technical architects across the Fabric / Foundry / Copilot / Purview / Entra ecosystem, and the Deloitte Independence Office. What this guide is not

This guide is not a legal document. Every Independence reminder points back to the Independence Office for authoritative interpretation. Every regulatory reference (Appendix P) is informational, not legal advice. Every commercial framework (Appendix N) passes through Deloitte Commercial QR before client proposal.

This guide is not a client-facing artifact. It is a Deloitte-internal document. When you need client-facing material, use the adapted decks referenced in Appendix O, adapted per pursuit with client-specific substance and reviewed through standard QR channels.

This guide is not static. It evolves quarterly at minimum, and whenever Microsoft platform or Deloitte service catalog changes warrant. Contribute back (Appendix X) when your pursuits produce patterns worth codifying.

The moment

In April 2026, the Microsoft four-plane architecture is the only enterprise stack that natively composes data, reasoning, governance, and identity for agentic AI. Deloitte Independence obligation with Microsoft means the commercial path is services-only, two-contract, ECIF-prohibited — the discipline that makes the services relationship durable. And Deloitte Agentic AI Delivery Services, accelerated internally by APEX and (in automotive) AXLE, represents the path to production in under twelve months for clients who otherwise would spend two years building.

That is the moment. This guide is how sellers engage with it.

— Keven Markham VP, Enterprise Transformation Deloitte Microsoft Technology & Services Practice April 2026

Chapter 0A

About This Edition — APEX-M and the APEX Platform Family

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Names this book explicitly: APEX-M, the Microsoft Platform edition of the APEX framework. Every page that follows assumes a Microsoft-anchored pursuit.

APEX is a framework name. APEX-M, APEX-G, APEX-A are editions — each tuned to one hyperscaler's native agentic stack. A seller's job is to know which edition fits which pursuit and to read the right trilogy before stepping into the client meeting.

0A.1.1 Why Platform-Aligned, Not Platform-Neutral

Every multi-cloud RFP eventually asks the question: "Can APEX run on any cloud?" The defensible answer is no, and that is a feature. A platform-neutral agentic framework has to optimise for the lowest common denominator across hyperscalers: it cannot use Microsoft Entra agent identities (those are Microsoft Entra-specific), it cannot use BigQuery's native ML.GENERATE_TEXT (that is BigQuery-specific), it cannot use Bedrock's Knowledge Bases (those are Bedrock-specific). What you get is a portable framework that loses each platform's native-integration leverage — exactly the leverage that makes the agent decision plane cohere into one auditable surface.

APEX is platform-aligned by deliberate choice. Each edition (APEX-M, APEX-G, APEX-A) maximises the native integration of its target platform. Sellers position APEX-M against a Microsoft-anchored client because APEX-M can use Microsoft Entra Agent ID, Purview lineage, Fabric Direct Lake, and Foundry hosted agents end-to-end — none of which a portable framework can. Sellers pick APEX-G for Google-anchored clients for the symmetric reason.

Objection — "Our client is multi-cloud, won't APEX-M lock them in?"

Response. APEX-M is anchored to the Microsoft Platform for the decision plane — the surfaces where agents reason, where governance flows, where the audit row writes. Data can still live across clouds; APEX-M reads from S3 / BigQuery / Snowflake via Fabric Mirroring or shortcuts (per Services Guide Ch 1A). What APEX-M does not portably support is moving the agent plane itself off Microsoft. If the client requires that, the right answer is APEX-A (Bedrock-native) or APEX-G (Vertex-native) — not a portable abstraction over all three. The two-contract Independence model (per §1.2) is platform-aligned by design; one decision plane, one tenant, one set of auditable identities.

0A.2 Microsoft Agent Framework — The Runtime APEX-M Leads With

APEX-M's agent runtime is Microsoft Agent Framework — Microsoft's open-source agent SDK that became Generally Available in 2026, available in .NET, Python, and Java. It is the canonical orchestration runtime across every Microsoft agent surface (Foundry Agent Service · Microsoft 365 Copilot · Copilot Studio · Microsoft Agent365 / Entra Agent ID). Sellers should treat "Agent Framework" as the answer to "what agent platform does APEX-M run on?" and as the differentiator against competitor agent SDKs (LangChain · LlamaIndex · CrewAI · Mosaic AI Agent Framework · AWS Bedrock Agents).

Key Play — when the client asks "why Microsoft Agent Framework over LangChain?"

"Three reasons. One: Microsoft Agent Framework agents are first-class governance subjects — every published agent gets a Microsoft Entra Agent ID, Conditional Access policies, and Purview classifications applied automatically. Two: the Foundry + Agent Framework + Purview integration is Microsoft-engineered end-to-end — the audit row, the lineage, the content-safety verdicts, the cost-per-decision metering all wire together without custom integration. LangChain is a SDK; it doesn't carry that platform-level wiring. Three: our delivery economics — APEX-M's 38-Service catalog already runs on Microsoft Agent Framework. We don't have to rebuild on LangChain to deliver Wave 2."

1.0 What Deloitte Sells, What APEX Accelerates

Before any seller reads further, the positioning of this guide must be unambiguous.

Deloitte does not sell APEX. APEX is not a product. Clients do not buy APEX. APEX does not appear on SOWs, in proposals, or in executive conversations. When sellers are tempted to say "we sell APEX to clients," they are stating the positioning incorrectly.

Deloitte sells Deloitte Agentic AI Delivery Services. Advisory, implementation, sustain, and managed services for the deployment of agentic agents on the Microsoft technology platform. That is the service catalog clients procure from Deloitte.

Clients license the Microsoft platform directly from Microsoft. Microsoft Fabric, Azure AI Foundry, Microsoft 365 Copilot, MCP servers, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Entra — all contracted between the client and Microsoft, never through Deloitte.

APEX is Deloitte's internal delivery accelerator. It is the proprietary methodology, semantic-model library, agent catalog, MCP tool library, HITL gate framework, audit-row discipline, and Wave 1/2/3 delivery playbook that Deloitte teams use internally to accelerate client deployments from 18–24 months to 9–12 months. Sellers learn APEX internally so they can confidently describe what Deloitte will deliver and why Deloitte delivers faster than the client could build it themselves.

The three-way relationship in one diagram

  • Client procures Microsoft platform licenses from Microsoft and Agentic AI Delivery Services from Deloitte.
  • Microsoft provides the platform (Fabric, Foundry, Copilot, MCP, Purview, Entra) directly to the client.
  • Deloitte delivers advisory, implementation, and operate services to the client — using APEX internally as the accelerator that makes delivery faster, cleaner, and more defensible.
  • Deloitte audits Microsoft — the relationship that makes the two-contract discipline non-negotiable.

The client sees agents on their Microsoft platform, delivered by Deloitte consultants. The client does not see a named "APEX product."

What sellers tell clients

  • "Deloitte will deliver your agentic-AI program on your Microsoft platform."
  • "Deloitte has invested in proprietary accelerators that let us deploy in months, not years."
  • "Your agents run on Fabric, Foundry, Copilot, MCP, and Purview — everything you've already licensed from Microsoft or will license directly."
  • "Deloitte's services contract covers the delivery; Microsoft's licensing covers the platform. Two separate agreements, one coherent program."

What sellers DO NOT tell clients

  • "Buy APEX."
  • "APEX is Deloitte's product for you."
  • "We'll give you an APEX license."
  • "APEX costs $X per user/month."
  • "APEX comes with Microsoft."

Any of these statements is a positioning error. Correct sellers to the accurate framing above.

Why the positioning matters

Three reasons this discipline is non-negotiable:

  1. Commercial clarity. Clients who believe they are buying "an APEX product" have mismatched expectations. Deloitte sells services; APEX is how we deliver them.
  2. Independence protection. Deloitte is Microsoft's auditor. The commercial structure must be clean: platform from Microsoft, services from Deloitte. APEX as an internal accelerator preserves that boundary; APEX as a sold product blurs it.
  3. Client ownership. What the client licenses from Microsoft is the client's — forever. What Deloitte delivers onto the client's platform is the client's — forever. APEX IP is Deloitte's and stays with Deloitte. At engagement exit the client owns their agents, their data, their Microsoft platform; Deloitte retains the framework methodology for the next engagement.
Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. Every statement made to a client — verbal, written, or slide — should pass the test: "If the SEC or PCAOB read this, would they conclude Deloitte and Microsoft have a commingled commercial offering?" The answer must always be no. "Deloitte delivers services; Microsoft provides the platform; the client contracts both separately" is the sentence that keeps the answer no.

With positioning established, the rest of this chapter covers the forces that make today the right moment for clients to engage Deloitte for agentic-AI delivery.

1.1 What APEX actually is (for sellers' internal understanding)

APEX is a manifest-driven agentic delivery accelerator that turns enterprise events into decisions — auditable, reversible, and governed. It was built by Deloitte's Microsoft Technology Services Practice (DMTSP) to address a specific gap every large enterprise has but few have named: the distance between "we have the data" and "we made the right decision in time." APEX closes that gap with a programmatic, contract-enforced system of agents, orchestrations, human-in-the-loop gates, and auditable decision rows — all used by Deloitte internally to accelerate client deployments of agentic AI on the Microsoft platform.

APEX leverages the Microsoft technology platform (Fabric, Azure AI Foundry, Purview, Copilot, Entra) as its runtime substrate. The client licenses the platform directly from Microsoft; Deloitte sells APEX — the services, IP, semantic models, agent library, and delivery methodology — on a separate contract. This two-contract model is not a convenience. It is an Independence requirement that reflects Deloitte's role as Microsoft's external auditor, codified in SEC Rule 2-01 and PCAOB Rule 3520.

What makes APEX different from "another AI platform"

Every hyperscaler, every SI, and every system vendor has an "AI platform" pitch in 2026. APEX is distinctive on four dimensions:

  1. Manifest-driven, not model-driven. An APEX service is defined by four manifests (event, orchestration, agent, tenant) that together specify the contract between the data plane and the decision. The model behind the agent is a detail; the manifest is the governance artifact.
  2. Audit row, not log line. Every APEX decision writes a row with inputs, reasoning trace, model version, tool version, policy version, HITL status, and downstream effect. This row survives audit, regulatory inspection, and internal post-mortem.
  3. HITL is first-class, not bolted on. APEX's human-in-the-loop gates are contracted in the manifest, not coded ad-hoc. Sellers should never describe APEX as "autonomous AI." It is adaptive human-supervised decisioning.
  4. Fabric + Foundry + Purview + Entra composition. APEX is architecturally native to the Microsoft four-plane pattern. This is an architectural observation, not a commercial assertion. See Chapter 4 for the competitive framing.
Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. The sentence "APEX is a Deloitte product that leverages the Microsoft technology platform" should be memorised verbatim. It accurately describes the relationship, passes Independence review, and sets up the two-contract framing without implying a joint commercial bundle.

1.1A.2 A Practice is a bundle of five reusable assets

A Practice is not a product the client buys. It is an internal Deloitte asset that accelerates delivery. Each Practice is composed of five things Deloitte maintains across engagements and reuses on every new pursuit:

  1. Canonical schemas. Semantic models that normalize the Practice's domain regardless of the client's source systems. Examples: SCML (Supply Chain), MERML (Merchandising), CXML (Customer) for RC; PatientML, ClaimML, StudyML for HLS; AXLEML sub-models for AXLE; UOGML, P&UML, MiningML for ER. See Appendix G for the full schema inventory.
  2. Agent catalog. Pre-built, tested, governance-wrapped agents addressing the Practice's top decisions. RC ships ~40 agents; HLS ~35; AXLE ~30; ER, TMT, TH, and ICE each ship 20–30.
  3. Orchestration catalog. Sequential / parallel / hierarchical / feedback orchestrations assembled from the 47 APEX archetypes. Each Practice publishes its own catalog of ~15–25 orchestrations. See Appendix T.
  4. Service catalog. Agents and orchestrations grouped into named, productized services with defined personas, KPIs, SLOs, and commercial envelopes. Example service codes: RC-E2E-03 Assortment & Pricing, HLS-E2E-02 Clinical Decision Support, AXLE-Connected-Factory-01, TMT-TEL-CC-03 Contact Center Intelligence.
  5. Delivery playbook. Wave 1 / 2 / 3 sizing, discovery prompts, objection handlers, reference-architecture sketches, and pre-clearance checklists specific to the Practice.

1.1A.3 Why Practices exist — the acceleration argument

Without a Practice, every client engagement begins from a blank Fabric workspace, a blank Foundry project, and a blank Power BI tenant. The first twelve to eighteen months are spent building:

  • A semantic model for the client's domain
  • A catalog of agents with HITL gates and audit discipline
  • A library of orchestrations that compose agents into end-to-end outcomes
  • A service definition that the client's business leaders can buy
  • A delivery method with governance, Independence, and commercial envelope

A Practice collapses this work. The client inherits Deloitte's engineering-year investment on day one. Deloitte delivers the first outcome in Wave 1 (4–12 weeks) rather than Wave 2 or 3. This is the reason a Practice exists: time-to-value compression.

1.2 The five forces that make APEX sellable today

The reason APEX closes now — and not in 2027 — is the convergence of five forces. You do not need to recite all five in a first meeting. You need to name the two that apply most to the prospect in front of you and be able to defend all five if challenged.

Force 1: The decision-velocity gap

Events outpace human triage in every operations-intensive enterprise. In a large-format retailer, the store operations team receives 2,500–4,000 signals a day per store across inventory, safety, labor, customer service, and regulatory categories. Internal benchmarks indicate under 20 % are triaged in time to act. The remaining 80 % become aged work, write-offs, customer complaints, or regulatory findings.

This force resonates with COOs, VPs of Operations, Store Operations directors, and Plant Managers. Translate it to their vocabulary: "How much of what your stores/plants/hospitals see in a day actually gets acted on before the window closes?" The honest answer is always "less than we'd like."

Force 2: Agentic AI inflection

The underlying technology crossed the enterprise-viability threshold in late 2024. Model tool-calling, function schemas, long-context grounding, and multi-agent orchestration are now production-grade. The operating model has not caught up. Most enterprises have one or two isolated agent pilots that have not scaled because they lack the semantic model, governance, and HITL discipline APEX provides.

This force resonates with CIOs, Chief Digital Officers, and Chief AI Officers who have been asked by their boards "what's our agentic strategy?" A credible answer requires not just a pilot story but an operating framework. APEX is the framework.

Force 3: Regulatory acceleration

Reporting windows have shortened across every regulated industry. 21 CFR Part 11 (Life Sciences), FERC reliability (Power & Utilities), HIPAA breach notification (HLS), EU DSA (TMT-MED), SOX §302 and §404 (public-company financial reporting), PCI DSS (payment-handling). A decision-automation platform whose audit trail is regulator-ready is a decision-automation platform you can actually deploy in production in these industries.

This force resonates with Chief Compliance Officers, Chief Legal Officers, and audit-committee-adjacent executives. The APEX audit row is the artifact; Purview's lineage plus Fabric's time-travel plus the manifest itself constitute a defensible evidentiary chain.

Force 4: Data sovereignty and PII complexity

Every decision crosses regulatory boundaries. A marketing segmentation touches PII; a clinical decision touches PHI; a payment routing touches PCI. APEX's tokenization-at-Silver pattern and native Purview integration mean sensitive data is classified, labeled, and governed before it reaches the agent layer — and the agent cannot bypass DLP controls.

This force resonates with Chief Data Officers, Chief Privacy Officers, and Chief Information Security Officers. The conversation is technical and fast; do not try to oversell.

Force 5: Knowledge-worker shortage

The people who hold institutional judgement are retiring. Pharmacist, credit-risk-officer, category-manager, radiologist, pilot-scheduler, grid-dispatcher — the median tenure of these roles is dropping, and the mid-career pipeline is thin. APEX's HITL gate captures their reasoning as they use the system; over time the judgment is codified into policy, not lost with the person.

This force resonates with Chief People Officers, Chief Human Resources Officers, and line-of-business leaders whose operating plan assumes talent they cannot actually hire.

1.3 The three executive pains APEX solves

The five forces are the market context. The three pains are what land in the room.

CIO pain: Tool sprawl. A typical Fortune 500 function runs 12–20 point tools. Rules engines, BI tools, ML workbenches, integration middleware, alerting platforms, workflow systems, policy engines. Each has an operating cost, an integration surface, and a dependency graph the CIO inherits but did not design. APEX collapses the agentic-decision layer into one platform with one semantic model and one audit trail. The TCO story is concrete: deprecate N tools, consolidate onto Fabric + Foundry, offload governance to Purview.

CFO pain: Untracked decision-ROI. CFOs can tell you the cost of their analytics estate to the dollar. They cannot tell you the aggregate dollar value of decisions taken against that estate. This is the audit-row gap. APEX's audit row ties every decision to its measurable downstream effect — write-offs avoided, disputes recovered, stale tags remediated, denials prevented, stockouts averted. When a CFO asks "what am I getting for the AI spend?", APEX answers in dollars per decision row, not in hours saved.

COO pain: Capacity-for-judgement. Operators — store managers, plant supervisors, hospital charge nurses, grid dispatchers — spend 55–70 % of their shift gathering data. They decide with partial information because gathering complete information is infeasible. Deloitte's agent delivery inverts the ratio. Agents handle the gathering, the operator handles the deciding. The ratio flips from 65 / 35 gathering / deciding to 25 / 75 deciding / gathering. The COO gets judgment capacity back without hiring.

Note

Example in the field — Big Box Store Store 100. Marisol Reyes, Operations Lead at Big Box Store Store 100, handled 8 operational events in a single shift — cold-chain excursion, receiving discrepancy, ESL failure, phantom OOS, FDA recall, BOPIS substitution, shrink pattern, foreign-object incident. Total manager touch across all 8 events: approximately 1 hour. Manager time returned vs pre-agent baseline: 5.2 hours per shift. See §16.13 for the full narrative. Agents delivered by Deloitte on Big Box Store's Microsoft platform; APEX was the internal accelerator that made the delivery feasible.

Key Play

Key Play. Lead with the pain that matches the exec you're sitting with. Do NOT recite all three. If you cover all three, you sound scripted. If you lead with the wrong one — CFO math to a COO, sprawl to a CFO — you sound like you did not prepare.

The 60-second pitch, three variants

To a CIO: "APEX is Deloitte's agentic platform. It runs on Microsoft Fabric, Foundry, Purview, and Entra. It collapses twelve to twenty point tools into one governed platform. Every decision is audited, reversible, and traceable to policy. Wave 1 is four to eight weeks and produces a concrete architecture and business case. Your Microsoft licensing is separate — that stays between you and Microsoft."

To a CFO: "APEX ties every AI decision to a dollar of measurable downstream effect. We write an audit row per decision with the input, the reasoning, the outcome, and the attributable value. For a Wave 2 deployment in your industry, we typically see 12–18 month payback on the first service alone. The platform license for Microsoft Fabric is your contract with Microsoft; our fees are fixed on Wave 1 and gated on Wave 2."

To a COO: "APEX reverses the ratio of data-gathering to deciding for your front-line operators. Your managers spend 65 % of their shift on data gathering today; APEX gets that to 25 %. The operator stays in the loop — every decision has a human-in-the-loop gate where it matters. Wave 1 picks one operational workflow, instrumented end-to-end, measurable in six weeks."

1.4 When APEX is NOT the right pitch

Qualification is a resource-allocation decision. Partners and Practice Leaders have a finite number of Wave 1 envisioning slots per quarter. Spending one on a bad-fit pursuit costs you two pursuits: the wasted one and the good one you could not serve.

APEX is NOT the right pitch when:

  • The prospect is still debating cloud migration at all. APEX assumes the client has decided on a cloud strategy. If they have not, help them with cloud strategy first.
  • The prospect has strategic AWS/GCP commitments that block Azure platform deployment. Architecturally honest disqualification. Chapter 4 covers the language.
  • The prospect's last three AI projects were canceled for governance reasons. This is a change-management problem, not a platform problem. APEX will not survive the same organization that killed the prior three.
  • The prospect wants a POC. APEX is a program, not a POC. If the only commercial envelope on offer is $150K for a six-week proof, qualify out or reframe to Wave 1 envisioning.
  • The prospect is a Deloitte audit client without pre-clearance. Hard gate. Do not engage commercially until Independence confirms pre-clearance.
  • The prospect's timeline is "let's see something next month". APEX Wave 1 delivery is four weeks minimum, and that is discovery. If the timeline cannot accommodate, qualify out.

The qualify-out script

"I appreciate the interest. The way APEX delivers value is through a four-to-eight-week envisioning that produces a concrete architecture and business case. The shortest credible commitment is Wave 1 at that scale. If the timeline or budget isn't there today, I'd rather hold the conversation for a quarter than deliver something that won't land. Can we revisit in Q3?"

This preserves the relationship. Most "not now" becomes "yes" when a trigger event lands — a new CIO, a regulatory finding, a board mandate.

1.5 The first-meeting qualifier checklist

Every first meeting should leave you able to answer seven questions. Rehearse them. Listen for the answers; do not ask them like a survey.

  1. What public 2026 commitment does the CEO have that this work could serve?
  2. Who is the single-threaded executive sponsor?
  3. What is the state of the Microsoft footprint — EA in place, Fabric capacity, Copilot licenses?
  4. What is the incumbent SI on adjacent scope?
  5. Is Deloitte the auditor? If so, is pre-clearance in place?
  6. What is the budget posture — funded in current fiscal, pending approval, pipeline only?
  7. What is the realistic decision window — this quarter, next quarter, next fiscal?

If three or more of these answers are "unknown" or "no", slow down. You are not yet qualified.

1.6 Why Canonical Schema Is the Acceleration Kernel

This is the core architectural concept that explains why Deloitte accelerates agentic-AI delivery from 18-24 months to 9-12 months. Sellers who cannot explain this lose architect-credibility conversations even when the rest of the pitch is clean. The concept is not abstract — it determines every downstream economic and technical outcome.

1.6.1 What a canonical schema is

A canonical schema is an opinionated, typed, classification-aware, relationship-defined specification of the business entities that matter in an industry. SCML (Supply Chain Merchandising Language), MERML (Merchandising), CXML (Customer Experience), AXLEML (AXLE Practice), and their peers across HLS, ER, TMT, TH, ICE are canonical schemas.

Each schema specifies, for its Practice domain:

  • The entities that matter — SKU, Category, Store, Customer, Patient, Encounter, Well, Asset, etc.
  • The attributes each entity carries — typed, with defaults, nullability, allowed values
  • The relationships between entities — cardinality, temporal validity, foreign-key paths
  • The classifications that apply — PII, PHI, PCI, SOX-controlled, trade-secret
  • The business-term bindings in Purview Unified Catalog
  • The pre-measure derivations — computed columns like stock-days-remaining, days-since-last-encounter, RUL
  • The post-measure definitions — DAX / SQL / KQL for period-over-period, rolling-window, attribution calculations

A canonical schema is not a database schema. It is a semantic contract — a shared definition of what "SKU" means in retail, what "Encounter" means in healthcare, what "Well" means in energy. The contract is enforced in code (Fabric artifacts), in governance (Purview labels), and in agent behavior (MCP tool bindings).

1.6.2 The acceleration math — with vs without

Without canonical schema. A client's first agentic use case requires authoring the semantic model for that specific agent's needs. The second use case on adjacent data requires authoring a SIMILAR semantic model — but with subtle differences because no one coordinated the first effort. By the fifth or tenth use case, the client has multiple overlapping semantic models, inconsistent entity definitions, duplicated transform logic, and a governance nightmare where "Customer" means one thing in agent A and a slightly different thing in agent B.

Time per new use case in this world: the first one takes 6-9 months of semantic-engineering work. Subsequent ones don't accelerate because each new one finds novel semantic territory and often re-opens entity definitions the first agent thought were settled. Scale economics break down.

With canonical schema. The first agentic use case authors OR consumes a Practice-standard canonical schema. All subsequent use cases in that Practice consume the same schema. The second use case starts with entities, relationships, classifications, and business terms already defined. Implementation effort shifts from "author a semantic model" to "implement a use case within the schema."

Time per new use case in this world: the first one takes the same 6-9 months (or a few months if consuming an already-delivered Practice schema). The second takes 2-3 months. The third takes weeks. By the time the client is at their fifth use case, new capabilities deploy in under a month because everything needed — entities, transforms, classifications, governance, tool bindings — is already there.

This is the acceleration kernel. The first-use-case timeline looks similar either way; the 5th-and-beyond timeline differs by 10-50×. APEX's economic advantage compounds because the canonical schema framework exists from Wave 1 Day 1.

1.6.3 Why this matters SPECIFICALLY for agentic AI

Traditional BI and analytics also benefit from canonical schemas. Agentic AI is different — the benefit is categorically larger, for six specific reasons:

1. Agents reason across entities, not within them. A BI dashboard typically visualizes one entity at a time. An agent routinely reasons across 5-10 entities in a single decision ("what is the inventory position of this SKU at these stores, given the demand forecast, competitive price, supplier reliability, and the lot-level provenance if recall-sensitive"). Without canonical relationships between entities, cross-entity reasoning requires the agent to do its own join-logic at query time — slow, error-prone, non-auditable.

2. Agents need typed interfaces. A human BI user can interpret ambiguity in a column ("is this price pre-tax or post-tax?"). An agent cannot. Typed schema contracts are mandatory for agent reliability, not nice-to-have.

3. Classification propagation is life-or-death for governance. A BI dashboard might tolerate a minor classification lapse. An agent that includes cleartext PHI in a response has created a HIPAA breach. Canonical schema carries classifications through every derivation so that an agent's output inherits correct handling automatically.

4. Audit-row attribution requires stable entity IDs. The CFO-credible "this specific margin dollar was saved by this specific agent decision" answer requires the decision to reference a specific, canonical, stable SKU ID and Store ID. Ad-hoc semantics produce ad-hoc IDs that don't support longitudinal attribution.

5. Agent evaluation requires schema stability. Testing an agent's behavior across 10,000 synthetic scenarios requires the schema those scenarios are expressed against to be consistent. Canonical schema is the substrate of reproducible agent evaluation; without it, agents can't be improved systematically.

6. Cross-Practice reasoning depends on federated canonical views. When a diversified client has RC + HLS-Provider + AXLE agents that occasionally need to reason across Practice boundaries (e.g., an employee who is also a customer, or an equipment failure whose warranty impact crosses Practice SORs), federation requires canonical schemas that can be meaningfully joined. Ad-hoc semantics cannot federate.

1.6.4 How canonical schema composes with the envelopes

Recall from §2.2A the five envelopes: Commercial, Scope, Data, Schema, Trust. Canonical schema is the lens through which the schema envelope becomes actionable. A service's schema envelope (the entities it reads and writes) only has operational meaning when those entities are defined by a canonical schema.

Specifically:

  • Trust envelope (classification + identity + DLP) is ENFORCEABLE only because canonical schema specifies per-column classification
  • Data envelope (what an agent can read) is DEFINABLE only because canonical schema enumerates the entities
  • Scope envelope (services + use cases) is PRICEABLE only because canonical schema bounds the implementation effort
  • Commercial envelope is CREDIBLE only because the scope-envelope math traces to canonical-schema counts

Schemas that are not canonical break this chain. The client ends up with nominal envelopes that can't be enforced at runtime.

1.6.5 Concrete acceleration example — RC Practice

A retailer engages Deloitte for Wave 2. The SCML canonical schema already exists (delivered in Wave 1). Five services are scoped: Assortment & Pricing, Unified Customer, Product Tracking, Demand Sensing, Markdown.

Without canonical schema, the retailer would need:

  • 5 service teams each authoring their own semantic model
  • 5 inconsistent versions of "SKU", "Store", "Customer", "Category"
  • 5 separate classification policies requiring per-service Purview work
  • 5 agent fleets that can't reason across each other's data
  • Composite decisions (e.g., "recommend markdown taking into account demand signal AND customer-cohort affinity") would require ad-hoc join work and custom integration

With SCML + MERML + CXML canonical schemas (APEX-delivered), the retailer gets:

  • One SKU entity definition consumed by all 5 services
  • Shared Store, Customer, Category canonical entities
  • One classification taxonomy applied uniformly (SupplierConfidential, CommercialSensitive, PII)
  • Agent fleets that reference the same entity IDs — cross-service reasoning is natural
  • Composite decisions work because the semantic model connects Demand Signal (MERML) to Customer Cohort (CXML) through shared Transaction and Store entities

The resulting Wave 2 timeline is 9-12 months instead of the 24-36 months the first scenario would require. The Wave 2 commercial envelope is ~70% smaller because the per-service implementation effort is dramatically lower. And — critically — the Wave 3 expansion to additional services becomes near-instant because the canonical schema is already there.

1.6.6 The anti-pattern — what happens without canonical schema

Deloitte teams have occasionally landed at clients who attempted agentic-AI deployment without canonical-schema discipline. The pattern is consistent:

  • First use case ships in 9-12 months (same as APEX)
  • Second use case takes 9-12 more months (no acceleration)
  • At 18-month mark, technical debt becomes visible — three semantic models diverging, governance inconsistent, agents can't compose
  • Third use case stalls because cross-agent reasoning doesn't work
  • Leadership concludes "enterprise agentic AI is hard" or "AI maturity takes time"
  • The real problem was skipping the canonical-schema discipline at the start

APEX's internal delivery accelerator exists precisely because Deloitte has seen this pattern enough times to know the discipline matters. The 18-24 month ground-up timeline that APEX compresses includes the implicit cost of first-principles canonical-schema authoring. APEX ships the canonical schemas in the box.

1.6.7 Why Fabric specifically matters for canonical schema

Canonical schema as a concept is platform-agnostic — it could be implemented on any data platform. But Fabric's architecture makes canonical schema operationally viable at enterprise scale in ways competing platforms don't:

  • OneLake gives the canonical schema one physical home; no cross-platform replication or synchronization drift
  • Fabric Mirrored Databases bring source data into the canonical-schema's landing zone without custom ETL; Silver transforms produce canonical entities from raw source with minimal glue code
  • Direct Lake serves canonical Gold views to Copilot, Power BI, and MCP tools with sub-second latency and zero data duplication
  • Purview integration propagates classifications through the canonical schema at the platform level — not as application-layer afterthought
  • Unified Catalog exposes business glossary terms linked to canonical entities so clients can govern vocabulary as part of the schema
  • Fabric Eventhouse extends canonical schema to real-time data with the same governance model as batch

Canonical schema authored on Fabric is operationally tractable; canonical schema authored from scratch on a composed non-Fabric stack requires the client to integrate those guarantees themselves.

1.6A Industry-Standard Schemas and the APEX / AXLE Canonical Design

Canonical schemas (SCML, MERML, CXML, PatientML, UOGML, AXLEML, TELML, TravelerML, ConnectedICEML, and the other ~35 APEX/AXLE schemas) are not invented from scratch. Each is designed on top of the industry-standard schemas that already govern the vertical. This section describes those standards, why they matter, and how APEX and AXLE incorporate them.

1.6A.1 Why industry-standard schemas matter

Three reasons a seller or architect should know the relevant standards for every Practice:

  1. Regulator recognition. Regulators (FDA, FERC, DOT, EPA, FCC, EU agencies) recognize standardized schemas as evidentiary baselines. A canonical schema that derives from HL7 FHIR or EPCIS or CIM has intrinsic defensibility; one that doesn't requires the client to justify every design choice.
  2. Interoperability economics. Enterprise clients have 10–30 years of investment in SORs that already speak standards (HL7 v2, EDI X12, ISA-95, OPC UA, OpenTravel). A canonical schema that aligns with those standards costs 30–70% less to integrate than a bespoke one.
  3. Regulator-recognized vocabulary. SNOMED-CT, LOINC, ICD-10, CPT, GS1 identifiers, ISO codes — these are the controlled vocabularies regulators expect. APEX schemas carry these codes as first-class attributes so agent outputs are regulator-ready from day one.

The table below names the standards that materially shape each Practice's canonical design. This is reference material; sellers don't need to recite it, but architects do.

1.6A.3 How APEX and AXLE canonical schemas are built on top of these standards

Every APEX or AXLE canonical schema follows the same three-step design pattern:

  1. Consume. Entity definitions are derived from the dominant industry standard. Example: SCML's Item entity inherits GS1 identifier structure (GTIN-14 with indicator digit) and GDSN attribute hierarchy. PatientML's Patient inherits FHIR Patient resource structure. AXLEML's Station inherits ISA-95 Equipment Hierarchy. TELML's Service inherits TM Forum SID Service/ServiceSpecification.
  2. Extend. APEX/AXLE adds metadata the standard doesn't carry: sensitivity labels, consent pointers, agent-safe flags, audit-row bindings, model-version constraints, HITL-gate declarations, manifest cross-references. These extensions make the schema governable and agent-consumable.
  3. Translate. Where multiple standards compete (HL7 v2 vs FHIR vs CDA; EDI X12 vs XML; WITSML versions), APEX/AXLE ship pre-built bidirectional mappings. The canonical form is one, but clients can keep their existing standards-speaking SORs intact.

The practical consequence: an RC client with SAP item master already GS1-conformant, a Salesforce Commerce Cloud catalog already Schema.org-conformant, and an EDI X12 inbound already conformant — all three integrate to SCML through off-the-shelf APEX adapters, not custom engineering.

1.6A.4 Standards that AXLE carries forward specifically

AXLE's canonical design is especially standards-heavy because discrete-manufacturing clients carry more standards than any other industry vertical:

  • ISA-95 Level 0–4 hierarchy is the spine of every AXLE plant data model (Enterprise → Site → Area → Work Center → Equipment Module → Control Module).
  • AutomationML is the exchange format between CAD / PLM / MES during commissioning.
  • STEP AP242 is the engineering bill-of-material exchange between Teamcenter / Windchill / 3DEXPERIENCE and downstream MES.
  • OPC UA is the runtime communication standard at Level 2 / 3 (PLC ↔ SCADA ↔ MES) that AXLE consumes through Fabric Real-Time.
  • IATF 16949 shapes QMSML-A's audit-trail requirements.
  • VDA / Odette message sets are the European auto-supplier EDI baseline that SupplyML-A speaks natively.

When an AXLE client says "we're standardized on ISA-95 and AutomationML, can APEX integrate?" the answer is: AXLEML was designed on ISA-95, consumes AutomationML for CAD/MES handoff, and AXLE's reference integrations are certified against both. The client keeps its standards investment; AXLE leverages it.

1.6A.5 Standards as regulator evidence

For regulated industries the standards carry legal weight beyond convenience:

  • FSMA 204 (US food traceability) explicitly references GS1 EPCIS as an acceptable event schema. SCML publishing EPCIS events directly is a regulator-ready deliverable.
  • FDA 21 CFR Part 11 electronic-record requirements are met in part by CDISC ODM-conformant audit trails. StudyML audit rows exported as ODM are 21 CFR Part 11 defensible.
  • FERC reliability standards require CIM (IEC 61968-13) Common Information Model for grid-topology exchange. P&UML materializes CIM-conformant outputs for state-PUC and FERC reporting.
  • EU DSA (Digital Services Act) mandates specific takedown-notice schemas. TMT's ContentSafetyML adopts the EU-published notice format.
  • DOT / EU261 disruption-compensation audit trails are straightforwardly derivable from IATA PADIS-conformant disruption records in IROPsML.

1.6A.6 The one-paragraph summary for standards

Note

"APEX and AXLE canonical schemas are designed on top of the industry standards that already govern each vertical — GS1 and ARTS for RC, HL7 FHIR and CDISC for HLS, CIM and WITSML for ER, ISA-95 and STEP for AXLE, TM Forum SID for TMT, IATA and OpenTravel for TH, AEMP and SAE J1939 for ICE. The canonical schemas consume, extend, and translate these standards so clients keep their standards investment and regulators recognize APEX outputs as evidentiary-grade by design. Deloitte's engineering value is in the extension and translation layer, not in redesigning the standards."

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. When describing APEX, refer to Deloitte's relationship with Microsoft as a "technology platform relationship" or "collaboration." Never use "partner," "alliance," or "joint venture." APEX is Deloitte IP; it runs on the Microsoft platform the client licenses directly. These word choices matter legally and regulatorily — they are not stylistic preferences.

Key Takeaways

  • APEX is a contract between data and decisions, not a bolted-on AI feature
  • Manifest-driven + audit row + first-class HITL + four-plane Microsoft composition
  • Lead with the pain that matches the exec; don't recite all five forces
  • Three executive pains map cleanly: CIO=sprawl, CFO=ROI attribution, COO=judgement capacity
  • APEX is a program, not a POC — qualify out prospects wanting a POC
  • The seven-question first-meeting checklist tells you whether to proceed

Seller Actions

  1. Memorise the sentence "APEX is a Deloitte product that leverages the Microsoft technology platform"
  2. Rehearse your 60-second APEX pitch in all three variants (CIO, CFO, COO)
  3. Identify two forces that apply most to each of your top three accounts
  4. Build the seven-question first-meeting qualifier into your call-prep template
  5. Practice Independence-compliant language in every APEX conversation
  6. Write a qualify-out script you can deliver without hesitation

The APEX Commercial Arc

2.1 The commercial posture

Deloitte sells Agentic AI Delivery Services. These are productised services delivered using APEX as the internal accelerator. When the client engages Deloitte on an agentic-AI program — say, "Assortment & Pricing Intelligence for a large retail merchant" — what the client procures is a complete delivery outcome: the designed agents, the configured Fabric semantic model, the trained workforce, the HITL governance, and the audit-row attribution that proves the business outcome. APEX is what Deloitte uses internally to deliver that outcome in 9–12 months rather than the 18–24 months a ground-up build would take.

This matters commercially because it changes the conversation. A ground-up build is priced on hours and risk-padded by both sides; a Deloitte delivery using APEX acceleration is priced on outcome envelope and paid back by measurable business result. The client is not buying the consultants' hours; they are buying an operational agent fleet on their Microsoft platform, delivered faster by Deloitte than they could build it themselves.

The two-contract model — memorise this

Every agentic-AI delivery engagement involves TWO separate contracts:

  1. Client ↔ Microsoft: platform licenses (Fabric capacity, Copilot seats, Foundry consumption, MCP hosting infrastructure, Purview entitlements, Entra licenses). The client procures these directly from Microsoft through their EA, MCA, or CSP arrangement. Deloitte does not quote, invoice, or commit to these terms on Microsoft's behalf.
  2. Client ↔ Deloitte: Deloitte Agentic AI Delivery Services (Wave 1 envisioning, Wave 2 implementation, Wave 3 sustain, managed services). Deloitte contracts for advisory, implementation, and managed services. Deloitte uses APEX internally to accelerate delivery; APEX is not a line item on the SOW, it is Deloitte's proprietary methodology.

This is not a stylistic preference. It is an Independence requirement. Deloitte audits Microsoft. No commercial flow may bundle the two in a way that implies a joint revenue arrangement. When procurement asks "can you quote us a single number that includes the Microsoft licensing?", the answer is always "no, those contracts are separate; here is our services fee, and here is the Microsoft contact for platform licensing."

2.2 The three-wave envelope

The envelopes below represent Deloitte advisory and implementation fees only. The Microsoft platform consumption runs on the client's direct contract with Microsoft. Envelopes vary by Practice — the numbers here are median RC-class; see industry chapters for Practice-specific ranges.

WaveNameDurationDeloitte envelope per PracticeWhat ships
1Envision & Land (Foundation)4–8 weeks (envisioning) + 3–4 months (first services)$500K–$2M (envisioning + first 2 services)Target-state architecture, 2–3 services live at pilot tenant, business case, Wave 2 roadmap
2Enable & Scale (Intelligence)6–15 months$5–15MFull Practice catalog at pilot scale, HITL tuning, expansion to adjacent sites
3Sustain & Transform (Optimisation)Multi-year (ongoing)$8–30MEnterprise rollout, second Practice, autonomy pilots, managed services

Total 18–36-month arc per Practice: $13–47M. A 3-Practice client over 3 years: $40–140M. These are ranges, not price lists. Each engagement is scoped to the Practice, the site count, and the service mix.

What Wave 1 actually delivers

Too often Wave 1 is sold as "a discovery" and delivered as slides. That is a loss. A proper Wave 1 produces:

  1. Target-state architecture diagram — one diagram, APEX services layered on the Microsoft stack, specific to this client's data estate.
  2. Selected services roster — 2–3 services chosen with rationale, each with baseline KPI, target KPI, and attribution confidence.
  3. Business case — benefit magnitude, investment envelope, payback window, risk register.
  4. Roadmap — quarter-by-quarter for Waves 2 and 3.
  5. Draft Wave 2 SOW — legally reviewable, not a slideware "next-steps".
  6. Executive readout — 12–15 slides with decision ask baked in.
  7. First service live at pilot tenant — when scope permits, one of the 2–3 selected services is already in pilot by end of Wave 1. This is the proof.

What Wave 2 actually delivers

Wave 2 is where the revenue compounds and where the client sees returning benefit. Wave 2 delivers:

  1. Full Practice catalog at pilot scale — all 5–7 services of the selected Practice running at one tenant with real data.
  2. HITL calibration — the gates are tuned to the client's operating discipline; autonomy rate (the percentage of decisions that pass without human review) is measured and trended.
  3. Site / geography expansion — from one pilot to 10 / 50 / 250 sites depending on the Practice and the client scale.
  4. Measured KPI uplift — baseline-to-target on the KPIs committed in Wave 1.
  5. Operational runbooks — so delivery can exit and the client (or a managed-service arrangement) can run.
  6. Wave 3 SOW — if both parties want to continue.

What Wave 3 actually delivers

Wave 3 is the sustain phase, often bundled with a managed-service run. Wave 3 delivers:

  1. Full enterprise rollout — the selected Practice is in production across the full site footprint.
  2. Second Practice initiation — a parallel track in a new Practice, typically starting with its own Wave 1.
  3. Autonomy pilots — selective experiments at raising autonomy rate on the most trusted services.
  4. Managed service run — Deloitte runs the platform on the client's behalf under an SLA, or co-runs with a client team we have trained.

2.2A Understanding "Envelope" — Commercial, Data, and Schema Dimensions

The word "envelope" appears throughout this guide in multiple senses. Sellers frequently conflate them, which creates confusion in pursuit conversations. This section disambiguates the term and explains how the commercial envelope connects back to the data and schema envelopes that sit beneath it.

2.2A.1 What an envelope actually is

An envelope in APEX terminology is a bounded scope — a deliberately-constrained perimeter around a thing. The perimeter has rules about what is inside, what is outside, how things cross the boundary, and who authorized what crosses. Sellers encounter five distinct envelope types in pursuit conversations. Each plays a different role, but they are not independent — they nest within each other and their boundaries reinforce.

2.2A.2 The six envelopes in APEX

Addendum update (v1.5)

The envelope taxonomy was extended from five to six in the Runtime Addendum. The sixth envelope — Cost — is the FinOps boundary that every runtime decision burns against. Prior references to "the five envelopes" elsewhere in the book are retained for continuity but should be read as "the six envelopes" going forward. See §2.2A.2.6 below and §AA for the change rationale.

1. Commercial Envelope. The money-and-time boundary of a Wave. Wave 1 commercial envelope = $500K–$2M over 4–8 weeks for the envisioning plus first services. Wave 2 commercial envelope = $5M–$15M over 6–15 months. Wave 3 commercial envelope = $8M–$30M over multi-year. The commercial envelope sets the maximum investment and timeline for a defined scope of outcomes. It is the primary frame of CFO conversations.

2. Scope Envelope. The functional-scope boundary of what the engagement delivers. Which services, which agents, which MCP tools, which Gold views, which classifications, which KPIs. Scope envelope is what the SOW documents; it is what procurement negotiates against; it is what Wave 1 envisioning crystallizes. A scope envelope is narrower than "everything we could possibly do" and wider than "one service." Scope envelope sets commercial envelope.

3. Data Envelope. The boundary around the data an agent fleet may read and the data an agent may write. A retail pricing agent's data envelope might include SKU, Category, Price, Competitive Signal, and Demand Signal — but not Member PII, Employee HR data, or Financial-ledger data. Data envelope is enforced at the MCP tool layer (what tools exist and what they return) and at the Purview / Entra layer (what classification and identity scope allow). Data envelope is narrower than the client's full Fabric estate by design.

4. Schema Envelope. The boundary around the canonical-entity subset an APEX service depends on. The Assortment & Pricing service has a schema envelope containing SCML Category, SCML SKU, MERML Price, MERML Promotion, MERML Markdown, and MERML Competitive Signal. It does NOT include CXML Customer, CXML Transaction, CXML Loyalty Member — those belong to a different service's schema envelope. Schema envelope determines which Silver + Gold artifacts the service authors and reads.

5. Trust Envelope. The boundary of classification + identity + DLP that governs every action inside the engagement. Trust envelope is enforced by Purview (what classifications apply), Entra (which identities authenticate), and the HITL gate framework (which decisions require human approval). Trust envelope is orthogonal to the other four; it intersects every one of them.

6. Cost Envelope. The FinOps boundary that every runtime decision burns against. Tokens, Fabric Capacity Units, MCP invocations, storage, network egress — all metered per service_code and bound to cost_per_decision on the audit row (see §6.10.12). Service P&L is a query, not a reconciliation. The Cost envelope is measured in real time through Azure API Management token metering (§5A.2) and surfaced to the CFO via the Power BI observability dashboards (§5A.5).

All six envelopes, applied simultaneously. When an agent executes a tool call in production, all six envelopes apply at once. The call must:

  • Fit the commercial envelope — paid for
  • Be in the scope envelope — approved functional scope
  • Return data inside the data envelope — identity-authorized
  • Reference entities inside the schema envelope — canonical-defined
  • Be governed by the trust envelope — classification-appropriate, HITL-correct
  • Fit within the cost envelope — within the token-budget and CU-budget for this service_code

Break any envelope, break the decision.

2.2A.3 How envelopes nest

The envelopes are not parallel — they nest:

Commercial envelope ← contains ← Scope envelope ← contains ← Data envelope ← derived from ← Schema envelope ← governed by ← Trust envelope ← metered by ← Cost envelope

The Cost envelope is the last link in the chain because it measures what every one of the other five allows. Commercial sets the ceiling (the money you can spend); Cost measures the floor (the money each decision actually spends). If Cost > Commercial over the window, the service is underwater and the commercial envelope needs revisiting.

How to read the diagram. Commercial contains Scope contains Data — those three nest as concentric boxes. A tool call that isn't in scope of the SOW can't fit in the Commercial envelope; data a managed identity can't reach can't fit in the Data envelope. Schema is not contained in Data — the Data envelope is derived from a pre-existing Schema envelope (entities, relationships, Gold views authored before the engagement). Trust is not contained at all — it governs Schema, and through Schema it governs everything else: classification propagates from Trust down through Schema into the Data envelope, into the Scope envelope's allowed services, and into the Commercial envelope's contractable surface.

An agent operating in production sits at the intersection of all five. When the agent reads data through an MCP tool, five boundaries apply simultaneously:

  • The tool call must fit within the commercial envelope for which it was paid (i.e., the service was in scope of the SOW)
  • The tool must be in the scope envelope of the engagement (i.e., it was approved for delivery)
  • The data returned must be inside the data envelope of the agent (i.e., the managed identity has scope to read it)
  • The data's canonical entity must be in the schema envelope of the service (i.e., the Silver and Gold artifacts were authored)
  • The data, the tool call, the agent's output must be governed by the trust envelope (i.e., classification, identity, HITL all apply)

Sellers who understand this nesting can describe agent behaviour precisely in architect conversations. Sellers who conflate the envelopes produce answers that are either too narrow or too broad.

2.2A.4 How the envelope connects to schemas

The schema envelope is the architectural kernel of the commercial envelope. That relationship is the single most important thing sellers need to understand about how APEX works commercially. Walk the chain:

  • A Wave 2 commercial envelope ($5–15M, 6–15 months) exists because a specific scope envelope was agreed (say, "five RC Practice services at pilot scale: RC-E2E-03 Assortment, RC-E2E-09 Product Tracking, RC-E2E-05 Unified Customer, RC-TTP-02 Demand Sensing, RC-TTP-07 Markdown").
  • Each service in the scope envelope has a defined schema envelope (the set of canonical entities it reads from and writes to). RC-E2E-03 Assortment reads Category, SKU, Price, Promotion, Markdown, Competitive Signal; RC-E2E-09 Product Tracking reads SKU, Supplier, Shipment, Lot, Inventory Position.
  • The union of all service schema envelopes defines the Wave 2 data platform scope — which Silver models must be built, which Gold views materialized, which MCP tools authored, which classifications applied, which agents trained, which HITL gates designed.
  • That data platform scope drives the delivery effort estimate — how many consultant weeks to build each Silver table, each Gold view, each MCP tool, each agent, each gate.
  • Delivery effort multiplied by blended rate plus risk adjustment produces the commercial envelope estimate the CFO sees.

The schema envelope is what the commercial envelope is buying. When a client asks "why is Wave 2 at the upper end of the range for us?" — the answer traces back to schema breadth. More canonical entities in scope means more Silver models, more Gold views, more MCP tools, more agents. The money buys the data structure that makes agentic reasoning possible.

2.2A.5 Why this matters in pursuit conversations

Three conversational moments where this nesting matters:

When a CFO challenges the envelope. The honest answer is "the commercial envelope is driven by the schema breadth we've scoped." If they want a smaller envelope, the conversation shifts to narrowing schema scope — which means narrowing services, which means narrowing measurable outcomes. Cost / scope / outcome triangle becomes concrete.

When a CIO asks "what agents can do." The honest answer is "an agent's capability is bounded by its schema envelope and trust envelope." An assortment-pricing agent cannot reason about a customer complaint because customer-experience schemas are outside its envelope. This is a feature, not a limitation — predictable scope makes governance tractable.

When a CCO asks "how we keep sensitive data from leaking." The honest answer is "trust envelope enforcement through Purview + Entra + HITL — evaluated at every tool call, every data crossing, every agent output." Classification at the schema-envelope boundary combined with DLP at the data-envelope exit prevents leakage by design.

2.2A.6 Envelope expansion — how scope grows across Waves

Wave 1 establishes a narrow scope envelope — 2–3 services, narrow schema envelope, narrow data envelope, narrow agent fleet. Commercial envelope matches.

Wave 2 expands schema envelope to the full Practice catalog for the selected Practice. Commercial envelope expands to match. Trust envelope tightens (more classifications, more DLP rules, more HITL gate patterns).

Wave 3 expands across Practices (adds a second, third Practice's schema envelope), across sites (scales the data envelope to more tenants), across autonomy (selectively loosens HITL gates where operational maturity supports). Commercial envelope expands to match; trust envelope remains authoritative.

Sellers scoping pursuits should estimate the Wave 2 and Wave 3 commercial envelopes by asking, at each Wave, "which additional schemas are in scope, what trust rules apply, and what's the resulting data-and-agent footprint." That's how credible multi-year commercial envelopes get built.

2.2A.7 The one-sentence summary

An envelope is a bounded scope; the five APEX envelopes nest commercial-inside-scope-inside-data-inside-schema-inside-trust; the schema envelope is what determines everything downstream including the commercial envelope the CFO sees.

2.2B The APEX Value-Delivery Chain — Scenario → Solution → Use Case → Service → Persona → KPI

The envelope chain explained in §2.2A describes how scope nests structurally. This section explains how value flows through the engagement — the chain that connects a real-world business scenario all the way to a measurable KPI in the client's P&L.

Every successful Deloitte Agentic AI Delivery engagement is a specific instance of this chain. Sellers who can walk it top-to-bottom and bottom-to-top in a pursuit conversation carry architectural credibility that generalized "we do AI" positioning cannot match.

2.2B.1 The chain, defined

Scenario — the real-world business situation or operational context where a decision needs to be made. Not a hypothetical; not a pitch-slide abstraction. A concrete event: "Reefer 14 was warm for 4 hours at 05:58 AM." Scenarios come from observing how the client actually operates.

Solution — the APEX-delivered response pattern that addresses the scenario. A solution is broader than any single service — it's the shape of how APEX answers this class of business problem. "Cold Chain Excursion Response" is a solution; it combines sensor telemetry + classification logic + disposition recommendation + human-in-the-loop approval + regulatory-trail preservation + write-off pre-approval.

Use Case — a specific, reusable workflow pattern within the solution. Use cases are what engineers and architects implement; they are concrete enough to code and test. "Temperature excursion triage + save/destroy disposition + customer notification for loyalty-identified purchasers" is a use case. The solution contains multiple use cases; the use case is the implementation unit.

Service — the productized APEX offering that delivers the use case. Services are what Deloitte commercializes. Each service has a catalog code (e.g., RC-E2E-03, HLS-Payer-UM-01), a defined set of use cases it implements, a commercial envelope, measurable KPIs, and specific persona ownership. Services are the units that sell and the units that get delivered in Wave 2.

Persona — the human role(s) the service serves. Personas are named, specific, and carry authority. Marisol Reyes (Store Operations Lead) is a persona; "retail manager" is not specific enough to be a persona. Each service has a primary persona (who uses it) and secondary personas (who oversee, benefit, or approve). Persona depth is what makes the service land operationally rather than just technically.

KPI — the measurable business outcome the service drives, attributable to specific agent decisions through the audit row. Write-off avoided per event: $1,313. Handle time reduced: -21%. Recall-scope time: 22 minutes vs 4-6 hours historic. KPIs close the loop back to the scenario — a measurable improvement in the very class of situation the scenario described.

2.2B.2 Why the chain matters

Every element in the chain has a specific commercial and architectural function:

  • Scenario grounds the conversation in what the client actually faces. Sellers who start at "AI platform capabilities" lose the room; sellers who start at "what does your operations lead face at 7 AM Monday" own the room.
  • Solution frames what Deloitte delivers in response — the approach, not the product. Solutions let clients understand the shape of help before diving into SKUs and pricing.
  • Use case translates to engineering — it's the bridge from business language to implementation plan. Wave 1 envisioning workshops produce use-case-level agreement.
  • Service commercializes the use case — the SOW references services by code. Commercial envelope, delivery timeline, KPI commitments attach to services, not use cases.
  • Persona drives adoption — a service delivered without persona-specific design won't be adopted. Change management, training, and HITL design follow from persona.
  • KPI creates accountability — the audit row traces the agent's decision to the persona's action to the measurable outcome. The CFO's ROI question answers here.

2.2B.3 The chain walked end-to-end — Worked Example 1 (RC)

Scenario: At a large-format grocery store at 05:58 AM, a refrigeration case (Reefer 14) has held at 48–52°F against a 41°F threshold for 4 hours 12 minutes. 412 units across 28 SKUs are at risk. The store opens at 7:00 AM.

Solution: Cold Chain Excursion Response. A pattern combining IoT telemetry ingest + FDA food-safety threshold classification + save-viable vs destroy disposition logic + inventory-at-risk quantification + HITL approval on write-off + vendor ticketing with root-cause evidence + regulatory evidence preservation.

Use Cases within the solution:

  • UC-1: Threshold-breach detection + severity classification
  • UC-2: Affected-inventory enumeration with SKU-level typing
  • UC-3: Save-viable vs destroy disposition per sub-category
  • UC-4: Quarantine task assignment + case-label pre-print
  • UC-5: Write-off pre-approval routing to manager
  • UC-6: Refrigeration vendor ticketing with time-series evidence

Service delivering these use cases: RC-E2E-ColdChain Excursion Response (catalog code; part of the RC E2E service family).

Personas served:

  • Primary: Marisol Reyes, Store Operations Lead (event recipient, HITL decider)
  • Secondary: Pull-team lead (task executor), Store Manager (escalation path), Inventory Control (write-off approver), Refrigeration Vendor (external ticketed party), Food Safety Compliance Lead (audit-trail consumer)

KPIs:

  • Write-off avoided per event: $1,313 (71% of $1,847 at-risk inventory saved)
  • Time-to-brief: 8 minutes (from excursion-end to manager-ready disposition package)
  • Manager touch-time: 90 seconds per event (HITL approval tap)
  • Audit-trail completeness: 100% regulator-ready evidence preserved

Chain closure: The audit row for Marisol's 6:08 AM approval attributes the $1,313 saved to this specific agent decision at Store 100 on this specific morning. The KPI connects back to the scenario; the chain loops.

2.2B.4 Worked Example 2 (HLS Provider)

Scenario: Room 7 patient admitted for UTI, stable at 06:00. By 09:45 nursing notes a +0.9°C temperature, heart rate 85→112 over 3 hours. No clinician has flagged concern.

Solution: Sepsis Early-Warning Pattern Detection. IoT + clinical-stream correlation + ML risk scoring + clinical-pattern-library matching + HITL clinician alert with explainability.

Use Cases:

  • UC-1: Continuous vital-sign + medication + lab stream ingest
  • UC-2: Sepsis-risk prediction with contributing-factor attribution
  • UC-3: Pattern-library cross-match for known-trajectory signatures
  • UC-4: Threshold-crossing alert with clinical explanation (not just score)
  • UC-5: Bedside action-recommendation (page, bundle, escalate)

Service: HLS-Provider-Sepsis-EW-01 (Early Warning).

Personas served:

  • Primary: Raj Patel, Charge Nurse (alert recipient, bedside assessor)
  • Secondary: Hospitalist (orders initiation), Rapid Response Team (escalation path), CMIO (clinical-governance owner), Quality Officer (outcome tracker)

  • Sepsis-recognition lead time: 2-4 hours earlier than baseline
  • MICU transfer avoidance rate: +8-15% in detected cases
  • Mortality-associated bundle compliance: +10-15 points
  • Clinical alert-fatigue rate: <5% false-positive threshold

Chain closure: Each alert writes an audit row attributing early detection to specific vital-sign + trajectory signals. Hospital reports quarterly sepsis KPIs back to the service.

2.2B.5 Worked Example 3 (ER)

Scenario: Lightning strike at 09:45 during severe storm triggers breaker open at substation feeder. Auto-sectionalization restores 30% of affected customers within 90 seconds. Remaining outages need crew dispatch sequencing.

Solution: Outage Triage + Restoration Sequencing. SCADA + AMI + OMS correlation + priority-customer ranking + crew-proximity optimization + HITL dispatcher approval.

Use Cases:

  • UC-1: Fault-location correlation across SCADA + AMI last-gasp
  • UC-2: Affected-customer enumeration with criticality classification
  • UC-3: Restoration-sequence generation with priority weighting
  • UC-4: Crew assignment with proximity + fatigue constraints
  • UC-5: Customer-communication draft with ETR

Personas served:

  • Secondary: Field Crew Leads, Customer Care, Commission Liaison (regulatory), Operations Manager, Communications team

  • Priority-customer restoration time: < 60 min for healthcare/water
  • Customer-call reduction during events: -40% (from proactive communication)
  • Commission-reporting-ready package: complete within 24 hours

2.2B.6 Worked Example 4 (AXLE / Automotive)

Scenario: At 07:15 on Line 3, Robot 14 accelerometer signals show early-stage bearing wear. No immediate production impact; failure likely within 2-3 weeks without intervention.

Solution: Predictive Maintenance with Workflow-Aware Scheduling.

Use Cases:

  • UC-1: Vibration + motor-current signature correlation
  • UC-2: Remaining-useful-life estimation with confidence band
  • UC-3: Maintenance-window optimization (next planned stop)
  • UC-4: Parts-availability verification + ordering
  • UC-5: Technician-schedule deconfliction
