  • Primary: Sam Chen, Shift Supervisor Line 3
  • Secondary: Maintenance Lead, Parts Manager, Production Planner, Plant Manager

KPIs:

  • Unplanned downtime: -15-25% (Wave 2) / -30-45% (mature)
  • MTBF improvement: +20-35%
  • Emergency maintenance spend: -30-50%
  • OEE uplift attribution: +3-7 points at Wave 2

2.2B.7 How sellers use the chain in pursuits

First meeting with an executive sponsor. Walk the chain top-down from a scenario they face. Start with "what does your ops lead face at 7 AM Monday" — if the sponsor confirms the scenario, continue to solution, service, persona, KPI. If the sponsor doesn't recognize the scenario, you have the wrong scenario — reset and ask.

Architect workshop. Walk the chain bottom-up. Start with "which KPIs drive your CFO conversations" — trace back to persona, service, use case, solution, scenario. The architect confirms each link or flags a gap. Gaps become Wave 1 envisioning agenda items.

Wave 1 envisioning. The workshop output IS a catalog of chains — for each in-scope service, a documented chain from scenario through KPI. These chains become the Wave 2 implementation acceptance criteria.

Wave 2 implementation. Each service implements its use cases, serves its personas, drives its KPIs. The audit row attributes outcomes back up the chain.

Wave 3 sustain. Continuous-improvement discipline watches each chain's KPI performance; when a KPI drifts, the investigation traces back up the chain to find root cause — often a persona-adoption issue, sometimes a use-case gap, occasionally a scenario that has evolved.

2.2B.9 Cross-reference to schema envelope

The chain connects back to the envelope discussion in §2.2A. Every service (element 4 in the chain) carries its schema envelope — the canonical entities it reads and writes. The schema envelope connects the Service row to the Fabric data platform. A service's KPI is measurable precisely because the service's schema envelope is well-defined: audit-row attribution queries depend on the entities being canonical, classified, and lineage-tracked.

A good way to say this in an architect conversation: "The chain you care about — scenario to KPI — executes on the envelope we described earlier. The schema envelope is where value delivery meets data architecture."

2.2B.10 The one-sentence summary

Every Deloitte Agentic AI Delivery engagement is a concrete instance of the chain Scenario → Solution → Use Case → Service → Persona → KPI; sellers who can walk this chain top-down in an executive conversation and bottom-up in an architect conversation carry architectural credibility generalized AI pitches cannot match.

2.2C The Human Oversight Spectrum — HITL, HOTL, and HIC

Every discussion of agentic AI eventually reaches the question "how much autonomy are we giving this thing?" APEX's answer is a spectrum of three oversight modes, not a binary. Sellers who can name all three and map them to specific services scale past the ceiling where "we need a human to approve everything" conversations stall.

2.2C.1 The three modes

Human-In-The-Loop (HITL). The agent pauses mid-flow; a human approves, rejects, or modifies; only then does the action execute. The human is a mandatory checkpoint. Latency is measured in seconds to hours. Scale ceiling is bounded by human bandwidth.

Human-On-The-Loop (HOTL). The agent acts autonomously within defined constraints; a human supervises — monitoring dashboards, reviewing exceptions, intervening only when anomalies or policy breaches occur. The human is above the flow, not in it. Latency on agent action is near-zero; the human's observability window is measured in minutes.

Human-In-Command (HIC). The human retains strategic authority — can pause the fleet, redirect the orchestration, shut down an agent class, or change the policy bundle — but does not monitor individual decisions. The human is outside the flow, governing it.

2.2C.2 The spectrum at a glance

ModeHuman roleAction latencyScale ceilingCanonical example
HITLApproves / modifies each gated actionSeconds–hoursLow (human-bandwidth-bound)Clinical denial, recall decision, pricing change above threshold
HOTLMonitors, intervenes on exceptionAgent runs full-speedMedium–highDemand-sensing forecast refresh, grid-telemetry anomaly watch
HICSets policy, pauses fleetNone on actionsHigh (policy-bandwidth-bound)Quarterly agent-portfolio review, Board-level risk sign-off

2.2C.3 Which mode for which workload

The oversight mode is not a service preference; it is an architectural property of the decision's risk profile:

  • HITL is required when an individual decision is consequential, irreversible, or regulator-scrutinized. Clinical denial. Customer-facing recall. Pricing change above threshold. Credit-limit modification. Engineering-change release.
  • HOTL is appropriate when decisions are routine, reversible, and volumetric. Forecast refresh every 15 minutes. Shelf-allocation recommendation. Anomaly detection. Telemetry triage. Loyalty personalization.
  • HIC is appropriate as the strategic wrapper around the above — the governance rhythm that approves policy versions, manifest changes, new service rollouts, and portfolio expansion.

Most APEX services combine all three in one service: HOTL on routine, HITL on consequential, HIC on quarterly governance. Sellers describing a service should be able to name which mode applies to which decision class inside the service.

2.2C.4 Why this matters to the CFO

A common CFO question: "How does APEX scale past what a human can approve?" A sophisticated answer:

Note

"It doesn't try to. Routine decisions run Human-On-The-Loop — the agent acts, the human monitors exceptions. Consequential decisions run Human-In-The-Loop — the agent prepares, the human approves. Strategic governance runs Human-In-Command — the human sets policy, the agents inherit it. We design each service with an explicit split. Scaling is about getting more decisions into the HOTL bucket safely, not about removing human oversight."

That answer converts the autonomy conversation from a binary to a design conversation.

2.2C.5 Why this matters to the CCO and regulator

The EU AI Act explicitly recognizes the spectrum: high-risk AI systems must have "appropriate human oversight" — which the Act defines to include HITL, HOTL, and HIC modes. Being able to map a service's decision classes to the three modes is part of the defensibility package for an EU AI Act regulator. APEX's manifest schema carries the mode per decision class as a first-class field; see §6.10 for how the audit row captures which mode fired on each decision.

2.2C.6 Common misuses to avoid

  • "APEX is fully autonomous." No — sellers must never say this. APEX is always human-governed across the spectrum.
  • "Everything runs Human-In-The-Loop." Wrong and commercially ceiling-limiting — routine workloads must run HOTL to scale.
  • "HOTL means no oversight." Wrong — HOTL is oversight; it is exception-based rather than checkpoint-based.
  • "The mode is a platform feature." Wrong — the mode is an orchestration-design choice encoded in the manifest. Foundry enforces it.

2.2C.7 The one-sentence summary

Oversight in APEX is a designed spectrum — HITL for consequential decisions, HOTL for routine monitoring, HIC for strategic governance — and every service combines all three with explicit mode declarations in the manifest.

2.3 Service tiers and volume pricing

Within the Wave 2 and Wave 3 envelopes, APEX services carry three tiers:

  • Essentials — single-site pilot, annual term, minimum viable configuration
  • Pro — multi-site, 2-year standard, full service capability
  • Enterprise — full enterprise, 3-year standard, cross-service integration

Volume tiers scale with the unit count — sites, plants, hospitals, facilities, whatever the Practice's natural unit is. Standard breakpoints: 10 / 50 / 250 / 1000 units per Practice. Above 1,000 units, commercial arrangements shift to enterprise-wide bundles.

2.4 The CFO conversation — ROI math

CFOs want two numbers: the investment and the payback window. The APEX audit-row discipline makes both defensible.

Example: RC client with 400 stores, Wave 1

  • Services selected: CXP (customer-experience) + RVD (retail-viability dashboard) + ESL (electronic-shelf-label intelligence)
  • Deloitte Wave 1 investment: $4–6M
  • First-year annualised benefit at Wave 2 scale: $4–7M
  • Payback window: 12–18 months on Wave 1 alone
  • Wave 2 compound benefit (year 2): $15–25M annualised
  • Three-year cumulative ROI: 2.5–4.0×

Example: HLS Payer, Wave 1

  • Services selected: HLS-Payer-UM (utilization management) + HLS-Payer-M360 (member 360)
  • Deloitte Wave 1 investment: $1.5–2.5M
  • First-year annualised benefit at Wave 2 scale: $8–15M (UM automation + denial reduction)
  • Payback window: 9–14 months on Wave 1
  • Wave 2 compound benefit (year 2): $30–50M annualised
  • Three-year cumulative ROI: 4.0–6.0×

Example: AXLE OEM, Wave 1

  • Services selected: AXLE-Product-GEA (generative engineering) + AXLE-Mfg-CF (connected factory)
  • Deloitte Wave 1 investment: $2–3.5M
  • First-year annualised benefit at Wave 2 scale: $6–12M (engineering cycle time + OEE)
  • Payback window: 14–20 months
  • Three-year cumulative ROI: 2.8–4.5×

Why the math is defensible

The audit-row attribution makes benefit claims concrete:

  • Every write-off avoided has an audit row
  • Every dispute recovered has an audit row
  • Every stale-tag remediation has an audit row
  • Every prevented stockout has an audit row

When the CFO's FP&A team asks "show me the number," Deloitte can produce the attribution query against the audit tables. The attribution is auditable because Purview governs the underlying data, and every agent action is logged in the Foundry observability layer.

2.5 Funding paths (Independence-compliant)

Client funding reaches Deloitte through one of four compliant channels only.

Direct client funding

The cleanest path. The client's budget funds Deloitte's SOW. Independence-neutral.

DCIF — Digital Cloud Investment Fund

Microsoft field allocates DCIF to a client to underwrite cloud investment. The client then engages Deloitte directly with their internal budget or the DCIF credit. Funds flow Microsoft → client → Deloitte, never Microsoft → Deloitte direct. Compliant because the client is the contracting party for the Deloitte services.

ISV Marketplace co-sell

Revenue is transacted through Azure Marketplace where an ISV (not Microsoft Corporation) is the contracting party. Deloitte may co-sell or subcontract to the ISV. Compliant because Microsoft is not the direct counterparty to Deloitte.

SI teaming

Deloitte subcontracts to, or co-delivers with, a non-restricted SI (Accenture, Infosys, HCLTech, Cognizant, Capgemini) who holds the Microsoft funding relationship. Deloitte's fees flow through the lead SI, not Microsoft.

Why ECIF is prohibited

ECIF (Enterprise Customer Investment Fund) is a Microsoft funding mechanism that credits the Microsoft customer for deployment activities. It cannot flow directly from Microsoft to Deloitte because it would constitute a commercial transaction between the auditor (Deloitte) and the audit client (Microsoft) — a direct Independence violation under SEC Rule 2-01(c)(4).

If a Microsoft seller offers ECIF funding for a Deloitte-led engagement, the correct response is:

"Deloitte cannot accept ECIF because of the audit relationship. The approved paths are direct client funding, DCIF allocated to the client, ISV Marketplace, or SI teaming with a non-restricted partner. Which of those works for this opportunity?"

This conversation should happen early — ideally during the pursuit-initiation call with the Microsoft field team — not during contract negotiation.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. The Deloitte engagement is contracted between Deloitte and the client. The Microsoft platform licenses are contracted between the client and Microsoft. Never pitch a bundled "Deloitte + Microsoft" commercial that blurs this. Procurement teams will test this in negotiation; your answer must be consistent every time.

2.6 The value-share option

For select services where measurable benefit is tightly attributable, value-share commercial is available:

  • RVC-03 (Recovery & Value Capture) — lower base fee + percentage of dispute/recovery dollars recaptured
  • SHK-07 (Shrink Intelligence) — lower base fee + percentage of shrink reduction vs baseline
  • ICE-WCP-03 (Warranty Cost Prevention) — lower base fee + percentage of warranty cost avoided
  • HLS-Payer-Denial-01 — lower base fee + percentage of denied-claim revenue recovered

When value-share is appropriate

  • The baseline KPI is clearly measurable and agreed in writing
  • Attribution to APEX services is unambiguous (no confounding concurrent initiatives)
  • The client has audit-quality data on the baseline
  • Deloitte's Commercial QR and Risk have signed off

When value-share is inappropriate

  • The baseline is disputed or unmeasured
  • Attribution requires assumptions the client may later challenge
  • The service's benefit is leading-indicator (e.g., customer satisfaction) rather than direct-dollar
  • The commercial duration is too short to see meaningful benefit

Value-share is a sophisticated commercial mechanism, not a discount-dressed sales ploy. Do not offer it casually.

2.7 Procurement defense script

Procurement teams will test the two-contract framing. A common challenge:

Procurement: "We want one number that includes everything." Seller: "Understood, and I want to be straightforward with you. Microsoft's platform licensing is a contract between your team and Microsoft; that's not something Deloitte can legally bundle into our services fee. What I can give you is a clean Deloitte fee with assumptions about Microsoft platform costs that you validate directly with Microsoft. That keeps the math transparent and avoids an Independence issue for our audit relationship with Microsoft."

Procurement: "Other SIs give us one number." Seller: "Other SIs may, and they have different regulatory obligations. Deloitte audits Microsoft, so our Independence rules require this separation. It's not a procurement preference; it's a legal requirement for us. I can help you assemble a combined total-cost view that includes Microsoft's quote and Deloitte's fee side by side."

Procurement: "Will Microsoft discount if we commit to more Deloitte services?" Seller: "That's a question for your Microsoft account team; I can't and won't represent Microsoft's pricing. Happy to make the introduction if one's not already in place."

Key Takeaways

  • Three waves: Wave 1 envisioning + first services; Wave 2 Practice at scale; Wave 3 sustain and expand
  • Two-contract model — Deloitte services and Microsoft platform are separate contracts, always
  • ROI math is audit-row-defensible; CFO gets a number that traces to specific decisions
  • ECIF cannot flow Microsoft-to-Deloitte; use direct / DCIF / ISV Marketplace / SI teaming
  • Value-share option on denial recovery, shrink, warranty — used selectively, not casually
  • Procurement will test two-contract framing; rehearse the defense script

Seller Actions

  1. Memorise approved funding paths (no ECIF direct)
  2. Build an ROI calculator using per-service annualised benefits
  3. Practice the "two-contract" framing until it is automatic
  4. Prepare a qualify-out script for sub-$1M POCs
  5. Rehearse the procurement defense script verbatim
  6. Know the value-share-appropriate services and the value-share-inappropriate situations
Chapter 3

The Microsoft Technology Stack APEX Leverages

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Explain APEX's relationship to the Microsoft stack with Independence-compliant language
  • Identify which platform capabilities APEX requires versus prefers
  • Position APEX as Deloitte IP that runs on Microsoft — not a joint offering
  • Navigate co-sell conversations with Microsoft field counterparts
  • Handle procurement questions about "who sells what" without stumbling

3.1 Deloitte delivers agentic AI on the Microsoft platform — start here

Deloitte Agentic AI Delivery Services is what Deloitte sells. It is the advisory, implementation, and managed-services motion for deploying agentic agents on the Microsoft technology platform. APEX is the proprietary internal accelerator Deloitte uses to deliver these services faster than a ground-up build would allow. APEX — the methodology, the semantic-model library, the agent catalog, the MCP tool library, the HITL gate framework, the audit-row discipline, the Wave 1/2/3 playbook — is Deloitte-owned, Deloitte-maintained, Deloitte-internal.

The Microsoft technology platform is the necessary substrate for Deloitte's agent delivery because that platform uniquely combines the data plane (Fabric), the intelligence plane (Azure AI Foundry + Azure OpenAI), the productivity layer (Copilot), the governance layer (Purview), and the identity layer (Entra) that agentic decision-automation requires at enterprise scale. MCP servers hosted in Azure Container Apps or Azure Functions glue the data plane and intelligence plane together with a model-agnostic tool contract.

Deloitte does not sell Microsoft licenses. Clients procure Microsoft platform entitlements directly from Microsoft. Deloitte delivers Agentic AI Delivery Services as advisory and implementation services that run on top of those entitlements. APEX, as Deloitte's internal accelerator, makes that delivery feasible in months rather than years.

The vocabulary that keeps you safe

Every sentence you speak about the Deloitte-Microsoft relationship has regulatory weight. The SEC and the PCAOB interpret language describing the relationship as evidence of the relationship's character. Use these approved formulations:

  • "Deloitte delivers agentic-AI services on the Microsoft technology platform."
  • "Your agents will run on Microsoft Fabric, Foundry, Copilot, MCP, and Purview — all platform you license directly from Microsoft."
  • "Deloitte has a technology platform relationship with Microsoft."
  • "Deloitte's delivery accelerates your deployment on the Microsoft stack you license directly."
  • "Microsoft is a technology platform provider for Deloitte's agentic AI delivery practice."

Do NOT say:

  • "Buy APEX" / "APEX product" / "APEX license"
  • "Microsoft is our partner" / "Deloitte-Microsoft partnership"
  • "Our alliance with Microsoft"
  • "The Deloitte-Microsoft joint venture"
  • "A co-branded solution"
  • "Microsoft-authorized Deloitte services"

These are not stylistic preferences. Every one of them would be a finding in an Independence review, or a positioning error that creates client expectation mismatch.

3.2 What APEX requires (mandatory)

These Microsoft platform capabilities are not optional. APEX as shipped today requires all of them, in combination, to function.

Microsoft Fabric (the data plane)

  • OneLake — unified lakehouse for all Practice data
  • Lakehouse — Bronze / Silver / Gold medallion architecture
  • Warehouse — T-SQL serving layer for Gold
  • Eventstream / Eventhouse — real-time event ingestion and KQL analytics
  • Pipelines / Dataflows Gen2 — batch and REST ingestion
  • Mirrored Databases — CDC from transactional SORs without ETL authoring
  • Shortcuts — cross-workspace and cross-cloud data reference without copying

Azure AI Foundry + Azure OpenAI (the intelligence plane)

  • Foundry Agents — agent authoring, orchestration, evaluation
  • Azure OpenAI Service — foundation models (GPT-4 class, reasoning models, embeddings)
  • Model catalog — curated selection of open and frontier models
  • Evaluation and monitoring — content safety, prompt-injection defense, drift detection

Azure AI Agent Service (agent runtime)

  • Agent registration and lifecycle
  • Canary and progressive rollout
  • Cross-agent orchestration with observability

Microsoft Purview (the governance plane)

  • Data Map — inventory, classification, lineage
  • Data Loss Prevention — sensitivity-aware policy enforcement
  • Information Protection — labeling and protection across Microsoft 365 and Azure
  • Audit — administrative and operational audit trails

Entra ID P2 (the identity plane)

  • Managed Identity — workload identity for agents and services
  • Conditional Access — risk-based access enforcement
  • Identity Governance — access reviews, lifecycle, entitlement management
  • Agent identity (emerging) — first-class identity for autonomous agents

Azure Container Apps or Azure Functions (MCP hosting)

  • MCP server hosting with managed identity
  • Auto-scale serverless and container-native options
  • Private Link and VNet integration

3.3 What APEX optionally leverages

These enhance the APEX experience where available but have fallback options when a client's posture differs.

  • Microsoft 365 Copilot — HITL adaptive cards in Teams; alternative: email-based approval workflows
  • Copilot Studio — conversational surfaces on customer-facing services; alternative: Foundry-direct agent with custom UI
  • Power Platform — dashboards, approval flows, low-code extensions; alternative: Fabric Power BI + custom apps
  • Microsoft Sentinel + Defender for Cloud — security posture monitoring; alternative: Splunk, Elastic, or any SIEM/XDR
  • GitHub Enterprise + GitHub Copilot — developer productivity for the internal build-out; alternative: Azure DevOps

3.4 Why this stack (the architectural argument)

The argument for Microsoft is architectural, not commercial. APEX's four-layer manifest model requires four platform capabilities to compose natively:

  1. Data plane with Delta-native storage, cross-workspace shortcuts, CDC mirroring, and T-SQL serving — all under one capacity envelope. Fabric delivers this with OneLake, Mirrored Databases, and Warehouse.
  2. Agent runtime with tool-calling, model-tier selection, registration, canary, and audit — under one orchestration and observability umbrella. Azure AI Agent Service + Foundry deliver this.
  3. Governance plane that propagates sensitivity labels from data-classification at Silver through to agent-output DLP — without hand-written policy plumbing. Purview delivers this natively because it sees Fabric data and Foundry outputs as the same governance surface.
  4. Identity plane with managed identity, conditional access, and per-tenant scoping — for users, agents, and service principals in one directory. Entra delivers this.

No other hyperscaler today composes these four planes natively. AWS has strong primitives across the categories but not native composition; GCP is similar; IBM's watsonx is strong in specific verticals; Oracle's strength is application-layer rather than platform-level; Salesforce is CRM-native rather than enterprise-cross-SOR.

This is an architectural observation, not a marketing claim. Clients evaluating APEX for other technology stacks should expect significant re-engineering. The APEX team has not produced a validated port to AWS, GCP, IBM Cloud, Oracle Cloud, or Salesforce Data Cloud.

3.5 What APEX is NOT

Be explicit with the client about what APEX is not. Ambiguity here causes Independence issues later.

  • NOT Microsoft's product. Microsoft does not sell APEX. Microsoft's Industry Solutions team may reference APEX in client conversations because the APEX reference architecture validates the Microsoft stack for agentic workloads; that reference is informational, not a Microsoft commercial offering.
  • NOT a Microsoft alliance or partnership. Deloitte's relationship with Microsoft in this context is a technology-platform relationship — we selected Microsoft as the runtime substrate for APEX. Microsoft does not co-own, co-brand, or co-market APEX.
  • NOT a bundled commercial. The client contracts two things separately: Deloitte services (APEX) and Microsoft platform entitlements. One contract never covers both.
  • NOT a joint offering. There is no combined Deloitte-Microsoft go-to-market motion in which Deloitte's fees are embedded in Microsoft's pricing or vice versa.
  • NOT an ISV product. APEX is a services engagement, not a software subscription. There is no APEX SKU on Azure Marketplace. (Some component assets may surface on Marketplace, but the platform itself is delivered as services.)

3.6 The client view

From the client's side, purchasing APEX looks like this:

  1. The client evaluates their strategic cloud and data platform commitments.
  2. If Microsoft is already their primary Azure + Fabric estate (or they are adopting it), APEX is a natural fit.
  3. The client signs a direct agreement with Deloitte for APEX advisory and implementation services.
  4. The client consumes Microsoft platform services under their existing EA, MCA, or CSP arrangement with Microsoft.
  5. Deloitte does not invoice the client for Microsoft licenses; Deloitte's invoice covers only Deloitte-delivered services.
  6. The Microsoft account team handles platform expansion (additional Fabric capacity, Copilot seats, Foundry consumption) as the APEX Practice scales.

3.7 Co-selling with Microsoft field

Co-selling between Deloitte practitioners and Microsoft field teams is permitted and frequent under the compliant funding paths established in Chapter 2. Microsoft's Industry Solutions Delivery (ISD) organization may provide:

  • Executive air cover for CXO-level introductions
  • Account-team coordination and deal registration
  • Technical validation of Fabric / Foundry / Copilot fit
  • Demo environments and reference architectures
  • DCIF funding allocation to the client (which then funds Deloitte)

What co-selling does NOT include:

  • Microsoft invoicing the client for Deloitte services
  • Microsoft paying Deloitte directly for customer delivery
  • Bundled Microsoft-Deloitte SOWs
  • Joint pricing commitments where Deloitte fees flex based on Microsoft commitments

The co-sell scripts

When a Microsoft seller asks about deal structure: "Deloitte contracts directly with the client for services. Microsoft's platform licensing is a separate client-Microsoft arrangement. Happy to align on timing so the two contracts close together, but they're independent commercially."

When a Microsoft seller offers ECIF: "Deloitte can't accept ECIF because of the audit relationship. The approved paths are direct client funding, DCIF allocated to the client, ISV Marketplace, or SI teaming with a non-restricted partner. Which fits this opportunity?"

When a Microsoft seller wants a joint pitch deck: "Happy to build a technology-and-services story together. Our references to the Deloitte-Microsoft relationship need to use specific approved language — I'll route the draft through our Independence Office before we take it external."

When a client asks "are you the same team as Microsoft?": "No. Deloitte is a separate firm. APEX is Deloitte intellectual property that leverages Microsoft's platform. We work closely with Microsoft's field team on accounts like yours, but the services contract is with Deloitte directly."

3.7A The Microsoft field org — who does what

Co-selling requires knowing which Microsoft role does what. The mental map:

3.7B The co-sell motion — step by step

  1. Pre-qualify the Microsoft team alignment. Before the first client meeting, call the GPL or Partner Development Manager to confirm Microsoft field awareness and appetite for the account. If Microsoft is cold on the account, co-sell motion is not available.
  2. Confirm the ATU's appetite. The ATU Lead decides whether to bring Deloitte into the account. Their questions: "What's your 30/60/90 value hypothesis? What Microsoft consumption does it drive? Which of my sellers do you want engaged?"
  3. Identify the Microsoft champion. One named individual — typically the ATU Lead, a GBB, or a CSA — becomes the co-sell counterpart. Build that relationship.
  4. Co-plan before co-pitch. Before any joint client meeting, hold a 30-minute internal Microsoft-Deloitte session to align on message, owner of each slide, and boundary lines.
  5. Joint client meeting. Microsoft leads the platform story; Deloitte leads the services, IP, and delivery story. Do not cross boundaries.
  6. Debrief and align on next steps. After the meeting, 15-minute Microsoft-Deloitte debrief. Agree next touchpoint.
  7. Track consumption. Wave 1 and Wave 2 drive measurable Microsoft consumption (Fabric CU, Foundry tokens, Copilot seats). Share consumption telemetry with the Microsoft ATU quarterly; this is the basis for continued co-sell investment.

3.7D Common co-sell failure modes

  • "Microsoft's here, so the deal is ours." No. Microsoft presence establishes access; Deloitte still has to earn the services contract independently.
  • "Let Microsoft own the first meeting." No. A first meeting with only Microsoft + client without Deloitte presence means Deloitte shows up as an appendix in the client's memory.
  • "Microsoft promised us ECIF." Stop. ECIF direct to Deloitte is prohibited. Reconfirm through Independence before proceeding.
  • "The ATU Lead said they'd route the services scope to us." Nice, but not binding. Build the client relationship directly; never rely on Microsoft routing alone.
  • "We'll figure out boundaries in the meeting." No. Co-plan before co-pitch. Every single time.

3.7E The quarterly motion

A healthy APEX account runs a quarterly Microsoft-Deloitte business review at each tier-1 client:

  • Wave status (Deloitte delivery)
  • Platform consumption trend (Microsoft view)
  • Next-quarter expansion pipeline (joint view)
  • Field-alignment issues escalated to GPL
  • Independence pre-clearance status refresh

This rhythm is what separates accounts where the co-sell motion compounds from accounts where each new pursuit re-introduces Deloitte cold.

3.8 What procurement will ask

Procurement teams ask the same seven questions on every APEX engagement. Rehearse.

  1. "Who is the contracting entity?" — Deloitte (Deloitte Consulting LLP or regional equivalent). Not Microsoft.
  2. "Is this a joint offering with Microsoft?" — No. Deloitte product, Microsoft technology substrate, separate contracts.
  3. "Can you include Microsoft licenses in your fee?" — No. Independence prohibits it.
  4. "Can Microsoft give us a discount if we use Deloitte?" — Separate conversation with Microsoft account team. Deloitte does not negotiate Microsoft pricing.
  5. "Who owns the IP created during the engagement?" — Deloitte retains APEX framework IP (semantic models, agent library, orchestration patterns, methodology). Client retains all client-specific configurations, data, and customisations deployed to their tenant.
  6. "Can we exit cleanly?" — Yes. Client retains all their data, their configurations, and their Microsoft platform entitlements. Deloitte's IP remains Deloitte's.
  7. "Will you indemnify us for Microsoft platform failures?" — No. Deloitte indemnifies for Deloitte-delivered services. Microsoft platform indemnities are in the client-Microsoft contract.

3.9 The "multi-cloud enterprise" reality

Most Fortune 500 clients run two or three hyperscalers. APEX lands cleanly in multi-cloud enterprises by being explicit about scope:

  • "APEX is the Microsoft-stack agentic platform. It runs where your Microsoft footprint runs."
  • "Your AWS workloads continue where they are; APEX doesn't need to touch them."
  • "Where your data crosses between clouds, Fabric's shortcuts or mirroring lets APEX reach it in place without moving it."

This framing is credible and commercially accurate. Trying to reposition APEX as a replacement for what the client already has elsewhere is a losing play.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. Marketing, proposal, and client-facing materials referencing APEX on Microsoft must avoid terms like "partner," "alliance," "joint venture," or any language implying a joint-commercial relationship. Approved terms: "APEX leverages Microsoft Fabric," "APEX runs on the Microsoft platform," "Deloitte's technology platform relationship with Microsoft." When in doubt, route draft materials through the Independence Office before external release.

Key Takeaways

  • APEX is Deloitte IP that leverages Microsoft as the runtime platform — always Deloitte-owned, always contracted separately
  • Client contracts Deloitte and Microsoft separately — two agreements, not one
  • Fabric, Azure AI Foundry, Purview, Entra ID are mandatory; Copilot is preferred but optional
  • Use "technology platform relationship" — never "partnership" or "alliance"
  • Co-selling with Microsoft field is encouraged under compliant funding paths; joint commercials are not
  • Procurement will test the two-contract framing with seven predictable questions — rehearse all seven

Seller Actions

  1. Memorise Independence-compliant language for every APEX conversation
  2. Eliminate "partner" and "alliance" from your pitch decks and remove them from email signatures
  3. For each pursuit, confirm the client understands the two-contract model in writing
  4. Route any Microsoft-field ECIF offer to approved funding paths within 24 hours
  5. Rehearse the four co-sell scripts and the seven procurement answers
  6. Brief your Microsoft field counterpart on the Independence constraints BEFORE joint calls
Chapter 4

Competitive Differentiation: Microsoft vs AWS, GCP, IBM, Oracle, Salesforce

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Handle "why Microsoft and not AWS/GCP/Oracle?" as the technical question it is
  • Articulate the architectural reasons APEX is platform-specific today
  • Respond respectfully when a client has strategic non-Microsoft commitments
  • Navigate multi-cloud pursuits with architectural honesty
  • Know when to disqualify the pursuit rather than force the pitch

4.1 The seller's posture

APEX sellers are not Microsoft sellers. Your job is not to defeat AWS, GCP, Oracle, IBM, or Salesforce on their own merits. Your job is to explain — accurately and without bias — why APEX as an agentic decision-automation platform runs today only on the Microsoft stack, and what that means for a client already invested in another hyperscaler.

The posture matters because of Independence. Deloitte audits Microsoft. Disparaging Microsoft's competitors in a sales conversation creates an appearance problem that runs beyond the deal you are working. A seller who attacks AWS to close a Deloitte audit client's APEX deal puts the audit practice's credibility at risk. The correct posture is: respectful architectural honesty about what APEX requires, and graceful disqualification when those requirements do not match the client's strategic commitments.

4.2 The core architectural argument

APEX's four-layer manifest model depends on four platform capabilities composing natively:

  1. A data plane with Delta-native storage, cross-workspace shortcuts, CDC mirroring, and T-SQL serve-layer — all under one capacity envelope (Fabric)
  2. An agent runtime with tool-calling, model-tier selection, registration, canary, and audit (Azure AI Agent Service + Foundry)
  3. A governance plane that can propagate sensitivity labels from Silver to agent-output DLP (Purview)
  4. An identity plane with managed identity, conditional access, and per-tenant scoping (Entra ID)

No other hyperscaler today composes these four in a single native stack. That is not a marketing claim; it is an architectural observation.

4.3 Platform-by-platform comparison

For each platform, this chapter states (a) what the platform is strong at, (b) the architectural gap relative to APEX's four-plane requirements, and (c) the correct posture when the client is primarily invested there.

4.3.1 Amazon Web Services (AWS)

Strengths. AWS has the deepest primitive-service catalog of any hyperscaler. Redshift and Athena for analytical workloads; Glue and Lake Formation for data governance; Bedrock as a serious model-orchestration layer with AgentCore maturing; SageMaker for ML lifecycle; IAM as an identity service that the rest of AWS integrates deeply. Many APEX-candidate clients have significant AWS investment, especially in RC, TMT-MED, and TMT-TEC.

Architectural gap. The gap is integration maturity across the four planes. AWS's data plane is composed (S3 + Lake Formation + Redshift + Athena + Glue); APEX's data plane is Fabric as a single product. An AWS equivalent requires the client and system integrator to author the integration between planes — governance labels from Lake Formation must be propagated by custom code to Bedrock output moderation; identity federation between IAM and application agents is workable but not native. A Bedrock agent cannot natively propagate Lake Formation sensitivity tags to output moderation the way Foundry + Purview can.

Co-existence pattern. Fabric shortcuts reach S3 data in place without duplication. Many APEX clients keep AWS workloads where AWS is load-bearing (media encoding, consumer mobile backends, existing analytical estates) and add Fabric for the APEX workload specifically.

Posture when AWS-primary. Be honest. APEX as shipped today is not the right platform for a client whose strategic AI trajectory is Bedrock / AgentCore. Offer an agentic discovery engagement that assesses what replicating APEX's four-layer model on AWS would require. Many clients conclude the architectural lift is too costly and shift some strategic workloads to Microsoft; some remain AWS-primary, and the APEX pursuit ends gracefully. You accept that outcome.

4.3.2 Google Cloud (GCP)

Strengths. GCP has excellent primitives — BigQuery is a category-leading analytics warehouse; Vertex AI and Gemini represent serious foundation-model investment; Dataplex has matured as the governance layer; Google's data engineering heritage is deep. Vertex AI Agent Builder and Agent Space are maturing quickly. Retail, consumer-internet, and technology clients running on GCP often have sophisticated internal AI teams.

Architectural gap. Two gaps. First, enterprise operational tooling — no equivalent to Fabric's OneLake cross-workspace model for multi-tenant APEX-style governance at enterprise scale. Second, enterprise identity federation at the depth of Entra ID — Google Workspace identity is strong for Google-centric estates but less deeply federated with on-prem Active Directory in the way most enterprises need.

Co-existence pattern. BigQuery-centric clients commonly federate Fabric onto BigQuery via shortcuts or Iceberg interop, keeping analytical processing in BigQuery while APEX services orchestrate through Foundry.

Posture when GCP-primary. Similar to AWS — honest assessment, acknowledge GCP strengths, note APEX runs on Microsoft today, invite a discovery on the gap. For consumer-internet and tech companies where GCP commitment is strong and deep, APEX often does not fit; disqualify gracefully.

4.3.3 IBM Cloud and watsonx

Strengths. IBM Cloud's agentic story is centerd on watsonx.ai, watsonx.data, and watsonx.governance as an integrated AI-and-governance play. IBM has particular strength in regulated financial services and public sector. IBM Consulting's scale is material.

Architectural gap. Two gaps. First, scale of the native hyperscale services — IBM Cloud's breadth across general enterprise workloads is narrower than Azure, AWS, or GCP. Second, enterprise ecosystem breadth beyond regulated verticals — IBM's strength in financial services and government does not extend to the retail / manufacturing / healthcare / TMT / TH breadth APEX targets.

Co-existence pattern. Many IBM-heavy clients carry IBM for legacy mainframe adjacency and are open to multi-cloud for new workloads. APEX on Microsoft can coexist with watsonx where watsonx owns specific regulated workloads.

Posture when IBM-primary. These clients often run IBM for mainframe and legacy analytical workloads and are selecting Azure or AWS for new AI investment. APEX fits the new-investment side cleanly.

4.3.4 Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI)

Strengths. Oracle's strength is deep vertical integration for Oracle-application customers (ERP, HCM, SCM, EBS, NetSuite, Fusion). OCI's price-performance on Oracle workloads is competitive. Oracle's ecosystem of application connectors is rich for Oracle-application-centric back-office workloads.

Architectural gap. The gap is native cross-application agent runtime. Oracle's agentic capabilities are application-embedded (Fusion AI Agents within Fusion modules) rather than platform-level and cross-SOR. APEX's cross-application agentic orchestration model does not have a clean home on OCI today — each Fusion module has its own AI capabilities that do not orchestrate together the way APEX agents do.

Co-existence pattern. Oracle Fusion apps remain on OCI as the transactional SOR; APEX leverages Fabric Mirroring or shortcuts to bring Oracle transactional data into the APEX semantic model without moving it.

Posture when Oracle-primary. Most Oracle-heavy clients run Oracle for core transactional systems and separately run Microsoft for analytics / AI / productivity. APEX fits alongside Oracle, not in place of it. The typical play is: "Oracle runs ERP, Microsoft runs the APEX agentic layer, Purview governs both."

4.3.5 Salesforce Platform (Data Cloud, Agentforce, Einstein)

Strengths. Salesforce's Data Cloud + Agentforce is rapidly maturing as an agent platform for CRM and front-office workflows. Einstein Trust Layer addresses enterprise safety concerns. Clients with large Salesforce footprints find the Salesforce agent story increasingly compelling for customer-facing workflows.

Architectural gap. The gap is breadth of SOR coverage. APEX ingests from WMS, MES, EHR, SCADA, AMI, PSS, pharmacy systems, historian systems, and dozens of non-CRM systems that Salesforce Data Cloud does not attempt to canonicalize. Agentforce is naturally CRM-centric; APEX is naturally enterprise-cross-SOR.

Co-existence pattern. Clients use Agentforce for Salesforce-resident workflows (sales cloud agents, service cloud agents, marketing agents); APEX handles cross-SOR orchestration that reaches beyond Salesforce's transactional boundary.

Posture when Salesforce-Agentforce-committed. Agentforce is best-in-class for customer-facing agentic workflows inside Salesforce. APEX complements Agentforce for non-CRM decision surfaces. The two coexist cleanly when scoped accordingly. If a client expects to use Agentforce for all agentic workloads including non-CRM, disqualify APEX on scope mismatch.

4.4 How to respond in the room

Client statementHonest, Independence-compliant response
"We're an AWS shop""APEX as shipped today runs on the Microsoft platform. If your strategic AI workloads are heading to Bedrock and SageMaker, APEX may not fit. I can explain why the platform choice is architectural, not commercial, and we can assess where APEX would require porting"
"We prefer Google Cloud"Same posture — honest, non-defensive, architectural framing
"Why not Oracle or IBM?""APEX's four-layer model requires specific native platform capabilities. Oracle and IBM have strong components but don't natively compose the full stack today. APEX can run alongside them for complementary workloads"
"We're standardizing on Salesforce Data Cloud""Agentforce is excellent for CRM-native workflows. APEX covers non-CRM decision surfaces. They coexist well when scoped accordingly"

4.5 What NOT to say

  • "Microsoft is better than AWS/GCP/Oracle." (Not your assertion to make; not Independence-appropriate.)
  • "Microsoft is our partner." (Independence violation.)
  • "You should move everything to Microsoft." (Not the APEX sale; you'll lose credibility.)
  • "APEX will work on AWS, we can port it." (Unvalidated; don't promise.)
  • "AWS/GCP/Oracle can't do this." (Factually sloppy; the architectural argument is subtler.)
  • "Their governance is weaker." (Disparagement; undermines Deloitte's audit credibility.)
  • "We've seen bad projects on their platform." (Anecdote, not argument.)
Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. Your job is to honestly position APEX as a Deloitte product that runs on the Microsoft platform. You are not defending Microsoft's competitive position against AWS/GCP/Oracle/IBM/Salesforce. If a client chooses a non-Microsoft strategic commitment, accept the outcome gracefully; there are many Deloitte offerings that fit those clients.

4.6 The multi-cloud reality

Most Fortune 500 clients run two or three hyperscalers. This is the normal case, not the exception. APEX fits into a multi-cloud posture as the agentic-decision-automation capability on the Microsoft stack, alongside whatever the client has committed to elsewhere.

Framing APEX as "the Microsoft-stack agentic platform in a multi-cloud enterprise" is more credible than framing it as a replacement for whatever they have elsewhere. It respects the client's existing investment, sets realistic scope, and gives the architect counterpart a clean story to tell their cloud-strategy committee.

The multi-cloud positioning paragraph

"APEX is architecturally native to the Microsoft four-plane stack — Fabric, Foundry, Purview, Entra. In an enterprise running AWS, GCP, or Oracle alongside Microsoft, APEX handles the agentic decision layer on the Microsoft footprint without displacing what you have elsewhere. Fabric's shortcuts and mirroring let APEX reach data in place on S3, BigQuery, or Oracle without moving it. The architectural question is where the four-plane integration lives; the commercial question is which workloads are a fit for APEX and which stay where they are."

Memorise this. It is Independence-compliant, architecturally accurate, and respects the client's strategic commitments.

4.7 When to disqualify — decision tree

Not every prospect is a fit. Disqualification is not failure; unqualified pursuits waste Deloitte delivery capacity and damage client relationships when they inevitably collapse.

Disqualify APEX when:

  1. Client has explicit strategic commitment to AWS / GCP / Oracle / IBM for new AI workloads. Honest disqualification. Offer platform-agnostic Deloitte advisory.
  2. Client requires APEX to run on a non-Microsoft stack. APEX is not ported. Do not commit to porting.
  3. Client's Salesforce Agentforce footprint is expected to cover all agentic workloads including non-CRM. Scope mismatch. APEX does not displace Agentforce in its home territory.
  4. Client's governance framework explicitly prohibits adding a new cloud footprint. Independent of platform preference, if no new footprint is permitted, APEX requires Fabric — disqualify.
  5. Client's procurement requires bundled Microsoft-Deloitte commercials. Independence prohibits. If the client insists after explanation, disqualify.

Keep a short list of trusted Deloitte advisory offerings to redirect disqualified prospects to. Most "APEX is not the fit" conversations end with a different Deloitte engagement, not a lost client.

4.8 Complementary Platforms — Palantir, C3.ai, and the Ecosystem Around APEX

The earlier sections of this chapter covered platforms that compete with the Microsoft stack as the primary AI substrate (AWS Bedrock, GCP Vertex, Oracle, IBM, Salesforce Agentforce). This section covers a different category: platforms clients already own that coexist with APEX rather than compete with it. The correct seller posture is not "displace these" — it is "compose APEX with these, so the client's prior investment is leveraged, not wasted."

4.8.1 Why the ecosystem question matters in Wave 1

Most large enterprise clients arrive at an APEX conversation with at least one non-Microsoft AI or data platform already deployed somewhere. A credible seller does not pretend these do not exist. A credible seller does not argue they should be ripped out. A credible seller shows how APEX composes with them — through MCP tools, Delta Share, standard APIs, and Purview lineage federation — so the client's strategic investments in other platforms are additive to the APEX delivery, not subtracted from it.

The positioning language for this conversation is consistent:

Note

"APEX is Microsoft-native because of Fabric + Foundry + Purview + Entra composition. But APEX's design explicitly supports integration with the other major platforms your organization has invested in. In a multi-platform enterprise, APEX doesn't replace what you have — it orchestrates across it."

4.8.2 Palantir Foundry

What Palantir does well. Graph-backed ontology layer; operational workflows (Workshop, Quiver, AIP); complex joins across historically-siloed systems; federal / intelligence-community workloads; high-touch forward-deployed-engineer delivery model. Many industrial, energy, healthcare, and government clients have meaningful Palantir investment.

How it coexists with APEX. Three integration patterns:

  1. Palantir ontology ↔ APEX canonical schema. The Palantir ontology can be mirrored to Fabric OneLake via shortcut; APEX canonical schemas (SCML, PatientML, etc.) materialize Silver views that reference the ontology. Purview lineage captures the join.
  2. Palantir actions as APEX MCP tools. A Palantir action (write-back to Foundry) becomes an APEX MCP action tool. An APEX agent can invoke a Palantir-authored transformation or decision pipeline, preserving the audit row.
  3. APEX agents surface inside Palantir Workshop. Workshop surfaces can embed APEX agent outputs through Copilot Studio or direct API, giving Palantir users APEX-generated recommendations without platform-switching.

When to lead with Palantir. Deep graph-analytics workloads where the ontology is the primary artifact; federal / intel clients with existing Palantir investment and strict classification models; complex multi-silo integrations where Palantir's forward-deployed-engineer model is already in motion.

When to lead with APEX. Microsoft-anchored clients (M365 / Fabric / Copilot footprint already dominant); regulated industries where Purview + Entra governance fits the client's existing compliance posture; agentic orchestration at scale with HITL discipline and audit-row attribution as first-class requirements.

The coexistence pitch. "Your Palantir investment stays. APEX agents can call Palantir pipelines through MCP, and Palantir Workshop can surface APEX agent outputs. One tenant, two complementary capabilities."

4.8.3 C3.ai

What C3.ai does well. Pre-packaged industry-specific AI applications — C3 AI Suite with vertical accelerators for energy, manufacturing, financial services, defense; strong predictive-maintenance heritage; well-defined data-model templates per industry.

How it coexists with APEX. Two integration patterns:

  1. C3 outputs as APEX agent inputs. A C3 predictive-maintenance score or financial-crime prediction is published to a C3 API; APEX exposes it as an MCP tool; an APEX agent reasons about the score in context and drives downstream workflow through Copilot.
  2. C3 data-model mapping to APEX canonical schema. C3's pre-built industry models are frequently translatable to APEX canonical schemas (e.g., C3 Energy Management ↔ P&UML; C3 Manufacturing Operations ↔ AAML). Where the client has already sunk investment into C3 models, APEX absorbs them through adapter schemas rather than re-designing.

When to lead with C3. Pre-packaged vertical ML applications where time-to-first-prediction matters more than agentic orchestration; clients already standardized on C3 platform; narrowly-scoped predictive-model workloads without multi-agent composition needs.

When to lead with APEX. Agentic reasoning workloads beyond predictive ML; multi-agent orchestration across verticals; HITL-governed decisions with audit-row defensibility; Microsoft-anchored enterprise platforms.

The coexistence pitch. "C3's models produce predictions; APEX's agents reason about those predictions in business context and drive action with human-in-the-loop. The two are designed for different workloads."

4.8.4 Databricks + Mosaic AI Agent Framework

What Databricks does well. Unified data + ML lakehouse on any cloud; Delta Lake open format (the same format Fabric OneLake uses); MLflow lifecycle; Mosaic AI Agent Framework for agent development; Unity Catalog for governance.

How it coexists with APEX. Databricks is the most architecturally-aligned complementary platform to APEX because both use Delta Lake. See Appendix F for the full Fabric + Databricks co-existence pattern. In summary:

  1. Delta Share / OneLake shortcut. Databricks Delta tables are visible to Fabric via shortcut with zero duplication. APEX canonical schemas can materialize either place.
  2. Databricks agents as APEX MCP tools. Mosaic-built agents become MCP-exposed tools; APEX orchestrations call them like any other tool.
  3. Unity Catalog ↔ Purview lineage federation. Governance labels cross the boundary.

When to lead with Databricks. Clients with deep existing Databricks investment and Unity Catalog governance; lakehouse-first architectures where the client's data estate already lives in Databricks.

When to lead with APEX. Governance-first, HITL-first, Copilot-experience-first pursuits where Fabric + Foundry + Purview + Entra composition is the architectural requirement.

4.8.5 Snowflake + Cortex

What Snowflake does well. Multi-cloud analytical warehouse with strong data-sharing; Cortex for in-warehouse LLM functions; Snowpark for ML; Horizon Catalog for governance.

How it coexists with APEX. See Appendix F. Two primary patterns:

  1. Snowflake-to-Fabric mirroring. Near-real-time replication via Fabric Mirror so APEX canonical schemas in Silver can join Snowflake-resident data without replatforming.
  2. Cortex functions as APEX MCP tools. In-warehouse LLM functions are wrapped as MCP tools; APEX agents invoke them when the workload is best served inside the warehouse.

Coexistence posture. "Your Snowflake investment stays. APEX does not require Snowflake to go away; it requires the data Silver layer to be queryable from Foundry, which Fabric Mirror to Snowflake satisfies."

4.8.6 Salesforce Einstein / Data Cloud / Agentforce

What Salesforce does well. In-platform CRM agents; customer-facing workflows; Data Cloud as a CDP; Einstein / Agentforce for in-flow AI.

How it coexists with APEX. Salesforce is both a SOR (for CXML customer data) and a destination (for agent-initiated next-best-action writes). Patterns:

  1. Data Cloud → Fabric. Via MuleSoft / native connector. Customer 360 attributes flow to CXML Silver.
  2. APEX agent outputs → Salesforce. Case creation, lead enrichment, next-best-action surfacing — APEX writes back via Salesforce API behind a HITL gate.
  3. Agentforce in the CRM surface; APEX in the enterprise surface. Agentforce handles in-CRM user-facing agent flows; APEX handles cross-domain orchestration that spans CRM, ERP, supply chain, service.

When to lead with each. Agentforce if the workload lives entirely inside CRM. APEX if the workload spans CRM plus anything else (supply chain, finance, operations, regulatory). Most enterprise workloads are the latter.

4.8.7 ServiceNow Now Assist / Virtual Agent

What ServiceNow does well. ITSM, HR Service Delivery, Customer Service Management workflow platform with Now Assist AI tightly integrated.

How it coexists with APEX. ServiceNow workflow becomes an APEX action target. APEX agents create / update / close ServiceNow records as HITL-gated actions; ServiceNow Now Assist operates inside the ITSM surface while APEX orchestrates cross-platform (e.g., a factory-floor incident that requires both ServiceNow work-order creation and AXLEML-based production-line impact analysis).

4.8.8 UiPath / Blue Prism / Automation Anywhere (RPA)

What RPA platforms do well. Screen-scraping, legacy-system automation, UI-level process execution where no API exists.

How it coexists with APEX. RPA becomes an APEX action tool of last resort. When a required SOR has no API, APEX calls the RPA platform through MCP to execute a legacy-UI transaction. The audit row captures the RPA invocation; Purview tracks the lineage from agent decision to legacy system change.

4.8.9 IBM watsonx / Cloud Pak for Data

What IBM does well. watsonx.ai governance platform; watsonx.data lakehouse; long-term relationships in regulated industries (finance, insurance, healthcare); deep IBM-consulting bench.

How it coexists with APEX. Two patterns:

  1. watsonx governance as a parallel control plane. For clients with watsonx.governance already in production, APEX agent outputs can be logged to watsonx.governance in addition to Purview. The client gets two compatible audit stores.
  2. watsonx.data as a data source. Lakehouse tables mirrored / shortcutted to Fabric OneLake.

4.8.10 Google Vertex AI / Agent Builder

What Google does well. Foundation-model research lineage (Gemini); BigQuery analytics; Vertex AI Agent Builder; multimodal capabilities.

How it coexists with APEX. In multi-cloud clients, Vertex agents can be exposed to APEX through Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol or through MCP tool wrappers. APEX orchestration treats a Vertex agent as just another tool; the governance and audit row remain in Purview.

4.8.12 The language to use in the meeting

When a client asks "How does APEX compete with Palantir / C3 / Databricks / Snowflake?" — the seller's answer is:

Note

"APEX doesn't compete with those. APEX is the Microsoft-native agentic-AI delivery framework. It orchestrates across the platforms you already have. If you use Palantir for ontology, APEX calls Palantir. If you use C3 for predictive maintenance, APEX reasons about C3's outputs. If you use Databricks as your lakehouse, APEX shortcuts to Databricks. What APEX brings is the four-plane Microsoft composition (Fabric + Foundry + Purview + Entra), the canonical-schema library, the agent catalog, and the delivery discipline. The other platforms stay where they are load-bearing."

That sentence reframes the conversation from displacement to composition, which is both architecturally accurate and commercially larger.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. When naming these platforms in client conversations, avoid any suggestion of preferred commercial arrangement. Deloitte has professional-services relationships with multiple platform providers; Independence rules require those relationships be disclosed where relevant but never positioned as commercial bundles.

Key Takeaways

  • APEX runs on Microsoft today because of architectural composition, not commercial bias
  • Four-plane native integration (data/intelligence/governance/identity) is the architectural gap for AWS/GCP/Oracle/IBM/Salesforce
  • Honest assessment beats defensive posturing; accept non-Microsoft clients gracefully
  • APEX often coexists with non-Microsoft platforms in multi-cloud enterprises

Seller Actions

  1. Memorise the four-plane argument for architectural differentiation
  2. For each pursuit, confirm the client's hyperscaler strategic commitments
  3. Prepare graceful "APEX doesn't fit here" pivots for non-Microsoft-first clients
  4. Never disparage AWS/GCP/Oracle/IBM/Salesforce competitively
Chapter 4A

The APEX Stack at a Glance — One Diagram Every Seller Needs

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Gives sellers the one-page APEX stack diagram — ten layers, top to bottom, that anchor every architecture conversation with a CIO/CDO/CTO/Chief Architect.
  • Decodes the A.P.E.X. acronym as four design commitments — what APEX stands for and what it stands against.
  • Walks the runtime view — how a single decision flows from event ingress through the data plane, the contract surface, the reasoning plane, the experience plane, and back out as an audit row.
  • Sources this chapter directly from docs/reference/APEX-Stacked-Architecture-Narrated.html — the canonical reference diagram all three trilogy volumes share.
Where this chapter sits

Part I closes by saying "this is why APEX wins." Part II opens by drilling into the four Microsoft pillars (Fabric · Foundry · Copilot · Purview). This chapter is the bridge: one diagram of the full ten-layer stack that lets a seller hand-wave the whole architecture in 90 seconds, then point at the layer the executive asked about and drill in. Every Part-II chapter expands a layer from this diagram; every Part-III Practice Playbook lands services on it.

4A.1 A.P.E.X. — Four Letters, Four Design Commitments

Before the diagram, the name. APEX = Agent-based Platform for EXecution. Each letter is a commitment — what the platform stands for, and what it stands against. The whole architecture is these four commitments, composed.

4A.2 The Ten-Layer APEX Stack

The stack reads top-down. Every arrow of data flows up; every line of governance flows down. The top is where humans meet agents (Experience). The bottom is identity and trust (Foundation) — always on, always underneath. The middle is the agent value-creation engine.

4A.2.1 How to Read the Stack in a Client Conversation

The stack is intentionally read from top to bottom in an executive conversation and from bottom to top in an architect conversation. Same diagram, two narratives:

AudienceRead directionWhat you say
CIO / CDO / CFO10 → 1 (top down)"Your operators see Copilot. Behind Copilot are 38 productized services. Behind the services, the agents that compose them. Below the agents, the data and tools they call. At the bottom, Entra and Purview that keep everything auditable. Each layer is a Microsoft platform investment you already have or are about to make."
Chief Architect / CTO1 → 10 (bottom up)"Entra and Purview are the substrate. On that, Fabric and the medallion. On top of Fabric, the canonical schemas — the acceleration kernel that lets the 2nd use case ship in 3 weeks instead of 6 months. Above schemas, the typed MCP contract. Above MCP, Foundry agents. Above agents, orchestration. Above orchestration, productized services. At the top, Copilot."
Compliance / CISO1 ↔ all (cross-cutting view)"Entra gives every agent a managed identity. Purview classifications flow from Silver up through Gold, MCP tools, agent outputs, and the audit row. Every decision is regulator-answerable from the Foundation layer up."

4A.3 The Runtime View — How a Single Decision Moves

The stack diagram is the static view (layers, components, products). The runtime view shows the dynamic path — an event arrives, data flows up through the medallion, the agent reasons, the audit row writes, the operator sees the result. Same architecture, different lens.

4A.4 The Seven Practices on the Stack

A Practice is not what the client buys. It is a bundle of five reusable assets Deloitte reuses across every pursuit in a vertical: canonical schemas · agent catalog · orchestration catalog · service catalog · delivery playbook. Each Practice lands on the stack the same way; the content per layer differs.

4A.5 Using the Stack in Pursuits

Sellers should print the ten-layer stack (Figure 4A.2) and keep it in front of them for every CIO/CDO/CTO conversation. The discipline is to point at the layer the executive named — not jump levels.

What the executive saidLayer to point atWhat you say next
"We've already invested in Fabric / OneLake."Layer 2 · Data Plane"Great — APEX is Fabric-native. The acceleration is at Layer 3, the canonical schemas, that turn your second use case from a 6-month build into a 3-week config."
"We're standing up Copilot already."Layer 10 · Experience"Then APEX is the engine behind Copilot. Layer 9 is the productized service catalog Copilot calls into; Layer 5 is the reasoning that produces the answer."
"Our concern is audit and lineage."Layer 1 · Foundation (Purview half)"Purview is the substrate, not an add-on. Every layer above writes lineage downward into the audit row. Show me your most sensitive Service and I'll walk the lineage with you."
"How do agents talk to our SOR data?"Layer 4 · MCP Tool Binding"They don't, directly. One typed MCP tool per Gold view, identity-scoped, classification-aware. The agent cannot touch Bronze or Silver."
"What's the difference between APEX and just-build-it-yourself?"Layer 3 · Canonical Schemas"This layer. APEX ships ~35 canonical schemas across seven Practices. That's 18–24 months of engineering effort, already done. Build-it-yourself starts at Layer 2."
"How do you handle multi-agent coordination?"Layer 8 · Orchestration"47 archetypes built on Microsoft Agent Framework's five builder classes. Parent/child topology with a Redis control plane at Layer 7 carrying state and a LEDGER carrying document lineage."
Best Practice — every Wave-1 anchor names a Service at Layer 9

The most common Wave-1 scoping error is anchoring on a layer rather than a Service. "Let's stand up Fabric" is a layer; "let's deploy RC-E2E-03 cold-chain markdown decisioning" is a Service at Layer 9. The Service implies all the layers below it. The layer implies nothing about value or KPI. Always anchor Wave 1 to a named Service from APEX-Scenario-Chains.xlsx (per Ch 9–15) and let the stack be the platform argument that supports it.

Key Takeaways

  • APEX = A.P.E.X. — Agent-based · Platform · Enterprise · eXecution. Four letters, four design commitments, each with what the platform stands for and what it stands against.
  • The ten-layer stack (Foundation · Data Plane · Canonical Schemas · MCP Tool Binding · Reasoning · Runtime · Control Plane · Orchestration · Service Catalog · Experience) is the one diagram every seller needs. Read top-down for executives, bottom-up for architects.

Chapter 5

Fabric — The Data Plane APEX Requires

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Explain Fabric as APEX's data plane in 90 seconds
  • Know the five Fabric integration patterns APEX uses and when each applies
  • Position client-direct Fabric capacity as the platform foundation
  • Handle Fabric-vs-Databricks-vs-Snowflake co-existence fluently
  • Size Fabric capacity for a discovery conversation

5.1 What Fabric is to APEX

Fabric is the data plane APEX requires. Every APEX deployment lands SOR data in Fabric's Lakehouse, canonicalizes in Silver, materializes in Gold, and serves Gold to agents via MCP. No Fabric, no APEX. This is not negotiable — APEX's semantic models (SCML, MERML, CXML, and their HLS, ER, AXLE, TMT, TH, ICE equivalents) are authored as Fabric artifacts.

The client licenses Fabric capacity directly from Microsoft. Deloitte's APEX engagement does not include Fabric licensing; Deloitte delivers the advisory, schemas, and implementation that run on client-owned Fabric capacity. This is the two-contract model in operation.

Why Fabric specifically

Fabric unifies five Microsoft data-platform capabilities that used to be separate products. OneLake provides a single logical data lake across the enterprise. Direct Lake lets Power BI read Parquet without ETL. Shortcuts let Fabric reference data in place across clouds. Mirrored Databases give CDC from transactional SORs without ETL authoring. Real-Time Intelligence (Eventhouse, KQL, Reflex) handles streaming and alerting natively.

That consolidation matters for APEX because the APEX agent patterns assume a single semantic surface — one place agents query, one governance boundary, one identity model. Fabric is the only hyperscaler data platform that composes these natively without client-side integration work.

5.2 The five Fabric integration patterns (deep dive)

APEX uses five integration patterns chosen by how the SOR emits data. Sellers should be fluent in identifying which applies to the client's top SORs during first-meeting discovery.

Pattern 1: Mirrored Database (CDC)

What it is. Fabric Mirroring replicates a source database's tables into OneLake as Delta tables with sub-minute latency. CDC (change data capture) is the underlying mechanism; the source's transaction log is streamed to Fabric continuously.

When APEX uses it. For transactional SORs where agent-grade freshness matters. Examples:

  • Manhattan WMS (RC, ICE)
  • SAP ISU / S/4HANA (ER, AXLE, RC)
  • Epic Clarity (HLS Provider)
  • Oracle Fusion ERP (AXLE, TMT, HLS)
  • Snowflake databases (RC, TMT)
  • SQL Server / Postgres / Cosmos DB (multi-industry)

Latency. 60–180 seconds typical.

Seller talking point. "For your top transactional system, Fabric mirroring replicates the tables into our semantic model in under three minutes without any ETL authoring. Your DBAs don't build pipelines; Fabric reads the CDC stream natively."

Pattern 2: Eventstream / Eventhouse

What it is. Fabric's real-time pipeline for high-volume event data. Eventstream handles ingestion; Eventhouse is the KQL-queryable landing zone. Reflex provides event-triggered actions.

When APEX uses it. For IoT, telemetry, click-stream, and high-frequency operational data. Examples:

  • Monnit / IoT gateways (RC cold-chain, ER predictive maintenance)
  • POS streams (RC)
  • Epic ADT notifications (HLS Provider)
  • SCADA event streams (ER)
  • Plex MES events (AXLE manufacturing)
  • Network alarms (TMT-TEL)

Latency. Sub-second to seconds.

Seller talking point. "For your real-time telemetry, we land the stream in Fabric Eventhouse and reflex-trigger APEX agents. The alert-to-decision loop runs in seconds, not minutes."

Pattern 3: Data Pipeline (scheduled batch)

What it is. Scheduled ETL/ELT for SORs that produce batch outputs on a schedule.

When APEX uses it. For end-of-day files, reporting extracts, external data feeds. Examples:

  • End-of-day inventory snapshots
  • Supplier master file refreshes
  • Regulatory report extracts
  • Third-party market data feeds

Latency. Minutes to hours, depending on schedule.

Seller talking point. "Overnight batch feeds land in the Bronze lakehouse via scheduled pipelines. APEX services consuming them run on a cadence that matches the client's operating rhythm."

Pattern 4: Dataflow Gen2 (REST pull)

What it is. Fabric's managed ETL for REST and SaaS APIs. Schedule, transform, and land.

When APEX uses it. For SaaS SORs without CDC — CRMs, HR systems, marketing platforms, third-party services. Examples:

  • Salesforce (read-only), HubSpot
  • Workday, SuccessFactors
  • ServiceNow, Jira
  • Marketing platforms (Adobe, Braze, Segment)

Latency. Minutes, schedule-dependent.

Seller talking point. "Where your SaaS systems expose REST, Fabric's Dataflow Gen2 pulls them into the lakehouse on schedule. No middleware, no custom Python."

Pattern 5: Custom Endpoint (webhook)

What it is. Push-only SORs that emit webhooks land in Fabric via a custom endpoint (Azure Functions or API App).

When APEX uses it. For systems with no pull API — webhook-only integrations, IoT devices, legacy systems. Examples:

  • Legacy industrial equipment
  • Some medical-device feeds
  • SMS / email event streams
  • Third-party notification services

Latency. Sub-second to seconds.

Seller talking point. "Where the SOR only pushes webhooks, we stand up a lightweight Azure Functions endpoint to receive and land. It's a well-trod pattern — no custom middleware."

The pattern-selection decision

SignalLikely pattern
Source is SQL database with CDCPattern 1 (Mirroring)
Source is Kafka, MQTT, or equivalent event busPattern 2 (Eventstream)
Source is SaaS REST APIPattern 4 (Dataflow Gen2)
Source produces scheduled filesPattern 3 (Data Pipeline)
Source can only push webhooksPattern 5 (Custom Endpoint)

In a first-meeting conversation, ask: "What are your top three operational SORs and how do they expose data?" The answer maps to patterns.

5.4 Fabric workspace pattern for APEX

APEX uses a specific Fabric workspace topology that sellers should be able to describe at a high level.

  • Platform workspace — shared services, the APEX runtime control plane, Purview policy artifacts
  • Practice workspace (per Practice, per tenant) — the Bronze/Silver/Gold medallion for that Practice at that tenant
  • Service workspace (optional) — for service-specific Gold views that multiple Practices consume
  • Dev / test / prod — three-environment deployment within each Practice workspace for safe change

The workspace topology matters for Independence and for Purview governance; it is not just a technical detail.

Fabric + Databricks co-existence on Azure

Databricks runs natively on Azure as Azure Databricks — a first-party Microsoft service in the Azure Portal with Entra identity, Private Link networking, and Azure billing. Many APEX prospects have material Azure Databricks investment for data engineering, ML feature pipelines, or Delta Lake lakehouses. The APEX posture is explicit: Databricks stays, Fabric is added, and the two interoperate.

The three interoperation patterns

  1. OneLake Shortcuts to ADLS Gen2. Databricks clusters commonly write Delta tables to ADLS Gen2. Fabric reaches these tables in place via OneLake shortcuts — no copy, no ETL, no duplicate storage bill. The Delta format is native to both sides.
  2. Mirrored Azure Databricks Unity Catalog. Fabric provides native mirroring of Unity Catalog schemas. Databricks remains the system of record for the data; Fabric sees a read-optimized replica suitable for APEX Gold serving and Power BI Direct Lake.
  3. Databricks as upstream producer, Fabric as APEX serving layer. Databricks continues to own ML training and batch feature engineering; APEX Gold views in Fabric consume Databricks-produced Delta tables and serve them to MCP for agent use.

Limitations of Databricks for APEX-style workloads

  • Copilot grounding. Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio ground natively against Fabric OneLake. Databricks Delta tables become Copilot-grounded only indirectly (through Fabric shortcuts or replication). On its own, Databricks has no Copilot-grounded answer for knowledge-worker surfaces.
  • Purview integration. Purview data-map coverage of Unity Catalog exists but is less mature than Purview over Fabric. Classification, lineage, and DLP on Databricks-resident data require more configuration work and in some cases Databricks-side agents.
  • Real-time intelligence. Databricks Structured Streaming is powerful for engineering; Fabric's Real-Time Intelligence (Eventhouse, KQL, reflex rules) is a more integrated pattern for the alerting and live-dashboard use cases APEX Practices lean on.
  • Semantic model authoring. APEX ships its semantic models (SCML, MERML, CXML, and their peers) as Fabric artifacts. A Databricks-only implementation would require re-authoring the semantic layer on Databricks-native tooling, which is not on the APEX roadmap.
  • Licensing doubling. Running both is two bills. Position honestly: Databricks earns its keep on engineering workloads it already owns; Fabric is added for the APEX workload. Right-sizing prevents duplicate spend.

Fabric + Snowflake co-existence on Azure

Snowflake runs on Azure as a first-class region choice. Many APEX prospects run the bulk of their analytics estate on Snowflake-on-Azure. Again, Snowflake stays, Fabric is added.

The three interoperation patterns

  1. Mirroring Snowflake into Fabric. Fabric provides native Snowflake mirroring. Snowflake remains the analytical system of record; Fabric sees a near-real-time replica with Delta format and OneLake addressing. No ETL pipelines to author.
  2. Iceberg interop via OneLake. Snowflake's Apache Iceberg support plus Fabric's Iceberg support means tables can be read by both engines from the same storage.
  3. Snowflake as source, Fabric as APEX serving layer. Snowflake serves traditional BI and analytical workloads; APEX-specific Gold views live in Fabric, grounded by Snowflake data through mirroring or Iceberg.

Limitations of Snowflake for APEX-style workloads

  • Agent runtime. Snowflake Cortex provides in-platform AI functions, but it is not a substitute for the Azure AI Foundry agent runtime APEX uses. APEX's 47 orchestration patterns and 165+ MCP tools target Foundry.
  • Copilot grounding. Microsoft 365 Copilot grounds natively against Fabric, not against Snowflake. Snowflake data reaches Copilot only through Fabric mirroring or OneLake integration.
  • Purview governance. Purview's native integration with Snowflake is less deep than with Fabric. Classification and DLP on Snowflake-resident PII or PHI require Snowflake-side governance tooling in addition to Purview.
  • Microsoft 365 integration. Snowflake excels at analytical SQL workloads, not at serving knowledge-worker agents through Teams, Outlook, SharePoint, and the Microsoft 365 graph. That integration is the Fabric + Foundry + Copilot story.
  • Data movement cost. Without mirroring, making Snowflake data agent-accessible requires duplication. Mirroring removes that cost but adds a Fabric capacity bill.

5.5 Why APEX on Fabric — the architectural acceleration case

This section is the seller's reference for the question every sophisticated architect or CTO asks within the first two meetings: "Fabric already does most of this. Why do I need APEX?" The answer has four parts: what Fabric alone does not provide, what APEX adds natively, why this combination cannot be replicated cheaply on AWS / GCP / IBM / Oracle / Salesforce, and why Fabric specifically is the right substrate. Sellers should be able to deliver this argument in 10 minutes to a technical audience.

5.5.1 What Fabric out-of-the-box does and does not provide

Fabric is a data platform. It is not a decision platform. The distinction is the entire APEX value proposition.

Fabric ships with the data-platform primitives APEX needs: OneLake, Lakehouse, Warehouse, Eventhouse, Data Factory, Real-Time Intelligence, Direct Lake, Shortcuts, Mirroring, Purview integration, Entra integration. An architect with Fabric can build a medallion architecture, land Bronze data, canonicalize Silver, materialize Gold, and serve Power BI. That is the shipping value of Fabric.

What Fabric does NOT ship:

Missing capabilityWhat it means in practiceBuild cost on raw Fabric

Retail needs category/SKU/customer/store semantics; HLS needs patient/encounter/claim/RWE; ER needs asset/process/event/outage. Fabric doesn't ship these.6–12 months per Practice for a 6-person data team

Foundry provides the agent runtime, but the agents themselves — price-recommend, assortment-optimize, demand-sense, markdown-cadence, shrink-detect, denial-predict, RWE-signal-detect — are application IP you author.9–15 months for the first Practice's agent set
