The sum of what Fabric does not ship, done by the client themselves, is 18–24 months of engineering effort per Practice for a competent team, plus the organizational learning to deploy that effort in regulated industries without breaking governance. That is the time-to-first-production-service gap APEX closes.

5.5.2 What APEX adds — specifically and concretely

APEX is not "a layer of consulting" on top of Fabric. It is a framework of Fabric-native artifacts plus delivery methodology. The pieces:

On the Fabric side (what APEX writes INTO Fabric):

  • Semantic models authored as Fabric Lakehouse + Warehouse schemas per Practice (SCML for supply-chain, MERML for merchandising, CXML for customer, and their HLS / ER / AXLE / TMT / TH / ICE equivalents)
  • Gold views materialized as Warehouse views or Direct-Lake-backed Delta tables, optimized for agent low-latency queries
  • KQL functions in Eventhouse for real-time reasoning over event streams
  • Pipeline artifacts in Data Factory for Bronze → Silver → Gold refresh orchestration
  • Data Activator rules for event-triggered agent invocations
  • Power BI certified datasets using Direct Lake for Copilot-grounded executive dashboards

On the Foundry side (what APEX writes for agent runtime):

  • ~40 agent definitions per Practice as Foundry Agent objects with system prompts, tool bindings, evaluation criteria
  • 47 orchestration patterns as Foundry multi-agent workflows
  • Agent-level evaluators measuring groundedness, safety, and business-outcome attribution

On the Purview side (what APEX writes for governance):

  • Classification rules for Practice-specific sensitive data (PHI for HLS, CPNI for TMT-TEL, PCI-adjacent for RC payments)
  • DLP policies on agent outputs
  • Lineage registrations across Bronze → Silver → Gold → agent output
  • Compliance assessments mapped to HIPAA / GDPR / SOX / 21 CFR Part 11 as applicable

On the Entra side:

  • Managed identities per agent, per MCP server, per tenant
  • Conditional access policies scoped to APEX workloads
  • Access review schedules for APEX-relevant roles

Above all these — the methodological IP:

  • Manifest contracts (event, orchestration, agent, tenant) — four-layer governance model
  • HITL gate patterns — eight standard gate types with audit-row contracts
  • Audit-row schema — the defensible-outcome attribution mechanism
  • Delivery methodology — Wave 1 / Wave 2 / Wave 3 cadence, envisioning templates, change-management playbook
  • Independence compliance — audit-client scope discipline, funding-path compliance, language rules

5.5.3 The composition — how APEX and Fabric work together

APEX is Fabric-native in a specific technical sense: APEX's artifacts ARE Fabric artifacts, not adjacent code that calls Fabric. When APEX ships "RC-E2E-03 Assortment & Pricing Intelligence," what the client receives is:

  1. Lakehouse tables conforming to SCML + MERML (Silver) and RC Gold views (Warehouse materialisations)
  2. Foundry agents that query those Gold views through MCP tool bindings
  3. Data Factory pipelines that refresh Silver and Gold
  4. Eventhouse functions if the service has real-time components
  5. Power BI Direct Lake datasets for merchant dashboards
  6. Purview classification rules for SKU / customer / supplier data
  7. Entra managed identities for the agents
  8. Copilot Studio surfaces grounded on the Direct Lake datasets
  9. Manifest artifacts committed to the client's Git repository
  10. A decision-audit-row table with attribution queries

The composition means there is no "APEX runtime" separate from Fabric and Foundry. APEX services ARE the Fabric tables, ARE the Foundry agents, ARE the Purview policies. When Fabric or Foundry releases a new capability, APEX services can adopt it directly because they are native to the platform.

This composition property is what lets APEX deploy in 9–12 months where a build-from-scratch equivalent takes 18–24 months: APEX inherits the Fabric + Foundry + Purview + Entra composition instead of re-authoring it.

5.5.4 Why this cannot be done with Fabric out-of-the-box alone

Architects who have deployed Fabric for analytics sometimes ask "why can't our data team just build this on Fabric themselves?" The honest answer has five parts:

(a) Time-to-value gap. A competent six-person data-engineering team, starting from scratch on raw Fabric, needs 18–24 months to author one Practice's semantic model, agent library, orchestration patterns, MCP tools, HITL gates, and audit-row discipline at APEX catalog depth. That is the gap. Clients with a public KPI commitment in the current fiscal year do not have 18 months.

(b) Cross-Practice consistency. A team building one Practice often produces a bespoke solution that does not generalize to the next Practice. APEX's seven Practices share a common manifest framework, common MCP tool catalog, common audit-row schema. The cross-Practice pattern reuse compounds Wave 3 value.

(c) Governance completeness. Purview integration, HITL gate design, audit-row attribution, and Independence-compliant delivery are framework concerns that an in-house team may underinvest in. Regulated-industry deployment (HLS, ER, regulated TMT) requires all of these to be first-class from day one. A build-your-own effort often rebuilds the governance layer in production after the first regulatory inquiry.

(d) Operating-model learning. Running an agentic platform in production — evaluation, drift detection, model-upgrade handling, safety monitoring, cost discipline — is operating-model IP. APEX carries it from prior engagements. A client building their own absorbs that learning the hard way.

(e) Independence protection. For Deloitte audit-client engagements, the scope discipline and language compliance are not optional. An in-house team or a non-Deloitte SI does not carry the same Audit-Committee-pre-clearance track record. This is a structural advantage Deloitte brings that no platform vendor can provide alone.

None of this is an argument that the client cannot build it themselves — they absolutely can. The argument is that the time, cost, and risk of doing so exceed what APEX Wave 1 + Wave 2 would cost to deploy the same capability faster, more consistently, and with better governance from day one.

5.5.5 Why APEX + Fabric accelerates over AWS / GCP / IBM / Oracle / Salesforce

The competitive-differentiation argument at Chapter 4 level is architectural — Fabric composes four planes natively. At the APEX-level, the acceleration argument has a concrete edge: APEX's 18–24 months of engineering is pre-built against Fabric specifically. Replicating APEX on an alternative stack requires re-authoring against that stack's primitives.

vs AWS (Bedrock + Redshift + Glue + Lake Formation + IAM):

AWS has strong primitives. A competent team can build a medallion on S3 + Glue, reason with Bedrock agents, govern with Lake Formation, authenticate with IAM. But there is no APEX-equivalent IP on AWS. The acceleration gap for a client picking AWS + AWS-SI vs Fabric + APEX is roughly:

  • 6–9 months for AWS-side semantic-model authoring that APEX ships on Fabric
  • 9–12 months for agent library on Bedrock / AgentCore that APEX ships on Foundry
  • 6–9 months for governance plumbing that APEX + Purview inherit
  • Total: 18–30 months longer time-to-first-production-service on AWS

Sellers should frame this as: "If AWS is your strategic commitment, there is no APEX-equivalent; the build-from-scratch timeline is 18–30 months longer. APEX exists because Microsoft's four-plane composition is what makes the 9–12 month timeline achievable."

vs GCP (Vertex AI + Agent Space + BigQuery + Dataplex + IAM):

GCP's strength is analytics (BigQuery) and the Gemini family. Vertex Agent Builder and Agent Space are maturing. Gap for a GCP-centric deployment:

  • Enterprise-identity federation depth (Entra ID on-prem AD federation is deeper than Google Workspace identity in most enterprises)
  • Cross-plane governance integration (Dataplex governs BigQuery; less native coverage of agent-output DLP)
  • Copilot-equivalent knowledge-worker surface (Gemini in Workspace is good but narrower than M365 Copilot in enterprise M365 estates)
  • APEX has not validated a port to GCP; timeline penalty is 18–30 months

vs IBM (watsonx.ai + watsonx.data + watsonx.governance):

IBM's strength is regulated-financial-services and public sector. watsonx is a serious integrated play. Gaps for APEX-equivalent:

  • Hyperscale enterprise breadth (retail / manufacturing / media less mature than financial services on IBM)
  • Knowledge-worker productivity surface (watsonx Orchestrate for Microsoft 365 estates is workable but not Copilot-native)
  • APEX-equivalent IP does not exist on watsonx for the seven APEX Practices; build timeline penalty similar to AWS/GCP

vs Oracle (OCI + Fusion AI Agents):

Oracle's agentic capabilities are application-embedded (Fusion HCM Agents, Fusion ERP Agents, NetSuite AI) rather than platform-level cross-SOR. The gap for an APEX-equivalent:

  • Cross-SOR orchestration is not OCI's native strength (Fusion Agents are inside Fusion modules)
  • Microsoft 365 / Copilot integration is absent
  • APEX coexists with Oracle (Oracle ERP as SOR → Fabric → APEX services) rather than competes

vs Salesforce (Agentforce + Data Cloud + Einstein):

Agentforce is strong within Salesforce's transactional boundary. Gap for enterprise-scale APEX-equivalent:

  • Non-CRM SOR breadth (APEX ingests from WMS, MES, EHR, SCADA, PSS, pharmacy, historian, etc. — Agentforce is CRM-centric)
  • Cross-SOR reasoning is not Agentforce's design point
  • Coexistence pattern works: Agentforce handles Salesforce-resident workflows, APEX handles cross-SOR decisions

5.5.6 Why Fabric specifically — the deep technical reasons

Fabric is not interchangeable with "any modern data platform." Six specific Fabric properties make it the substrate APEX requires. Sellers should know all six.

(1) OneLake unifies storage across workloads without ETL. In Fabric, a Delta table written by a Spark notebook in a Lakehouse is queryable by T-SQL through the SQL Analytics Endpoint, by Power BI through Direct Lake, by notebooks in any authorized workspace, and by Foundry agents through MCP tools — all reading the same Parquet files. No inter-workload ETL, no dataset refresh, no data duplication. Alternative platforms require inter-service ETL that the client authors.

(2) Direct Lake makes agent queries and Copilot grounding near-instant. Direct Lake reads Parquet directly with column-store optimization. For APEX agents and M365 Copilot grounded on Fabric data, this means sub-second queries on Gold without the dataset-refresh delay of Import mode or the per-query SQL overhead of DirectQuery. This is the query-path property that makes Copilot-grounded knowledge-worker experiences feasible.

(3) Mirroring gives CDC from major SORs without authored pipelines. Azure SQL DB, Cosmos DB, Snowflake, Azure Databricks Unity Catalog, PostgreSQL, MongoDB mirror to OneLake as Delta tables in near-real-time (60–180s typical). APEX's Bronze landing for transactional SORs uses Mirroring as the first choice. The client's DBA team does not author pipelines; Fabric reads the transaction log natively.

(4) Shortcuts give cross-cloud read-in-place without data movement. Shortcuts to ADLS Gen2, S3, GCS, Dataverse, and other OneLake workspaces mean APEX can reach a Databricks-resident table on S3, a Snowflake Iceberg table, or a BigQuery-fed GCS export in place. This is the property that makes Fabric + Databricks + Snowflake coexistence real at enterprise scale (see Appendix F).

(5) Entra-native identity propagates to every workload uniformly. Every Fabric query, every agent invocation, every MCP tool call authenticates against the same Entra tenant. Managed identities per agent, conditional access per workload, access reviews across the estate — all delivered through a single identity plane. Alternative platforms require identity federation the client authors.

(6) Purview integration propagates classification from Silver to agent output natively. Purview classifies Fabric data at the Lakehouse / Warehouse / Eventhouse layer; the same classification propagates to Direct Lake datasets, Power BI, Copilot grounding, and Foundry agent outputs. No manual policy plumbing. DLP policies apply consistently. This is the governance property that makes HLS and regulated-industry deployment feasible from day one.

5.5.7 The "why not just Fabric" conversation — rehearsed responses

Architect / CTO saysSeller response

5.5.8 Why Fabric — the deeper Fabric-specific briefing

For conversations where the architect wants Fabric deep-dive beyond APEX context, sellers should be able to brief on six Fabric-specific points.

OneLake architecture. Tenant-wide logical data lake, Delta / Parquet / Iceberg native, hierarchical workspaces, path-level ACLs via Entra, shortcuts for cross-cloud federation. Single copy of data queryable by every Fabric workload.

Capacity model. F-SKUs (F2 through F2048) sold as CU (Capacity Unit) reservations. Compute is shared per capacity; workspace-to-capacity binding determines isolation. F64 is typical Wave 2 Practice scale; F128+ for multi-Practice enterprise.

Workload engines. Lakehouse (Spark), Warehouse (T-SQL MPP), Eventhouse (KQL), Data Factory (pipelines), Dataflow Gen2 (Power Query M), Eventstream (stream processor), Real-Time Intelligence (Eventhouse + Activator), Mirrored Database (CDC), Data Science (notebooks), Power BI (semantic model + viz). Each workload draws from the same OneLake storage.

Query-path triangle. Import (in-memory, fast, refresh-bounded), DirectQuery (at-query, slower, always fresh), Direct Lake (reads Parquet directly, near-Import speed, near-DirectQuery freshness). APEX defaults to Direct Lake for Gold serving.

Integration fabric. Fabric + Azure AI Foundry + Microsoft Purview + Microsoft Entra + Microsoft 365 Copilot compose natively. No inter-service ETL or policy plumbing.

SaaS delivery. No clusters to manage, no storage accounts to provision, no VMs to patch. Fabric capacity is the only billable resource; everything else is tenant configuration through Fabric REST API, PowerShell Az.Fabric, or Fabric admin portal.

The technical briefing should be 10–15 minutes. Sellers who cannot deliver it will lose credibility with sophisticated architect audiences.

5.5.9 When APEX + Fabric is NOT the right answer

Intellectual honesty matters. Sellers should know the three conditions under which the APEX + Fabric pitch should be declined, not forced:

  1. Client strategic platform is explicitly AWS or GCP for new AI investment. APEX does not port. Decline gracefully; offer platform-agnostic Deloitte advisory.
  2. Client has an in-flight in-house agent platform that is 12+ months into production. APEX is an accelerator; duplicating already-built work wastes client investment. Evaluate co-existence or narrow-scope complement.
  3. Client's timeline is less than 6 months from discovery to measurable outcome. APEX Wave 1 is 4–8 weeks; Wave 2 first service is 4–6 months after Wave 1 close. If the client needs production value inside 6 months total, scope accordingly or decline.

5.6 When Fabric is a blocker

If the client has a strategic commitment that excludes Microsoft Fabric entirely, APEX is not a viable pitch. Qualify this in the first meeting. Having Databricks or Snowflake already is NOT a Fabric-blocker — APEX coexists. A hard "no Microsoft Azure data services" posture IS a blocker.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. Do not quote Fabric, Databricks, or Snowflake pricing to the client on Deloitte letterhead. Refer the client to their Microsoft account team (Fabric, Azure Databricks) or Snowflake account team for capacity licensing. Deloitte's scope is advisory and implementation, not license resale.

  • Five integration patterns — know which applies to client's top SOR
  • Deloitte advises on sizing; does not quote or resell Fabric licensing
  • AWS/GCP/Oracle/Databricks/Snowflake alternatives don't replace Fabric for APEX

Chapter 5A

The Runtime Plane — Gateway, Safety, Evaluation, Observability

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Answer the four operational questions sophisticated buyers always ask
  • Position Azure API Management as the model-egress plane with token metering
  • Explain the safety primitives (Content Safety, Prompt Shields, Groundedness Detection, Protected Material)
  • Make the eval story credible: golden datasets, PyRIT red-teaming, shadow + canary rollout
  • Distinguish audit rows (decision evidence) from observability (operational evidence)
  • Close the feedback loop: production decision → audit row → LEDGER → eval case → next version
Addendum note

This chapter was added in the Runtime Addendum (v1.5). Suggested reading order: read Chapters 5 and 6 first, then return here to see how the four Microsoft pillars compose into a single operational plane. The content here answers the four questions that move CIO / Chief Architect / CISO conversations forward: "what does it cost to run", "what about hallucinations", "how do you know it's actually working", and "what happens when it breaks".

5A.1 Why this matters in a sales conversation

Every sophisticated agentic-AI buyer eventually asks four operational questions. Sellers who can answer them cleanly move the pursuit forward; sellers who cannot, don't. APEX's Runtime Plane is how Deloitte answers all four — with Microsoft-native primitives, not custom engineering.

The four questions, mapped to the four sub-planes of this chapter:

  1. What does it cost to run? → §5A.2 Model Gateway (APIM token metering → cost_per_decision)
  2. What about hallucinations? → §5A.3 Safety Plane (Groundedness Detection + HITL gate on failure)
  3. How do you know it's actually working? → §5A.4 Evaluation Plane (golden datasets + shadow + canary)
  4. What happens when it breaks? → §5A.5 Observability Plane (App Insights + Log Analytics + SLOs)

5A.2 Model Gateway — the egress plane

Azure API Management sits in front of every Azure AI Foundry agent call. One egress point, one governance surface, one place to meter and control.

  • Rate limits per service_code and per tenant — noisy-neighbor protection for shared model capacity
  • Token metering rolls up to cost_per_decision on the audit row (see §6.10.12)
  • PII redaction at the prompt boundary — before data leaves the tenant
  • Model version routing — primary (GPT-4o), fallback (GPT-4o-mini), cheap-tier for structured extraction
  • Response caching for deterministic-prompt calls (cache-hit flag on audit row)
  • Circuit breakers fail-soft to fallback models instead of blocking orchestrations
Objection handler — "what does it cost to run?"

APEX meters every model call through APIM with token-level granularity. Cost per decision is bound to the audit row, which means the CFO view is a Power BI dashboard over Log Analytics — not a quarterly reconciliation. Sellers should never quote agentic-AI cost as an abstract number; always reference cost_per_decision and offer to walk the dashboard.

5A.3 Safety Plane — input and output inspection

Every prompt and every response passes through Microsoft-native safety primitives at the boundary of the agent call. Safety verdicts are written to the audit row, bound to the decision_id (see §6.10.12 for the safety_verdict field).

  • Azure AI Content Safety — text and image moderation across four harm categories; tunable thresholds per service
  • Prompt Shields — detects jailbreak attempts and indirect prompt injection from retrieved documents or context
  • Groundedness Detection — verifies agent output is supported by retrieved context; flags hallucination before release
  • Protected Material Detection — flags copyrighted text or code in outputs (critical for IP-exposed surfaces)
  • Custom safety policies — per-Practice overlays on top of the Microsoft baseline
Objection handler — "what about hallucinations?"

APEX does not assume the model is trustworthy. Every response flows through Groundedness Detection before release to the user. If the output is not supported by retrieved context, the HITL gate fires. The safety verdict is on the audit row — meaning "we checked" is a query, not an assurance.

5A.4 Evaluation Plane — continuous quality

No production APEX agent ships without a continuously-running evaluation harness. Offline and online, pre- and post-deployment.

5A.4.1 Offline evaluation

  • Golden datasets per Practice — curated input-output pairs reviewed by SMEs
  • Regression suites on every agent version; breaking changes blocked at CI
  • Red-team prompts generated by PyRIT (Microsoft's AI red-teaming toolkit)
  • Foundry Promptflow evaluators — relevance, coherence, fluency, groundedness scored per response

5A.4.2 Online evaluation

  • Shadow mode — new agent version runs alongside production with zero user impact
  • A/B testing — traffic-split experiments with statistical-significance gates on KPI impact
  • Canary rollouts — 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% with automated rollback on safety or quality regression
  • Drift detection — input distribution, output distribution, and KPI-correlation shifts surfaced to the service owner
Objection handler — "how do you know it's actually working?"

Every production APEX agent runs a continuously-executing eval harness. Nothing ships without passing golden-set regression. Nothing rolls out without shadow-mode validation. And the feedback loop closes: audit rows become eval cases, eval cases shape the next version. The agent materially improves month over month. Ask about the current golden-set size for the relevant Practice — that is the credibility signal.

5A.5 Observability Plane — always-on telemetry

Runtime telemetry across every agent, every tool call, every orchestration. The distinction from audit rows: audit rows are decision evidence; observability is operational evidence. Both exist.

  • Application Insights — traces, metrics, logs per agent, per orchestration, per tool call
  • Log Analytics — cross-service KQL queries; joins across Fabric, Foundry, APIM, and Entra logs
  • Foundry tracing — hierarchical spans (agent → tool → model call) with full input/output capture
  • Token and cost metering — per service_code, per tenant, per identity; real-time P&L
  • Latency percentiles — p50, p95, p99 per agent; SLO dashboards per service
  • Tool-call success rates — MCP-tool-level reliability; flag degradation before users notice
  • Power BI dashboards over Log Analytics — service-owner view, CFO view, SteerCo view
Objection handler — "what happens when it breaks?"

Runtime telemetry is distinct from audit rows. Audit rows are decision evidence. Observability is operational evidence. When an agent starts degrading — tool-call failures, latency drift, token-spend spike — the service owner sees it in Application Insights and Log Analytics before any user does. SLOs are measured, not promised.

5A.6 The feedback loop — what makes APEX adaptive

Production decision → audit row written → LEDGER bound by ledger_ref → sample reviewed by SME and automated evaluator → finding becomes eval case → golden dataset updated → next agent version → shadow mode → canary rollout → production.

Without this loop, the LEDGER accumulates but the agent stands still. With it, the agent materially improves month over month.

Year one: instincts. Year two: record. Year three: superagent. This is the sentence to memorize. Full mechanics of how the loop formalizes inside §6.12 are in §6.12.7.

Key Takeaways

  • Four operational questions, four sub-planes: Gateway, Safety, Evaluation, Observability
  • Every primitive is Microsoft-native — APIM, Content Safety, Prompt Shields, Groundedness Detection, Application Insights, Log Analytics, Foundry Promptflow, PyRIT
  • APEX adds the composition — the audit-row fields, the HITL triggers, the eval loop back into LEDGER
  • Decision evidence (audit row) and operational evidence (observability) are distinct systems by design
  • Feedback loop — production → audit → LEDGER → eval → next version — is what makes the "superagent year three" narrative credible

  2. For the current pursuit, know which Practice's golden-set size you can cite as the credibility signal
  3. Walk the CFO view (Power BI dashboard over Log Analytics) at least once before quoting cost_per_decision

6.1 What Foundry is and what it is not

Azure AI Foundry is where APEX-M agents run. Every agent invocation is a Foundry Agent Service call backed by a foundation model hosted in Foundry. Microsoft Agent Framework is the SDK the agent's code is written in; Foundry is the hosted runtime that executes it. The client contracts Foundry and Azure OpenAI directly from Microsoft; Deloitte's APEX-M engagement delivers the Microsoft-Agent-Framework agent designs, prompts, MCP servers, and orchestrations that run on that runtime.

Foundry is NOT just a model endpoint. It is the enterprise agent platform — authoring, orchestration, evaluation, monitoring, governance. A seller who describes Foundry as "Microsoft's version of OpenAI" misses the distinction that matters to enterprise buyers: Foundry adds the production-grade operational tooling that raw model APIs lack.

The Foundry value proposition in one sentence

"Foundry is to agents what Kubernetes was to containers — the production runtime with authoring, orchestration, observability, evaluation, and governance all integrated."

6.2 Foundry capabilities APEX uses

Core platform

  • Azure AI Foundry Portal — the agent authoring and management UI
  • Azure AI Foundry SDK — programmatic authoring for advanced teams

  • Meta Llama — Llama 3.x family for open-weight workloads
  • Mistral — Mistral Large, Mistral Small for European clients with data-residency concerns
  • Specialized models — embeddings, vision, speech, document understanding

Agent runtime

  • Azure AI Agent Service — the hosted agent runtime with registration, canary, A/B testing
  • Azure AI Search + Embeddings — semantic grounding, retrieval-augmented generation
  • Azure AI Content Safety — input and output moderation, prompt-injection defense
  • Azure AI Evaluation — built-in evaluation harnesses (relevance, groundedness, safety)

Observability and governance

  • Foundry tracing — per-invocation trace with model, tool, latency, cost
  • Foundry monitoring — production metrics, alerting, drift detection
  • Purview integration — classification labels propagated to agent outputs
  • Entra integration — managed identity for agents, conditional access on tool calls

6.3 Why APEX is Foundry-native

APEX could, in principle, run on any hosted-model API. It runs on Foundry because four integration points matter:

  1. Purview integration for content-safety and lineage. Every agent invocation's input and output is inspectable by Purview classification. Competing model endpoints require custom policy plumbing.
  2. Entra managed identity for agents. Agents can authenticate to downstream systems (Fabric, Purview, third-party APIs) as themselves, with per-tool conditional access. No shared API keys, no service-principal sprawl.
  3. Fabric-native grounding. Foundry agents ground on Fabric data via managed connections without custom RAG pipelines. Note: RAG supports unstructured-content retrieval within APEX's hybrid context model; agent identity and canonical schema are carried by the file-first context architecture (§6.12), not by RAG.
  4. Production-grade evaluation and monitoring. Model drift, groundedness regressions, and safety violations are detected by Foundry's built-in evaluation harnesses.

A Bedrock agent, a Vertex agent, or a self-hosted LangChain app can reach similar functionality, but the integration work is client-owned and ongoing. Foundry inherits the integration as a platform property.

The composition is what unlocks deployment in HLS (PHI handling), ER (critical infrastructure), and regulated TMT. Competing platforms require the client to author the equivalent composition.

6.7 The prompt-injection defense conversation

Savvy CIOs and CISOs will ask about prompt injection and jailbreak resistance. The honest answer:

"Foundry has built-in prompt-injection defense through Azure AI Content Safety's jailbreak-shield classifier. Even if a prompt-injection attack got past the classifier, the agent's tool permissions are bounded by its manifest — it can't call tools outside scope. Third layer: every tool call is logged, and Purview inspects the output. We can show you the trace for a real injection attempt we caught."

This is a seller-critical conversation because it addresses the executive-level discomfort around "letting AI do things." The three-layer answer (content safety + manifest scoping + audit) is the standard pitch.

6.9 Agent Orchestration — The Multi-Agent Pattern Library

This is the deep-dive on how individual agents compose into complete workflows — the architectural concept that makes APEX services more than single-agent wrappers. Sellers who can explain orchestration in an architect conversation carry credibility that abstract "AI platform" pitches cannot match. For the complete per-schema catalog of specific orchestrations Deloitte delivers, see Appendix T.

6.9.1 What orchestration is (and isn't)

Orchestration in APEX is the composition of multiple agents into a governed multi-step workflow that produces a coherent decision or action. An orchestration is not a single agent with a complex prompt, and it is not a workflow-engine pipeline moving data through transforms. It is the pattern by which reasoning agents hand off context to each other, route to human approval gates at the right moments, invoke action tools, and emit audit rows that trace the full decision path.

Orchestration is distinct from:

  • Data orchestration (Fabric Data Factory pipelines, Data Activator rules) — those move data between Bronze / Silver / Gold
  • BPM / workflow engines (like UiPath or Camunda) — those automate deterministic business processes
  • Single-agent chains (one agent, multiple prompts) — those are prompt-engineering, not orchestration

An orchestration's defining property is multi-agent composition with explicit manifest governance. Each step in the orchestration is performed by a distinct agent with its own identity, tools, classification scope, and audit emission. The orchestration manifest is the contract that binds them together.

6.9.2 The four primitive orchestration patterns

Every APEX orchestration is constructed from four primitive patterns — and usually combines two or three. Sellers should memorise all four.

1. Sequential. Output of agent A feeds agent B which feeds agent C. Each agent refines or transforms the previous agent's output. Used when reasoning steps have a strict dependency order — e.g., detect → classify → disposition → notify.

2. Parallel. A dispatch node fans out to multiple independent agents, whose outputs merge downstream. Used when independent investigations can happen concurrently — e.g., in a recall scenario, agent A traces upstream lot, agent B enumerates affected customers, agent C drafts regulator communication, all concurrent, merge at the HITL gate.

3. Hierarchical. An orchestrator agent plans the work and dispatches to specialist agents, receiving their outputs back. Used for complex decisions where the plan itself requires reasoning — e.g., in a disruption-recovery scenario, the orchestrator chooses which specialist to consult based on the disruption type.

4. Feedback loop. An agent produces output, an evaluator agent assesses it, and either accepts or sends back for refinement. Used when quality thresholds matter — agent drafts, evaluator reviews, loop until quality threshold or iteration limit.

Real orchestrations compose these. An APEX recall orchestration is typically parallel (trace + enumerate + draft concurrent) inside a sequential (detect → parallel-work → HITL → execute) inside a hierarchical (orchestrator coordinating the whole).

6.9.3 The 47 APEX orchestration patterns

APEX's internal accelerator library contains 47 reusable orchestration patterns — the productised IP that Deloitte applies across engagements. These 47 patterns are not 47 different workflow implementations; they are 47 archetypes from which specific orchestrations are composed.

Examples of the 47 archetypes:

  • "Anomaly-detection + disposition + HITL-approval + action"
  • "Multi-source identity-resolution with confidence-weighted merge"
  • "Pattern-match on event cluster → regulatory-scope compute → multi-stakeholder notification"
  • "Predictive-trigger + workflow-aware scheduling + resource confirmation"
  • "Classification-change propagation across dependent services"
  • "Cross-Practice entity federation with trust-boundary enforcement"

Each archetype specifies the primitive patterns it uses, the general step-shape, the typical HITL insertion points, the classification handling, and the audit-row emission pattern. When Deloitte delivers a Practice-specific orchestration — say, an RC recall workflow — the implementation starts from the relevant archetype(s) and specialises to the Practice's semantic model and SOR landscape.

Why 47? The number is a consequence of how decisions actually cluster at enterprise scale. Seven Practices × roughly seven decision-shape categories per Practice ≈ 47 distinct archetypes that, together, cover the vast majority of real operational decisions. Rare edge-case decisions get one-off treatment; the 47 archetypes cover the rest.

This is the acceleration kernel for orchestration. A Practice-specific orchestration ships in weeks-to-months because it specialises an existing archetype, not because someone invents a new workflow pattern from scratch.

6.9.4 The orchestration manifest — how patterns become governable

Every APEX orchestration has a manifest — a Git-versioned declarative artifact that defines:

  • Steps — which agents participate, in what order, under which pattern
  • Tool bindings — the MCP tools each step may invoke
  • HITL insertion points — which step boundaries require human approval, and who approves
  • Classification policy — the trust envelope applied at each step boundary
  • Audit emission — per-step audit-row fields and format
  • Failure modes — step-failure behavior (retry, skip, escalate, halt)
  • Evaluation hooks — what gets measured, at which step, by which evaluator
  • Version — orchestration manifest version for agent pinning

The manifest is the governance artifact. An orchestration without a manifest is an undocumented multi-agent workflow — which means it cannot be audited, versioned, or safely evolved. APEX's production discipline does not permit agents to compose informally; every composition is manifest-declared.

6.9.5 HITL gates as orchestration checkpoints

Human-in-the-loop gates are not afterthoughts in APEX orchestration — they are first-class checkpoints specified in the manifest. Gate placement is a design decision that balances:

  • Regulatory requirements — some decisions MUST have human approval (FDA recall initiation, clinical-medication changes, PSPS de-energisation)
  • Reversibility cost — gates before irreversible actions (delete, pay, dispatch, notify)
  • Client policy — organisational rules about who approves what
  • Autonomy maturity — as clients build confidence, selective gates can become notification-only

Gate types in APEX orchestrations:

  • Hard gate — orchestration pauses; cannot proceed without explicit approval
  • Soft gate — orchestration continues after acknowledgement; can be deferred
  • Policy gate — automatic approval against a codified policy, but reviewable after the fact
  • Escalation gate — human approver can escalate to higher authority

A parallel orchestration might have multiple gates firing concurrently (different approvers for different parallel branches). A hierarchical orchestration has gates at both the orchestrator level (strategic approval) and specialist level (execution approval). Gate design reflects the orchestration's shape.

6.9.6 How orchestration ties back to APEX — the acceleration story

Orchestration is the third acceleration kernel (alongside canonical schema from §1.6 and the manifest framework). The acceleration math:

Without pattern library. Each Practice-specific workflow is designed from scratch. The designer must decide what should be sequential vs parallel, where to put HITL gates, how to emit audit rows, how to handle failures. Some of these decisions are correct; many are subtly wrong and reveal themselves only in production. Each workflow takes weeks of design before implementation begins.

With 47 pattern archetypes. The designer starts from an archetype that has been stress-tested across many prior engagements. Pattern selection takes hours, not weeks. Specialisation to the Practice takes weeks, not months. Implementation proceeds directly.

Beyond per-workflow savings, the pattern library creates compositional leverage. A new business need often maps to combining existing patterns rather than designing a new one. The second recall-adjacent workflow at a client reuses the recall archetype. The third cross-shift coordination workflow reuses the coordination archetype. The tenth use case deploys in weeks because it combines patterns already proven.

This compounding is why APEX commits to 9–12 month Wave 2 timelines. The first orchestration takes longer; the fifth and beyond deploy fast because orchestration-reasoning is done.

6.9.7 Concrete example 1 — RC recall orchestration (Store 100 Event 05)

Walking through the orchestration that executed during the FDA Class II infant formula recall at Store 100 (§16.13.6) exposes how the primitive patterns compose:

Top-level shape: hierarchical. A recall-orchestrator agent receives the FDA notice, plans the recall execution, dispatches specialist agents, collects their outputs, routes to HITL, then orchestrates execution.

Inside the "plan phase": parallel. Specialists fire concurrently:

  • Lot-trace agent (walks upstream from lot to shipment to supplier)
  • Inventory-enumeration agent (quantifies on-shelf, backroom, and sold units)
  • Customer-identification agent (joins sold-unit transactions to loyalty members)
  • Quarantine-planning agent (designates quarantine bay, assigns pull team)
  • Communication-draft agent (produces bilingual customer notification)
  • POS-rule agent (posts register-level hold)
  • Regulatory-trail agent (assembles FSMA 204 evidence package)

Merge point: HITL gate. Store operations lead (Marisol) receives the consolidated disposition package. Hard gate — execution blocked pending approval.

Post-approval: sequential. Execute quarantine → send customer notifications (after Corporate Comms pre-release review) → post POS rules → emit regulator-ready evidence package.

Archetype used: "regulatory-triggered multi-stakeholder response with mandatory HITL and audit-preservation." One of the 47 archetypes. Specialised here to FDA recall semantics; the same archetype specialises to HLS Provider recall workflows, to AXLE framework recall workflows via WLML, to CVML connected-vehicle campaigns, and others.

Manifest fields specific to this orchestration: FDA-specific trigger signature, FSMA-204 audit-preservation requirements, retail-specific customer notification templates, Purview classifications for FDA-notice + customer-PII + SupplierConfidential. All specialisation; the skeleton is the archetype.

6.9.8 Concrete example 2 — HLS sepsis early-warning (Hospital §10.9.4)

Top-level shape: feedback loop. A monitor agent continuously evaluates vital-sign + medication + lab streams. A classification agent scores sepsis risk. An evaluator agent validates the score against historical cases. If confidence insufficient, the loop continues. If confidence sufficient and threshold crossed, exit the loop into action.

Inside the evaluator phase: hierarchical. An orchestrator evaluator may dispatch to:

  • Pattern-library specialist (match against known sepsis-trajectory signatures)
  • Differential-diagnosis specialist (consider alternative explanations — dehydration, medication effects)
  • Severity-classifier specialist (SIRS, severe sepsis, septic shock)

Exit from loop: sequential with HITL. Alert generation → HITL gate (Charge Nurse Raj receives alert with pattern explanation) → bedside assessment → escalation (if Raj concurs) to hospitalist → sepsis-bundle initiation.

Archetype used: "continuous-monitoring + pattern-match + HITL-expert-confirmation + protocol-initiation." Another of the 47 archetypes. Specialised for sepsis; the same archetype serves cardiac-arrest prediction, patient-deterioration scoring, fall-risk monitoring, and delirium detection.

The feedback loop matters specifically for clinical decisions because false-positive alerts fatigue clinicians and lose trust. The evaluator agent's job is to ensure only high-confidence alerts fire. This discipline is encoded in the archetype; specialisation tunes the threshold.

6.9.9 Orchestration's relationship to the envelopes

The envelope framework from §2.2A intersects orchestration at every level:

  • Commercial envelope — orchestrations are the delivery unit that drives effort estimation. Wave 2 pricing = sum of orchestration-specialisation effort + agent-authoring effort + testing + deployment.
  • Scope envelope — which orchestrations are in scope defines the service selection in the SOW.
  • Data envelope — orchestrations declare which Gold views they consume; the union is the service's data envelope.
  • Schema envelope — the orchestration's data envelope is expressed in terms of canonical schema entities. No canonical schema → no coherent orchestration.
  • Trust envelope — gates, classifications, identity scopes are all manifest-declared per orchestration step.

A seller can honestly describe Wave 2 pricing as "a specific count of orchestration patterns specialised for your Practice semantic model, each with gate-placement design, classification enforcement, and audit-row emission." That framing resists the "why so expensive" challenge because the work is countable.

6.9.10 Architect conversation template

When an architect asks how agents compose into services, the rehearsed explanation:

  1. "Agents don't act in isolation in production." State this upfront.
  2. "They compose into orchestrations — multi-agent workflows with manifest governance." Introduce the term.
  3. "Every orchestration is built from four primitive patterns — sequential, parallel, hierarchical, feedback-loop — and most combine two or three." Show the diagram.
  4. "APEX's internal accelerator includes 47 reusable orchestration archetypes that cover the vast majority of decision patterns we see across our seven Practices." Quantify.
  5. "When we deliver a Practice-specific workflow, we specialise an archetype rather than designing from scratch. That's why the second and third orchestrations in your Wave 2 deploy faster than the first." Name the acceleration.
  6. "Every orchestration has a Git-versioned manifest that specifies the steps, HITL gates, classifications, and audit behavior. That's what makes the system governable." Operational maturity.
  7. "For the complete catalog of orchestrations per schema, Appendix T lists approximately 150 specific orchestrations with their triggers, data used, actions invoked, and HITL patterns. We reference them by ID in Wave 1 envisioning." Point to the catalog.

This framework converts abstract "AI does the work" conversations into architect-credible specificity — at the level of architecture any senior technologist can evaluate.

6.10 The APEX Audit Row — How Agents Emit Audit and How Orchestrations Compose It

The audit row is the single most important governance artifact APEX produces. Every seller has heard it mentioned; fewer can describe what it actually contains and how it's produced. This section fills that gap. It lives in Chapter 6 because the agent runtime (Foundry) is where the audit row is emitted; §8.8 covers where it is stored, retained, and presented to auditors (Purview's domain).

6.10.1 What the audit row is (and isn't)

The APEX audit row is not a log line. It is a structured, tamper-evident, signed record of a decision — the unit of work an agent performs. A log line records "something happened"; an audit row records "this agent, reasoning this way, over this data, under this policy, with this human oversight, produced this decision, which drove this downstream effect."

The operational test: an APEX audit row is the minimum artifact a regulator, auditor, or post-incident forensic review needs to reconstruct and evaluate the decision. If the row is sufficient to that test, it is an APEX audit row. If it isn't, it's a log line.

6.10.2 Audit row anatomy — the 14 required fields

Every APEX agent emits an audit row with at least these fields. Deloitte's delivery standard enforces them through the manifest schema:

FieldContent
trace_idUUID binding every step of an orchestration into one forensic thread
decision_idUUID of this specific agent decision
agent_idEntra Agent ID of the emitting agent
invoking_identityEntra principal (user or upstream agent) that invoked this agent
manifest_versionGit SHA of the orchestration manifest version in effect
policy_versionGit SHA of the Purview/DLP/HITL policy bundle in effect
model_versionSpecific Foundry-deployed model (e.g., gpt-4.1-2025-xx-xx) including any fine-tune ref
prompt_versionGit SHA of the system-prompt / few-shot bundle
inputs_refContent-hash reference to the input payload (actual data stored in Gold view snapshot)
tools_calledOrdered list of (mcp_tool_id, tool_version, parameters_hash, result_hash) tuples
reasoning_trace_refReference to the captured reasoning trace (redacted per DLP)
decision_outputStructured output the agent produced
hitl_statusOne of {none, pending, approved, modified, rejected, overridden} with approver identity + timestamp
downstream_effect_refReference to the action-tool call or write-back that resulted (null if advisory)

Three additional optional fields frequently carried: cost_attribution (PTU / token cost), sensitivity_label_propagation (labels inherited from inputs), confidence_score (where applicable).

6.10.3 How each agent emits the row

Every APEX agent's manifest carries an audit_emit section that specifies what the agent must capture. The Foundry runtime enforces emission — an agent that fails to emit a row cannot write its output downstream; the invocation is quarantined. This is not opt-in logging. It is a contractual gate in the runtime.

The emission path on each agent invocation:

  1. Pre-invocation. Foundry resolves manifest, policy, prompt, and model versions. Stamps them on the row-in-progress.
  2. Tool calls. Each MCP tool invocation produces a (tool_id, version, params_hash, result_hash) entry. The actual parameters and results are content-addressed into an immutable store; the row carries the hashes.
  3. Reasoning capture. The model's reasoning trace (where the model produces one) is captured, DLP-scanned against the propagated sensitivity labels, and stored by reference. Sensitive tokens never appear inline in the row.
  4. Decision output. The structured output is validated against the manifest's output schema and stored.
  5. HITL gate. If a gate fires, the row is marked hitl_status=pending and paused until a Teams card / Copilot Studio action / dashboard approval returns.
  6. Downstream effect. If the decision drives an action (MCP action tool, system write, communication), the action's own audit row is cross-referenced via downstream_effect_ref and trace_id.
  7. Seal. The row is signed, hashed, and written to the immutable audit store (see §8.8).

6.10.4 Reasoning-trace capture — what actually gets stored

Reasoning traces are the part of the audit row most often misunderstood. What gets captured is not the raw chain-of-thought text (which may contain PHI, PCI, trade-secret, or hallucinated content). What gets captured is:

  • Tool-call sequence — verifiable and high-value for forensic review.
  • Decision justification — a constrained, post-reasoning summary the model is instructed to produce in structured form.
  • Cited-evidence pointers — which Gold-view records / documents the decision references, by content hash.
  • Model confidence or uncertainty signal — where the model or a downstream classifier produces one.

The raw internal reasoning (where available from the model) is captured separately into a restricted store with stricter access controls — accessible only for incident investigation by authorized roles. This separation is deliberate: raw traces can contain sensitive echoes of input data that DLP should not expose to general audit-review users.

6.10.5 How orchestrations compose audit rows

An orchestration is a composition of agents. Its audit artifact is a composite audit row — a parent record that references every participating agent's row through the shared trace_id.

The composite row adds orchestration-specific fields:

FieldContent
orchestration_idWhich orchestration (e.g., RC-E2E-09-OR-05 lot-trace-recall) fired
archetype_idWhich of the 47 archetypes this orchestration specializes
triggerWhat fired the orchestration (event, user action, schedule)
participating_agentsOrdered list of agent decision_ids with their trace_id join
orchestration_outcomeFinal composite result
latency_breakdownPer-step wall-clock
hitl_gates_firedOrdered list of HITL events
policy_exceptionsAny policy-engine deferrals or escalations

The pattern: every agent emits its own row; the orchestration emits a wrapping row that cross-references them. An auditor who wants to reconstruct a recall event starts at the orchestration's composite row and walks to each participating agent's row; each agent's row walks to its MCP tool calls; each tool call walks to Purview-registered Gold view versions.

6.10.6 Cross-agent correlation — the trace_id discipline

All agents in an orchestration inherit the same trace_id. This is the forensic thread. A trace_id carries across:

  • Synchronous agent calls (parallel, sequential, hierarchical patterns)
  • Asynchronous handoffs (agent queues up work for a downstream agent)
  • HITL gate pauses and resumes
  • Retries and alternate-path executions
  • Action-tool invocations against external systems

Any audit row not carrying a trace_id is a bug. Foundry's runtime rejects emission of audit rows without one.

6.10.7 Version stamps — the three-version rule

Every APEX audit row carries three Git-versioned stamps: manifest_version, policy_version, prompt_version. A regulator asking "under what rules was this decision made on April 15, 2026?" gets a precise answer:

  • Check the decision_id.
  • Resolve the three SHAs.
  • Check out each SHA from the Git repository that stores the versioned artifacts.
  • Read the exact manifest, exact policy bundle, exact prompt that was in effect.

No "we think this was the policy at the time." No reconstruction from change logs. The bytes of the governing artifacts are immutably pinned per decision.

6.10.8 Audit-aware tool design — the MCP contract

Each MCP tool participates in the audit row by contract:

  • Tool version is stamped. Tools are immutable by version; a behavior change gets a new version string.
  • Parameter hashes are emitted. The agent does not need to expose the params directly; the hash lets an auditor verify later what was actually sent.
  • Result hashes are emitted. Same rationale on the output side.
  • Sensitivity labels propagate. The label on the Gold view backing the tool flows into the audit row, which downstream DLP consumes.
  • Identity is scoped. The tool enforces the invoking agent's scope (unit, region, plan, program, etc.); unauthorized scopes fail fast and the failure is itself audit-rowed.

See Appendix H for the full MCP tool-binding pattern; audit emission is a first-class requirement of every tool in the APEX catalog.

6.10.9 HITL-decision capture

When a HITL gate fires, the audit row captures:

  • The approving / rejecting / modifying identity (Entra principal).
  • The decision timestamp and latency (how long did it wait).
  • The modification (if the human altered the agent's recommendation — the delta is captured).
  • The justification (optional but strongly encouraged free-text the human provides).
  • The channel (Teams card, Copilot Studio, dashboard, mobile app).

Over time, the HITL-decision ledger becomes a training corpus: patterns in human modifications feed the next version of the agent's prompt/policy. This is how Deloitte's delivery improves the service quarter over quarter without retraining the foundation model.

6.10.10 What the CFO, CCO, and CISO each get from the audit row

RoleWhat they pull from the audit row
CFOdownstream_effect_ref → dollar impact; cost_attribution → agent operating cost per decision; net ROI traceable decision-by-decision
CCO / Chief Compliancepolicy_version + hitl_status + sensitivity_label_propagation → defensible evidence that policy was followed
CISOinvoking_identity + agent_id + tools_called → who acted, what tools ran, from which identity; correlates to Entra risk signals
Chief Data Officerinputs_ref + Purview lineage → full upstream provenance of every input
Chief Audit Executive / external auditorThe full row + three version stamps → sufficient to reconstruct decisions retrospectively

6.10.11 What makes this meaningfully different from "logs"

Three differences that matter:

  1. Structure-first. Logs are text; audit rows are typed records validated against a schema at emission time.
  2. Version-pinned. Logs describe what happened; audit rows additionally pin the exact rules that governed what happened.
  3. Human-decision inclusion. Logs record machine actions; audit rows record the human's participation (approve / modify / reject / override) with the same rigor as the machine's.

6.10.12 Runtime Addendum — cost + safety fields

Addendum update (v1.5)

The typed audit row in §6.10 was extended in the Runtime Addendum with two additional fields to reflect the Runtime Plane (Chapter 5A) and the Cost envelope (§2.2A.2.6). All other audit row fields remain unchanged. These two fields become the sellable answer to "what does it cost to run?" and "what about hallucinations?" — both answers flow from a SQL query against the ledger.

FieldSchemaPopulated by / purpose
cost_per_decision{tokens, fabric_cu, usd}Model Gateway (APIM, §5A.2) at decision write time. Enables per-service P&L queries and per-tenant cost allocation.
safety_verdict{content_safety, prompt_shield, groundedness}Content Safety, Prompt Shields, Groundedness Detection (§5A.3) at the input / output boundaries. Enables "did we check?" queries to return evidence.

Both fields are stamped by the Foundry runtime at emission time — they are not opt-in. An agent that disables cost metering or skips safety inspection cannot pass the emission gate. This is a contractual runtime property, not a policy overlay.

This is why regulators recognize APEX audit rows as evidentiary artifacts, and why the audit row is the single most-cited artifact in APEX's Independence defensibility. See §8.8 for storage, retention, tamper-evidence, and regulatory mapping.

6.11 Microsoft Orchestrator Agent Types — Semantic Kernel, Copilot Studio, Agent365 (E7)

Microsoft ships three distinct orchestrator runtimes for agentic AI, each with a different authoring model, deployment target, governance posture, and scale profile. A credible architect conversation in 2026 requires knowing when to use which — and, more importantly, knowing that APEX engagements at scale use all three composed together, not one in isolation. This section is the deep dive.

6.11.1 The three runtimes at a glance

RuntimeTypeTarget userDeploymentAPEX fit
Semantic KernelCode-first SDKDevelopersAzure compute (App Service / Container Apps / AKS / Foundry Agent Service)Custom IP-sensitive orchestrations
Copilot StudioLow-code + pro-codeMakers + developersMicrosoft cloud (Power Platform managed)Conversational front-end, M365 surface
Agent365 (E7)Enterprise agent platformIT admins + makersMicrosoft 365 tenantGoverned workforce agents at enterprise scale

None of the three is a replacement for the others. They compose vertically: Semantic Kernel at the core, Copilot Studio at the surface, Agent365 as the governance + identity layer.

6.11.2 Semantic Kernel — the code-first core

What it is. Microsoft's open-source agent SDK available in .NET, Python, and Java. Provides a composable kernel abstraction, plugin system, planners, memory stores, filters, prompt templating, and (as of the 1.0+ Agent Framework) first-class multi-agent orchestration primitives.

Key building blocks.

  • Kernel — the core runtime binding a model (ChatCompletion service pointing at Azure OpenAI, Foundry-hosted Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) to registered plugins, memory, and filters.
  • Plugins — the function-calling surface. Each plugin function is a callable the agent can invoke with structured parameters. In APEX, plugins wrap MCP tools, SOR APIs, and Fabric Gold-view queries.
  • Planners — produce goal-directed multi-step plans from a natural-language goal. Used for dynamic orchestrations where the plan itself requires reasoning.
  • Agent Framework — the 1.0+ abstraction that promotes an individual kernel + instructions + tools into a first-class "Agent" that can be composed with other agents.
  • Orchestration primitives — Sequential, Concurrent, GroupChat, Handoff, Magentic (the SK-native multi-agent coordination patterns).
  • Memory & Vector stores — ephemeral conversation memory + persistent vector-backed semantic memory. (APEX's durable agent memory is file-first — memory/MEMORY.md curated by the operator per §6.12.2. Vector stores support unstructured-content retrieval; they are not the durable memory layer.)
  • Filters — pre/post hooks on function calls, prompts, and outputs. Where APEX inserts audit-row emission, PII scrubbing, and classification propagation.
  • Prompt templates — Handlebars/Jinja-style parameterized prompts versioned in Git.

How it's built.

  1. Developer writes the kernel bootstrap in .NET/Python/Java: chat-completion service, model deployment reference, execution settings.
  2. Plugins registered — either from attribute-decorated classes (code-first) or imported from OpenAPI specs.
  3. Prompt templates and instructions stored as files alongside the code, Git-versioned.
  4. Agents defined with role, instructions, allowed plugins, and execution constraints.
  5. Orchestrations composed — the Sequential / Concurrent / Handoff / GroupChat / Magentic orchestrator wraps multiple agents.
  6. Filters registered for audit emission, DLP, classification propagation.

How it's deployed.

  • As Azure App Service, Azure Container Apps, or AKS workload — standard .NET/Python deployment pipelines.
  • Alternatively wrapped in Foundry Agent Service for Microsoft-managed runtime (recommended for enterprise scale; lifts operational burden).
  • Identity via managed identity or Entra Agent ID (see Appendix K).
  • Endpoints exposed via APIM + private-endpoint routing.

How it's managed.

  • CI/CD via Azure DevOps / GitHub Actions / GitLab CI — standard code pipeline.
  • Versioning through Git commit SHAs (the same SHAs that pin the manifest, policy, and prompt per §6.10).
  • Observability through Application Insights + OpenTelemetry; Foundry dashboards for agent-specific views.
  • Evaluation through Foundry's Agent Evaluation SDK + custom eval harnesses.
  • Canary rollout via deployment slots or feature flags.

Subagent calling — the deep dive.

SK's Agent Framework exposes multiple orchestrator classes, each enforcing a distinct composition pattern:

  • SequentialOrchestration. Agent A produces output → passed as input to Agent B → passed to Agent C. Used for strict pipeline decisions (detect → classify → disposition → notify). Trace_id binds all three; each agent emits its own audit row; the orchestration emits a wrapping composite row per §6.10.5.
  • ConcurrentOrchestration. A dispatcher agent fans out to multiple specialist agents in parallel; their outputs are merged by a reducer. Used when concurrent independent investigations can proceed — e.g., "query three SORs simultaneously for a lot-trace event." Parallel trace_ids roll up to the parent.
  • GroupChatOrchestration. Multiple agents participate in a structured chat, taking turns by role. A manager agent (or round-robin policy) governs turn-taking. Used for adversarial review patterns — e.g., "a drafter agent produces recommendation; a reviewer agent critiques; a synthesizer produces final."
  • HandoffOrchestration. One agent decides when to pass control to another based on its internal reasoning — e.g., a triage agent classifies the incoming message and routes to billing, scheduling, or clinical agents. Handoffs preserve conversation context + trace_id.
  • MagenticOrchestration. A supervisor agent plans a multi-step workflow dynamically, dispatching to specialist agents as the plan evolves. Used for complex reasoning where the plan itself is emergent. This is SK's closest pattern to a hierarchical orchestration (Appendix T archetype families F3, F7, F10).

Subagent invocation mechanics. A subagent call in SK resolves through the orchestrator's routing, with each hop:

  1. Parent agent completes its reasoning step.
  2. Orchestrator selects the next agent (per pattern rules).
  3. Context object (conversation history, kernel args, classification labels) is forwarded.
  4. Audit filter fires on entry — records the handoff in the audit row.
  5. Subagent executes with full tool access defined in its own plugin list.
  6. Subagent output returns to the orchestrator.
  7. Audit filter fires on exit — records output hash, sensitivity label, latency.
  8. Orchestrator decides next step (continue, handoff again, terminate).

Strengths for APEX.

  • Maximum control — Practice-specific orchestrations with deep domain logic are built in code.
  • Deep Foundry and Azure OpenAI integration; first-class support for Anthropic Claude and Meta Llama in Foundry.
  • Version-pinnable in Git — fits APEX's three-version-stamp discipline (§6.10.7).
  • Filter model is the natural APEX audit-emission insertion point.
  • Works with any model across Practices.

When to use SK in an APEX engagement.

  • Custom Practice-specific orchestrations with complex domain logic (RC-E2E-03 assortment + pricing with elasticity reasoning; HLS clinical-decision-support with guideline adherence).
  • Agents that call MCP tools with complex parameter shaping.
  • Reasoning-heavy workloads where the agent code is Deloitte IP.
  • Any orchestration with IP-sensitive prompt design that should not leave Deloitte-managed code.

6.11.3 Copilot Studio — the experience-surface platform

What it is. Microsoft's low-code (with pro-code extension) platform for authoring custom Copilots and agentic applications that surface inside Microsoft 365, Teams, web, mobile, and voice channels. Successor to Power Virtual Agents; now the backbone of the M365 Copilot customization story.

Key capabilities.

  • Topic authoring — intent triggers + response flows; hybrid of rule-based and generative.
  • Generative orchestration — an AI-driven runtime that selects topics, tools, and knowledge sources dynamically from instructions (no explicit flow authoring).
  • Actions — Power Automate Cloud Flows triggered by the agent; Dataverse writes; API calls.
  • Knowledge sources — SharePoint, websites, Fabric lakehouse, Dataverse, files, public web, enterprise graph.
  • Plugins — call external agents, external APIs, or other Copilots (including Foundry-hosted SK agents).
  • Agent Flows — multi-step agentic workflows within the Copilot Studio environment.
  • Channels — Teams, web chat embed, mobile, M365 Copilot surfaces, voice via Azure Communication Services.
  • Authentication options — anonymous, Entra, MSA, external SSO.

How it's built.

  • Maker portal (web UI) provides visual authoring.
  • Topic designer for declarative intent → response flows.
  • Generative orchestrator — author writes an instruction ("You are a store-ops assistant; use these knowledge sources; invoke these plugins when users ask about inventory"); runtime AI decides the flow.
  • Plugins registered from AI Hub, API spec imports (OpenAPI / Swagger), or custom connector references.
  • Knowledge sources configured by URL / SharePoint site / Fabric lakehouse.
  • Pro-code extension via Copilot Studio Kit (SDK) for advanced behaviors and Power Fx custom logic.

How it's deployed.

  • Maker publishes to a Power Platform environment (dev/test/prod per standard ALM).
  • Solution-packaged for cross-environment deployment.
  • Published to channels (Teams org-wide / specific users, web embed, M365 Copilot custom-copilot registration, API).
  • Managed Environments provide tenant-level governance.

How it's managed.

  • Power Platform ALM — solutions, environments, deployment pipelines.
  • Copilot Studio Analytics — conversation volumes, completion rates, escalations to human, customer satisfaction.
  • Admin Center — DLP policies (what connectors a maker can use), environment strategy, managed environments, tenant isolation.
  • Purview compliance — sensitivity labels propagate through Copilot Studio; DLP enforced.

Subagent calling — the deep dive.

Copilot Studio invokes subagents through four distinct mechanisms:

  1. Plugins. A plugin encapsulates an external capability — typically an API, another agent endpoint, or a Foundry/SK agent. The Copilot Studio agent decides to call a plugin based on instruction + user utterance; generative orchestrator handles parameter extraction from conversation context.
  2. Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. Copilot Studio can call other Copilot Studio agents, Foundry agents, or SK agents that expose an A2A-compliant endpoint. A2A preserves delegation identity (user's Entra token flows through); trace_id is propagated in the A2A call headers.
  3. Connectors. The Power Platform connector catalog (~1,400 connectors) is a subagent-adjacent primitive — a connector invocation is effectively a capability call. Used for SaaS integrations (Salesforce, ServiceNow, SAP, etc.).
  4. Actions / Power Automate flows. A flow may itself orchestrate multiple subsequent calls, forming a lightweight orchestration within Power Platform.

Invocation mechanics for a Copilot Studio → SK subagent call.

  1. User utters "show me markdown cadence for personal care this week" in a Teams-embedded Copilot Studio agent.
  2. Generative orchestrator maps the utterance to the Practice service + plugin.
  3. Plugin is a registered A2A endpoint to an SK-hosted APEX orchestration (RC-TTP-07 Markdown).
  4. Copilot Studio calls the SK endpoint with user delegation token (Entra OBO — on-behalf-of flow).
  5. SK orchestration plans, dispatches to MarkdownCadenceAgent + ElasticityReasoningAgent + SellThroughAgent concurrently.
  6. Each subagent calls MCP tools that resolve Fabric Gold views.
  7. SK returns the composed recommendation; audit rows emitted.
  8. Copilot Studio renders the response in Teams; HITL gate on merchant-approval fires if required.
  9. Trace_id spans all hops — Teams → Copilot Studio → SK → subagents → MCP tools.

Strengths for APEX.

  • Fastest path from APEX agent to worker-facing surface.
  • Native M365 / Teams integration — no custom UI.
  • Citizen-developer accessible; key for scaling the agent catalog beyond Deloitte's delivery bench.
  • Governance through Power Platform admin + Purview.
  • Handles channel complexity (Teams, web, mobile, voice) without custom code.

When to use Copilot Studio in an APEX engagement.

  • Conversational front-end for APEX services.
  • M365 Copilot custom-copilot surfacing.
  • Teams-embedded HITL gates (merchant / clinician / operator approvals).
  • Store-associate / clinical-staff / field-worker assistants.
  • Voice channel deployment via ACS.

6.11.4 Agent365 (E7) — the enterprise agent platform

What it is. Microsoft's newest enterprise agent platform, launching under the Microsoft 365 E7 licensing tier. Positions agents as first-class workforce principals with:

  • Entra Agent ID as first-class identity (not just a managed service principal).
  • M365 Copilot as the default surface.
  • Purview governance, DLP, sensitivity labels applied natively.
  • Compliance Manager assessments at the agent level.
  • Agent Monitor — a central admin console for the tenant's agent population.
  • Agent Builder — enterprise-grade agent authoring with configuration-first UX.
  • Marketplace of pre-built agents (Microsoft, ISV, Deloitte-authored).
  • Unified M365 audit integration.

Key capabilities.

  • Per-agent Entra Agent ID — each agent is a first-class identity with lifecycle, conditional access, audit scope.
  • Scope binding — agents are scoped to user context, tenant context, or data context as declared in the agent manifest.
  • Classification propagation — sensitivity labels from inputs flow to agent outputs automatically.
  • Conditional access for agents — Entra policies restrict when / where / how an agent can be invoked.
  • Unified audit — agent activity merges into the M365 compliance audit log.
  • Cost attribution — per-user / per-department cost visibility for agent usage.
  • Managed lifecycle — deployment, updates, retirement handled through admin console.
  • SLA + monitoring — enterprise-grade observability and availability.

How it's built.

  • Agent Builder in M365 admin center — configuration-first authoring with pro-code hooks.
  • Import existing agents from Copilot Studio or wrap SK-hosted orchestrations.
  • Purview sensitivity labels applied at agent registration.
  • Entra Agent ID auto-provisioned at publish time.
  • Scope declaration in manifest (user-delegated / app-delegated / data-scoped).
  • Publisher attestation (vendor / internal / Deloitte-authored).

How it's deployed.

  • Published to tenant's agent catalog.
  • User / group assignments handled like M365 app licenses (Entra license-group model).
  • Rollout rings — pilot → specific departments → enterprise.
  • Versioned — each agent publish is a new immutable version; previous versions retained per retention policy.

How it's managed.

  • Agent Monitor dashboard — single admin pane for the tenant's agent fleet.
  • M365 compliance center integration — agent activity feeds the same eDiscovery, retention, and legal-hold pipelines as user activity.
  • Purview DLP policies apply natively to agent outputs.
  • Retirement workflow — agents can be retired with grace periods; users redirected to successor agents.
  • Cost attribution — usage metered per agent; rolled up to department or cost center.

Subagent calling — the deep dive.

Agent365 subagent orchestration routes through the Agent Orchestration Hub — a tenant-level layer that:

  1. Federates calls across agents regardless of underlying runtime (SK, Copilot Studio, Foundry custom, third-party MCP endpoints).
  2. Inherits parent delegation context — a subagent called from a user-delegated parent inherits the same user token with scope-preserved authorization.
  3. Propagates classification labels automatically — a sensitivity label on an input flows to every downstream subagent and every resulting output.
  4. Emits correlated audit rows at both parent and subagent level, joined by trace_id and surfaced in unified M365 audit.
  5. Enforces governance on every hop — conditional access, DLP, sensitivity-aware routing, agent-class-specific retention.
  6. Supports cross-runtime chains — an Agent365-registered Copilot Studio agent can call an Agent365-registered SK agent through the Hub; the Hub is the trust boundary.

Invocation mechanics for an Agent365 parent → Agent365 subagent call.

  1. User invokes parent agent through M365 Copilot (Teams / Word / Outlook / Agent365 app).
  2. Entra OBO issues a delegation token scoped to the parent agent's allowed resources.
  3. Parent agent's runtime (SK or Copilot Studio or bespoke) runs in Agent365 container.
  4. Parent decides to call a subagent; invocation routes through the Hub.
  5. Hub validates: is the subagent in the tenant's catalog? Does the parent have authorization to call it? Does the current classification of the context permit the call?
  6. Hub issues a scoped delegation to the subagent (preserving user context, narrowed scope if configured).
  7. Subagent executes; tool calls, MCP interactions, Fabric Gold views all inherit the scoped identity.
  8. Subagent output flows back through Hub; classification labels applied; audit rows emitted.
  9. Parent receives response; any HITL gates in Agent365 manifest fire.
  10. Final response rendered to user; unified audit records every hop.

Strengths for APEX.

  • Ready-to-use governance — fastest path to enterprise-grade compliance.
  • Licensed via M365 E7 — no separate Azure agent-runtime spend (simplifies CFO conversation).
  • Unified with workforce identity, M365 audit, Purview — dramatically reduces integration lift.
  • Best fit for workforce-facing agents at scale.
  • Agent Marketplace enables Deloitte-authored APEX agent templates to distribute.

When to use Agent365 in an APEX engagement.

  • Enterprise-wide workforce agent rollouts.
  • Agents that must inherit M365 user context and delegation.
  • Governance-first deployments where Purview / Entra native integration is critical.
  • Clients with E7 licensing footprint or plans to acquire E7.
  • Scenarios where centralized agent administration (Agent Monitor) drives operational efficiency.

6.11.7 How subagent calls propagate across all three — a full trace

The canonical cross-runtime invocation pattern in an APEX engagement:

  1. User action. Store associate asks the store-manager assistant in Teams: "Why is personal-care category showing margin exposure?"
  2. Copilot Studio receives. Generative orchestrator maps to the category-exposure plugin.
  3. A2A call through Agent Orchestration Hub. Copilot Studio invokes the registered APEX RC-E2E-03 Assortment & Pricing orchestration; Entra OBO carries the user's delegation.
  4. Hub validation. Agent365 Hub checks policy: is the associate's role authorized to invoke this orchestration? Is the requested category in scope? Are classification labels compatible?
  5. SK orchestration runs. MagenticOrchestration supervisor plans: needs category exposure, elasticity signals, and competitor pricing.
  6. Concurrent dispatch. Supervisor invokes CategoryExposureAgent, ElasticityReasoningAgent, CompetitorPriceAgent in parallel.
  7. MCP tool calls. Each subagent calls MCP tools resolving Fabric Gold views (e.g., vw_agent_category_exposure).
  8. Audit rows emit at every hop. Trace_id binds all — Copilot Studio hop, A2A handoff, SK orchestration, each subagent, each MCP tool call, each Fabric view access (§6.10, §8.8).
  9. Synthesizer. Supervisor merges the three subagents' outputs into a single recommendation.
  10. Response flows back. Through Hub → Copilot Studio → Teams.
  11. HITL fires if required. Merchant approval on recommended markdown cadence.
  12. Unified audit log. M365 audit consolidates every hop; Purview lineage binds every Gold-view access to the orchestration decision.

One forensic thread across three orchestrator frameworks. That is the architectural win — composition without gaps.

6.11.9 Common pitfalls

  • The all-Copilot-Studio trap. Clients attempt to build everything in Copilot Studio. Works for conversational scenarios; breaks at scale on IP protection, reasoning depth, and governance at the orchestration layer.
  • The all-Semantic-Kernel trap. Developers build deep SK agents with no workforce-facing surface. Agents are architecturally sound and operationally unreachable.
  • Ignoring Agent365. Treating Agent365 as optional — at enterprise scale, the governance it provides (Entra Agent ID, unified audit, Hub routing) is difficult to reproduce in custom orchestration.
  • Parallel disconnected stacks. Building SK agents and Copilot Studio agents in parallel without A2A integration or trace_id correlation — produces two ungoverned fleets.
  • Recommending before discovery. Prescribing a specific composition before understanding the client's existing Power Platform estate, E7 posture, and workforce-surface requirements.
