Chapter 29

Qualifying

What This Chapter Does for You
  • The MEDDPICC-adapted APEX qualification framework
  • How to qualify out early and save the pipeline
  • The five hard-gate questions
  • Independence qualification as a non-negotiable first gate

29.1 The qualification posture

Qualification is not lead-scoring. It is an explicit act of deciding whether this pursuit gets scarce Deloitte delivery capacity. Over-qualification is cheap; over-committed capacity is expensive.

29.2 The five hard-gate questions

  1. Independence — is the prospect a Deloitte audit client, and if so, is pre-clearance in place?
  2. Sponsor — is there a named, single-threaded executive sponsor with budget authority?
  3. Pain — is there a publicly committed KPI or board-level mandate that the pursuit ties to?
  4. Budget — does the prospect have Wave 1 budget in the current fiscal, or is the pursuit pending approval?
  5. Timing — does the prospect want a material outcome inside 9 months?

If three or more of these are "no" or unknown, the pursuit is not qualified. Continue qualifying, do not accelerate to proposal.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder: Question 1 is a hard gate, not a scoring input. No Independence clearance = no pursuit, regardless of the other four answers.

29.3 MEDDPICC adapted for APEX

  • Metrics — the publicly committed KPI
  • Economic buyer — sponsor with sign authority
  • Decision criteria — documented, or still forming?
  • Decision process — known gates, committees, timing?
  • Paper process — procurement approach, MSA status
  • Identify pain — tied to metrics above
  • Champion — named, coachable, at the right level
  • Competition — incumbent SI, hyperscaler alignment, platform commitments

29.4 The cost of continuing an unqualified pursuit

  • Partner time reduction on qualified pursuits
  • Delivery leader fatigue
  • Discovery budget burn without close
  • Client frustration when timelines slip

29.5 How to qualify out gracefully

  • Offer a reduced-scope engagement (paid discovery only) that matches the client's current readiness
  • Preserve the relationship; most "not now" becomes "yes" when a trigger event lands
  • Document the disqualification reason for pipeline reporting

29.6 Pre-qualification: who should be in the first meeting

A qualified meeting has the right people in the room. Before accepting a first meeting, clarify who will attend. The pattern that works:

  • Executive sponsor — the person who can sign off on Wave 1 investment
  • IT / platform representative — so Microsoft footprint and architecture questions get answered
  • Business-outcome owner — the P&L leader who owns the KPI the pursuit serves
  • Deloitte account team — the client partner and any existing relationship holders

Missing any of the first three is a signal the meeting will not produce decisions. Offer to postpone until the room is right.

29.7 First-meeting execution

Run the first meeting to three outcomes, in priority order:

  1. Establish credibility — APEX is serious, Deloitte is the right team, Independence is handled
  2. Confirm or deny the pain — does the pressure point we think we're solving actually exist for this client
  3. Qualify for Wave 1 — is this pursuit ready for a Wave 1 envisioning commitment

A meeting that achieves 1 but not 2 or 3 is still a successful meeting — it earns the next meeting. A meeting where you try for 3 before 1 or 2 often loses the relationship.

29.8 The qualification scorecard

Use a consistent scorecard across pursuits so partners and practice leaders can compare like with like:

Dimension0 (miss)1 (weak)2 (adequate)3 (strong)
IndependenceAudit client, no pre-clearanceAudit client, pre-clearance in progressAudit client, pre-clearedNot an audit client
SponsorNo named sponsorSponsor named, no budget authoritySponsor named with budgetSponsor named, budget confirmed, priority committed
PainSpeculativeDescribed, not measuredMeasured, not ownedMeasured, owned, publicly committed
BudgetNo posturePending future fiscalBudget identified, approval pendingBudget approved, in current fiscal
TimingNo window9–12 months out3–9 months outImmediate decision window

Score 12–15: proceed to Wave 1. 8–11: continue qualifying. <8: disqualify or slow down.

29.9 The qualification handoff

Once qualified, the handoff to delivery is explicit. The qualifying partner transitions the pursuit to a named delivery lead with:

  • Qualification scorecard filled in
  • Sponsor map and stakeholder notes
  • Competitive context
  • Commercial envelope estimate
  • Known risks

This handoff is a Deloitte process moment, not a client-facing one. It ensures delivery starts informed.

Key Takeaways

  • Qualification is a resource-allocation decision, not a lead-score
  • Five hard-gate questions; three "no"s disqualifies
  • Independence is the first, non-negotiable gate

Seller Actions

  1. Memorise the five hard-gate questions
  2. Qualify out gracefully — offer a smaller scope or defer
  3. Always check Independence FIRST
Chapter 30

Discovery and the Four-Week Workshop

What This Chapter Does for You
  • The structure of a four-week APEX envisioning workshop
  • What to produce by end-of-workshop
  • How to run discovery without overrunning scope
  • Common discovery failure modes

30.1 Workshop shape

A four-week envisioning is the APEX Wave 1 default. Breakdown:

  • Week 1 — current state. Data estate, pain inventory, executive interviews.
  • Week 2 — target state. Candidate service selection, architecture sketch, process re-imagining.
  • Week 3 — business case. Benefits, costs, risks, commercial envelope.
  • Week 4 — close. Executive readout, Wave 2 scope, SOW drafted.

30.2 End-of-workshop deliverables

  1. Target-state architecture (single diagram, APEX services layered on Microsoft stack)
  2. Selected services list with rationale
  3. Business case (benefits, investment, payback, risks)
  4. Wave 2 roadmap (quarter-by-quarter)
  5. Executive readout deck (12-15 slides)
  6. Draft Wave 2 SOW

30.3 Discovery guardrails

  • One sponsor interview per week; agenda locked 48 hours ahead
  • All interviews captured in a living synthesis doc; no side-channel notes
  • Architecture sketched by end of Week 2, not Week 4
  • Business case anchor: single KPI, single benefit magnitude, single payback
  • Commercial envelope anchored to benefit, not to hours

30.4 Common failure modes

  1. Scope sprawl — discovery "just one more interview" that pushes timeline
  2. Architecture paralysis — Week 2 architecture converted into Week 4 architecture with no scope decision
  3. Benefit inflation — business case padded to hit a threshold the client did not ask for
  4. Champion isolation — discovery team talks only to the champion, not adjacent decision makers
  5. Independence late — pre-clearance not confirmed until Week 3
Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder: For audit clients, pre-clearance MUST be confirmed BEFORE Week 1 kick-off. Any discovery activity that crosses Independence boundaries unapproved creates exposure.

30.5 The executive readout

Keep it concrete:

  • Slide 1: pain restated in client's language
  • Slides 2-4: target state
  • Slides 5-7: roadmap and services
  • Slides 8-10: business case
  • Slides 11-13: Wave 2 scope
  • Slides 14-15: decision ask

30.6 Workshop cast: who should be in the room

A proper envisioning workshop has ten to fifteen participants across three categories:

Client side (6–10 people):

  • Executive sponsor (at least the final read-out)
  • Business-outcome owner (P&L leader)
  • Chief Data Officer or designated data architect
  • Chief Information Security Officer or designated security architect
  • Chief Compliance Officer representative (especially HLS, ER, regulated TMT)
  • 2–3 line-of-business practitioners who will use the services
  • Change-management or adoption leader

Deloitte side (3–5 people):

  • Engagement partner
  • Delivery lead (Wave 2 owner)
  • Industry Practice lead
  • Data / architecture lead
  • Governance / Purview lead (especially regulated industries)

Microsoft side (1–2 people, optional):

  • Account technology strategist or industry specialist
  • Co-sell lead if DCIF or other funding is in play

30.7 Workshop outputs — expanded

Each of the six deliverables has expected depth:

  1. Target-state architecture — one diagram, APEX services layered on the Microsoft stack, specific to this client. 5–7 layers visible; IP-level detail elsewhere.
  2. Selected services roster — 2–3 services with: persona, KPI, baseline, target, Foundry-tier, Purview-intensity, integration dependencies.
  3. Business case — spreadsheet with: benefit model per service, risk-adjusted NPV, payback window, Wave 2 and Wave 3 extension estimates.
  4. Roadmap — quarter-by-quarter chart for Waves 2 and 3; extension points called out.
  5. Draft Wave 2 SOW — legally reviewable draft with scope, deliverables, timeline, fees, assumptions, acceptance criteria, client dependencies, commercial terms.
  6. Executive readout deck — 12–15 slides sized to the sponsor's attention budget.

30.8 When Wave 1 exposes a blocker

Not every Wave 1 concludes with a signed Wave 2. Sometimes envisioning surfaces a blocker:

  • Data-estate immaturity makes Wave 2 infeasible in the proposed window
  • Organisational-change appetite is too low for Wave 2 scale
  • Regulatory posture requires additional compliance work before Wave 2
  • The selected services do not carry enough benefit to justify Wave 2 investment

When this happens, the honest move is to close Wave 1 with a readout that says so. Propose a remediation program — often smaller and specific to the blocker — and invite the client to re-enter APEX Wave 2 when ready. Attempting to force Wave 2 into a non-viable context is a guaranteed failed engagement.

Key Takeaways

  • Four-week envisioning with explicit weekly deliverables
  • End of workshop produces six artifacts and a draft SOW
  • Guardrails prevent scope sprawl and architecture paralysis

Seller Actions

  1. Memorise the week-by-week workshop shape
  2. Template the six deliverables
  3. Confirm Independence pre-clearance BEFORE Week 1
Chapter 31

Proposal and Commercial Framing

What This Chapter Does for You
  • The two-contract commercial model in practice
  • How to frame the Deloitte services SOW
  • Pricing approach — fixed, T&M, outcome-based
  • Contract artifacts the pursuit team owns

31.1 Two-contract framing

As established in Chapter 2, APEX engagements use a two-contract commercial model:

  1. Client ↔ Microsoft — platform licenses (Fabric, Copilot, Foundry, Purview)
  2. Client ↔ Deloitte — services (advisory, implementation, managed services)

Deloitte sellers own Contract 2. We do not quote, commit, or negotiate Contract 1 on Microsoft's behalf. Microsoft sellers handle that.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder: Deloitte must not represent Microsoft licensing terms in the services SOW. Cross-reference Microsoft's contract, but keep commercial commitments separated.

31.2 The services SOW structure

  • Scope — services delivered, in-scope / out-of-scope, assumptions
  • Deliverables — concrete artifacts per phase
  • Timeline — waves with explicit gates
  • Investment — pricing structure
  • Roles — named Deloitte leaders
  • Client dependencies — platform licenses, data access, SME time
  • Commercial terms — change control, acceptance, payment

31.3 Pricing models

  • Fixed-fee Wave 1 — standard for four-week envisioning
  • T&M Wave 2 — standard for implementation
  • Outcome-linked Wave 3 — selective; requires measurable KPI and clear attribution
  • Managed-service run — recurring monthly fee post-Wave 2

Outcome-based pricing is attractive to clients but creates attribution risk. Use sparingly and only with clear baselines.

31.4 Wave-gated commercial logic

Deloitte commits to Wave 1 at SOW. Wave 2 SOW follows Wave 1 readout. Wave 3 SOW follows Wave 2 mid-point. This gates cost exposure and gives the client contractual off-ramps — reducing perceived risk.

31.5 The investment narrative

Build the investment framing as:

  1. Wave 1 investment: benefit from discovery clarity alone (avoided cost, opportunity sizing)
  2. Wave 2 investment: benefit from first service in production
  3. Wave 3 envelope: benefit from portfolio

Client sees each wave paying for itself.

31.6 Proposal cover letter pattern

Every proposal benefits from a cover letter that anchors decision criteria. The template:

"Dear [Sponsor],

Attached is our proposed Wave 1 envisioning for APEX in your [segment]. It reflects the scope and outcomes we discussed on [date] with [stakeholders].

The engagement delivers [2–3 concrete deliverables] over [duration] at a fixed fee of [$X]. Platform licensing for Microsoft Fabric, Foundry, Copilot, and Purview is a separate contract between [client] and Microsoft; your account team at Microsoft is the contact for those terms.

We have verified [Independence status: not an audit client / audit client with pre-clearance in place] and the engagement falls within approved scope.

We recommend starting [specific week] to align with [trigger: fiscal timing, regulatory deadline, peer-pressure event]. The next decision point is [specific item] by [date].

[Deloitte partner signature]"

This cover letter makes the commercial decision concrete and surfaces the two-contract framing before procurement raises it.

31.7 Handling procurement RFP cycles

Some APEX pursuits enter through a formal RFP rather than a direct-partnership conversation. RFPs reward a different discipline:

  • Read the evaluation criteria before the response; match the response to what will be scored
  • Never invent scope the RFP did not ask for; scope creep loses points
  • Always answer Independence questions explicitly; ambiguity loses points
  • Provide named delivery leads with credentials; avoid generic "Deloitte will assign"
  • Price explicitly to the RFP structure; never embed Microsoft platform costs

RFP-originated pursuits often run longer and carry lower close rates than partnership-originated. Resource accordingly.

31.8 The commercial risk register

Every proposal should include an internal commercial risk register — not shared with the client but guiding negotiation:

  • Scope-expansion risk — how much change-request budget do we expect?
  • Client-dependency risk — what SME time or data access are we assuming?
  • Independence risk — what if the audit-client status changes mid-engagement?
  • Platform risk — what if Microsoft pricing changes during the engagement?
  • Attribution risk — for value-share services, can we actually measure the outcome?
  • Adoption risk — what if the client's business-outcome team does not adopt the service?

This register should inform the pricing envelope, the acceptance criteria, and the change-control provisions.

Key Takeaways

  • Two-contract model — Deloitte owns services, Microsoft owns platform
  • Wave-gated commercial logic reduces perceived risk
  • Outcome pricing used sparingly

Seller Actions

  1. Template the services SOW structure
  2. Rehearse the wave-gated investment narrative
  3. NEVER quote Microsoft licensing on behalf of the client
Chapter 32

Competitive Positioning

What This Chapter Does for You
  • The three competitive categories APEX faces
  • Positioning against hyperscaler services arms
  • Positioning against boutique AI consultancies
  • Positioning against large SIs with their own platforms

32.1 Three competitive categories

  1. Hyperscaler services arms — AWS Pro-Serv, GCP Pro-Serv, Microsoft Industry Solutions
  2. Large SIs — Accenture, IBM Consulting, TCS, Infosys, Capgemini — some with their own AI platforms
  3. Boutique AI consultancies — specialists in vertical segments

32.2 Against hyperscaler services arms

Hyperscaler pro-serv arms have architectural depth but limited industry-vertical IP. Differentiate on:

  • Vertical depth — APEX's 45 services concentrated in 7 Practices
  • Independence-compliant delivery on audit clients
  • Outcome orientation — Deloitte sells business outcomes, hyperscaler pro-serv sells platform migrations

32.3 Against large SIs

Competing SIs often bring their own AI platforms. Differentiate on:

  • Microsoft-stack native architecture, not platform-agnostic veneer
  • Single-vendor trust boundary (Microsoft) for regulated data
  • APEX's 165+ MCP tools and 47 orchestration patterns — comparable only if competitor has invested similarly
Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder: Do not disparage competitors. Frame differentiation on what Deloitte brings, not on what competitors lack.

32.4 Against boutique AI consultancies

Boutiques are nimble and cheap. Differentiate on:

  • Scale delivery — Deloitte runs multi-hundred-consultant programs
  • Independence process and QR depth
  • Multi-year sustain and change capability
  • Acknowledge boutiques may win first pilots; position Deloitte for Wave 2 production

32.5 Architectural positioning vs alternative clouds

As established in Chapter 4, when a prospect considers AWS, GCP, IBM Cloud, OCI, or Salesforce, the position is architectural:

  • APEX is built for the Microsoft four-plane architecture (Fabric, Foundry, Copilot, Purview + Entra)
  • An equivalent pattern on alternative clouds is theoretically possible but would require re-authoring APEX
  • Position as: "APEX is native here; we would not recommend re-authoring for a different cloud; if your platform commitment is elsewhere, we are not the right partner for this workload."

This is respectful disqualification, not hostile competition.

32.6 Win-theme patterns

  • "Fastest to outcome" — when timeline is client's stated pain
  • "Lowest regulatory risk" — when compliance is client's stated pain
  • "Deepest vertical IP" — when competitor can match platform but not Practice depth
  • "Single trust boundary" — when data sensitivity is stated pain

32.7 The competitive-landscape conversation with the client

When a client openly compares Deloitte's APEX proposal to another SI's proposal, the posture is:

  1. Do not attack the competitor directly. Independence concerns aside, it sounds desperate.
  2. Ask what the client sees in the other proposal that matters to them. Listening reveals their decision criteria.
  3. Describe APEX on its own merits against those criteria. Not "we're better than X" but "here's how APEX addresses that criterion."
  4. Acknowledge genuine strengths of the alternative. Credibility is worth more than false confidence.
  5. Close on differentiation that matters to this client. Not generic; specific to their stated criteria.

32.8 When you lose

Not every pursuit wins. When you lose:

  • Debrief the client (when they will take the call); learn the real reason
  • Document in the opportunity record for future pipeline analytics
  • Preserve the relationship — your win rate improves when losers return
  • Check the Independence log — some losses are Independence-protected wins (disqualified rather than defeated)
  • Re-qualify the pipeline with the learning

Key Takeaways

  • Three competitive categories — hyperscaler pro-serv, large SIs, boutiques
  • Differentiate on vertical depth, Independence, architectural fit
  • Respect competitors; frame differentiation on Deloitte's strengths

Chapter 33

Objection Handling

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Top ten objections and rehearsed responses
  • How to handle Independence challenges
  • Handling "we already have Snowflake/Databricks"
  • Handling "why not do this ourselves"

33.1 Top ten objections and how to handle them

1. "We already have Snowflake (or Databricks) — why Fabric?"

Response: APEX is Fabric-native for good architectural reasons (OneLake addressing, Direct Lake, native Copilot grounding, Purview integration, Foundry-runtime proximity). Your existing Snowflake or Databricks investment stays — both run on Azure alongside Fabric, and both interoperate with Fabric through native mechanisms. Fabric mirrors Snowflake natively. Fabric shortcuts reach Databricks Delta tables in ADLS Gen2 without copying. Databricks keeps ML training and engineering; Snowflake keeps analytical SQL and data sharing; Fabric hosts the APEX Gold views and agent serving. The APEX services assume Fabric for the primary semantic model — re-authoring APEX on Snowflake Cortex or Databricks-only is not on the roadmap. See Appendix F for the co-existence patterns in detail.

2. "We'll build this ourselves"

Response: Acknowledge that is viable; estimate time-to-first-value honestly (typically 18-24 months for a comparable agent library). APEX Wave 2 delivers first production service in 9-12 months. If speed is a KPI the executive has committed publicly, that gap is the business case.

3. "Microsoft is too expensive"

Response: Microsoft licensing is between the client and Microsoft. We don't negotiate that. What we can commit to is ensuring the APEX services deliver measurable benefit larger than the platform investment over the first 24 months.

4. "Copilot is over-hyped"

Response: Fair. The APEX position is not Copilot-as-magic but Copilot as the user surface on Foundry-orchestrated reasoning. The value is in the agents, not the chatbot.

5. "What about data sovereignty?"

Response: Purview is the control plane, and Fabric supports regional residency. We scope sovereignty constraints in Week 1 discovery.

6. "We tried AI before and it failed"

Response: Most early AI efforts were notebook-to-nowhere. Deloitte's agent delivery is production-first: Fabric pipelines, Foundry orchestration, Purview governance, MCP tool catalog, HITL gate framework, audit-row attribution. APEX as the internal accelerator brings 280+ production-grade agents, 165+ MCP tools, and manifest-driven governance that the notebook-to-nowhere efforts lacked.

Note

Example in the field — Big Box Store Store 100. 8 operational events delivered in one shift — cold-chain write-off, DSD dispute, price integrity, phantom OOS, FDA recall, BOPIS substitution, shrink signal, customer incident. 6 events agent-resolved or decision-prepared; 2 fully autonomous; $18,400 impact protected in a single shift. See §16.13 for the production-grade narrative. This is what agent delivery looks like after the notebook-to-nowhere era ends.

7. "Your Microsoft posture conflicts with our (AWS/GCP) commitment"

Response: Acknowledged. APEX is native to Microsoft; we do not re-author it. If platform commitment is elsewhere, we are honest partners for advisory but not the right choice for APEX implementation on an alternative cloud.

8. "How do we know you won't lock us in?"

Response: APEX IP is codified in Fabric artifacts, Python/C# code, and documented agents. At exit, client retains everything deployed to their tenant.

9. "Independence — aren't you our auditor?"

Response: If Deloitte audits the client, we follow the audit-independence process with pre-clearance from the Audit Committee. Services we can and cannot perform are defined explicitly; we do not work around them.

10. "What's your implementation risk?"

Response: Wave 1 delivers a concrete envisioning deliverable. Wave 2 breaks into two-month increments. Wave 3 is incremental. Risk is bounded at each wave commitment.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder: Objection 9 is ALWAYS answered with the Independence office's language, not improvised. Rehearse exactly.

33.2 Objection-response framework

Every objection response follows a three-step pattern:

  1. Acknowledge the concern genuinely. "That's a fair question" or "I understand the concern." Do not start with "but."
  2. Reframe to the underlying decision. Surface what the client is actually trying to decide, which may differ from the surface objection.
  3. Answer with specifics. Generalities lose; specific references to services, clients, or evidence land.

33.3 Objections you should see more of

Some objections indicate a serious buyer:

  • "How does this integrate with [specific existing system]?" — they are planning integration
  • "What happens in Wave 3 when we want to extend?" — they are planning expansion
  • "How do we train our team to operate this?" — they are planning adoption
  • "What's the exit path if APEX doesn't perform?" — they are de-risking internally

When these objections come up, lean in. They are signals of a sophisticated buyer.

33.4 Objections that signal qualify-out

Other objections indicate the pursuit will not close:

  • "We want it cheaper than any precedent" — budget is not real
  • "We need to see a POC first" — program commitment is absent
  • "We haven't decided on a cloud strategy" — foundational prerequisite is missing
  • "Our audit committee is currently reviewing Deloitte's independence" — active Independence concern

These are not objections to overcome; they are signals to disqualify gracefully and return to pipeline later.

33.5 The objection post-mortem

After every deal close or loss, document the top three objections and how they were handled. Build a pursuit-specific objection library for the account team. Over time, this becomes a competitive edge — partners arrive pre-prepared for the exact objections the account has raised historically.

Key Takeaways

  • Ten rehearsed objections cover ~90% of what sellers hear
  • Independence objection always uses Independence-office language
  • Respect the objection — do not dismiss

Seller Actions

  1. Memorise all ten objection responses
  2. Rehearse the Independence objection verbatim
  3. Bring the objection responses to pursuit-team kickoff
Chapter 34

Procurement and Close

What This Chapter Does for You
  • How procurement negotiations typically run
  • What to concede and what to defend
  • Managing the contract-signing timeline
  • Closing the deal cleanly

34.1 Procurement posture

Procurement is not the adversary. Procurement is a buyer with a job to do. Treat with respect and expect them to push on price, terms, and IP.

34.2 What procurement typically pushes

  • Fixed-fee on scope procurement considers ambiguous
  • Risk allocation (liability caps, indemnification, acceptance)
  • IP ownership of deliverables
  • Benchmarking clauses against market rates
  • Service-level commitments for managed services
  • MSA alignment vs bespoke terms

34.3 What to concede

  • Reasonable scope clarifications (write them down)
  • Reasonable benchmarking for managed-service run
  • Reasonable acceptance criteria tied to deliverables
  • Payment terms within Deloitte norms

34.4 What to defend

  • Unlimited liability (always cap)
  • IP transfer of Deloitte-proprietary APEX code and methods
  • Services that would create Independence conflicts
  • Commercial outcomes Deloitte cannot attribution-control (e.g., market-share uplift)
Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder: For audit clients, procurement terms must be consistent with pre-cleared scope. Never negotiate scope outside of what Independence cleared without going back for re-clearance.

34.5 The signature push

  • Align on signature date 2 weeks ahead; ensure legal, finance, and sponsor all in motion
  • Weekly cadence: what's open, what's next, what's blocked
  • Escalate gracefully via the sponsor if procurement stalls for non-substantive reasons
  • Celebrate signature with sponsor + Microsoft counterpart + delivery lead

34.6 What not to do

  • Do not accept unlimited indemnification "just to get it signed"
  • Do not sign a SOW with acceptance criteria you cannot measure
  • Do not concede Deloitte IP retention to close
  • Do not promise outcomes Deloitte cannot control

34.7 Procurement escalation patterns

When procurement escalates beyond normal negotiation, patterns emerge:

Pattern 1: Price-only escalation

Procurement focuses exclusively on Deloitte fees. Response: route the conversation to the executive sponsor with the business case that anchors value to outcome. Price-only escalation typically collapses when the sponsor re-enters.

Pattern 2: IP-transfer demand

Procurement demands transfer of APEX IP to the client. Response: clarify the IP-retention boundary. Client retains their data, their configurations, their Microsoft platform — Deloitte retains the APEX framework IP. This is non-negotiable.

Pattern 3: Terms-only escalation

Procurement focuses on commercial terms (indemnification, liability caps, acceptance criteria). Response: partner with Deloitte Legal and Commercial QR early. Do not negotiate terms on the fly.

Pattern 4: Timeline pressure

Procurement invents urgent signature deadlines. Response: verify the deadline with the sponsor. Invented urgency is a negotiation tactic; real urgency is sponsor-confirmed.

34.8 Close-out cadence

Two weeks before target signature:

  • Legal review complete
  • Financial terms final
  • Risk / Independence sign-off documented
  • Sponsor aligned on signature date

One week before:

  • Final-form contracts with signature blocks
  • Exchange-of-counterpart protocol confirmed
  • Celebration / kick-off logistics planned

Day of signature:

  • Confirm receipt of signed documents
  • Transition to delivery team (see Chapter 35)
  • Client communication: thank-you and next-step schedule

34.9 When procurement wins

Sometimes procurement succeeds in extracting concessions that damage engagement economics. Document for internal post-mortem. Lessons:

  • Where did we start negotiating from too weak a position?
  • What intelligence about procurement's approach did we miss?
  • What would we do differently next time?

This is institutional learning, not finger-pointing.

Key Takeaways

  • Procurement is a buyer with a job — respect, don't adversarialise
  • Defend liability caps, IP retention, Independence-pre-cleared scope
  • Concede on clarifications, benchmarking, reasonable acceptance

Seller Actions

  1. Memorise the four "defend" items
  2. Rehearse the signature-push cadence
  3. Never close at the cost of IP or Independence
Chapter 35

Delivery Handoff

What This Chapter Does for You
  • What the selling team owes the delivery team
  • Delivery kickoff artifacts
  • How to stay involved as the relationship owner
  • Avoiding the handoff gap

35.1 The handoff obligation

Selling does not end at SOW signature. The selling team is the relationship owner. Delivery is accountable for execution, but the seller is accountable for:

  • Continuity of sponsor relationship
  • Expanding scope into Wave 2 and Wave 3
  • Protecting the account from competitor inroads during delivery
  • Being the client's escalation path

35.2 Delivery kickoff artifacts

At SOW signature, the selling team produces:

  1. Account strategy doc — the why, the sponsor, the roadmap
  2. Discovery synthesis — the findings from Wave 1
  3. Stakeholder map — power, influence, sentiment
  4. Commercial commitments doc — what Deloitte promised
  5. Risk register — what could go wrong
  6. Independence status — pre-clearances, pending items, escalation path

35.3 Staying involved

  • Biweekly check-in with sponsor for the first 3 months
  • Monthly review with delivery lead on Wave 2 scope expansion
  • Quarterly account-strategy review with Practice leader
  • Year-end review with executive sponsor on business-case realisation

35.4 The handoff gap

The common failure: seller disappears post-signature, delivery lead is new to sponsor, client sentiment drifts. By the time anyone notices, competitor has landed Wave 2 somewhere else.

Prevention: signed-and-delivered calendar of seller touchpoints. Non-negotiable.

35.5 Expanding the account

Wave 2 scope expansion is the seller's job, not delivery's. Delivery generates reference cases; seller converts reference cases into next-wave commitments.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder: Any Wave 2 scope expansion on audit-client accounts requires its own Independence review. Do not promise verbally; route through the process.

35.6 The handoff meeting

A proper delivery kickoff meeting includes the seller, the delivery lead, and the client sponsor. The agenda:

  1. Introductions — seller introduces delivery lead; client sponsor meets the team
  2. Context transfer — seller summarizes the pursuit narrative for the delivery team
  3. Scope walkthrough — delivery lead confirms scope and surfaces any ambiguity
  4. Cadence agreement — weekly / biweekly check-in schedule
  5. Escalation path — who to call when issues arise
  6. Celebration — acknowledging the signed engagement

This meeting is 60–90 minutes. It is not optional; skipping it is the single most common cause of early delivery friction.

35.7 Seller's ongoing role during delivery

For the first 12 months after Wave 1 close:

  • Monthly — account-strategy review with delivery lead and Practice lead
  • Quarterly — sponsor check-in (business-outcome focus, not delivery status)
  • Semi-annual — Practice leader review of expansion opportunities
  • As needed — crisis escalation support

The seller's calendar should have these checkpoints scheduled as non-negotiable before delivery starts.

35.8 Measuring the handoff

A successful handoff is visible in outcomes:

  • Delivery kick-off happens within 2 weeks of SOW signature
  • Client sponsor sentiment remains positive through the first 90 days
  • No surprises for the client (scope, personnel, timeline) during the first quarter
  • Wave 2 scope expansion conversation begins within the first 6 months
  • Delivery team rates the handoff "complete" on post-close survey

These metrics should feed back into the seller's qualification discipline — a seller whose handoffs consistently produce positive downstream outcomes earns more Wave 1 allocation.

35.9 The career arc

Sellers who maintain account continuity beyond signature build compounding client relationships. The senior Deloitte sellers with the largest APEX books-of-business have been present in their client's life for 5–10 years across multiple wave cycles. The selling motion is not transactional; it is a long-term professional relationship with the client's executive team. The handoff discipline described in this chapter is what makes that longevity possible.

35.10 Delivery Team Composition — Who Actually Shows Up

Sellers get asked in every procurement conversation: "who will actually do the work?" Having a credible answer differentiates pursuits. This section describes the canonical Deloitte delivery-team composition by Wave and by Practice intensity.

Chapter 36

Microsoft Contact Center + Voice — Agentic AI in the Customer Service Channel

What This Chapter Does for You
  • The Microsoft Contact Center stack — Dynamics 365 Contact Center, Copilot Studio, Azure Communication Services, Voice AI
  • Why the contact center is one of the highest-ROI APEX-accelerated deployment sites
  • How Deloitte accelerates contact-center agentic AI using APEX methodology
  • Core capabilities Deloitte delivers — real-time voice assist, post-call summarisation, case orchestration, IVR-to-agent transitions, voice-of-customer intelligence
  • Commercial envelope and typical outcomes for contact-center deployments

36.1 Why contact center matters

The contact center is where customer experience, operational cost, and regulatory exposure all converge in a single workflow. A mid-size enterprise contact center handles 5–50 million interactions per year; a large enterprise handles 100M+. Every interaction carries a cost (labor, licensing, infrastructure), a customer-experience outcome (NPS, first-contact resolution, handle time), and a regulatory footprint (CPNI, HIPAA, PCI, state privacy rules). Contact centers are also where AI value becomes immediately measurable because handle-time, FCR, and CSAT are already instrumented.

Why this chapter. Sellers routinely encounter contact-center conversations in RC, HLS Payer, HLS Provider, TMT-TEL, TH, and ICE pursuits. The Microsoft Contact Center stack plus voice + agentic AI is a high-leverage entry point — and Deloitte's delivery accelerates deployment substantially through APEX methodology.

36.2 The Microsoft Contact Center stack

Microsoft's contact-center offering is a portfolio assembled from several products working together:

36.2.1 Dynamics 365 Contact Center

The core customer-service platform — case management, agent desktop, knowledge base, routing, workforce management. Runs on Dataverse with native Copilot integration.

36.2.2 Copilot Studio

Conversational agent authoring for customer-facing (bot-first) and agent-assist (in-context for human agents) surfaces. Grounded on Dataverse, Fabric, Microsoft Graph, and custom MCP sources.

36.2.3 Azure Communication Services (ACS)

Voice, SMS, email, chat, WhatsApp, Microsoft Teams integration. Programmable communications platform — voice calls in particular — that APEX-delivered agents can interact with directly.

36.2.4 Azure AI Speech

Speech-to-text, text-to-speech, speaker identification, custom voice, real-time transcription. Load-bearing for voice-AI contact-center scenarios.

36.2.5 Azure OpenAI / Foundry

Reasoning for real-time assist, summarisation, sentiment analysis, intent classification, orchestration of complex interactions.

36.2.6 Dataverse + Power Platform

Operational data store, low-code customisation, Power Apps surfaces for supervisor and specialist workflows.

36.2.7 Microsoft 365 + Teams

Agent collaboration, expert escalation, training, knowledge sharing — particularly where Teams-based "call intent experts" support front-line agents.

The stack composes: ACS handles voice; Speech handles transcription; Foundry handles reasoning; Copilot Studio or custom Foundry agents drive conversation; Dataverse + Fabric hold data; Dynamics 365 is the agent desktop; Purview governs; Entra authenticates.

36.3 Where the agentic-AI opportunity lives

36.3.1 Pre-call routing and intent capture

Before the call reaches a human agent, a Copilot Studio voice bot gathers the intent, authenticates the caller, pulls relevant context from Fabric, and routes to the right specialist with the context pre-staged on the agent desktop. Reduces misroute, reduces handle time.

36.3.2 Real-time agent assist

During the call, an assist agent listens to the live transcript, surfaces relevant knowledge-base articles, suggests next best responses, flags compliance concerns (e.g., "the caller asked about investment advice — regulatory disclosure required"), and automates the post-call note draft.

36.3.3 Bot-handled resolution

For well-understood interaction types (balance inquiry, appointment reschedule, order status, refund requests under threshold), a Copilot Studio bot can handle the full interaction with backoff to human escalation. Reduces cost-per-interaction dramatically; preserves human capacity for complex interactions.

36.3.4 Post-call summarisation and case creation

After the call, summarize the interaction, extract key decisions, populate Dataverse case fields, trigger follow-up workflows. Handled automatically — human agent confirms, doesn't author.

36.3.5 Voice-of-customer intelligence

At aggregate scale, analyze all transcriptions for emerging themes, product-issue signals, competitive moves, regulatory-concern patterns. Feeds product, marketing, quality, and compliance teams as intelligence flow.

36.3.6 Supervisor and coaching surfaces

Real-time visibility into agent performance, quality-of-interaction scores, coaching recommendations, exception-pattern surfacing. Supervisors focus on coaching the issues the data surfaces rather than hunting for issues.

36.3.7 Compliance and call-recording intelligence

Real-time detection of regulatory-sensitive phrases, automated quality-check against script compliance, PII / PHI / PCI-detection and protection in transcripts.

36.4 How APEX accelerates contact-center delivery

Deloitte's agent-delivery methodology — when applied to contact-center pursuits — reuses many of the patterns APEX accelerates elsewhere:

36.4.1 Conversational semantic models

APEX's CXML (customer experience) and equivalent Practice semantic models extend to cover conversation entities — interaction, session, turn, resolution, escalation. The Silver → Gold pipeline already handles these patterns.

36.4.2 MCP tool catalog for contact center

APEX's MCP tool library extended with contact-center-specific tools:

  • get_caller_context — pull 360 context at call start
  • classify_intent — intent classification agent
  • get_knowledge_article — knowledge-base retrieval
  • suggest_next_response — agent assist
  • detect_compliance_flag — real-time compliance scan
  • summarize_interaction — post-call summary
  • create_follow_up_case — workflow trigger
  • route_to_specialist — transfer with context
  • flag_quality_concern — supervisor surface
  • extract_voc_themes — aggregate VoC

36.4.3 HITL patterns for contact center

Deloitte's HITL gate framework adapts to voice context — soft HITL (assist agent suggests, human accepts), hard HITL (bot escalates to human), approval HITL (supervisor approves compensation above threshold).

36.4.4 Purview classification for conversation data

Real-time call transcripts are PII-rich and often contain PHI (HLS), PCI (RC payment data), or CPNI (TMT-TEL). APEX's classification taxonomy extends to conversation data with DLP policies applied to transcript storage, agent-assist outputs, and summarisation results.

36.4.5 Audit-row attribution

Every bot-handled resolution, every agent-assist suggestion accepted by a human, every compliance flag raised — all write to APEX audit rows attributing customer outcomes to specific agent actions.

36.4.6 Wave-1 envisioning adapted for contact center

Deloitte's standard Wave 1 four-week envisioning adapts cleanly — the specific Practice services selected shift (contact-center-oriented), but the methodology, discovery pattern, and business-case assembly are the same.

36.5 Key contact-center capabilities Deloitte delivers

CC-CCX-01 Real-time Voice Assist. Live-transcript-driven agent assist with knowledge retrieval, response suggestion, compliance flag. Typical uplift: handle-time -15% to -25%, FCR +5 to +10 points, CSAT +10 points.

CC-CCX-02 Bot-First Resolution. Copilot Studio voice bot handling balance, status, appointment, and basic transaction categories. Typical uplift: bot-resolution rate 40-65% of eligible interactions; cost-per-interaction reduced materially.

CC-CCX-03 Post-Call Intelligence. Summarisation, case-field population, follow-up triggering. Typical uplift: after-call work time reduced 60-80%.

CC-CCX-04 Voice-of-Customer Intelligence. Aggregate VoC pattern detection feeding product / marketing / quality teams. Typical uplift: emerging-theme detection lead time from weeks to hours.

CC-CCX-05 Supervisor Intelligence. Real-time performance visibility, coaching recommendations, exception surfacing. Typical uplift: supervisor time-on-coaching +40%, time-on-admin -50%.

CC-CCX-06 Compliance Shield. Real-time regulatory detection (disclosures, script compliance, PII/PHI/PCI handling). Typical uplift: compliance incidents reduced 60-85%.

CC-CCX-07 Workforce-Management Intelligence. Schedule optimization, attrition prediction, hiring-need forecasting. Typical uplift: scheduling accuracy improved, attrition reduced measurably.

36.6 Commercial envelope for contact-center pursuits

  • Wave 1 (Envision & Land): 4–8 weeks; $400K–$1.5M; delivers envisioning + first assist / bot capability in pilot channel
  • Wave 2 (Enable & Scale): 6–15 months; $4M–$18M; deploys across contact-center footprint with multiple capabilities
  • Wave 3 (Sustain & Transform): Multi-year; $6M–$25M; enterprise-wide, integrated with product / marketing / quality workstreams

Business case anchors vary by industry and scale:

  • RC contact center: $10M–$60M annualised at Wave 2 scale
  • HLS Provider / Payer call center: $15M–$100M annualised
  • TMT-TEL care operation: $20M–$200M annualised
  • TH reservations / service: $10M–$50M annualised

36.7 Qualifying a contact-center pursuit

Six-question qualifier:

  1. What is the interaction volume (annual calls / chats / emails)?
  2. What is the current technology stack (Genesys / NICE / Cisco / Avaya / custom)?
  3. What is the agent desktop footprint today?
  4. Is Dynamics 365 Contact Center in flight or in consideration?
  5. Is there a board-level customer-experience initiative with committed KPI?
  6. Are there specific regulatory pressures (TCPA, PCI, HIPAA, CPNI)?

If 4–6 crisply answered, the pursuit is real. Qualify out if the client's contact-center technology is committed to non-Microsoft path without hybrid coexistence openness.

36.8 Coexistence with non-Microsoft contact-center platforms

Many clients run Genesys, NICE CX, Cisco Webex Contact Center, Avaya, or vendor-specific contact-center software. Deloitte's delivery accommodates:

  • Dynamics 365 Contact Center replacement — where client is ready to migrate the agent desktop to Microsoft
  • Microsoft-powered overlay — Copilot Studio + Foundry agents + ACS overlaid on incumbent contact-center platform for assist, intelligence, and voice-AI capabilities without replacing the call-routing fabric
  • Hybrid — most common; Microsoft handles specific capabilities (assist, voice-AI, analytics) while incumbent handles call-routing and core agent desktop

The overlay pattern is the most flexible and preserves client investment in existing contact-center licensing.

36.9 Objection handling specific to contact center

Client saysResponse
"Our Genesys deployment was expensive; we can't replace it""Understood. Our most common deployment pattern is overlay — your Genesys continues to handle call routing; Microsoft handles assist, intelligence, and voice-AI. Coexists; doesn't displace."
"Customer-facing voice AI is brand risk""Agreed. Our HITL pattern for voice has the bot handle well-defined intents only; complex or emotionally-sensitive interactions escalate to human immediately with full context pre-staged."
"We have compliance concerns with call transcription""Purview governs classification and DLP on transcripts. Real-time detection of PII / PHI / PCI handles the concern. We've delivered compliance-sensitive contact-center AI at clients with the most restrictive frameworks."
"We can't afford another migration""Your existing contact-center stays. We add Microsoft capabilities as overlay. Wave 1 is a 4-6 week envisioning that scopes the overlay specifically; it doesn't require replacement."

36.10 Independence considerations for contact center

Standard DMTSP Independence discipline applies:

  • Client licenses D365 Contact Center, Copilot Studio, ACS, Speech, Foundry, Purview from Microsoft directly
  • Deloitte's contact-center services contracted separately
  • Audit-client pre-clearance required for call-center scope at audit clients
  • Conversation-data PII / PHI handling gets enhanced Purview scrutiny
  • No ECIF for contact-center implementation funding (standard approved paths only)
Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. When positioning contact-center offerings, maintain the two-contract framing. Microsoft Contact Center stack is licensed from Microsoft; Deloitte accelerates deployment. Never present as bundled.

Chapter 37

Conclusion — The Seller Compact

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Revisit the positioning compact: what Deloitte sells, what APEX accelerates, what clients experience
  • Crystallise the single-sentence seller message
  • Frame the seller professional arc through this guide
  • Establish the continuous-improvement disciplines that keep this guide current

37.1 What this guide has been about

Thirty-six chapters and twenty-one appendices is a lot of content. Before closing the book, the seller should be able to state the essence of this guide in three sentences without looking it up.

Sentence one. Deloitte sells Agentic AI Delivery Services; clients contract Microsoft directly for the platform; APEX is Deloitte internal delivery accelerator that never appears in client conversations, proposals, or SOWs.

Sentence two. Microsoft four-plane architecture (Fabric data plane, Foundry reasoning plane, Purview governance plane, Entra identity plane) is the only stack that natively composes the capabilities enterprise agentic AI requires — and Deloitte accelerates delivery from the 18–24 month ground-up baseline to a 9–12 month Wave 2 timeline through APEX methodology.

Sentence three. Every agent decision writes an audit row that attributes measurable business outcome; every data element carries a Purview classification that governs access and output; every action flows through a human-in-the-loop gate where judgment matters — and this discipline is what makes enterprise agentic AI defensible at the Chief Compliance Officer, Chief Financial Officer, and Board level.

If the seller can deliver these three sentences credibly in the first ninety seconds of a pursuit conversation, the rest of the guide content informs the subsequent hour, week, and year.

37.2 The seller professional arc through this guide

Sellers engage with this guide at three career stages, and the emphasis shifts at each stage.

The seller learning the offering. Part I (Ch 1–4) and Part II (Ch 5–8) are the foundation. The positioning of §1.0, the commercial arc of Ch 2, the technology stack fluency of Ch 3–8 are what make a seller credible in the first meeting. A new seller should read these chapters end-to-end before an outbound call; experienced sellers revisit them when positioning shifts.

The seller running pursuits. Part III (industry playbooks, Ch 9–15), Part IV (account playbooks, Ch 16–28), and Part V (pursuit motion, Ch 29–35) are where the seller spends most time. Industry chapter depth, account-specific intelligence, qualification discipline, discovery workshop execution, proposal framing, objection handling, procurement navigation, and delivery handoff — the operating material for every active pursuit.

The seller maturing the practice. Ch 36 (Contact Center), Ch 37 (this conclusion), and the appendices (A–U) are the material the seller uses to deepen specialisation, consult on cross-practice or regulatory-sensitive pursuits, mentor junior sellers, and contribute back to Deloitte methodology. A seller who reads this guide in their first year and returns to contribute in their fifth has completed the arc.

37.3 The disciplines that survive this guide revision cycles

Content in this guide will change. Microsoft platform evolves; Deloitte service catalog evolves; client industries evolve; regulatory frameworks evolve. Certain disciplines, however, should survive every revision:

Independence discipline. Deloitte audits Microsoft. The two-contract commercial model, the language rules ("technology platform relationship," never "partnership"), the funding-path compliance (no ECIF direct to Deloitte), and the audit-client pre-clearance requirement are non-negotiable. Every seller preserves these.

Honest architectural argument. APEX methodology is Microsoft-native because Microsoft is the only platform that natively composes the four planes enterprise agentic AI requires. Not because Deloitte has a commercial relationship with Microsoft that favours the platform. When a client strategic commitment is AWS, GCP, or another stack, the honest answer is that APEX does not fit; Deloitte has platform-agnostic advisory services available separately.

Client-outcome discipline. Every deployment carries measurable business outcomes attributed through the audit row. No "we improved AI maturity" hand-waving. CFO-credible dollar-per-decision attribution is the discipline.

HITL-first agentic AI. Agents prepare, humans decide — until the client, the regulator, and Deloitte delivery leadership all agree that a specific agent action is appropriate for autonomy. The default posture is HITL. The burden of proof is on autonomy, not on human-in-loop.

Cross-practice coherence. A Deloitte engagement at an enterprise client often spans multiple practices (APEX Industry Practices, AXLE automotive framework, adjacent Deloitte offerings). Cross-practice coordination is how the total client value is greater than any single practice engagement alone.

37.4 Three closing recommendations

Read the appendices out of order. The appendices are reference material, not narrative; read them when pursuits require them, not sequentially. Appendix G (Schemas) and Appendix H (MCP Tools) in particular are mid-pursuit architect-credibility references, not front-to-back reading.

Rehearse the rehearsed scripts. The objection-handling tables (Ch 33, Appendix C), the five seller positioning scripts (Ch 12.9.9, Appendix I.9, elsewhere), and the procurement defense scripts (Ch 31.3) are rehearsal material. Reading them once does not work; repetition until the responses are automatic is the only method.

Contribute back. Every successful pursuit produces pattern-level learning. New objections the client raised that we had not rehearsed. New Practice-specific framings that worked. New reference-deployment narratives that illustrate outcomes. Send these to the author (Appendix V) for incorporation into the next revision. The guide improves by collective contribution.

37.5 The compact

Sellers are Deloitte front door to enterprise agentic AI. The client experience with Deloitte begins with the seller, and the trajectory of a multi-year strategic relationship is often set in the first ninety seconds of the first conversation. The content of this guide — all thirty-six preceding chapters and twenty-one appendices — exists to make those ninety seconds credible, those first meetings consequential, those pursuits closable, and those deliveries defensible.

Everything else follows from that.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. The positioning discipline established in §1.0 is the single most important thing in this guide. When in doubt about language, structure, or commercial framing, the default answer is the one that preserves the two-contract model and the Independence Office approved vocabulary. Nothing else — not a bigger close, not a faster deal, not a more compelling pitch — is worth compromising that discipline.

Key Takeaways

  • Three sentences capture the entire guide: what Deloitte sells, why Microsoft, how decisions stay defensible
  • Sellers use the guide differently at different career stages — foundation, pursuit-running, practice-maturing
  • Four disciplines survive every revision: Independence, honest architecture, client-outcome focus, HITL-first
  • Rehearse the scripts; read appendices out of order; contribute back

Seller Actions

  1. Memorise the three-sentence compact
  2. Identify which of the three career stages you are in and read accordingly
  3. Commit the four revision-survival disciplines to practice
  4. Contribute one learning back to the author quarterly

38.1 Why this chapter exists

The preceding chapters cover each pursuit stage in isolation. This chapter walks through one continuous pursuit — from the initial email to the first Wave 1 kickoff meeting — so a seller new to APEX has a concrete reference for the whole motion. The pursuit is composite — drawn from multiple real engagements, genericized, time-compressed, and Independence-scrubbed.

38.2 The pursuit at a glance

-3Outbound email to client VPQualifying email (§X.2)

38.3 The scenario

Client. A mid-size regional retail chain — 240 stores, $3.8B annual revenue, publicly traded. CFO committed to 150bp margin improvement over 24 months on the last earnings call. Chief Merchant named in her own letter to store directors as responsible for category margin uplift. Current state: SAP S/4 Retail, Oracle Retail Xstore POS, Salesforce Commerce Cloud e-commerce, Adobe Experience Platform for MarTech, mature Microsoft Fabric footprint (F128 reserved) from a prior data-platform project. Not a Deloitte audit client (simplifies Independence).

The trigger. A Microsoft GPL who supports the account calls the Deloitte APEX lead: "My ATU thinks this account is ready for agentic AI. Chief Merchant has a margin target and is frustrated by the pace of the current vendor. Can you take a look?"

38.4 Week −4 — Internal qualification

The APEX lead, before any outbound contact, runs §1.5 qualifier internally with the Microsoft GPL's input:

  1. Public CEO commitment? Yes — 150bp margin on earnings call.
  2. Single-threaded executive sponsor? Maybe — Chief Merchant is the budget owner; CFO is the funding gate.
  3. Microsoft footprint? Strong — F128 Fabric, E5 across workforce, Copilot deployed to 800 seats.
  4. Incumbent SI? Yes — Accenture on adjacent scope. Neutral, not hostile.
  5. Auditor? Not Deloitte. Independence footprint limited to standard tax / advisory separation.
  6. Budget posture? Funded through Merch OpEx for FY27; unused. Ready to deploy.
  7. Decision window? Signed by end of Q2; delivery start Q3.

6/7 green. The lead makes internal "GO." Pursuit team assigned: lead (Principal), RC SME (Senior Manager), Fabric Architect (Manager).

38.5 Week −3 — Outbound email

The lead writes a variant of §X.2 qualifying email to the Chief Merchant, referencing the Microsoft GPL introduction and a specific RC framing — assortment-and-pricing intelligence (RC-E2E-03) because it aligns directly to the margin-improvement commitment. Length 140 words; scheduled for Tuesday 7:45am local; CC'd to the Chief Merchant's EA at her request.

Reply Wednesday morning: "Looks interesting. EA will find 30 minutes."

Meeting scheduled for the following Tuesday afternoon.

38.6 Week −2 — First meeting

Deloitte team: Principal + RC SME. Client team: Chief Merchant + VP Category Management (observer).

Agenda executed per §X.3. The Principal's 3-slide framing:

  • Slide 1: APEX framework (Practice = RC, Services catalog, Wave 1/2/3 envelope)
  • Slide 2: Reference architecture sketch — Fabric + Foundry + Copilot + Purview + Entra with the client's named SORs filled in during the meeting (live, on the whiteboard surface)
  • Slide 3: RC-E2E-03 narrative — category margin exposure detection as decision surface; Chief Merchant as lead persona; margin uplift KPI as commitment

Chief Merchant engages on slide 3. Her question: "If we did this, when would I see the first margin number move?" The Principal's answer is calibrated: "Wave 1 produces the scaffolding — architecture, service design, team alignment. First margin signal is 12–16 weeks after Wave 2 kickoff. So about 4 months into Wave 2, around 6 months from today if we move now."

Chief Merchant: "OK. Run the discovery. My EA will set up the workshop."

End-of-meeting verdict: discovery workshop scheduled.

38.7 Week −1 — Internal pursuit-team forming

APEX lead staffs the four-week discovery workshop team per §35.10.1: Principal (0.1), Delivery Manager (0.5), RC Practice SME (0.5), Fabric / Foundry Architect (1.0), Purview governance architect (0.3), data engineer (0.5), use-case lead (0.5). Total ~3.4 FTE for the 4-week workshop.

Deal-qualify checkpoint with pursuit QR: go. Budget assigned to pursuit. Microsoft GPL briefed; Microsoft team ready to join Week 2 architecture session.

38.8 Week 0 — Discovery Week 1 (Context and pain)

Client team: Chief Merchant, VP Category, VP Pricing, Director of Merchandising Operations, Director of Store Operations. Deloitte team: 4 people per above.

3-hour session produces:

  • Ranked pain list: (1) Category-level margin exposure discovery is too slow — "we see exposure in quarterly reviews, not in the week that matters"; (2) markdown cadence is reactive rather than predictive; (3) competitor price moves go uncorrelated with own-assortment decisions.
  • Candidate services from RC catalog: RC-E2E-03 Assortment & Pricing, RC-TTP-07 Markdown. (Chief Merchant asks about RC-TTP-02 Demand Sensing; team flags it as potential Wave 2 add, not Wave 1.)
  • SOR inventory (Bronze candidates): SAP S/4 (category, SKU, price, promotion), Xstore POS (transaction), Commerce Cloud (e-commerce transactions + audience signals), Adobe Experience Platform (segment membership), Revionics (active promo calendars), DataWeave (competitor pricing feed). 6 SORs for Wave 1. Seven others deferred to Wave 2.

Output delivered Thursday; pre-read sent to client team before Week 2.

38.9 Week 1 — Discovery Week 2 (Architecture alignment)

Microsoft team joins: CSA + GBB Data & AI. 4-hour session.

Architecture sketch drafted live:

  • Fabric Bronze: mirroring from SAP S/4 (SAP Datasphere), CDC from Xstore, API pull from Commerce Cloud, event stream from Adobe Experience Platform, file-drop from Revionics and DataWeave.
  • Fabric Silver: SCML (Item, Category, Price, Promotion, Markdown, CompetitorSignal) + MERML (Assortment, PriceRule, MarkdownCadence). Client has ~40% of SCML entities already modeled from the prior data-platform project — reduces Silver-layer effort by ~30%.
  • Fabric Gold: two agent-safe views for Wave 1 — vw_agent_category_exposure, vw_agent_markdown_cadence.
  • MCP tool binding: 4 tools for Wave 1 — category exposure query, elasticity lookup, markdown-cadence recommendation, competitor-signal correlation.
  • Foundry: 3 agents — CategoryExposureAgent, ElasticityReasoningAgent (reasoning tier for elasticity modeling), MarkdownCadenceAgent. Estimated peak PTU for Wave 1 pilot: 30 PTU, PAYG initially.
  • Copilot: Teams cards for merchant approvals, Power BI Direct Lake for executive dashboards.
  • Purview: PII classification on loyalty data (in scope later for RC-E2E-05 — not Wave 1); trade-secret classification on pricing rules; DLP policy preventing cross-category leakage in agent output.
  • Entra: agent identities scoped to category subset. Chief Merchant role; VP Category role; Director-level roles.

Microsoft GBB validates the architecture; suggests mirroring S/4 via the newer SAP Data Extractor approach; pushes back lightly on the F128 capacity being sufficient — team agrees F128 handles Wave 1 comfortably; F256 considered for Wave 2.

Output: architecture diagram v0.9, integration list, capacity sizing estimate.

38.10 Week 2 — Discovery Week 3 (Service selection and KPI commitment)

Client team + Chief Merchant sponsor presence at end.

Service commitment:

  • Wave 1 (4–12 weeks scaled to 10 weeks given complexity): RC-E2E-03 Assortment & Pricing as lead service; pilot scope = 3 categories (personal care, seasonal home, select electronics), representing ~22% of total chain margin.
  • KPI baseline: 2026 YTD margin on these 3 categories calculated at 31.8% weighted average.
  • Wave 1 target: infrastructure ready for measurement; no margin move expected in Wave 1 itself.
  • Wave 2 target: 80–180bp margin uplift on these 3 categories within 16 weeks of Wave 2 kickoff. (Aligned to §Appendix S RC KPI band.)

HITL design: agent recommends markdown cadence; VP Pricing approves; Chief Merchant reviews weekly roll-up. All via Teams card with audit row emission per §6.10. Oversight mode per §2.2C: HITL on markdown approval; HOTL on category exposure monitoring; HIC on monthly policy review with Chief Merchant.

Orchestration archetype selection: Continuous-monitor-threshold + HITL-alert (F1 archetype per Appendix T.W.10.3) for exposure detection; Predictive-trigger + workflow-aware scheduling (F3) for markdown cadence.

Output: service commitment document signed by Chief Merchant.

38.11 Week 3 — Discovery Week 4 (Wave 1 plan and Wave 2 roadmap)

10-week Wave 1 plan:

  • Weeks 1–2: Architecture and governance design (Silver / Gold / Purview / Entra)
  • Weeks 3–5: MCP tool development + agent prompt/manifest authoring
  • Weeks 6–7: Integration (SOR connectors) + Bronze ingestion
  • Weeks 8–9: Agent + orchestration + Copilot surface assembly
  • Week 10: Production go-live (3-category pilot) + Chief Merchant briefing

Wave 2 roadmap (preview):

  • Months 1–4: Expand to remaining categories (complete chain), add RC-TTP-07 Markdown, add RC-TTP-02 Demand Sensing as a companion to RC-E2E-03
  • Months 5–8: RC-E2E-05 Unified Customer (leveraging loyalty data)
  • Months 9–12: Scale monitoring, managed-services transition prep

Wave 1 commercial envelope: \$680K fixed fee. Wave 2 envelope projected \$4.8M–\$7.2M.

Deliverables list per §X.5 finalized.

38.12 Week 4 — SOW draft and QR review

Draft SOW (per §X.6) produced by Principal + Commercial QR. Route:

  • Principal review (Day 1)
  • Independence liaison review (Day 2) — no audit client; standard non-audit-service checklist passes
  • Commercial QR (Days 3–4) — minor adjustments to milestone language and payment schedule
  • Risk register finalized

Draft sent to client Friday Week 4.

38.13 Week 5 — Client procurement engagement

Procurement raises the seven predictable questions per §3.8:

  • MSA already in place from prior Deloitte engagement — reused with amendment.
  • Payment terms: 40% milestone-1 / 30% milestone-2 / 30% completion.
  • SLA on deliverables: weekly checkpoint; remedies for slippage.
  • Insurance / indemnity: standard Deloitte language.
  • Subcontractor disclosure: near-shore engineers disclosed.
  • IP: Deloitte retains APEX IP; client work product per standard terms.
  • Exit: termination-for-convenience with 30-day notice; pro-rated work product.

Three rounds of redlines. All manageable.

38.14 Week 6 — Negotiation

Final hitch: procurement asks for 10% fee reduction. Principal declines per §C.9 discipline, offers instead to narrow Wave 1 scope from 3 categories to 2 (which reduces fee 15% and pushes the omitted category to Wave 2). Chief Merchant overrides procurement — keeps 3 categories, accepts the fee.

Lesson the lead logs for the pursuit post-mortem: Chief Merchant's sponsorship overrode procurement friction because §C.9.13 escalation to the right level resolved it.

38.15 Week 7 — Signature

SOW signed Thursday. Kickoff scheduled Monday of Week 8.

38.16 Week 8 — Wave 1 kickoff

Kickoff deck delivered to combined team:

  • Principal opens: context, commitment, ways of working.
  • Delivery Manager: week-by-week plan, roles, contact list.
  • RC SME: service design overview.
  • Fabric / Foundry architect: architecture walk-through.
  • Purview architect: governance design.
  • Client lead (Chief Merchant delegate): client-side team, their commitments.
  • Q&A.

Named-individual team roster in SOW appendix. First working session Tuesday.

38.17 What to take from this walkthrough

Six pattern takeaways from this composite pursuit:

  1. The 11-week cadence is real. Outbound to kickoff in 8–12 weeks is the productive rhythm. Much longer signals qualification problems; much shorter signals under-discovered scope.
  2. Microsoft GPL introduction is high-leverage. The pursuit starts warm because the GPL had already assessed account readiness.
  3. The first meeting converts on slide 3, not slide 1. The Practice framework matters, but the industry-specific narrative is what lands.
  4. Discovery Week 2 is the architectural crux. The diagram that emerges on Day 2 of Week 2 is the one that carries through to the SOW.
  5. Service selection is more important than service count. One well-chosen Wave-1 service (RC-E2E-03 here) lands better than three hedged ones.
  6. Fee defense matters more than fee optimization. A 10% discount is a 10% relationship-credibility loss; scope adjustment preserves both.

38.18 The one-sentence takeaway

Every successful APEX pursuit follows this cadence with minor variation: qualify internally, email warmly, discover thoroughly, commit specifically, contract cleanly, kick off confidently — with the pursuit QR discipline holding every step to Independence and commercial standards.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. The composite pursuit in this chapter is fictitious, constructed to illustrate the motion. Client names, specifics, and financial figures are illustrative. Real pursuits are never shared in internal material without Independence-Office scrubbing.

Key Takeaways

  • The 11-week pursuit cadence from outbound email to Wave 1 kickoff
  • Every stage has a named artifact and a verdict decision
  • Discovery Week 2 is where the architecture gets drawn; Week 3 is where services commit
  • Fee defense through scope adjustment beats fee defense through discount
  • Microsoft GPL partnership is the lead multiplier on mid-market RC pursuits

Seller Actions

  1. Memorise the week-by-week cadence
  2. Rehearse the 30-minute discovery meeting agenda until reflexive
  3. Practice the architecture sketch live on a whiteboard
  4. Build a personal playbook of the six pattern takeaways
Appendix A

Microsoft Product Reference

This appendix summarizes the four Microsoft product pillars the APEX architecture leverages. Content is framed for seller conversation, not deep technical reference.

A.1 Microsoft Fabric

Fabric is Microsoft's unified data and analytics platform. Key concepts:

  • OneLake — single logical data lake spanning the organization
  • Workloads — Data Engineering, Data Factory, Data Warehouse, Real-Time Intelligence, Data Science, Synapse, Fabric Databases
  • Direct Lake — Power BI reads Parquet directly without ETL
  • Shortcuts — cross-cloud data reference without copying
  • Compute models — capacity-based, F-SKUs

Seller-relevant value: eliminates data-movement tax, native Copilot grounding, native Purview governance.

A.2 Azure AI Foundry

Foundry is Microsoft's enterprise AI platform. Key concepts:

  • Foundry Agents — build, deploy, and orchestrate agents
  • Model catalog — frontier and open models, with per-model governance
  • Agent orchestration — multi-agent patterns with observability
  • Evaluation and monitoring — safety, drift, cost
  • Integration — Fabric, Copilot, Azure services

Seller-relevant value: agent orchestration that production teams trust, not just a model endpoint.

A.3 Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio

  • Microsoft 365 Copilot — productivity surface (Word, Excel, Teams, Outlook, PowerPoint)
  • Copilot Studio — build custom copilots grounded in enterprise data
  • Agents in Copilot — surface Foundry agents inside Microsoft 365

Seller-relevant value: where knowledge workers already live.

A.4 Microsoft Purview

  • Data Map — data discovery, classification, lineage
  • Data Loss Prevention — sensitive data controls
  • Compliance — policies, audit, regulatory reporting
  • Insider Risk — user behavior analytics

Seller-relevant value: trust architecture; often the first workload in regulated industries.

A.5 Microsoft Entra (adjacent but critical)

  • Identity and access management
  • Conditional access
  • Identity governance
  • The identity plane that APEX's agents assume

A.6 Platform integration patterns

  • Fabric → Foundry: data grounding for agents
  • Foundry → Copilot: agent surfacing
  • Purview → Fabric and Foundry: governance across data and reasoning
  • Entra → all: identity for user, agent, and service principal
