Appendix C

Objection Handbook

Expanded from Chapter 33. Full verbatim responses to the most common 30 objections.

C.1 Platform objections

"We already have Snowflake — why Fabric?" APEX is Fabric-native. Snowflake stays. Both run on Azure. Fabric mirrors Snowflake natively, so you get APEX Gold views and Copilot-grounded serving over Snowflake data with no ETL to author. Snowflake continues to own analytical SQL and data sharing; Fabric adds the APEX agent-serving and governance layer. See Appendix F for patterns.

"Databricks is our standard" Azure Databricks and Fabric coexist explicitly. Databricks continues to own ML training and batch feature engineering. Fabric reaches Databricks Delta tables in ADLS Gen2 via OneLake shortcuts — no data copy — and mirrors Unity Catalog natively. APEX services run on Fabric; Databricks keeps its current job. See Appendix F for patterns.

"Why not run APEX on Snowflake Cortex or Databricks Mosaic directly?" APEX assumes Fabric as the data plane and Foundry as the agent runtime. Snowflake Cortex and Databricks Mosaic are in-platform AI — strong for their resident workloads, not substitutes for the integrated four-plane architecture APEX relies on. Copilot grounding, Purview integration, Foundry orchestration, and Entra agent identity all require Fabric-native authoring.

"We're all-in on AWS" APEX runs on the Microsoft stack architecturally. If the client's strategic platform choice is AWS, we are honest that APEX is not the right fit on AWS. We offer strategy and advisory services that are platform-agnostic.

"Our primary cloud is GCP" Same as AWS. Honest disqualification.

C.2 AI / Agent objections

"We tried AI and it didn't work" Most early efforts were notebook-to-nowhere. APEX is production-first: Fabric pipelines, Foundry orchestration, Purview governance. That operational maturity is what was missing.

"Copilot is hype" Not the value driver. The value is Foundry orchestration; Copilot is the user-surface layer.

"We can build this ourselves" Acknowledged and valid. The question is time-to-first-value and opportunity cost. APEX's agent library, semantic model, and MCP tool library represent roughly 18-24 months of engineering lead.

"Our models are better than anyone else's" Good. APEX isn't a model — it's an orchestration, data, and governance fabric that lets your models reach production faster.

"What about hallucination?" Foundry provides grounding, retrieval, and evaluation. APEX services use structured prompts and agent-chains with verification steps. Hallucination risk is bounded and monitored.

C.3 Commercial objections

"Microsoft is expensive" Microsoft licensing is between client and Microsoft. Our services business case is based on APEX outcome, not on platform investment. If Microsoft licensing is blocked, we route through Microsoft account team.

"Your fee is too high" Let's anchor to benefit. What is the public KPI the service ties to? What is a reasonable share of that benefit as services investment?

"We want outcome pricing" We do outcome-linked pricing selectively. Requires baseline, attribution, and measurement we both agree on upfront.

"We want multi-year commitment from you for a discount" We consider it. Requires wave-gated off-ramps so the client is not stuck.

C.4 Independence and trust objections

"Aren't you our auditor?" If Deloitte audits the client, we follow audit independence rules with Audit Committee pre-clearance. Services we can and cannot perform are explicit; we do not work around them.

"How do we know Deloitte won't share our data?" Standard engagement NDA; Deloitte data-handling protocols; client data never commingled with other clients; Independence office oversight on audit clients.

"Will we be locked into Deloitte?" APEX IP deployed to your tenant is yours. We retain the reference library, the methodology, the patterns; you retain the implementation.

C.5 Organisational objections

"We already have (a different SI)" Then we are not selling services — we are selling IP. APEX reference architecture can be deployed by your current SI if you choose.

"Our team isn't ready" Wave 1 four-week envisioning builds organizational readiness. Wave 2 integrates your team in delivery. Wave 3 transfers to your team.

"Change fatigue in our organization" Acknowledged. We scope Wave 2 deliberately small to prove value before scaling. Change is paced to org capacity.

C.9 Pricing Objections — The Dedicated Library

Pricing objections get their own section because they dominate late-stage pursuits and deserve rehearsed responses distinct from architectural or compliance objections. Every response below has been tested in the field.

C.9.1 "Your proposal is more expensive than the SI quote."

Note

"I'm not surprised — our proposal includes the canonical-schema library, the pre-built agent catalog, the orchestration archetypes, and the governance framework. An SI quote for the same outcome typically assumes the client funds the engineering year of semantic-model authoring, the agent catalog development, and the governance policy bundle. If you price the SI proposal with those line items added back, the gap closes or reverses. Would you like to walk through a line-by-line comparison against the SI scope?"

Never drop the price by reducing scope; shift the conversation to the scope the SI excluded.

C.9.2 "Can you match Accenture's / IBM's / Cognizant's day-rate?"

Note

"We don't compete on day-rate. We compete on fixed-fee outcome-linked delivery with Deloitte's IP included. Our Wave 2 isn't a staffing contract; it's a productized delivery of specific services (RC-E2E-03, RC-E2E-09, etc.) with defined outcomes, defined HITL patterns, and defined KPI measurement. If you want staffing against your backlog, we're not the right answer. If you want named business outcomes with audit-row attribution, we are."

C.9.3 "Why can't we bundle the Microsoft licensing with Deloitte services?"

Note

"Because Deloitte is Microsoft's external auditor. SEC Rule 2-01 and PCAOB Rule 3520 require strict separation between the audit-client relationship and service delivery. We cannot sell bundled commercials. You license Microsoft platform from Microsoft directly; you contract Deloitte services separately. Every other SI that says they can bundle is either (a) not Microsoft's auditor, or (b) misrepresenting what's contractually permissible. The two-contract model is a feature, not a constraint."

C.9.4 "Your Wave 1 envelope is 2–3× what we paid for our last advisory project."

Note

"The Wave 1 envelope funds a buildable production outcome — a working agent in an agreed-scope service, with manifests, governance, and audit row in production by Week 10. It isn't advisory. If what you want is a strategy document, Deloitte has an advisory offering at the price band you remember; APEX is a delivery offering. Which outcome does the board actually want?"

C.9.5 "The PTU costs look too high."

Note

"PTU costs scale with workload; they're not a fixed tax. In Wave 1 we operate pay-as-you-go — typically \$2K–\$8K per month for the pilot. We only recommend reserved PTU after Wave 2 workloads are measured and reservation economics beat PAYG. We don't ask the client to commit to reserved capacity until we can justify the break-even from actual telemetry. See Appendix U for the cost-calculation detail."

C.9.6 "Fabric is a new platform — why should we commit to F256 now?"

Note

"You don't. Wave 1 typically runs on F64 pay-as-you-go. F256 reservation is a Wave 2 decision when your consumption patterns are measured and the reservation economics are defensible. Reserving at signing is a rookie mistake we explicitly avoid recommending."

C.9.7 "We already budgeted for AI at half this amount."

Note

"Understood. The half-budget covers either (a) a narrower scope — one service instead of three — which we can deliver inside that envelope, or (b) a POC rather than a production deployment — which we don't sell because POCs don't produce durable value. Would you like to scope one service at your budget, or stage the current scope across two fiscal years?"

C.9.8 "Value-share — we want the whole engagement on value-share."

Note

"Value-share works on services with clean audit-row attribution to dollar outcomes — typically markdown (RC-TTP-07), shrink (RC-TTP-06), and recovery services. For services without direct dollar attribution, value-share creates perverse measurement incentives. We can structure a hybrid — fixed fee for foundation services, value-share on the attribution-clean services. Would that fit your commercial posture?"

C.9.9 "Your offshore blend is lower than Accenture's — what's the trade-off?"

Note

"Our blend reflects the work. Engineering of APEX manifests and agent governance is onshore because the IP is sensitive and the design is judgement-heavy. Pipeline integration and reporting is blended onshore / near-shore / offshore. Delivery quality is constant across the blend; we don't ship 80% offshore. Would you like the named-individual role card before Wave 1 kickoff?"

C.9.10 "Can you guarantee the KPI outcomes?"

Note

"We guarantee the delivery — scoped services in production by Wave 2, manifests committed, governance in place, audit row emitting. The KPI outcomes are conditional on factors outside our control (data quality, organizational adoption, operating-model commitment). What we do guarantee: if the KPI outcome is not achieved, we can trace why through the audit row and correct. That's stronger than a KPI guarantee because it tells you the actual cause. See Appendix S for the KPI expectation bands."

C.9.11 "Your Wave 3 annual ops cost — can that be bought down?"

Note

"Wave 3 ops cost is proportional to the service portfolio you operate. It scales down if the portfolio shrinks, or if your team takes over specific services. We explicitly design Wave 3 with a transfer option — named services can be handed to the client's internal team on an agreed timeline. Ops cost becomes 'build-new-services' cost only, which the client controls."

C.9.12 "Can we defer payment to outcome realization?"

Note

"Partially, through value-share (§C.9.8) on eligible services, or through milestone-gated commercial terms on Wave 2. Full outcome-deferral across the engagement is not workable — we'd be funding your program on our balance sheet, which breaks Deloitte's finance model. Milestone gating is the practical middle ground."

C.9.13 Escalation pattern

If pricing objections persist across three meetings without movement, that usually signals one of three underlying issues:

  1. Wrong sponsor. Go up one level. The person objecting may not own the budget.
  2. Wrong service scope. Smaller Wave 1 scope that fits their budget and lets them buy more later.
  3. Wrong timing. They are not ready to buy this fiscal. Reset to pipeline.

Do not keep discounting to close. Every point of discount is a point of future-engagement credibility lost.

Deloitte Independence Notes

Note

E.1 Audit-client engagement rule

  • Specific services are pre-cleared with the Audit Committee

  • NEVER say "partner", "alliance", "joint venture" in reference to Microsoft (in regulated contexts)
  • USE: "relationship", "collaboration", "teaming arrangement", "technology platform provider"

E.4 Funding paths

  • ECIF-funded engagements are prohibited on audit clients
  • Approved funding paths: DCIF, direct client, ISV Marketplace, SI teaming arrangement

E.5 Reporting obligations

  • Quarterly Independence reviews mandatory for audit-client engagements
  • Personal Independence compliance required for all Deloitte professionals on audit-client engagements

E.6 Escalation

  • When in doubt: Independence office
  • Never improvise

E.7 Non-audit clients

Even for non-audit clients:

  • Deloitte internal risk protocols apply
  • Data-handling protocols apply
  • Conflict checks apply
  • Client confidentiality protocols apply

The difference with audit clients is the additional layer of SEC / PCAOB-defined restrictions. Base level of professional conduct is identical across all engagements.

Appendix F

Data Platform Co-Existence — Fabric with Databricks and Snowflake on Azure

This appendix is the seller's reference for the most common data-platform incumbency pattern: a prospect already runs Databricks, Snowflake, or both — very often on Azure — and is asking how APEX fits. Short answer: APEX requires Fabric as the data plane, but Databricks and Snowflake keep their current roles. This appendix gives the sell-side talking points, the honest limitations, and the architecture patterns to reference in discovery.

F.1 Why this conversation matters

Three observations frame every conversation where Databricks or Snowflake is already present:

  1. Both platforms run on Azure. Azure Databricks is a first-party Microsoft service. Snowflake on Azure runs in every major Azure region. Being "on Azure" is not the differentiator — the differentiator is what each platform is optimized to do.
  2. Client investment is rarely abandoned. Existing Databricks or Snowflake estates represent meaningful spend, skills, and operational maturity. Suggesting the client tear them out is a lost deal. APEX's posture is explicit co-existence.
  3. APEX has architectural requirements, not platform preferences. APEX requires: (a) a data plane that OneLake addresses, (b) Copilot-grounded serving, (c) Purview governance native, (d) Foundry as the reasoning runtime. Fabric delivers all four natively; Databricks and Snowflake contribute to specific layers of the stack but not all four.

F.2 Azure Databricks + Fabric

What Azure Databricks is best at

  • Data engineering at petabyte scale (Spark-based ETL, streaming transforms)
  • ML training and batch feature engineering with MLflow
  • Unity Catalog as the lakehouse governance layer for Databricks-resident data
  • Delta Lake as a mature open-format lakehouse with time travel, ACID, and schema evolution
  • Data-science notebook experience for statistical and ML work

How Fabric coexists

  • OneLake Shortcuts to ADLS Gen2. Databricks clusters typically write Delta to ADLS Gen2. Fabric reads these tables in place via shortcuts. No duplication, no second storage bill.
  • Mirrored Azure Databricks Unity Catalog. Fabric mirrors Unity Catalog schemas natively. Databricks remains the data owner; Fabric surfaces a read-optimized replica for APEX Gold and Power BI Direct Lake.
  • Databricks as upstream producer, Fabric as APEX serving layer. Databricks continues to own ML training and batch feature engineering; APEX Gold views in Fabric consume Databricks Delta outputs and expose them to MCP for agent serving.

Honest limitations of a Databricks-only approach for APEX

  • No native Copilot grounding. Microsoft 365 Copilot grounds on Fabric OneLake, not on Databricks Delta. Reaching Copilot from Databricks requires Fabric in the middle.
  • Purview depth. Purview over Fabric is deeper than Purview over Unity Catalog. Classification, lineage, DLP on Databricks-resident data needs additional configuration and sometimes Databricks-side agents.
  • Real-time intelligence. Databricks Structured Streaming is strong for engineering; Fabric Real-Time Intelligence (Eventhouse, KQL, reflex) is a more integrated pattern for the live-dashboard, alerting, and reflex use cases APEX leans on.
  • APEX semantic models are Fabric artifacts. Re-authoring SCML, MERML, CXML (and HLS, ER, AXLE, TMT, TH, ICE equivalents) on Databricks-native tooling is not on the APEX roadmap.
  • Two bills if not right-sized. Fabric + Databricks costs more than either alone. Right-sizing matters. Deloitte's advisory role in discovery covers this.

The discovery question that matters

"What workloads do you want to keep on Databricks forever, and which are candidates to shift to Fabric over time?" Clients with a clear answer run healthy co-existence. Clients who answer "everything stays on Databricks forever" need APEX only as a thin serving layer — still viable, but the envelope shrinks.

F.3 Snowflake + Fabric

What Snowflake is best at

  • Analytical SQL at scale with separation of storage and compute
  • Secure data sharing (Snowflake Data Cloud) for inter-organization data exchange
  • Cross-cloud portability (AWS, Azure, GCP) for clients with multi-cloud posture
  • Mature role-based access control and governance internal to Snowflake
  • Data marketplaces and data-sharing arrangements

How Fabric coexists

  • Native Snowflake mirroring into Fabric. Fabric mirrors Snowflake databases into OneLake with Delta/Parquet materialisation. Near-real-time. No ETL to author.
  • Iceberg interop via OneLake. Snowflake's Apache Iceberg support and Fabric's Iceberg support let tables be read by both engines from the same storage location.
  • Snowflake as source, Fabric as APEX serving layer. Snowflake continues to serve traditional BI and analytical workloads; APEX-specific Gold views live in Fabric, grounded by Snowflake data through mirroring or Iceberg.

Honest limitations of a Snowflake-only approach for APEX

  • No Foundry-equivalent agent runtime. Snowflake Cortex provides in-platform AI functions but is not a substitute for Azure AI Foundry. APEX's 47 orchestration patterns and 165+ MCP tools target Foundry.
  • No native Copilot grounding. Microsoft 365 Copilot grounds on Fabric, not Snowflake. Snowflake reaches Copilot only through Fabric mirroring or Iceberg shared storage.
  • Purview over Snowflake is shallower than Purview over Fabric. PII/PHI classification and DLP on Snowflake-resident data need Snowflake-side governance tooling alongside Purview.
  • Microsoft 365 graph integration. Serving agents through Teams, Outlook, SharePoint, and the Microsoft 365 graph is a Fabric + Foundry + Copilot story; Snowflake does not natively play in that surface.
  • Data movement economics. Without mirroring or Iceberg, making Snowflake data agent-accessible means duplication. Mirroring removes duplication but adds Fabric capacity cost.

The discovery question that matters

"Is Snowflake your strategic analytical platform, or is it a load-bearing system in a broader portfolio?" If strategic, Snowflake stays and Fabric augments. If load-bearing but not strategic, Fabric is a viable successor for some workloads while Snowflake runs down.

F.4 Both at once: Databricks + Snowflake + Fabric

Several large enterprises run all three. The pattern that works:

  • Databricks owns engineering and ML
  • Snowflake owns analytical SQL and data sharing
  • Fabric owns APEX agent serving + Copilot grounding + Purview governance

Each platform plays to its strength. APEX's job is orchestration across all three through Fabric's OneLake as the integration substrate.

F.5 When to disqualify the pursuit

  • Client has strategic commitment to an Oracle Cloud-only, AWS-only, or GCP-only posture for new workloads
  • Client explicitly rejects any new Microsoft Azure footprint
  • Client requires APEX to run entirely on Databricks SQL or Snowflake Cortex without any Fabric

In these cases, APEX is not the right fit. Deloitte's broader platform-agnostic advisory remains available.

F.6 What to say in the first conversation

Client saysYou say
"We just invested in Databricks""Good. Databricks stays. APEX runs on Fabric alongside it; the two interoperate through OneLake shortcuts or Unity Catalog mirroring. Let's talk about what you want to keep on Databricks long-term vs what could shift."
"We're a Snowflake shop""Great. Snowflake stays. Fabric mirrors Snowflake natively — no ETL to author. APEX services run on Fabric and read Snowflake-mirrored data directly."
"Why do we need Fabric if we have Databricks?""Because APEX requires a Copilot-grounded, Purview-governed, Foundry-reasoning data plane. Databricks covers parts of that picture but not all of it. Fabric is the integration substrate, not a Databricks replacement."
"Can we run APEX only on Snowflake?""No — APEX's 45 services assume Fabric as the data plane and Foundry as the agent runtime. Snowflake stays for what it does best; Fabric is added for APEX."
"Isn't Fabric Databricks re-branded?""No. Fabric is a different product with OneLake, Direct Lake, Eventhouse, and integrated Copilot grounding. Databricks and Fabric coexist by design."
Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. Deloitte does not resell or commercially commit to Fabric, Databricks, or Snowflake licensing. Client contracts directly with Microsoft (Fabric, Azure Databricks) and Snowflake (when not on Azure Marketplace). Deloitte sells advisory and implementation services only.

Appendix G

APEX Schemas, Entities, and Agent Consumption Patterns

This appendix is the seller's reference for APEX's canonical schemas across all 7 Practices. Each schema is described by its canonical entities, the systems of record (SORs) those entities map from, how agentic agents consume the entities to produce decisions, and how entities combine for situation assessment. Sellers use this appendix in pursuit conversations when architects or Chief Data Officers ask "what data does APEX actually reason over."

G.1 How to read this appendix

Each Practice has one or more canonical ML schemas. Within each schema, this appendix covers the key entities using a consistent five-part template:

  • Description — what the entity represents in business terms
  • SOR mapping — source systems it typically draws from, and the Fabric integration pattern (Mirroring, Eventstream, Data Pipeline, Dataflow Gen2, or Custom Endpoint)
  • Agent decision use — how APEX agents query and reason over the entity
  • Situation assessment — how the entity combines with other entities to assess operational situations
  • Example decisions — concrete decision types the entity informs

The appendix closes with cross-Practice entity patterns (§G.9), five standard agent query patterns (§G.10), and five situation-assessment patterns (§G.11) that apply across all Practices.

Note

Naming convention. When an entity appears in multiple Practices, the description notes the cross-Practice reference. Where APEX schema names collide with adjacent frameworks (e.g., AXLE framework's SCML vs RC's SCML), this appendix prefixes with the schema family for disambiguation.

G.2 Retail & Consumer (RC) Practice Schemas

RC has three primary canonical schemas covering supply-chain, merchandising, and customer experience domains.

G.2.1 SCML — Supply Chain Merchandising Language

Foundational RC schema for physical-goods flow from supplier through store to customer.

Note

Example in the field — Big Box Store Store 100. SCML entities are the foundation of Events 01 (cold chain), 02 (receiving discrepancy), 05 (recall), 07 (shrink), and 08 (customer incident) in the Store 100 narrative (§16.13). When the agent resolved the FDA infant-formula recall in Event 05, it traversed COLD_CHAIN_TELEMETRY, LOT_TRACE, STORE_INVENTORY_POSITION, RECEIVING_EVENT, and DIM_CUSTOMER through the SCML + CXML semantic layers — producing the 208-unit, 29-customer scope in under 4 minutes.

Entity: Category

  • Description. A merchandising category — the grouping by which merchants plan, buy, price, and report. Categories form a hierarchy (department → class → subclass). Every SKU rolls up through this hierarchy.
  • SOR mapping. Typically from ERP master data (SAP MM, Oracle Retail Merchandising) via Mirrored Database or Data Pipeline. Enriched with competitor-category definitions from third-party data.
  • Agent decision use. Category anchors most RC agents. Price-recommend agents scope to a category; assortment-optimize agents produce category-level assortment; markdown-cadence agents reason per category.
  • Situation assessment. Combined with Store and Competitive Signal, Category assessments identify margin exposure where a specific category at specific stores is underperforming peer cohorts.
  • Example decisions. Re-price in category; shift shelf space between categories; re-negotiate supplier cost for a category; adjust category's markdown trigger threshold.

Entity: SKU

  • Description. Stock-keeping unit — the lowest-level merchandise identifier with unique attributes (size, color, pack, supplier). The atomic unit of assortment, pricing, and inventory.
  • SOR mapping. Item master from ERP (SAP, Oracle), POS master files, supplier catalogs. Mirrored Database for core master; Dataflow Gen2 for supplier catalog enrichment.
  • Agent decision use. SKU-level reasoning dominates RC agents. Demand-sensing produces SKU-store-day forecasts; markdown agents recommend per-SKU cadence; replenishment agents reason per SKU-store pair.
  • Situation assessment. SKU combined with Inventory Position and Demand Signal produces stock-out or over-stock assessments. SKU plus Competitive Signal surfaces pricing vulnerability.
  • Example decisions. Reorder SKU; clearance this SKU; substitute with alternate SKU; discontinue SKU; shift SKU between stores.

Entity: Store

  • Description. A physical or digital retail location. Has attributes (size, format, cluster, geography, demographics) that modulate how every other RC decision applies.
  • SOR mapping. Store master from ERP, real-estate systems, labor planning systems. Mirrored Database typical. Operational state (open/closed, hours, manager-on-duty) via Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Store scopes almost every RC decision. Store-operations agents reason at store level; BOPIS agents route per store; markdown agents tune per-store sell-through.
  • Situation assessment. Store plus Shift Summary plus Inventory Position yields store-performance assessments. Store plus Customer cohort yields trade-area assessments.
  • Example decisions. Allocate inventory to store; price promote at store-cluster; change store labor schedule; flag store for operational review.

Entity: Supplier

  • Description. A supplying entity (manufacturer, wholesaler, distributor) with commercial terms, performance history, and product-category scope. Supports supplier programs and compliance requirements.
  • SOR mapping. Supplier master from procurement (SAP Ariba, Coupa, Ivalua), ERP vendor master. Mirrored Database for master, Data Pipeline for performance scorecards, external feeds for risk and sustainability signals.
  • Agent decision use. Supplier anchors provenance, performance, and risk agents. Recall agents trace through Supplier; sustainability agents attest at Supplier level; contract-risk agents score Supplier credit and continuity risk.
  • Situation assessment. Supplier plus Shipment Track plus SKU produces supply-continuity assessments; Supplier plus Lot produces recall-scope assessments.
  • Example decisions. Switch to alternate supplier; escalate supplier for performance review; redirect shipment; initiate supplier recall workflow.

Entity: Shipment

  • Description. A movement of goods from one node to another — supplier to DC, DC to store, DC to customer (for DTC). Carries tracking, ETA, and exception data.
  • SOR mapping. TMS (Blue Yonder, Manhattan TMS, Oracle Transportation), WMS outbound, carrier APIs. Eventstream for real-time events, Data Pipeline for batch manifests.
  • Agent decision use. Shipment-tracking agents produce ETA updates; exception agents flag delayed or damaged shipments; routing agents suggest rerouting.
  • Situation assessment. Shipment plus Inventory Position plus Store produces fulfillment-risk assessments; Shipment exceptions plus Supplier context isolate chronic supplier issues.
  • Example decisions. Expedite shipment; reroute to alternate store; hold at DC; claim carrier damages.

Entity: Inventory Position

  • Description. On-hand quantity of a SKU at a node (store, DC, in-transit) at a point in time. Time-indexed; inventory reasons about historical and current state.
  • SOR mapping. WMS (Manhattan, Blue Yonder, SAP EWM), POS for store on-hand, ERP for DC positions. Mirrored Database where available; Eventstream for real-time movements.
  • Agent decision use. The most queried RC entity. Replenishment agents read position continuously; BOPIS agents check position at order time; shrink agents compare theoretical vs actual.
  • Situation assessment. Inventory Position plus Demand Signal drives stock-out predictions; plus Competitive Signal and Price drives markdown decisions; plus Shipment drives allocation choices.
  • Example decisions. Reorder to target; transfer between stores; trigger markdown; flag shrink variance for investigation.

Entity: Lot / Batch

  • Description. A lot or batch-traceable unit for serialised provenance. Required in grocery, pharmacy, and regulated retail. Foundation for recall and sustainability.
  • SOR mapping. WMS lot-tracking modules, supplier ASN (advanced shipping notice) feeds, batch-genealogy extracts. Data Pipeline for batch manifests; webhook for supplier-originated events.
  • Agent decision use. Recall agents trace impacted lots; sustainability agents attest at lot level; quality agents correlate field failures to manufacturing lots.
  • Situation assessment. Lot plus Supplier plus Store plus Customer (via transaction) produces recall scope and customer notification lists in minutes instead of days.
  • Example decisions. Trigger recall; notify affected customers; quarantine inventory at stores; initiate supplier investigation.

G.2.2 MERML — Merchandising

Schema covering pricing, promotion, assortment, and competitive response.

Entity: Assortment

  • Description. A bound set of SKUs approved for a store or store cluster, with effective dates. The answer to "what do we sell where."
  • SOR mapping. Assortment-planning systems (Oracle Retail Assortment, Blue Yonder Category), merchandising-ERP modules. Data Pipeline typical. Competitive-assortment observation from third-party data (NielsenIQ, Circana) via Dataflow Gen2.
  • Agent decision use. Assortment-optimize agents reason over assortment + sell-through to recommend SKU changes. New-store agents bootstrap assortment from peer clusters.
  • Situation assessment. Assortment plus Inventory Position plus Demand Signal produces assortment-gap assessments; Assortment plus Competitive Signal flags cannibalisation risk.
  • Example decisions. Add or remove SKU from assortment; expand assortment cluster; test SKU at regional subset before rollout.

Entity: Price

  • Description. The monetary amount asked per SKU at a store (or online) as of an effective date. Includes regular price, markdown, and promotional price history.
  • SOR mapping. Pricing systems (Oracle Retail Pricing, Blue Yonder Pricing), ERP pricing modules, POS price-book tables. Mirrored Database for current pricing; history in Lakehouse.
  • Agent decision use. Price-recommend agents produce price adjustments; elasticity agents model demand response; competitive-price agents monitor peer pricing.
  • Situation assessment. Price plus Competitive Signal plus Demand Signal produces margin-at-risk assessments; Price plus Promotion plus Transaction produces promotional-lift measurements.
  • Example decisions. Raise, lower, or hold price; match competitor; deepen markdown; end markdown early.

Entity: Promotion

  • Description. A time-bounded, scoped pricing event with specific mechanics (BOGO, percent-off, flat-off, bundled). Carries cost-to-serve and expected-lift parameters.
  • SOR mapping. Trade-promotion-management tools, promotional-calendar systems, POS promotion tables. Data Pipeline typical.
  • Agent decision use. Promotional-design agents recommend mechanics; promotion-timing agents recommend start/end; promotion-lift agents measure attributable lift.
  • Situation assessment. Promotion plus Transaction plus Demand Signal produces promotional-ROI assessments; Promotion plus Competitive Signal flags peer-response pressure.
  • Example decisions. Launch promotion; extend or shorten; deepen discount; limit to certain stores; pull due to margin erosion.

Entity: Markdown

  • Description. A permanent price reduction to clear aged or overstock inventory. Often on a stepped cadence (first markdown, second markdown, clearance).
  • SOR mapping. Markdown-management systems, ERP pricing, POS. Data Pipeline. Sell-through signals from POS via Mirroring.
  • Agent decision use. Markdown-cadence agents recommend timing and depth; sell-through-prediction agents forecast remaining lifecycle.
  • Situation assessment. Markdown plus Inventory Position plus Demand Signal produces margin-protection assessments. Markdown history plus seasonal Pattern produces cadence-tuning insights.
  • Example decisions. Trigger markdown; escalate to clearance; hold at current level; donate unsold.

Entity: Competitive Signal

  • Description. Observable competitor pricing, assortment, and promotion data. Usually third-party-sourced; sometimes from competitive-intelligence scraping programs.
  • SOR mapping. Third-party data (NielsenIQ, Circana, SimilarWeb), scraping services, loyalty-panel data. Dataflow Gen2 pull.
  • Agent decision use. Competitive-response agents compare our pricing, promotion, and assortment to peer. Competitive-monitoring agents flag sustained competitor moves.
  • Situation assessment. Competitive Signal plus Price plus Promotion drives competitive-response assessments; plus Market Share signals flags competitive pressure by category.
  • Example decisions. Match competitor; hold line; initiate counter-promotion; escalate to category review.

G.2.3 CXML — Customer Experience

Schema covering customer identity, loyalty, interaction, transaction, and preference.

Entity: Customer

  • Description. A resolved customer identity across channels (POS, e-commerce, app, loyalty, service). Integrates multiple source identities into one canonical person. Cross-Practice concept — appears in RC, TH, and TMT with Practice-specific attributes.
  • SOR mapping. Loyalty platforms (Kobie, Cheetah, Oracle CrowdTwist), e-commerce (Commerce Cloud, Shopify), POS, MarTech (Adobe, Salesforce), CRM. Mirrored Database plus identity-resolution agents.
  • Agent decision use. Customer anchors CX-side agents. Next-best-action agents query Customer for recent interactions; personalisation agents produce per-Customer recommendations.
  • Situation assessment. Customer plus Loyalty plus Transaction yields value-tier assessments; plus Interaction plus Preference yields service-priority assessments.
  • Example decisions. Extend retention offer; escalate service case; personalise communication; opt-in to research cohort; flag fraud investigation.

Entity: Loyalty Member

  • Description. Customer's loyalty-program membership with tier, points/miles balance, earn/burn history, and benefits eligibility.
  • SOR mapping. Loyalty ledger (proprietary, Tibco-backed, or SaaS). Mirrored Database plus real-time Eventstream for point events.
  • Agent decision use. Loyalty-economics agents model member value; tier-management agents recommend tier actions; redemption agents optimize offer timing.
  • Situation assessment. Loyalty Member plus Transaction plus Preference produces lifetime-value assessments; plus Interaction produces disengagement-risk assessments.
  • Example decisions. Bump tier; issue targeted bonus; expire dormant points; recover lapsing member.

Entity: Interaction

  • Description. A single touchpoint with the customer — web session, app session, service call, in-store visit, email open, chat. Time-stamped, channel-attributed.
  • SOR mapping. Clickstream (Adobe Analytics, Google Analytics), service tickets, call-center systems, email platforms. Eventstream for real-time, Data Pipeline for batched aggregates.
  • Agent decision use. Interaction context informs personalisation agents, service-prioritisation agents, and journey-stage agents.
  • Situation assessment. Interaction pattern across channels produces journey-stage and intent assessments; anomalous interaction flags fraud or abuse.
  • Example decisions. Serve next-best-action; surface contextual help; escalate service; suppress marketing.

Entity: Transaction

  • Description. A purchase event — line items, amounts, payment method, channel, store (or digital). The highest-volume RC entity.
  • SOR mapping. POS (NCR, Oracle Retail, Toshiba), e-commerce order tables, marketplace settlement feeds. Mirrored Database for transactional writes; Eventstream for real-time POS events.
  • Agent decision use. Transaction is the primary measurable outcome. Attribution agents tie decisions to transaction dollars; fraud agents inspect anomalous transactions; market-basket agents mine co-purchase patterns.
  • Situation assessment. Transaction plus Customer plus Interaction produces conversion-funnel assessments; plus Inventory Position produces forecast-accuracy measurements.
  • Example decisions. Attribute revenue to campaign; investigate fraud; include in market-basket recommendation; trigger loyalty benefit.

Entity: Preference

  • Description. Declared or derived customer preferences — communication channel, frequency, topic interests, substitution allowances, sustainability priorities.
  • SOR mapping. Preference centers, MarTech profiles, service-case notes. Data Pipeline plus derived-preference agents that infer from behavior.
  • Agent decision use. Personalisation agents select channel and cadence via Preference; substitution agents choose alternates per Preference; privacy-respect agents suppress undesired communication.
  • Situation assessment. Preference plus Interaction plus Customer yields respect-consent assessments; plus Transaction yields declared-vs-revealed-preference analysis.
  • Example decisions. Choose channel for outreach; select substitution when item unavailable; suppress a campaign; suggest sustainable alternative.

Entity: Session

  • Description. An in-channel session with sequence-of-events context — landing, navigation, cart-add, checkout, abandonment. Short-lived; analyzed in aggregate.
  • SOR mapping. Web analytics, app telemetry, POS visit sessions. Eventstream heavy.
  • Agent decision use. Session-state agents drive real-time next-action; abandonment-recovery agents trigger post-session messaging; session-anomaly agents flag fraud patterns.
  • Situation assessment. Session plus Interaction plus Customer produces engagement-quality assessments; plus Transaction produces conversion-attribution.
  • Example decisions. Serve abandonment offer; route to service; block suspected fraud session; surface personalised content mid-session.

G.3 Healthcare & Life Sciences (HLS) Practice Schemas

HLS has three sub-segments (Payer, Provider, Life Sciences) with distinct schemas. Below covers the key entities per sub-segment.

G.3.1 Payer schemas (MemberML, ClaimML, UtilizationML)

Entity: Member

  • Description. A health-plan member — enrolled individual with plan, benefits, eligibility period, and demographic attributes. Often spans commercial, Medicare Advantage, or Medicaid lines of business.
  • SOR mapping. Enrollment systems, eligibility platforms, state Medicaid files. Mirrored Database plus compliance-gated ingestion with Purview PHI classification from Bronze.
  • Agent decision use. Member-360 agents consolidate across claims, pharmacy, behavioral; utilization-management agents evaluate prior-authorization requests for the Member.
  • Situation assessment. Member plus Claim plus Care Gap Indicator produces star-rating and HEDIS readiness assessments; plus Social-Determinants produces health-equity opportunity assessments.
  • Example decisions. Approve or defer prior-authorization; enroll in care-management program; close care gap; outreach for wellness.

Entity: Claim

  • Description. A claim-for-payment from provider to payer with diagnosis codes, procedure codes, amounts billed, adjudication status, and denial reasons. High-volume, high-value.
  • SOR mapping. Core claim-adjudication system (proprietary or SaaS). Mirrored Database where possible; Data Pipeline for batch adjudication feeds. Purview classification for PHI at Bronze.
  • Agent decision use. Claim-triage agents route claims; denial-prediction agents flag likely denials pre-adjudication; fraud-waste-abuse agents score suspicious claims.
  • Situation assessment. Claim plus Authorization plus Provider Contract produces contract-compliance assessments; plus Member history produces medical-necessity context.
  • Example decisions. Pay, pend, or deny claim; route to investigation; apply contract rate; recover overpayment.

Entity: Authorization

  • Description. A prior-authorization or service-authorization request with clinical justification, urgency, and outcome. Governs pre-service medical necessity.
  • SOR mapping. UM platform, clinical-decision-support tools, provider-portal submissions. Data Pipeline plus webhook for real-time submissions.
  • Agent decision use. UM-agent evaluates against clinical guidelines; drafts approval or request-for-additional-info; escalates to medical director when needed. HITL gate at approval.
  • Situation assessment. Authorization plus Member plus Claim history produces medical-necessity context; plus Provider profile identifies unusual-practice patterns.
  • Example decisions. Approve authorization; pend for additional information; deny with appeal rights; escalate to medical director review.

Entity: UM Case

  • Description. A utilization-management case that aggregates authorizations, claims, and clinical context for a specific care episode or program.
  • SOR mapping. UM workflow systems, case-management platforms. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. UM-case agents maintain case state; recommend next clinical reviewer action; suggest care-management enrollment.
  • Situation assessment. UM Case plus Member plus utilization pattern produces program-eligibility assessments; plus care-quality scores produces outcome-likelihood assessments.
  • Example decisions. Enroll in care management; authorize additional services; transition to palliative; initiate discharge-planning.

Entity: Provider Contract

  • Description. The contracted relationship between payer and provider — reimbursement terms, quality incentives, referral networks, authorization requirements. Often complex with carve-outs.
  • SOR mapping. Contract-management systems, provider data management (PDM). Data Pipeline; limited real-time need.
  • Agent decision use. Contract-compliance agents evaluate claims against contracted terms; network-adequacy agents assess member access.
  • Situation assessment. Provider Contract plus Claim plus Member access produces network-adequacy and value-based-care assessments.
  • Example decisions. Apply contract rate; flag out-of-contract utilization; credentialing-review trigger; negotiation priority.

G.3.2 Provider schemas (PatientML, EncounterML, OrderML)

Entity: Patient

  • Description. Resolved patient identity across encounters, orders, documentation, and claims. Integrates Epic / Cerner (Oracle Health) / Meditech identities into one canonical patient. Always PHI.
  • SOR mapping. EHR (Epic Clarity, Oracle Health Cerner, Meditech) via Mirrored Database where supported, FHIR API via Azure Health Data Services. Purview PHI classification mandatory from Bronze.
  • Agent decision use. Clinical-documentation-assist agents ground on Patient record; denial-prevention agents correlate Patient with coding patterns; care-pathway agents recommend next clinical action.
  • Situation assessment. Patient plus Encounter plus Order plus Claim produces clinical-decision and revenue-cycle assessments simultaneously.
  • Example decisions. Suggest order; flag documentation gap; risk-stratify for care management; route for specialty consult.

Entity: Encounter

  • Description. A clinical encounter — inpatient stay, outpatient visit, ED visit, telehealth. Carries diagnosis, procedure, provider, and location.
  • SOR mapping. EHR encounter tables. Mirrored Database or FHIR API. ADT (admit/discharge/transfer) events via Eventstream for real-time.
  • Agent decision use. Encounter-based agents (documentation-assist, denial-prevention, LOS-optimization) activate on encounter events. Discharge-planning agents consider full-encounter context.
  • Situation assessment. Encounter plus Order plus Clinical Note produces clinical-quality and revenue-cycle assessments; plus Staffing produces throughput-capacity assessments.
  • Example decisions. Suggest discharge-planning action; flag LOS outlier; propose alternate care setting; schedule follow-up.

Entity: Order

  • Description. A clinical order — lab, imaging, medication, procedure, consult. The input to and output of most clinical workflows.
  • SOR mapping. CPOE (computerized physician order entry) within EHR. Mirrored Database for historical; Eventstream for real-time.
  • Agent decision use. Order-set-optimization agents recommend standard bundles; duplicate-order-prevention agents flag unnecessary repeats; pharmacy-optimization agents suggest formulary alternatives.
  • Situation assessment. Order plus Patient plus Clinical Note plus Cost produces value-based-care and waste-prevention assessments.
  • Example decisions. Suggest order; flag duplicate; propose formulary alternative; expedite for critical patient.

Entity: Clinical Note

  • Description. Unstructured (or semi-structured) clinical documentation — H&P, progress notes, discharge summaries, consultant notes. Primary source of clinical nuance.
  • SOR mapping. EHR document store. FHIR DocumentReference where supported; vendor-specific extract where not. Purview classification for PHI critical.
  • Agent decision use. Documentation-assist agents (often via Dragon Copilot) draft notes from conversation; coding agents extract billing codes from notes; signal agents find relevant historical notes for case review.
  • Situation assessment. Clinical Note plus Order plus Encounter produces clinical-coherence and documentation-quality assessments.
  • Example decisions. Draft note for physician review; suggest code; flag documentation deficiency; surface historical note for decision context.

Entity: Denial

  • Description. A payment denial from payer — reason code, appeal status, recovery likelihood, root cause. Revenue-cycle-critical.
  • SOR mapping. Revenue-cycle management systems, EHR billing modules, payer 835 transaction files. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Denial-prediction agents flag likely denials pre-submission; denial-management agents route appeals; root-cause agents identify systemic denial drivers.
  • Situation assessment. Denial plus Encounter plus Order plus Claim produces pre-submission denial-risk assessments; denial pattern plus Payer produces payer-specific operational insight.
  • Example decisions. Route to appeals; rework documentation; provider education trigger; adjust standard order sets.

G.3.3 Life Sciences schemas (StudyML, RWEML, HCPML)

Entity: Study

  • Description. A clinical study — protocol, sites, enrollment target, endpoints, regulatory status. The unit of clinical-development progress.
  • SOR mapping. CTMS (Veeva Vault CTMS, Oracle Health Sciences), eTMF, clinical-data-platforms. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Enrollment-prediction agents forecast site-level enrollment; site-selection agents rank candidates; protocol-deviation agents detect adherence anomalies.
  • Situation assessment. Study plus Subject plus Site plus Event produces enrollment-trajectory and risk-signal assessments.
  • Example decisions. Open new site; close underperforming site; amend protocol; expand inclusion criteria.

Entity: Subject

  • Description. A study subject (enrolled, screened, or randomised participant) with consent, visit history, and event log. PHI under Part 11.
  • SOR mapping. EDC (Electronic Data Capture) systems, ePRO platforms, central-lab feeds. Data Pipeline; Purview PHI classification + 21 CFR Part 11 controls.
  • Agent decision use. Subject-risk-stratification agents identify dropout risk; safety-signal agents correlate adverse events; adherence agents flag protocol deviations.
  • Situation assessment. Subject plus Visit plus Event plus Lab produces safety and efficacy assessments; plus Site produces site-performance context.
  • Example decisions. Retain at-risk subject; investigate adverse event; protocol deviation notification; interim analysis trigger.

Entity: RWE Cohort

  • Description. A real-world-evidence cohort — defined patient population from claims, EHR, registry data for post-market evidence generation.
  • SOR mapping. Claims data providers (Optum, IQVIA, Komodo), EHR federations, patient registries. Data Pipeline plus Purview for multi-source PHI.
  • Agent decision use. Cohort-definition agents propose inclusion/exclusion; signal-detection agents mine for efficacy or safety patterns; comparative-effectiveness agents compare treatment arms.
  • Situation assessment. RWE Cohort plus Outcome plus Cost produces comparative-effectiveness and value assessments; plus regulatory precedent produces submission-readiness assessments.
  • Example decisions. Size cohort; refine inclusion criteria; identify signal for investigation; prepare regulatory submission.

Entity: HCP (Healthcare Professional)

  • Description. A licensed healthcare professional — physician, pharmacist, nurse practitioner — with specialty, affiliations, prescribing patterns, engagement history. Basis for commercial engagement.
  • SOR mapping. HCP master data (NPI-registry-based), commercial engagement systems (Veeva CRM), congress-attendance records. Data Pipeline plus identity-resolution for cross-system HCP.
  • Agent decision use. HCP-segmentation agents prioritize engagement; next-best-action agents recommend rep actions; compliance agents enforce aggregate-spend limits.
  • Situation assessment. HCP plus Engagement plus prescribing Signal produces engagement-effectiveness assessments; plus Aggregate Spend produces Sunshine Act compliance context.
  • Example decisions. Schedule rep call; send KOL invitation; suppress commercial outreach (compliance); invite to advisory board.

Entity: Engagement

  • Description. An interaction with an HCP — rep call, medical-science-liaison meeting, digital engagement, congress touchpoint. Commercial-effectiveness foundation.
  • SOR mapping. CRM (Veeva, Salesforce), digital platforms, medical-affairs systems. Eventstream + Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Engagement-quality agents assess interaction outcomes; next-best-action agents plan subsequent engagement; cross-channel agents orchestrate rep + MSL + digital touchpoints coherently.
  • Situation assessment. Engagement plus HCP plus Study plus prescribing Signal produces commercial-effectiveness and scientific-exchange quality assessments.
  • Example decisions. Request follow-up; deliver specific scientific content; schedule MSL; adjust engagement cadence.

Entity: Site

  • Description. A clinical-trial site — with capabilities, principal investigator, enrollment history, quality metrics. Foundation for site-selection and site-management.
  • SOR mapping. CTMS, site-feasibility platforms. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Site-selection agents rank new sites; site-health agents monitor active sites; enrollment-forecast agents produce per-site projections.
  • Situation assessment. Site plus Subject plus Event plus Protocol Deviation produces site-quality assessments.
  • Example decisions. Select site for new study; close low-performing site; schedule monitoring visit; escalate quality concern.

G.4 Energy & Resources (ER) Practice Schemas

ER has three sub-segments (Upstream Oil & Gas, Power & Utilities, Mining) with sub-segment-specific schemas.

G.4.1 Upstream Oil & Gas (AssetML, WellML, ProcessML)

Entity: Well

  • Description. A producing or injecting well with location, completion history, production rates, pressure signatures, and decline profile.
  • SOR mapping. Well-history systems (Aries, Enertia, SAP UOG), SCADA historian (OSIsoft PI, AVEVA PI, GE Proficy). Mirrored Database for master; Eventstream for telemetry.
  • Agent decision use. Production-optimization agents identify wells underperforming type-curve; workover-candidacy agents rank wells for intervention.
  • Situation assessment. Well plus Production Event plus pressure Signal produces artificial-lift-optimization and decline-acceleration assessments.
  • Example decisions. Schedule workover; adjust artificial lift; shut-in for pressure maintenance; prioritize for recompletion.

Entity: Production Event

  • Description. A volumetric measurement of oil, gas, or water produced — per well per time interval (hourly, daily). Highest-volume ER entity.
  • SOR mapping. SCADA via Eventstream; daily production allocations via Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Production-accounting agents reconcile allocations; anomaly agents flag unexpected declines; decline-curve agents forecast future production.
  • Situation assessment. Production Event plus Well plus Process Step produces operational-excellence and revenue-impact assessments.
  • Example decisions. Flag deferred production; investigate decline; update decline forecast; trigger maintenance workflow.

Entity: Asset

  • Description. A physical asset — pump, separator, compressor, tank — with location, capability, maintenance history, and digital-twin reference.
  • SOR mapping. EAM systems (IBM Maximo, SAP PM, Infor EAM), equipment master. Data Pipeline plus Mirroring.
  • Agent decision use. Predictive-maintenance agents model Asset health; dispatch-optimization agents route work orders; asset-integrity agents assess regulatory compliance.
  • Situation assessment. Asset plus Process Step plus sensor telemetry produces remaining-useful-life (RUL) and safety-risk assessments.
  • Example decisions. Schedule maintenance; order spare parts; dispatch technician; flag safety risk; retire asset.

Entity: Process Step

  • Description. A defined step in a production or processing workflow — with setpoints, actual values, permit/approval context, and safety-critical flags.
  • SOR mapping. DCS/PLC systems, process-control historians. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Process-optimization agents tune setpoints; excursion agents flag deviations; energy-efficiency agents optimize across steps.
  • Situation assessment. Process Step plus Asset plus environmental Signal produces emissions-compliance and efficiency assessments.
  • Example decisions. Adjust setpoint; flag excursion for operator review; optimize for energy; trigger emissions-reporting.

G.4.2 Power & Utilities (GridML, OutageML, MeterML)

Entity: Grid Asset

  • Description. A grid element — transformer, breaker, recloser, regulator, substation — with location, capacity, age, criticality, and health signals.
  • SOR mapping. GIS systems, OMS (outage management), SCADA. Mirrored Database for GIS; Eventstream for SCADA.
  • Agent decision use. Reliability agents rank assets for replacement; wildfire-risk agents identify vegetation-adjacent high-risk assets; load-forecast agents predict stress.
  • Situation assessment. Grid Asset plus Weather plus Load plus Wildfire Risk Zone produces outage-risk and public-safety-shutoff assessments.
  • Example decisions. Schedule vegetation management; initiate PSPS (public-safety power shut-off); replace ageing asset; load-shed.

Entity: Outage Event

  • Description. An actual or threatened service interruption — start time, affected meters, probable cause, restoration estimate.
  • SOR mapping. OMS, SCADA fault-indicator events, customer-outage reports. Eventstream heavy.
  • Agent decision use. Outage-prediction agents anticipate events; restoration-optimization agents sequence crews; customer-communication agents generate updates.
  • Situation assessment. Outage Event plus Grid Asset plus crew Location plus Customer Priority produces restoration-sequencing and regulatory-reporting assessments.
  • Example decisions. Dispatch crew; reroute power; notify affected customers; escalate to regulator.

Entity: Meter Read

  • Description. AMI-origin time-series meter reading — interval consumption per service point. Very high-volume (96 reads per meter per day at 15-min intervals).
  • SOR mapping. AMI head-end systems (Itron, Landis+Gyr, Sensus). Eventstream essential at volume.
  • Agent decision use. Demand-forecast agents aggregate readings; anomaly agents detect theft or meter failure; DER-orchestration agents coordinate with behind-meter generation.
  • Situation assessment. Meter Read plus Customer plus weather plus DER Unit produces load-flexibility and non-technical-loss assessments.
  • Example decisions. Target DER-orchestration offer; investigate meter anomaly; update load-forecast; bill correction.

Entity: DER Unit

  • Description. A distributed energy resource — rooftop solar, battery, EV charger, demand-flexible load. Part of the emerging grid-flexibility landscape.
  • SOR mapping. DERMS (distributed energy resource management systems), utility-aggregator platforms. Data Pipeline plus Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. DER-orchestration agents signal availability, schedule dispatch; settlement agents calculate participation rewards.
  • Situation assessment. DER Unit plus Grid Asset plus Load plus Market Price produces dispatch-optimization and settlement assessments.
  • Example decisions. Dispatch DER for grid support; curtail during oversupply; settle aggregator payment.

Entity: Wildfire Risk Zone

  • Description. A geospatial zone with wildfire-risk attributes — fuel load, slope, weather-risk, historical ignitions, population density.
  • SOR mapping. GIS overlays, weather services, third-party risk data. Data Pipeline for base; real-time weather via Dataflow Gen2.
  • Agent decision use. PSPS-decision agents evaluate whether to de-energise; patrol-prioritisation agents route inspection; vegetation-management agents prioritize clearing.
  • Situation assessment. Wildfire Risk Zone plus Grid Asset plus Weather plus Customer produces public-safety-shutoff trade-off assessments.
  • Example decisions. Initiate PSPS; prioritize vegetation management; dispatch patrol; pre-position crews.

G.4.3 Mining (FleetML, OreBodyML, SiteML)

Entity: Fleet Unit

  • Description. A mining haul truck, loader, drill, or dozer with telematics, operator, maintenance state, and current task.
  • SOR mapping. Fleet-management systems (Caterpillar MineStar, Komatsu KOMTRAX, Modular Mining), OEM telematics. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Dispatch-optimization agents assign tasks; predictive-maintenance agents flag failures; shift-planning agents allocate across site.
  • Situation assessment. Fleet Unit plus Ore Body Cell plus Haul Cycle plus Operator produces site-productivity assessments.
  • Example decisions. Dispatch truck to shovel; schedule maintenance; re-route to avoid congestion; change operator.

Entity: Ore Body Cell

  • Description. A volumetric cell within the ore body — with grade, tonnage, recovery factor, mined/unmined status.
  • SOR mapping. Block-model databases (Micromine, Maptek Vulcan, Hexagon), mine-planning systems. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Mine-plan-optimization agents sequence extraction; grade-control agents reconcile planned vs actual; recovery agents optimize processing decisions.
  • Situation assessment. Ore Body Cell plus Dispatch Event plus Haul Cycle plus processing yield produces reconciliation and recovery assessments.
  • Example decisions. Prioritise cell for extraction; adjust processing recipe; reconcile grade estimate.

Entity: Dispatch Event

  • Description. A fleet-management-system assignment of a Fleet Unit to a task — load, haul, dump, tram — with expected and actual cycle time.
  • SOR mapping. Fleet-management systems. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Dispatch-optimization agents evaluate real-time task assignments; queue-minimisation agents reduce shovel idle.
  • Situation assessment. Dispatch Event plus Fleet Unit plus Haul Cycle produces cycle-time and productivity assessments.
  • Example decisions. Reassign truck; override dispatch; expedite maintenance to restore unit to service.

Entity: Haul Cycle

  • Description. A completed load-haul-dump-return cycle with GPS track, time stamps, tonnage, and fuel consumption.
  • SOR mapping. Telematics + dispatch system. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Productivity-analytics agents aggregate cycles; operator-coaching agents identify training opportunities; tire-management agents correlate wear to haul routes.
  • Situation assessment. Haul Cycle plus Fleet Unit plus Operator plus route produces productivity-variance and tire-management assessments.
  • Example decisions. Coach operator; change haul route; schedule tire rotation.

G.5 Industrial & Manufacturing (AXLE) Practice Schemas — AXLEML

AXLEML is APEX's unified canonical for the broad AXLE Practice scope (Auto + Aerospace + Industrial Products + Discrete Manufacturing). Sub-models below. For the adjacent AXLE framework's 9 specialized schemas (AAML, QEML, PDML, SCML, WOSFML, DTML, CVML, ESML, WLML), cross-reference §12.9 of this book.

G.5.1 Product sub-model

Entity: Item

  • Description. A product identifier — final good, assembly, sub-assembly, component — with engineering attributes, configuration rules, and lifecycle stage.
  • SOR mapping. PLM (Siemens Teamcenter, PTC Windchill, Dassault 3DEXPERIENCE, Aras), ERP item master. Mirrored Database.
  • Agent decision use. Generative-engineering agents reason over Item constraints; feasibility agents evaluate manufacturability; configuration agents produce buildable variants.
  • Situation assessment. Item plus BOM plus ECO plus Configuration produces engineering-change-impact and build-feasibility assessments.
  • Example decisions. Approve ECO; flag feasibility issue; create variant; retire item.

Entity: BOM (Bill of Materials)

  • Description. The parent-child structure of an Item — what components make up an assembly, at what quantities, with effectivity dates.
  • SOR mapping. PLM BOM structures, ERP BOM modules. Data Pipeline; Mirrored Database where supported.
  • Agent decision use. BOM-impact agents trace engineering changes; cost-rollup agents compute manufactured cost; sourcing agents identify supplier dependencies.
  • Situation assessment. BOM plus Item plus Supplier plus Cost produces change-impact and cost-engineering assessments.
  • Example decisions. Approve BOM revision; flag supplier single-source risk; trigger cost-reduction opportunity.

Entity: ECO (Engineering Change Order)

  • Description. A controlled change to Item, BOM, or specifications with review workflow, impact analysis, and effectivity date.
  • SOR mapping. PLM change management. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Change-impact agents summarize downstream effects; approval-routing agents identify stakeholders; simulation agents test change in digital twin.
  • Situation assessment. ECO plus BOM plus Work Order plus Inventory produces change-impact assessments — what's in production, what's on order, what's in field.
  • Example decisions. Approve / reject / escalate ECO; schedule cutover; initiate field-update program.

Entity: Configuration

  • Description. A configurable-product variant specification — options, constraints, pricing impact. Relevant for configure-to-order industries.
  • SOR mapping. Configuration-management systems, CPQ (configure-price-quote). Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Configurator agents validate buildability; pricing agents compute variant price; production-planning agents sequence configured orders.
  • Situation assessment. Configuration plus Item plus Work Order plus Operation produces build-complexity and cycle-time assessments.
  • Example decisions. Accept / reject configuration; schedule into production; price variant.

G.5.2 Manufacturing sub-model

Entity: Work Order

  • Description. A manufacturing order — product to build, quantity, planned operations, resource allocations, schedule.
  • SOR mapping. MES (Plex, Siemens Opcenter, SAP ME, Rockwell, Wonderware), ERP production. Mirrored Database plus Eventstream for operation events.
  • Agent decision use. Scheduling agents sequence work orders; priority agents re-rank based on customer-commit; anomaly agents flag work orders at risk.
  • Situation assessment. Work Order plus Operation plus Quality Event plus Equipment produces cycle-time, yield, and schedule-adherence assessments.
  • Example decisions. Expedite; pause; reassign to alternate line; flag for escalation.

Entity: Operation

  • Description. A manufacturing step — the atomic unit of work performed on a Work Order. Has planned and actual durations, equipment, operator, and outcome.
  • SOR mapping. MES operation log. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. OEE agents aggregate per operation; bottleneck agents identify constraint steps; quality agents correlate defects to operations.
  • Situation assessment. Operation plus Equipment plus Operator plus Quality Event produces process-control and labor-allocation assessments.
  • Example decisions. Dispatch to alternate operation; adjust cycle time; trigger maintenance on equipment.

Entity: Quality Event

  • Description. A manufacturing quality observation — inspection result, non-conformance, SPC out-of-control, first-article-inspection outcome.
  • SOR mapping. QMS (ETQ, Sparta, Veeva QualityOne), MES quality modules, inline-inspection systems. Eventstream plus Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Quality-containment agents isolate suspect production; root-cause-analysis agents correlate to operations and materials; corrective-action agents draft 8D reports.
  • Situation assessment. Quality Event plus Work Order plus Supplier plus Lot produces containment, recall-scope, and supplier-quality assessments.
  • Example decisions. Quarantine lot; notify customer; escalate to CAPA (corrective-and-preventive action); flag supplier.

G.5.3 Aftermarket sub-model

Entity: Service Record

  • Description. A post-sale service event — customer complaint, dealer service visit, field campaign, or recall action. Links build to field experience.
  • SOR mapping. DMS (dealer-management systems), field-service platforms (ServicePower, ServiceMax), warranty systems. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Warranty-pattern agents correlate field failures to manufacturing; dealer-effectiveness agents benchmark service performance; predictive-service agents flag next service.
  • Situation assessment. Service Record plus Warranty Claim plus Part Genealogy plus Manufacturing Lot produces warranty-root-cause and dealer-effectiveness assessments.
  • Example decisions. Initiate campaign; notify dealer; adjust warranty reserve; target predictive-service outreach.

Entity: Warranty Claim

  • Description. A warranty reimbursement claim from dealer to OEM with failure code, labor, parts, and root-cause attribution.
  • SOR mapping. Warranty-management systems, dealer portals. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Fraud-detection agents screen unusual claims; root-cause-correlation agents tie claims to manufacturing conditions; supplier-recovery agents identify supplier-responsible claims.
  • Situation assessment. Warranty Claim plus Part Genealogy plus Service Record plus Supplier produces supplier-recovery and recall-scoping assessments.
  • Example decisions. Approve claim; flag for investigation; recover from supplier; trigger engineering review.

Entity: Part Genealogy

  • Description. The traceability chain from raw material through manufactured component to installed position in a specific end-product vehicle or unit.
  • SOR mapping. MES serial-track-and-trace, supplier component IDs, dealer install records. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Recall-scoping agents identify exact impacted units; supplier-investigation agents trace failure to lot; warranty agents correlate field failure to part provenance.
  • Situation assessment. Part Genealogy plus Quality Event plus Warranty Claim plus Customer produces recall-scope and customer-notification assessments.
  • Example decisions. Scope recall; notify affected customers; quarantine remaining lot; investigate supplier.

G.5.4 Connected sub-model

Entity: Telemetry

  • Description. In-service product telemetry — vehicle CAN data, equipment sensor data, fleet-management feeds. Very high-volume.
  • SOR mapping. OEM telematics platforms, third-party fleet services (Webfleet, Samsara, Geotab). Eventstream at high volume.
  • Agent decision use. Health-scoring agents rank assets; usage-pattern agents feed predictive service; fleet-optimization agents dispatch.
  • Situation assessment. Telemetry plus Item plus Service Record plus DTC Event produces in-service-health and warranty-forecast assessments.
  • Example decisions. Schedule service; dispatch mobile tech; flag anomaly; update RUL estimate.

Entity: OTA Deployment

  • Description. An over-the-air software update with version, targeted vehicles/units, rollout phase, and success metrics.
  • SOR mapping. OTA platforms (OEM-proprietary or vendor-based). Data Pipeline + webhook for rollout events.
  • Agent decision use. Rollout-orchestration agents stage deployments; regression-detection agents compare pre-vs-post telemetry.
  • Situation assessment. OTA Deployment plus Telemetry plus DTC Event produces rollout-health assessments.
  • Example decisions. Pause deployment; expand cohort; roll back; escalate regression.

Entity: DTC Event (Diagnostic Trouble Code)

  • Description. A fault code raised by in-service product — DTC identifier, timestamp, frequency, severity. The signal of in-service issues.
  • SOR mapping. Telematics DTC feeds, dealer-scan-tool uploads. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. DTC-cluster agents detect emerging-issue patterns; severity agents prioritize response; recall-trigger agents flag when DTC volume warrants campaign.
  • Situation assessment. DTC Event plus Telemetry plus Service Record plus Warranty Claim produces emerging-issue-detection and campaign-scoping assessments.
  • Example decisions. Initiate TSB (technical service bulletin); launch campaign; expedite engineering investigation; update diagnostic guidance.

G.6 Technology, Media & Telecom (TMT) Practice Schemas

TMT has three sub-segments: TEC (technology vendors and internal enterprise), MED (media and entertainment), TEL (telecommunications).

G.6.1 TMT-TEC schemas (DeveloperML, ProductUsageML)

Entity: Developer

  • Description. An internal software engineer — with role, tenure, team, repository permissions, recent contribution history. Foundation for developer-productivity analytics.
  • SOR mapping. HR systems, GitHub Enterprise, identity platforms. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Productivity agents (Copilot / custom) ground on Developer context; onboarding agents identify skill gaps; code-review agents route based on expertise.
  • Situation assessment. Developer plus Code Artifact plus Commit History plus incident data produces productivity-trend and knowledge-concentration assessments.
  • Example decisions. Pair with senior; route review; suggest training; identify key-person risk.

Entity: Code Artifact

  • Description. A unit of code — function, class, module, repository — with ownership, complexity, test coverage, and change frequency.
  • SOR mapping. GitHub Enterprise, Azure DevOps, CI/CD systems. Data Pipeline plus webhook for PRs.
  • Agent decision use. Code-review agents ground on Code Artifact history; complexity agents flag technical-debt candidates; test-coverage agents recommend test additions.
  • Situation assessment. Code Artifact plus Developer plus Incident produces ownership-risk and quality assessments.
  • Example decisions. Prioritise refactor; flag missing tests; suggest review reassignment.

Entity: Product Usage Event

  • Description. A customer's use of a software product — feature invoked, session duration, error encountered. The telemetry of software product analytics.
  • SOR mapping. Product telemetry platforms, customer-success platforms. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Adoption agents identify under-used features; expansion-opportunity agents flag upsell candidates; churn-prediction agents detect declining engagement.
  • Situation assessment. Product Usage Event plus Customer plus Support Ticket produces customer-health assessments.
  • Example decisions. Outreach to at-risk customer; offer feature training; route to account team; flag churn risk.

G.6.2 TMT-MED schemas (ContentML, AudienceML, RightsML)

Entity: Title

  • Description. A piece of content — film, TV series, documentary, live event — with metadata, cast, genre, rating, and release windows.
  • SOR mapping. DAMs, content-management systems, metadata services (IMDb, proprietary). Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Programming agents recommend scheduling; rights agents check availability by market; personalisation agents match Title to Audience.
  • Situation assessment. Title plus Rights Window plus Audience Cohort plus Viewing Event produces programming-ROI assessments.
  • Example decisions. Schedule premiere; extend promotional window; license additional markets; retire from catalog.

Entity: Episode

  • Description. An individual installment of episodic content — season, episode number, run time, metadata. Foundation of episodic engagement tracking.
  • SOR mapping. Catalogue systems. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Drop-off agents identify episodes where viewers churn; binge-pattern agents recognize high-engagement series.
  • Situation assessment. Episode plus Viewing Event plus Audience Cohort produces engagement-quality assessments.
  • Example decisions. Recommend next episode; prompt viewer; optimize promotional placement.

Entity: Audience Cohort

  • Description. A defined group of viewers — demographic, behavioral, or preference-based. Basis for personalisation and advertising.
  • SOR mapping. DMPs, first-party CRM, third-party audience data. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Personalisation agents match Content to Cohort; advertising agents target campaigns.
  • Situation assessment. Audience Cohort plus Viewing Event plus Title produces cohort-level content-engagement assessments.
  • Example decisions. Target recommendation; commission new content for cohort; adjust advertising campaign.

Entity: Rights Window

  • Description. A licensing arrangement — content, territory, window (SVOD, AVOD, theatrical, broadcast), effective dates, exclusivity.
  • SOR mapping. Rights-management systems. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Rights-compliance agents enforce availability; rights-optimization agents identify re-licensing or exploitation opportunities.
  • Situation assessment. Rights Window plus Title plus Territory plus Viewing Event produces rights-utilisation and licensing-opportunity assessments.
  • Example decisions. License renewal; restrict availability; pursue additional territory; retire from catalog.

Entity: Viewing Event

  • Description. An individual watch session — user, Title or Episode, duration watched, device, moment-level engagement. Highest-volume MED entity.
  • SOR mapping. Streaming platform telemetry. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Personalisation agents; engagement-tracking agents; advertising-impression agents.
  • Situation assessment. Viewing Event plus Audience Cohort plus Title plus Session produces engagement and completion assessments.
  • Example decisions. Serve next recommendation; trigger in-session message; measure campaign reach.

G.6.3 TMT-TEL schemas (NetworkML, SubscriberML, ServiceML)

Entity: Network Element

  • Description. A network component — cell site, router, switch, optical node — with location, capacity, software version, and health state.
  • SOR mapping. NMS (network management systems), Cisco Crosswork, Nokia / Ericsson OSS. Eventstream + Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Network-incident-triage agents correlate Element events to root cause; capacity-planning agents forecast load.
  • Situation assessment. Network Element plus Alarm plus subscriber Impact produces incident-severity and customer-impact assessments.
  • Example decisions. Dispatch field; reroute traffic; schedule maintenance; escalate incident.

Entity: Alarm

  • Description. A fault or performance event from a Network Element — severity, affected service, duration, restoration status.
  • SOR mapping. NMS alarm streams. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Alarm-correlation agents group related alarms; noise-reduction agents suppress known cascades; root-cause agents rank probable causes.
  • Situation assessment. Alarm plus Network Element plus Subscriber plus Truck Roll Event produces incident-lifecycle assessments.
  • Example decisions. Acknowledge alarm; investigate root cause; dispatch truck; auto-remediate.

Entity: Subscriber

  • Description. A telecom customer — residential or business — with services, plan, tenure, payment, and network-experience attributes. Often multi-service.
  • SOR mapping. BSS (Amdocs, Netcracker), CRM, provisioning systems. Mirrored Database.
  • Agent decision use. Customer-care-assist agents ground on Subscriber; churn-prediction agents evaluate Subscriber context; retention agents target offers.
  • Situation assessment. Subscriber plus Service plus Alarm plus Truck Roll produces customer-experience assessments.
  • Example decisions. Proactive outreach; service credit; dispatch tech; offer upgrade.

Entity: Service

  • Description. A service instance for a Subscriber — plan, features, provisioning state, billing, SLA. Often many per Subscriber.
  • SOR mapping. Order-management, activation, billing. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Provisioning agents detect stuck orders; billing agents identify dispute patterns; upsell agents identify Service-expansion candidates.
  • Situation assessment. Service plus Subscriber plus Usage plus Alarm produces service-quality assessments.
  • Example decisions. Resolve stuck order; refund billing issue; recommend upgrade; disconnect.

Entity: Truck Roll Event

  • Description. A field-technician dispatch — location, issue category, resolution, actual-vs-estimated duration. Cost-center and customer-experience driver.
  • SOR mapping. Field-service management systems. Eventstream + Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Diagnostic agents pre-screen truck rolls to reduce unnecessary dispatch; routing agents optimize crew assignment.
  • Situation assessment. Truck Roll Event plus Alarm plus Subscriber plus Service produces dispatch-effectiveness and cost assessments.
  • Example decisions. Dispatch crew; resolve remotely; reschedule; escalate to repair team.

G.7 Travel & Hospitality (TH) Practice Schemas

TH's foundational schema is TravelerML (the resolved traveler identity). Other schemas cover operations, loyalty, and revenue.

G.7.1 TravelerML — the unified traveler

Entity: Traveler

  • Description. Resolved traveler identity — integrates PSS, loyalty, operational, and digital identities into one canonical person. Cross-Practice concept: related to RC Customer and TMT Subscriber but with travel-specific attributes.
  • SOR mapping. PSS (Sabre, Amadeus, Navitaire), loyalty ledger, PMS (Opera, Protel), CRM. Mirrored Database plus identity-resolution.
  • Agent decision use. Traveler anchors every customer-facing TH agent. Disruption-recovery agents need Traveler context; personalisation agents use Traveler preferences; service-recovery agents evaluate Traveler value.
  • Situation assessment. Traveler plus Journey plus Loyalty Status plus recent Interaction produces re-accommodation-priority and personalised-service assessments.
