  • Example decisions. Prioritise re-accommodation; personalise outreach; approve goodwill credit; upgrade upon availability.

Entity: Identity

  • Description. A source-system identity that maps to a Traveler — one Traveler may have 3–8 Identity records across PSS, loyalty, operations, digital. Persistent after resolution.
  • SOR mapping. Source-system identity records. Mirrored Database + dedicated resolution agents.
  • Agent decision use. Identity-resolution agents match records; audit agents explain resolution decisions; merge-control agents gate ambiguous matches.
  • Situation assessment. Identity patterns across a single Traveler produce data-quality and operational-fragmentation assessments.
  • Example decisions. Merge identities; flag ambiguous match for review; update preferences centrally.

Entity: Preference

  • Description. Traveler preferences — meal, seat, room type, loyalty tier benefits, communication channel. Declared and derived.
  • SOR mapping. Loyalty profiles, booking-system profile fields, in-app preference centers. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Personalisation agents apply Preference to journey; pre-arrival agents notify relevant staff; service-recovery agents respect Preference in alternatives.
  • Situation assessment. Preference plus Journey plus Loyalty Status produces personalised-service assessments.
  • Example decisions. Assign preferred seat; pre-stock preferred minibar; route to preferred staff member.

Entity: Journey

  • Description. A complete trip — origin, destination, segments (flights / stays / activities), dates, companions. The unit of traveler experience planning.
  • SOR mapping. PNR / booking records, OPUS systems, reservation APIs. Data Pipeline plus Eventstream for booking changes.
  • Agent decision use. Journey-stage agents know where in trip; upsell agents target appropriate products; disruption agents scope affected Journeys.
  • Situation assessment. Journey plus Traveler plus Disruption Event plus Loyalty Status produces re-accommodation and recovery-offer assessments.
  • Example decisions. Offer upgrade; proactive rebook; send update; target ancillary.

Entity: Loyalty Status

  • Description. Traveler's loyalty-program standing — tier, lifetime value, qualifying activity, elite benefits. Powers service differentiation.
  • SOR mapping. Loyalty ledger. Mirrored Database plus Eventstream for status changes.
  • Agent decision use. Prioritisation agents rank Traveler actions; benefit-application agents enforce tier benefits; retention agents target at-risk high-tier.
  • Situation assessment. Loyalty Status plus Journey plus Interaction produces customer-priority assessments.
  • Example decisions. Extend courtesy; expedite service; target retention; offer strategic upgrade.

G.7.2 OpsML — operational events

Entity: Flight

  • Description. A scheduled or operating airline flight — route, aircraft, crew, schedule, load factor, ops state. Foundation of airline operations.
  • SOR mapping. Ops-control systems (Sabre Movement Manager, AIMS, IFS), PSS, crew systems. Eventstream for events, Mirrored for master.
  • Agent decision use. Disruption-recovery agents reason over Flight network; gate-management agents optimize turn; crew agents match duty.
  • Situation assessment. Flight plus crew availability plus weather plus Traveler manifest produces operational-recovery assessments.
  • Example decisions. Delay; cancel; substitute aircraft; reassign crew; re-accommodate pax.

Entity: Stay

  • Description. A hotel stay — property, room, check-in/out, guest, rate, ancillary usage. Foundation of hospitality operations.
  • SOR mapping. PMS (Opera Cloud, Protel), CRS. Mirrored Database.
  • Agent decision use. Pre-arrival agents prepare; in-stay agents personalise; housekeeping optimization agents route.
  • Situation assessment. Stay plus Traveler plus Preference plus property capacity produces service-personalisation assessments.
  • Example decisions. Upgrade; welcome amenity; expedite housekeeping; flag service issue.

Entity: Disruption Event

  • Description. An operational disruption — weather cancellation, mechanical, crew shortage, ATC delay. Triggers recovery workflows.
  • SOR mapping. Ops systems, weather feeds, ATC-status feeds. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Recovery-plan agents produce re-accommodation options; proactive-communication agents notify affected travelers; resource-reallocation agents reassign crew and aircraft.
  • Situation assessment. Disruption Event plus Flight plus Traveler plus Crew plus partner availability produces recovery-sequencing assessments.
  • Example decisions. Initiate recovery plan; prioritize traveler class; schedule partner space; update communications.

Entity: Re-accommodation

  • Description. An action taken during disruption recovery — rebook, reroute, hotel voucher, compensation. Tracked for traveler-impact and financial settlement.
  • SOR mapping. Ops-control, compensation systems. Eventstream + Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Recovery-cost-optimization agents balance traveler satisfaction vs cost; compensation-policy agents enforce regulatory obligations.
  • Situation assessment. Re-accommodation plus Disruption Event plus Loyalty Status plus historical patterns produces cost-and-satisfaction assessments.
  • Example decisions. Offer rebook option; authorize voucher; decline request; escalate edge case.

Entity: Gate Event

  • Description. A gate-operations event — aircraft on-gate, boarding started, gate-change, departure. Drives on-time performance and traveler experience.
  • SOR mapping. Airport-ops systems, turn-management. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Turn-optimization agents reduce ground time; gate-assignment agents balance airport load.
  • Situation assessment. Gate Event plus Flight plus crew ready plus aircraft ready produces turn-performance assessments.
  • Example decisions. Expedite boarding; change gate; hold for connecting; schedule maintenance.

G.7.3 LoyaltyML & RevenueML

Entity: Loyalty Member — equivalent to RC Loyalty Member with TH-specific attributes (elite status, lifetime miles, status-qualification progress).

Entity: Earning Event

  • Description. A loyalty-point or mile earning transaction — flight, stay, partner, co-brand credit card. The program's fuel.
  • SOR mapping. Loyalty ledger, partner-integration feeds, co-brand card feeds. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Earning-accuracy agents verify partner settlements; promotion agents identify eligibility; fraud agents detect anomalous earning patterns.
  • Situation assessment. Earning Event plus Member plus Programme Rule produces earning-correctness and program-economics assessments.
  • Example decisions. Approve / reverse earning; flag for review; adjust partner settlement.

Entity: Redemption

  • Description. A loyalty-point or mile redemption — award flight, upgrade, hotel stay, partner product. Balance-sheet liability release.
  • SOR mapping. Loyalty ledger, award-inventory systems. Eventstream.
  • Agent decision use. Redemption-optimization agents match member requests to award inventory; valuation agents price strategic redemptions; liability agents monitor outstanding balance risk.
  • Situation assessment. Redemption plus Member plus inventory context produces redemption-satisfaction and liability assessments.
  • Example decisions. Approve redemption; offer alternative; adjust award pricing; flag liability concentration.

Entity: Fare Ladder

  • Description. A structured set of fare classes and prices for a specific market pair at a point in time. Foundation of airline revenue management.
  • SOR mapping. Revenue-management systems (PROS, Sabre Revenue Optimizer). Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Dynamic-pricing agents propose fare-ladder adjustments; competitive-monitoring agents flag peer moves.
  • Situation assessment. Fare Ladder plus Competitive Signal plus booking velocity produces pricing-opportunity assessments.
  • Example decisions. Raise / lower fares; close / open fare class; match competitor; protect premium.

Entity: Yield Signal

  • Description. Booking velocity and mix signals that indicate demand strength — pace vs forecast, class mix, booking horizon distribution.
  • SOR mapping. Revenue-management, GDS / NDC data, internal bookings. Eventstream + Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Pricing agents respond to yield signals; capacity-planning agents feed aircraft / property allocation.
  • Situation assessment. Yield Signal plus Fare Ladder plus Competitive Signal plus event context produces revenue-optimization assessments.
  • Example decisions. Price response; re-allocate capacity; open special fare; flag anomaly.

G.8 Industrial & Commercial Equipment (ICE) Practice Schemas

ICE covers heavy equipment (construction / agriculture / mining-equipment OEMs), commercial vehicles, building products, industrial distribution.

G.8.1 Connected Equipment (EquipmentML)

Entity: Unit

  • Description. A piece of industrial or commercial equipment — serial number, model, configuration, current owner, warranty status, service history.
  • SOR mapping. OEM product master, registration systems, dealer-held records. Mirrored Database.
  • Agent decision use. Lifecycle agents reason over Unit stage; warranty agents evaluate coverage; attach-opportunity agents identify aftermarket targets.
  • Situation assessment. Unit plus Telemetry Event plus Service Event plus Warranty Claim produces lifecycle-value and attach-opportunity assessments.
  • Example decisions. Target aftermarket offer; warranty determination; service-upgrade offer; trade-in evaluation.

Entity: Installed Base Record

  • Description. A tracked equipment unit in service — owner, operational state, connectivity, service agreement, dealer of record.
  • SOR mapping. Dealer management systems, fleet-management platforms (VisionLink, KOMTRAX, Deere Operations Center). Data Pipeline + Mirroring.
  • Agent decision use. Fleet-intelligence agents aggregate per-owner fleet; service-planning agents schedule maintenance across installed base.
  • Situation assessment. Installed Base plus Telemetry plus Dealer produces service-program and dealer-performance assessments.
  • Example decisions. Schedule service; expand service contract; flag dealer issue; target fleet-expansion offer.

Entity: Telemetry Event

  • Description. Sensor-origin telemetry from connected equipment — hours, load factor, fuel, faults, geolocation.
  • SOR mapping. Telematics platforms (OEM-proprietary, Uptake, Trimble). Eventstream heavy.
  • Agent decision use. Health-scoring, utilisation-analytics, anomaly-detection agents.
  • Situation assessment. Telemetry plus Unit plus environment plus Fleet context produces health and utilisation assessments.
  • Example decisions. Schedule service; recommend utilisation change; flag anomaly; validate warranty claim.

Entity: Utilisation Profile

  • Description. Aggregated utilisation pattern per Unit — hours worked, load spectrum, operator behavior, geography. Derived from Telemetry.
  • SOR mapping. Derived in Silver from Telemetry Event. Computed nightly or continuously.
  • Agent decision use. Utilisation-insight agents; predictive-service interval agents; warranty-adjudication agents.
  • Situation assessment. Utilisation Profile plus Unit plus Warranty plus Service History produces attach-opportunity and warranty-adjudication assessments.
  • Example decisions. Adjust service interval; offer program upgrade; deny warranty (abuse); recommend operator training.

G.8.2 Dealer (DealerML)

Entity: Dealer

  • Description. An authorized dealer — with territory, service capability, sales performance, program participation. Complex relationship governed by dealer contract.
  • SOR mapping. OEM dealer master, DBS. Mirrored Database.
  • Agent decision use. Dealer-development agents benchmark; program-participation agents recommend opportunities; data-sharing agents govern information flow.
  • Situation assessment. Dealer plus Dealer Performance Metric plus Territory plus Programme produces dealer-health and parity assessments.
  • Example decisions. Enrol program; coach on metric; escalate performance concern; target parity intervention.

Entity: Dealer Performance Metric

  • Description. A measured attribute of dealer performance — service-attach rate, parts-stock accuracy, NPS, training compliance.
  • SOR mapping. DBS, survey systems, training platforms. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Benchmarking agents compare cohorts; coaching-recommendation agents target improvement areas.
  • Situation assessment. Performance Metric plus Dealer plus peer cohort produces dealer-cohort assessments.
  • Example decisions. Develop dealer; flag for review; recognize high performer; provide training.

Entity: Territory

  • Description. A geographic area assigned to a Dealer with exclusivity or primary-coverage rights. Foundation of channel-conflict management.
  • SOR mapping. Dealer agreements, GIS. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Channel-conflict agents identify cross-territory issues; coverage agents recommend new-dealer locations.
  • Situation assessment. Territory plus Dealer plus Installed Base plus competitor presence produces channel-optimization assessments.
  • Example decisions. Add dealer; redraw territory; resolve channel conflict; expand coverage.

Entity: Dealer-OEM Data Contract

  • Description. Governs what data may be shared between Dealer and OEM — which signals, for which purposes, with what customer consent. Essential for APEX agent-scope design.
  • SOR mapping. Legal / contract systems. Data Pipeline; changes are rare.
  • Agent decision use. Agent-scope enforcement agents enforce data-contract boundaries; compliance agents track consent state.
  • Situation assessment. Data Contract plus Dealer plus agent access request produces permission-determination assessments.
  • Example decisions. Permit / deny data access; gate agent scope; trigger contract renegotiation.

G.8.3 Aftermarket (AftermarketML)

Entity: Service Event

  • Description. A post-sale service — warranty repair, scheduled maintenance, emergency repair. Logged by Dealer with parts / labor / root cause.
  • SOR mapping. DMS service systems, dealer-uploaded events. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Warranty-correlation agents link to manufacturing; service-quality agents monitor; attach-opportunity agents flag upsell.
  • Situation assessment. Service Event plus Unit plus Warranty Claim plus Part Genealogy produces warranty-root-cause and attach-value assessments.
  • Example decisions. Escalate to engineering; recover from supplier; target aftermarket program; adjust warranty reserve.

Entity: Part Demand Signal

  • Description. Forecast signal for parts stocking at Dealer level — from Telemetry, Service History, Utilisation Profile.
  • SOR mapping. Derived in Silver; may also incorporate Dealer order history. Eventstream + Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Parts-planning agents stage inventory; dealer-stocking agents recommend order levels.
  • Situation assessment. Part Demand Signal plus Dealer plus Installed Base produces parts-availability assessments.
  • Example decisions. Stage inventory; dealer-order recommendation; flag likely shortage; target mass-order offer.

Entity: Attach Opportunity

  • Description. A derived opportunity to attach an aftermarket service or product to a Unit — e.g., service contract, extended warranty, connected-service subscription.
  • SOR mapping. Derived from Installed Base, Utilisation Profile, lifecycle stage. Silver computation.
  • Agent decision use. Aftermarket-targeting agents rank opportunities; dealer-action agents notify sales.
  • Situation assessment. Attach Opportunity plus Dealer plus Customer value produces prioritized-target assessments.
  • Example decisions. Notify dealer; present in customer portal; trigger direct offer; prioritize sales-team attention.

G.8.4 Rental (RentalML)

Entity: Rental Asset

  • Description. An equipment unit in rental inventory — with rental-specific attributes (availability, rate, condition, meter).
  • SOR mapping. Rental-management systems. Mirrored Database.
  • Agent decision use. Utilisation agents optimize fleet; pricing agents set rates; redeployment agents move across locations.
  • Situation assessment. Rental Asset plus Utilisation Window plus market Demand produces rental-utilisation assessments.
  • Example decisions. Raise / lower rate; move to high-demand location; retire from rental; promote for sale.

Entity: Rental Transaction

  • Description. A rental contract — asset, customer, start/end, rate, add-ons. Revenue event.
  • SOR mapping. Rental-management. Data Pipeline.
  • Agent decision use. Rate-realisation agents compare actuals to target; customer-segmentation agents identify strategic renters.
  • Situation assessment. Rental Transaction plus Asset plus Customer plus market rate produces rate-realisation assessments.
  • Example decisions. Approve rate; require deposit; flag customer risk; target upgrade.

Entity: Utilisation Window

  • Description. A time window of rental-asset state — on rent / idle / service / sold. Foundation of fleet-productivity metrics.
  • SOR mapping. Derived from Rental Transaction. Silver computation.
  • Agent decision use. Fleet-balance agents redeploy; sales-conversion agents target underused units.
  • Situation assessment. Utilisation Window plus Asset plus cohort produces fleet-health assessments.
  • Example decisions. Redeploy; sell; keep in rental; service.

Entity: Pricing Signal

  • Description. Local market pricing signal for rental rates — competitor rates, demand velocity, seasonal patterns.
  • SOR mapping. Competitive-rate scraping, internal booking velocity. Data Pipeline + Dataflow Gen2.
  • Agent decision use. Dynamic-pricing agents adjust rates; market-response agents identify opportunities.
  • Situation assessment. Pricing Signal plus Rental Asset plus Utilisation produces rate-optimization assessments.
  • Example decisions. Raise / lower rate; match competitor; hold.

G.9 Cross-Practice entity patterns

Several entity concepts recur across multiple Practices with Practice-specific attributes. APEX's identity-resolution discipline is what makes cross-Practice engagement coherent.

Customer / Traveler / Subscriber / Member. RC's Customer, TH's Traveler, TMT's Subscriber, HLS's Member all refer to a person or organization the enterprise serves. In cross-Practice APEX deployments (e.g., a retailer-airline co-brand loyalty program), the canonical Customer entity federates Practice-specific attributes under a single resolved identity.

Asset / Unit / Equipment. ER's Asset, AXLE's Item, ICE's Unit, RC's Store (as a physical location) all refer to tangible things the enterprise owns or serves. Cross-referencing produces holistic fleet or facility views.

Workforce / Personnel. Most Practices have a workforce dimension — RC store associates, HLS clinicians, ER operators, AXLE / ICE technicians. APEX's shared Workforce concept unifies skill, schedule, ergonomics, and training across the Practices for a client operating multiple Practices.

Supplier / Partner / Vendor. RC suppliers, AXLE suppliers, ICE suppliers, HLS providers, TMT content partners — all shared the need for performance tracking, contract compliance, and sustainability attestation. The canonical Supplier entity federates.

Transaction / Event. Every Practice has a primary transactional event — RC Transaction, HLS Claim, ER Production Event, AXLE Work Order, TH Journey, TMT Service, ICE Rental Transaction. While the entities are distinct, APEX's audit-row discipline makes cross-Practice revenue and value attribution coherent.

G.10 Five standard agent query patterns

APEX agents query entities following five recurring patterns. MCP tools exposed to agents implement these query patterns.

Entity-read — retrieve a single entity by key. Agent calls tool with entity-key; returns full-entity payload. Low-latency Direct Lake serving from Gold.

Example: get_sku(sku_id='ABC123', store_id='STR-045') returns the SKU entity with current price, inventory position, and demand forecast.

Entity-search — find entities matching multi-attribute filter. Agent calls tool with predicate; returns matched entity list.

Example: find_claims(member_id='M-789', date_range='last-30-days', status='denied') returns matching Claim entities.

Cross-entity-join — reason across two or three entities through a relationship. Agent calls tool with entity-keys and join specification; returns joined view.

Example: get_sku_inventory_suppliers(sku_id='ABC123') returns SKU with current Inventory Position across stores plus Supplier information.

Temporal-window — aggregate entity state over a time window. Agent calls tool with entity-key and time-spec; returns aggregate.

Example: get_production_rate(well_id='W-100', window='7d') returns 7-day production aggregate with day-level resolution.

Cross-Practice federation — rare but high-value. Agent queries across two Practices via the cross-Practice entity pattern.

Example: get_traveler_loyalty_across_brands(traveler_id='T-500') returns Traveler's loyalty status across airline, hotel, and retail co-brands if APEX's identity resolution federates them.

G.11 Five situation-assessment patterns

APEX agents combine entity queries to assess operational situations and recommend decisions. Five recurring assessment patterns:

Threshold-breach assessment — one entity attribute crosses a defined threshold; agent assesses severity and proposes action.

Example: Inventory Position on SKU-ABC at Store-045 falls below reorder threshold. Agent assesses demand forecast, in-transit shipments, alternative substitutes, and proposes replenishment action.

Pattern-match assessment — multi-entity signal pattern matches a known condition; agent classifies the situation and proposes pre-defined response.

Example: DTC Event pattern on connected vehicle matches known-failure signature for component X manufactured between dates Y. Agent scopes impact, proposes TSB or campaign initiation.

Correlation assessment — agent identifies causal or probabilistic link across domains that manual analysis would miss.

Example: Warranty Claim spike on aerospace engine correlates to Quality Event batch in manufacturing six months prior, correlates to Supplier component lot. Agent assembles supplier-recovery case.

Anomaly assessment — agent detects a novel pattern deviating from expected behavior; flags for human investigation.

Example: Claim submission pattern from Provider X in last 30 days deviates from historical pattern. Agent assembles anomaly report for fraud investigator.

Scenario assessment — agent explores multiple "what-if" scenarios over entities and ranks by outcome.

Example: Given Disruption Event impacting 15 Flights, agent produces 5 re-accommodation scenarios varying by traveler-priority-policy and cost envelope, ranks by combined traveler-satisfaction and cost-to-airline.

Each pattern produces an APEX audit row with the input entities, reasoning trace, and proposed decision. HITL gates at the decision boundary; human approves, overrides, or escalates. This is how APEX decision-automation actually operates.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. Entity names and schema references in this appendix are APEX IP. Do not import client-confidential entity names into APEX semantic models without explicit client authorisation and Purview classification. APEX's canonical semantic models are Deloitte IP; client-specific extensions live in the client's own Fabric tenant with IP retention governed by the two-contract model.

Appendix H

MCP Server Tools — How Agents Call Gold-Tier Data

This appendix is the seller's reference for APEX's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server tools — the interface through which agents consume Gold-tier data and invoke actions in downstream systems. It covers how MCP fits into the APEX architecture, the five Silver-to-Gold transform patterns that create the data tools serve, the five standard MCP tool patterns, and a per-Practice catalog of tools with example invocations, response shapes, and Gold-view backing.

H.1 How to read this appendix

Each tool in the per-Practice sections follows a consistent ten-part template:

  • Tool name — canonical APEX MCP tool identifier
  • Purpose — what the tool enables an agent to do, in one sentence
  • Input schema — parameters, types, required vs optional
  • Output shape — response structure returned to the agent
  • Gold view backing — the Fabric Gold artifact the tool queries
  • Silver→Gold transform — which of the five standard patterns produces the Gold view
  • Example invocation — realistic agent call with parameters
  • Example response — abbreviated JSON of what the agent receives
  • Classification carry-through — Purview labels that propagate with the response
  • Typical consumer agents — which APEX agents use this tool

Sellers use this appendix in two situations: (a) pursuit conversations where client architects ask "how does the agent actually get data" and (b) Wave 1 envisioning workshops where MCP tool scope is being defined.

H.2 MCP architecture in APEX

Model Context Protocol is an open standard (introduced by Anthropic, broadly adopted across the industry including Microsoft's Foundry) that defines how agents invoke tools and receive structured responses. In APEX, MCP is the sole interface between agents and data / action. Agents never query Fabric directly; they never call SORs directly; every data read and every state change goes through an MCP tool.

The MCP layer in the APEX stack

From top to bottom:

  1. Agent (in Foundry) — reasons, decides, invokes tools
  2. MCP tool contract — input schema (what the agent provides), output shape (what it receives), authentication scope, rate limits
  3. MCP server (hosted in Azure Container Apps or Azure Functions) — implements the tool; exposes the MCP endpoint; authenticates as a managed identity
  4. Gold view (in Fabric Warehouse or Lakehouse) — the data the tool queries via T-SQL or SQL-over-Lakehouse
  5. Silver tables (in Fabric Lakehouse) — canonical entity data feeding the Gold view
  6. Bronze tables (in Fabric Lakehouse) — raw SOR landing
  7. Source systems of record — ERP, EHR, WMS, SCADA, etc.

Every step is Fabric-native and Entra-identified. Purview classification travels with the data from Silver through Gold to the MCP tool's response to the agent's output.

Why MCP specifically

Three properties of MCP matter for APEX:

  • Model-agnostic — any agent (Foundry-hosted, Anthropic Claude, GPT-class, Gemini) can invoke the same tools. APEX tools are not bound to a specific model family.
  • Structured I/O — tool inputs and outputs are typed JSON, not free-text. This makes tool calls reproducible and auditable. The audit row captures structured inputs and outputs with no parsing ambiguity.
  • Authorisation-scoped — each MCP server runs as a managed identity with scoped permissions on the underlying Gold views. An agent calling a tool inherits the tool's scope; it cannot escalate outside the tool's boundaries.

MCP server organization in APEX

APEX groups MCP tools into servers per Practice + functional area. A typical AXLE tenant might have:

  • axle-product-mcp — tools accessing Product sub-model Gold views
  • axle-manufacturing-mcp — tools accessing Manufacturing sub-model
  • axle-aftermarket-mcp — tools accessing Aftermarket sub-model
  • axle-connected-mcp — tools accessing Connected sub-model
  • axle-action-mcp — tools invoking actions (work-order dispatch, engineering-change approvals)

Similar pattern per Practice. RC tenants have rc-scml-mcp, rc-merml-mcp, rc-cxml-mcp, rc-action-mcp. HLS tenants have hls-payer-mcp, hls-provider-mcp, hls-ls-mcp, hls-action-mcp. And so forth.

Each server is independently deployable, independently identifiable (separate managed identity), and independently rate-limited. This separation is load-bearing for governance — a compromised or misbehaving agent interacting with one MCP server cannot reach tools on another.

Tool categories

Within each MCP server, tools fall into categories:

  • Read tools — query Gold views and return data. Predominantly these. Most of this appendix.
  • Action tools — invoke a state change in a downstream system (create work-order, approve engineering change, issue refund, dispatch truck). Governed by HITL gates.
  • Evaluation tools — compute assessments over Gold data (risk score, attribution calculation, anomaly detection). Reads that involve computation.
  • Session tools — maintain per-agent-session context (remember a decision context across multiple tool calls in an orchestration).

Sellers should know that approximately 80% of APEX's MCP tools are read tools; 10% are action tools; 10% are evaluation or session tools.

H.2A Gold Views and MCP Tools — The Binding Contract

This section is the seller's reference for the most architect-asked question after "how does the agent get data" — "how exactly does a Gold view become an MCP tool, and what governs the binding?" The answer involves a specific contract pattern that Deloitte authors during Wave 2 implementation.

H.2A.1 The core relationship

A Gold view is a queryable data artifact in Fabric (Warehouse view, Lakehouse SQL endpoint table, or Eventhouse KQL function). An MCP tool is a typed agent-invocable interface hosted on an MCP server. They are not the same thing — one is data, the other is an agent-callable contract.

The MCP tool wraps the Gold view with five things the raw view cannot provide:

  1. Input schema — typed parameters agents provide
  2. Output shape — typed response agents receive
  3. Authentication + authorization — managed-identity scope evaluation
  4. Classification enforcement — Purview-aware redaction before return
  5. Auditability — every invocation writes to audit trail

Without the MCP-tool wrapper, an agent would need to write raw T-SQL or KQL against a Gold view — which is neither typed, governed, nor auditable. With the wrapper, the agent calls a typed interface and receives a typed, scoped, audited response.

H.2A.2 The binding contract — what ties a tool to a view

Every MCP tool declares its Gold-view binding explicitly. The binding specification includes:

The backing view. Exact Fabric path — workspace / warehouse-or-lakehouse / schema / view name. Example: apex-rc-gold.scml.sku_with_enrichment.

The query template. The parameterized SQL or KQL the tool runs against the view. Parameters map 1:1 to the tool's inputSchema. Example:

SQL
SELECT * FROM apex-rc-gold.scml.sku_with_enrichment
WHERE sku_id = @sku_id AND (@store_id IS NULL OR store_id = @store_id)

The classification policy. Which Purview labels on the Gold view's columns apply to the response, and how (mask, redact, pass-through based on caller identity scope).

The latency SLO. Maximum acceptable p95 query latency. If a Gold view is slow enough that the SLO is violated, the binding either materializes a faster pre-computed view or fails the tool commit-stage.

The refresh contract. How fresh the data must be. Tied to the Silver → Gold transform pattern that produces the view (see §H.3).

Version stamp. Tool version + view version + transform version. Any mismatch after a schema change generates a canary alert until the chain re-stabilizes.

H.2A.3 The Gold-to-Tool mapping model — 1:1, N:1, 1:N

Most bindings are 1:1 — one Gold view backs one MCP tool. Example: rc_gold.category backs get_category. Clean, simple, predictable.

Some bindings are N:1 — one tool reads from multiple Gold views. Example: get_sku_with_enrichment reads SKU + Price + Inventory Position + Demand Signal Gold views. This usually means the tool's backing Gold is itself a composed view (Pattern B in §H.3 — multi-entity join).

Occasionally bindings are 1:N — one Gold view supports multiple tools with different projections / filters / aggregations. Example: rc_gold.transaction_history backs both get_transaction_history (detail) and get_transaction_summary (rollup). These exist when the base Gold is authoritative and the tool difference is projection/aggregation only.

APEX's default posture: prefer 1:1. Use N:1 when performance or query complexity demands. Avoid 1:N unless the tool-projection logic is trivial (same-table aggregation).

H.2A.4 The five transform patterns → MCP tool latency mapping

The Silver → Gold transform pattern that creates the view (from §H.3) determines the tool's latency profile:

Transform patternGold view typeTool latency profileTypical tool use
Pattern A (single-entity materialization)Direct Lake Delta tableSub-500msentity-read, get_* tools
Pattern B (multi-entity join materialization)Pre-joined Delta or Warehouse view500ms–2scross-entity tools
Pattern C (temporal aggregation)Aggregated Delta (refreshed on cadence)Sub-500ms for pre-aggregated; 2-10s if computed livetemporal-window tools (get_*_history)
Pattern D (cross-domain federation)Multi-workspace joined view1–5s typicalcross-Practice tools
Pattern E (real-time reflex)Eventhouse KQL functionSub-secondreal-time get_* tools

The SLO the tool commits to IS a function of which transform pattern produced its backing view. When a client asks "why is this tool fast but that one takes 3 seconds" — the answer traces to the transform pattern, not to the tool code.

H.2A.5 The classification flow through the binding

This is the part architects scrutinize most in HLS, TMT-TEL (CPNI), and regulated-industry engagements. Walk it step by step:

  1. Data lands in Bronze from a source system with source-native classification (Epic Clarity rows are PHI; Sabre PNR rows are PII + PCI-adjacent; SAP ECC rows may be SOX-controlled).
  2. Silver canonical model preserves + enriches classification. Each canonical attribute carries a Purview sensitivity label. Derived attributes inherit the most-restrictive label among inputs.
  3. Gold view materializes with propagated classification. Every column in the Gold view is labelled. Composite columns (e.g., a derived margin-exposure flag computed from regular price + promo + cost) inherit the most-restrictive label of the inputs.
  4. MCP tool binding specifies policy per column. For each column in the Gold view's response, the tool declares: pass-through (caller sees raw value), redact (replace with [REDACTED] token), mask (hash / partial-show), or deny (omit entirely, tool returns an error).
  5. At tool invocation time, the MCP server evaluates caller identity (Entra-backed managed identity or delegated user), retrieves the identity's effective scope from Purview, intersects with the tool's classification policy, and applies the correct per-column treatment before returning.
  6. The audit row captures tool name, caller identity, parameters, response shape (classification-aware; doesn't log redacted values), and downstream effect.

A seller describing this to a CISO says: "Every MCP tool invocation is evaluated at five points: identity authentication, scope lookup, Gold-view query authorization, classification-aware column-by-column response filtering, and audit logging. Nothing reaches the agent that the identity isn't scoped to see."

H.2A.6 Versioning — how Gold views and tools evolve together

Gold views and MCP tools version together. A breaking change to either requires explicit coordination:

Additive schema change on Gold view (new column). Tool's inputSchema unchanged. Tool's outputShape may OPTIONALLY include the new column (non-breaking; agents that don't know about it ignore it). No canary required.

Type change on existing Gold column. Breaking. Requires new tool version; old tool version deprecated over 2 quarters; agents pin to specific tool version via manifest.

Classification change on existing Gold column (e.g., column was "Internal" now "Confidential"). Non-breaking to tool interface but MAY change response content for some callers (scope-dependent masking). Deploy with explicit communication to affected agent manifests.

New tool wrapping existing Gold view. Non-breaking. New tool appears in the catalog; existing agents unaffected. This is how the catalog grows.

Removal of Gold column that a tool exposes. Breaking. Triggers tool version bump + agent manifest updates.

APEX's bump-classification framework (PATCH / MINOR / MAJOR from the APEX Core methodology) applies to tools and Gold views identically. A PATCH changes neither contract; a MINOR adds optionally-consumed capability; a MAJOR breaks the interface.

H.2A.7 Worked example — get_sku binding

Concrete illustration of the full binding for one of the most-used RC tools.

Tool: rc-scml-mcp.get_sku

Input schema:

JSON
{
  "sku_id": {"type": "string", "required": true},
  "store_id": {"type": "string", "required": false,
               "description": "If provided, scopes inventory to this store"}
}

Output shape:

JSON
{
  "sku": {
    "sku_id": "string",
    "description": "string",
    "category_id": "string",
    "supplier_id": "string (classified: SupplierConfidential)",
    "regular_price": "decimal (classified: CommercialSensitive)",
    "current_price": "decimal (classified: CommercialSensitive)",
    "inventory_position": {
      "on_hand": "integer",
      "on_order": "integer",
      "stock_days_remaining": "decimal (derived)",
      "margin_exposure_flag": "enum [LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH] (derived)"
    }
  }
}

Gold view backing: apex-rc-gold.scml.sku_with_enrichment (Pattern B: multi-entity join of SKU + Price + current-inventory rollup + demand-signal rollup).

Silver → Gold transform: Pattern B; refreshed on Silver inventory updates (Data Activator rule-triggered) every 5 minutes nominal; sub-500ms rebuild.

Classification policy:

  • supplier_id: pass-through to identities with SupplierConfidential scope; masked ([REDACTED]) otherwise
  • regular_price, current_price: pass-through to identities with CommercialSensitive scope; denied to identities without
  • Other columns: pass-through to any authenticated identity with RC-tenant scope

Latency SLO: p95 ≤ 500ms.

Versioning: get_sku@v2.1.0 — current; @v2.0.x supported through end of quarter; @v1.* deprecated.

Typical caller: APEX price-recommend agent (managed identity agent-rc-price-recommend-s100) during morning category review; APEX substitution agent during BOPIS pick; Copilot Studio SKU-lookup surface for merchandiser queries.

H.2A.8 Architect conversation template

Sellers can use this template when a client architect asks how Gold-views-to-MCP-tools actually work:

  1. "Every MCP tool binds to a specific Gold view." State this upfront.
  2. "The Gold view is produced by one of five Silver → Gold transform patterns." Reference §H.3 transform patterns.
  3. "The transform pattern determines the latency SLO the tool commits to." Latency isn't arbitrary; it's architectural.
  4. "The tool wraps the view with typed input, typed output, managed-identity auth, Purview-aware response filtering, and audit logging." Five guarantees.
  5. "Most bindings are 1:1; N:1 when the tool composes multiple views; 1:N rarely and only for trivial projection differences." Clarity on shape.
  6. "Versioning follows APEX bump classification — PATCH / MINOR / MAJOR — and Gold-view changes coordinate with tool-version releases through the manifest." Operational maturity.
  7. "Because the binding is explicit, every agent decision ultimately traces through a specific tool version reading a specific Gold view at a specific refresh state at a specific classification-filter outcome." Audit row defensibility.

This framework converts abstract "the agent queries data" conversations into architect-credible specificity.

H.2A.9 Summary table — Gold view ↔ MCP tool binding

Binding dimensionWhat it specifiesFailure mode if absent
Backing view pathFabric workspace + schema + view nameTool can't find data
Input schemaTyped parametersAgent calls with garbage inputs
Output shapeTyped responseAgent can't reliably parse response
Query templateParameterized SQL/KQLTool can't translate inputs to Fabric query
Auth + scopeManaged identity + Purview lookupUnauthorized data exposure
Classification policyPer-column pass/mask/redact/denySensitive data leaks to unauthorized caller
Latency SLOp95 boundTool unusable in production
Refresh contractFreshness guaranteeStale data drives bad decisions
Version stampTool + view + transform versionsIncompatible change breaks agents silently
Audit contractPer-invocation logged fieldsNo regulator-ready evidence

H.2A.10 The one-sentence summary

An MCP tool is a typed, authenticated, classification-aware, versioned, audited wrapper around a Fabric Gold view; the wrapper is where agent invocations become governed, observable, and defensible; the Gold view is where the canonical data lives; together they form the binding contract that defines what agents can and cannot do at production scale.

H.3 The five Silver→Gold transform patterns

Every APEX Gold view is produced by one of five canonical Silver-to-Gold transform patterns. Understanding the patterns matters because each has different refresh, latency, and governance properties that sellers explain to client architects.

Pattern A: Single-entity materialisation

What it is. A Gold view that materializes one Silver entity with its full attribute set, typically with computed enrichments (derived attributes, classifications applied, timestamps normalized).

Refresh. Event-driven via Fabric Data Pipeline triggered on Silver upsert, or scheduled (hourly / daily) for lower-volume entities.

Example. rc_gold.sku — the full SKU canonical view with derived attributes (stock-days-remaining, margin-exposure-flag) that tools like get_sku return.

Classification. Entity's classification labels carry through directly to Gold.

Pattern B: Multi-entity join materialisation

What it is. A Gold view that joins two or three Silver entities — typically a primary entity with its commonly-co-queried related entities.

Refresh. Scheduled (typically hourly) unless lower-latency requirement justifies event-driven via cross-entity reflex rules.

Example. rc_gold.sku_with_inventory — joins SKU with current Inventory Position across all stores. Tool get_sku_inventory_all_stores reads this.

Classification. The most restrictive classification across source entities wins.

Pattern C: Temporal aggregation

What it is. A Gold view that computes time-window aggregates — daily sales, 7-day demand, 30-day trend — over a Silver event stream.

Refresh. Scheduled at the aggregate's natural cadence (nightly for daily aggregates; hourly for 1-hour rolling windows; streaming for minute-level).

Example. rc_gold.demand_signal_7d — rolling 7-day demand per SKU-store-day. Tool get_demand_signal reads this.

Classification. Aggregate-level classification; individual-event classifications are collapsed.

Pattern D: Cross-domain federation

What it is. A Gold view that federates entities across sub-models or Practices to support cross-domain reasoning. Rare at small scale; essential at enterprise scale.

Refresh. Event-driven where low-latency cross-domain correlation matters; scheduled otherwise.

Example. axle_gold.warranty_to_manufacturing_correlation — links Warranty Claims (Aftermarket sub-model) to Quality Events (Manufacturing sub-model) via Part Genealogy. Tool get_warranty_root_cause_context reads this.

Classification. Most restrictive classification across federated domains.

Pattern E: Real-time reflex

What it is. A KQL-based Gold "view" in Eventhouse that serves near-real-time event aggregations. Not a materialized table — a queryable function over Eventhouse data.

Refresh. Streaming — queries return current state within seconds of event arrival.

Example. er_gold.production_event_realtime — KQL function returning last-hour production rates by well. Tool get_production_rate_realtime reads this.

Classification. Real-time classification via Eventhouse policies; Purview integration via batch sync.

H.4 The five standard MCP tool patterns

The query patterns from §H.10 map to five MCP tool patterns. Each tool in the per-Practice sections follows one pattern.

Pattern 1: Entity-read

Purpose. Retrieve a single canonical entity by its natural or surrogate key.

Input. Entity key(s) and optional attribute-projection.

Output. Full entity payload (or error if not found).

Backing. Gold view materialized via Pattern A (single-entity).

Latency. Low (Direct Lake or Warehouse query — typically sub-500 ms).

Pattern 2: Entity-search

Purpose. Find entities matching filter criteria, paginated.

Input. Filter predicate (typed attribute filters), pagination parameters, sort order.

Output. Matched entity list with pagination token.

Backing. Gold view materialized via Pattern A or B; typically with an index on filter attributes.

Latency. Low-to-medium (depends on filter selectivity; typically under 2 s for seller-class queries).

Pattern 3: Cross-entity-join

Purpose. Reason across two or three related entities through their relationships.

Input. Primary entity key(s) plus join specification.

Output. Primary entity with related entity collections inline.

Backing. Gold view materialized via Pattern B (multi-entity join).

Latency. Medium (pre-joined at refresh time; query is a filter on the joined view).

Pattern 4: Temporal-window

Purpose. Retrieve aggregates over a time window.

Input. Entity key plus time-window specification (relative or absolute).

Output. Aggregate values with window metadata.

Backing. Gold view materialized via Pattern C (temporal aggregation) or Pattern E (real-time reflex).

Latency. Low for pre-aggregated (Pattern C); low-to-medium for real-time (Pattern E).

Pattern 5: Action-execute

Purpose. Invoke a state change in a downstream system — create work-order, approve engineering change, dispatch crew.

Input. Action parameters plus authorisation context.

Output. Action outcome with execution identifier and any async-completion handle.

Backing. Not a Gold view. The tool invokes the downstream SOR API directly (ERP, EHR, MES, etc.) via managed-identity auth through Azure Functions.

Latency. Variable — depends on SOR responsiveness. Always wrapped with timeout and retry.

HITL. Action-execute tools almost always have a HITL gate before invocation. The agent produces the action proposal; a human approves (via Teams Copilot card or Power App); the tool executes post-approval.

With the foundation established, the remaining sections catalog the tools per Practice. Each Practice section is organized by MCP server; each server lists its tools with the ten-part template.

H.5 RC MCP Tools

RC Practice MCP tools are organized into four servers: rc-scml-mcp (supply and inventory), rc-merml-mcp (merchandising), rc-cxml-mcp (customer), and rc-action-mcp (state-change actions).

Note

Example in the field — Big Box Store Store 100. RC MCP tools are the tools Marisol Reyes's agents called during her shift (§16.13). The lot-trace tool during the Event 05 FDA recall; the shipment-status tool during Event 02 DSD dispute; the inventory-position tools during Event 04 OSA remediation; the customer-identity tool during Event 06 BOPIS substitution. Each tool reads a Gold view; each Gold view is materialized from Silver via one of the five transform patterns in §H.3. The agent fleet at Store 100 used approximately 35 distinct MCP tools across the eight events — all delivered by Deloitte onto Big Box Store's Microsoft platform.

H.5.1 rc-scml-mcp server

Tool: get_category

  • Purpose. Retrieve a merchandising category with its full hierarchy and attributes.
  • Input. category_id (string, required).
  • Output. Category entity with parent hierarchy, attributes, and child-category list.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.category — single-entity Pattern A.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern A single-entity materialisation from rc_silver.category.
  • Example invocation. get_category(category_id='DPT-014-C-042').
  • Example response. Category JSON with department, class, subclass names and roll-up path.
  • Classification. Trade-secret pricing policy labels carry through when present.
  • Consumers. price-recommend agent; assortment-optimize agent; margin-exposure agent.

Tool: list_categories

  • Purpose. Enumerate categories under a parent or matching a filter.
  • Input. parent_id (optional), filter (optional predicate).
  • Output. Category list with pagination.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.category.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern A.
  • Example. list_categories(parent_id='DPT-014', status='active').
  • Response. Array of Category entities.
  • Classification. Category-level only.
  • Consumers. merchant-planning agent; cross-category-assortment agent.

Tool: get_sku

  • Purpose. Retrieve a single SKU with current pricing, inventory summary, and derived enrichments.
  • Input. sku_id (required), store_id (optional — scopes inventory view).
  • Output. SKU entity with current price, total inventory, store-level inventory if store_id provided, stock-days-remaining, margin-exposure-flag.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.sku_with_enrichment.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern B multi-entity join (SKU + Price + Inventory Position rollup + Demand Signal).
  • Example. get_sku(sku_id='ABC-12345', store_id='STR-045').
  • Response. SKU JSON with price, store inventory, derived metrics.
  • Classification. Supplier-confidential attributes masked per agent scope.
  • Consumers. price-recommend; demand-sense; markdown-cadence; replenishment agents.

Tool: find_skus

  • Purpose. Search SKUs matching multi-attribute filter.
  • Input. filter (category, supplier, status, price-range), sort, pagination.
  • Output. SKU list with pagination token.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.sku_with_enrichment — indexed on filterable attributes.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern B.
  • Example. find_skus(filter={category_id: 'DPT-014-C-042', margin_exposure: 'high'}).
  • Response. Paginated SKU array.
  • Classification. Pricing masked where agent scope disallows.
  • Consumers. assortment-optimize; margin-exposure agents.

Tool: get_sku_inventory_all_stores

  • Purpose. Retrieve per-store inventory position for a SKU across the entire store network.
  • Input. sku_id (required).
  • Output. Array of {store_id, on_hand, on_order, safety_stock, reorder_point, stock_days_remaining}.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.sku_inventory_all_stores.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern B (SKU joined to Inventory Position across all stores).
  • Example. get_sku_inventory_all_stores(sku_id='ABC-12345').
  • Response. Store-by-store inventory array with computed stock-days.
  • Classification. Standard.
  • Consumers. rebalance-inventory agent; substitution-recommend agent; BOPIS-routing agent.

Tool: get_store

  • Purpose. Retrieve a store's master attributes and current operational state.
  • Input. store_id (required).
  • Output. Store entity with format, cluster, geography, hours, current ops-state flags.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.store.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern A.
  • Example. get_store(store_id='STR-045').
  • Response. Store JSON.
  • Classification. Standard.
  • Consumers. store-operations agents; allocation agents.

Tool: list_stores_by_cluster

  • Purpose. List stores within a named cluster (e.g., "urban-high-traffic").
  • Input. cluster_id (required), active_only (optional).
  • Output. Store list.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.store.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern A.
  • Example. list_stores_by_cluster(cluster_id='CLU-URB-HT').
  • Response. Array of Stores.
  • Consumers. cluster-level agents (assortment cluster, pricing cluster).

Tool: get_supplier

  • Purpose. Retrieve a supplier master record with current performance signals.
  • Input. supplier_id (required).
  • Output. Supplier entity plus current performance rollup (OTIF, chargeback history, risk score).
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.supplier_with_performance.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern B (Supplier joined to derived Supplier Performance Metric).
  • Example. get_supplier(supplier_id='SUP-00214').
  • Response. Supplier JSON with performance indicators.
  • Classification. Supplier-confidential; commercial terms masked per scope.
  • Consumers. supplier-development agent; chargeback agent; sourcing agent.

Tool: get_supplier_performance

  • Purpose. Retrieve supplier performance aggregates over a time window.
  • Input. supplier_id (required), window (e.g., '90d', '1y').
  • Output. Time-windowed performance aggregates: OTIF rate, chargeback $, quality hold count.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.supplier_performance_window.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern C temporal aggregation.
  • Example. get_supplier_performance(supplier_id='SUP-00214', window='90d').
  • Response. Aggregate metrics JSON.
  • Consumers. supplier-development; sourcing; chargeback-recovery agents.

Tool: get_shipment_status

  • Purpose. Retrieve current shipment state with ETA and exception flags.
  • Input. shipment_id (required) OR po_number (alt).
  • Output. Shipment entity with current status, ETA, exception history.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.shipment_current.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern E real-time reflex (Eventstream-fed Eventhouse).
  • Example. get_shipment_status(shipment_id='SHP-981223').
  • Response. Status + ETA + exception array.
  • Consumers. shipment-exception agent; fulfillment-risk agent.

Tool: get_inventory_position

  • Purpose. Retrieve current inventory position for a SKU at a specific store.
  • Input. sku_id, store_id (both required).
  • Output. Current on-hand, on-order, committed, available-to-promise.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.inventory_position_current.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern E real-time reflex.
  • Example. get_inventory_position(sku_id='ABC-12345', store_id='STR-045').
  • Response. Position JSON.
  • Consumers. replenishment; BOPIS; substitution agents.

Tool: get_inventory_history

  • Purpose. Retrieve inventory position time series for a SKU-store over a window.
  • Input. sku_id, store_id, window.
  • Output. Time-series of inventory position at day resolution.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.inventory_history.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern C temporal aggregation.
  • Example. get_inventory_history(sku_id='ABC-12345', store_id='STR-045', window='30d').
  • Response. Time-series array.
  • Consumers. demand-sense; forecast-accuracy agents.

Tool: get_lot_genealogy

  • Purpose. Retrieve lot-traceability chain from supplier to stores to customer transactions.
  • Input. lot_id (required).
  • Output. Genealogy graph — supplier → supplier lot → receipt → store distribution → customer transactions (if traceable).
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.lot_genealogy.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern D cross-domain federation (Lot + Shipment + Inventory + Transaction).
  • Example. get_lot_genealogy(lot_id='LOT-78832').
  • Response. Lineage JSON.
  • Classification. PII on customer transactions redacted for agent-scope.
  • Consumers. recall-scope agent; sustainability-attestation agent.

Tool: trace_recall_scope

  • Purpose. Given a trigger (lot, supplier, SKU range), compute full recall-affected scope.
  • Input. trigger_type ('lot' | 'supplier' | 'sku_range'), trigger_value, customer_notification_scope (optional bool).
  • Output. Scope summary: affected lots, affected stores, affected customers (count if scope, list if explicitly requested and scoped allowed).
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.recall_scope_computed.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern D.
  • Example. trace_recall_scope(trigger_type='lot', trigger_value='LOT-78832', customer_notification_scope=true).
  • Response. Recall scope JSON.
  • Classification. Customer PII available only with compliance-approved scope.
  • Consumers. recall-management agent; customer-notification agent.

H.5.2 rc-merml-mcp server

Tool: get_assortment

Tool: get_price_history

Tool: get_promotion

  • Purpose. Retrieve active promotion details including mechanics and expected lift.

Tool: get_markdown_status

  • Purpose. Retrieve markdown status for SKU-store including cadence history and sell-through.

  • Output. Markdown state — current tier, days-since-step, sell-through, recommended-next-action.

  • Example. get_markdown_status(sku_id='ABC-12345', store_id='STR-045').

  • Consumers. markdown-cadence agent.

Tool: get_competitive_signal

  • Purpose. Retrieve observable competitive pricing and assortment signals for a SKU or category.
  • Input. sku_id OR category_id, optional competitor_id, window.
  • Output. Competitive signal entries per competitor (price, promotional depth, assortment coverage).
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.competitive_signal_current.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern B.
  • Example. get_competitive_signal(sku_id='ABC-12345', window='7d').
  • Response. Competitive signals array.
  • Classification. Third-party data usage terms may restrict re-sharing.

Tool: compare_to_competitor

  • Purpose. Compare our SKU / price / assortment to named competitor.
  • Input. sku_id, competitor_id, comparison_type (price | assortment | promotion).

  • Gold backing. rc_gold.competitive_comparison.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern D.

  • Consumers. competitive-response agents.

H.5.3 rc-cxml-mcp server

Tool: get_customer

  • Purpose. Retrieve resolved customer identity with 360 attributes.
  • Input. customer_id OR one of source-system identifiers with resolution hint.
  • Output. Customer entity with loyalty summary, recent interaction summary, preference summary.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.customer_360.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern B.
  • Example. get_customer(customer_id='CUS-0003521').
  • Response. Customer JSON.
  • Classification. PII; strict scope enforcement.
  • Consumers. next-best-action; personalisation; service agents.

Tool: resolve_customer_identity

  • Purpose. Resolve ambiguous identity inputs to canonical customer.
  • Input. Any subset of email, phone, loyalty id, device id, email hash, order number.
  • Output. Resolved customer id with confidence score and match-evidence trail.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.customer_identity + identity-resolution service (reflex).
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern E.
  • Example. resolve_customer_identity(email='buyer@example.com', loyalty_id='LOY-0044123').
  • Response. Canonical customer id + confidence.
  • Classification. PII; HITL where confidence is low.
  • Consumers. identity-resolution agent; service-case routing agent.

Tool: get_loyalty_member

  • Purpose. Retrieve loyalty program standing for a resolved customer.
  • Input. customer_id.
  • Output. Loyalty Member entity: tier, points balance, qualifying activity.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.loyalty_member.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern A.
  • Example. get_loyalty_member(customer_id='CUS-0003521').
  • Response. Loyalty JSON.
  • Consumers. loyalty-economics; retention agents.

Tool: get_interaction_history

  • Purpose. Retrieve customer interaction history across channels over a window.
  • Input. customer_id, window, optional channel_filter.
  • Output. Chronological interaction array with channel, type, outcome.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.interaction_history.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern C.
  • Example. get_interaction_history(customer_id='CUS-0003521', window='30d').
  • Response. Interaction array.
  • Classification. PII + service-case content redaction.
  • Consumers. service agents; personalisation agents.

Tool: get_transaction_history

  • Purpose. Retrieve customer purchase history over a window.
  • Input. customer_id, window, optional category_filter.
  • Output. Transaction array with line items, amounts, channels.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.transaction_history.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern C.
  • Example. get_transaction_history(customer_id='CUS-0003521', window='1y', category_filter='DPT-014').
  • Response. Transaction array.
  • Classification. PII + PCI-adjacent. Payment method redacted.
  • Consumers. market-basket; LTV; next-best-action agents.

Tool: get_preference

  • Purpose. Retrieve customer declared and derived preferences.
  • Input. customer_id, optional preference_domain (comms, product, sustainability, etc.).
  • Output. Preference entity.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.preference.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern A.
  • Example. get_preference(customer_id='CUS-0003521', preference_domain='comms').
  • Response. Preferences JSON.
  • Classification. PII.
  • Consumers. channel-selection; substitution; personalisation agents.

Tool: get_session_state

  • Purpose. Retrieve current session state for customer with in-flight context.
  • Input. session_id OR (customer_id, active_only=true).
  • Output. Session entity with path, in-flight actions, cart state.
  • Gold backing. rc_gold.session_active.
  • Silver→Gold. Pattern E real-time.
  • Example. get_session_state(customer_id='CUS-0003521', active_only=true).
  • Response. Session JSON.
  • Classification. PII + session-sensitive.
  • Consumers. abandonment-recovery; real-time personalisation agents.

H.5.4 rc-action-mcp server (action-execute tools)

All action tools require HITL approval gate before execution.

Tool: create_replenishment_order

  • Purpose. Create a replenishment purchase or transfer order after HITL approval.
  • Input. sku_id, store_id, quantity, source_node_id (supplier or DC), approval_token.

  • Backing. No Gold view; invokes ERP replenishment API via Azure Functions.
  • Example. create_replenishment_order(sku_id='ABC-12345', store_id='STR-045', quantity=120, source_node_id='DC-02', approval_token='APR-883').
  • Response. Order confirmation JSON.
  • Classification. Standard.
  • Consumers. replenishment agent.

Tool: trigger_markdown

  • Purpose. Initiate markdown price change after HITL approval.
  • Input. sku_id, store_id OR cluster_id, markdown_tier, approval_token.
  • Output. Markdown activation confirmation with effective datetime.
  • Backing. Pricing system API invocation.
  • Example. trigger_markdown(sku_id='ABC-12345', cluster_id='CLU-URB-HT', markdown_tier=2, approval_token='APR-884').
  • Response. Activation JSON.
  • Consumers. markdown-cadence agent.

Tool: recommend_substitution

  • Purpose. Generate substitution recommendation for a customer order mid-fulfillment.
  • Input. customer_id, out_of_stock_sku_id, store_id.
  • Output. Ranked substitution options with preference-adjusted scoring.
  • Backing. Invokes substitution reasoning agent with Gold data.
  • Example. recommend_substitution(customer_id='CUS-0003521', out_of_stock_sku_id='ABC-12345', store_id='STR-045').
  • Response. Ranked substitution array.
  • Consumers. BOPIS-substitution agent; associate-facing Copilot Studio surface.

Tool: notify_customer_recall

  • Purpose. Trigger customer notification for a recall scope after compliance approval.
  • Input. recall_id, notification_channel (email, SMS, push, mail), approval_token.
  • Output. Notification job id and scope.
  • Backing. Notification-system API invocation.
  • Example. notify_customer_recall(recall_id='REC-001', notification_channel='email', approval_token='APR-885').
  • Classification. PII; compliance-approval gate mandatory.
  • Consumers. recall-management agent.

Tool: create_service_case

  • Purpose. Create a service case for a customer issue after HITL approval.
  • Input. customer_id, case_type, description, priority, approval_token.
  • Output. Case id from downstream service system.
  • Backing. Service-management system API invocation.
  • Example. create_service_case(customer_id='CUS-0003521', case_type='product-complaint', description='...', priority='p2', approval_token='APR-886').
  • Consumers. service-recovery agents.

H.13 MCP Governance — Auth, Rate Limits, Audit

APEX's MCP servers run under a common governance pattern:

Authentication. Every MCP server is hosted as an Azure Container App or Azure Function with a Managed Identity. Agents authenticate to MCP servers via Entra-issued tokens scoped to the agent's managed identity. Tools receive the agent's identity as part of the tool invocation context and can enforce per-identity authorisation.

Authorisation. Tools use Purview classification labels to determine what data the agent may see. A request for a PHI-classified entity from an agent without PHI scope returns a redacted response or a permission-denied error — both audit-logged.

Rate limits. Each MCP server enforces per-identity rate limits. Defaults: 100 requests per minute per identity for read tools, 10 requests per minute for action tools. Overridable per tenant.

Audit logging. Every tool invocation writes to the APEX audit-row system: tool name, input parameters (with sensitive-param redaction), output summary (with classification-aware redaction), agent identity, session id, HITL approval reference if applicable, and outcome.

HITL integration. Action-execute tools integrate with the APEX HITL gate framework. Agent prepares the action proposal; proposal is routed to a human (Teams Copilot card / Power Apps / email); human approves, modifies, or denies; approved actions execute with the approval token traveling with the audit row.

Versioning. MCP tools are versioned; breaking changes produce a new tool name; agent manifests pin tool versions for reproducibility.

Observability. Foundry tracing + MCP-server-side instrumentation produce per-tool latency, error-rate, cost (token / compute), and business-outcome attribution metrics.

H.14 Building Custom MCP Tools — Client-Specific Extensions

APEX's MCP tool catalog is designed for extension. Clients frequently require tools that reach client-specific SORs, client-specific decision logic, or client-proprietary models. The pattern:

  1. Define the Gold view. Author the Fabric artifact (Lakehouse table, Warehouse view, or Eventhouse function) the new tool will read.
  2. Define the MCP tool contract. Author an inputSchema and outputShape consistent with the APEX tool patterns.
  3. Implement the MCP server. Add a new tool to an existing MCP server (or stand up a new server for a new functional domain) with managed-identity auth, rate limits, and audit logging.
  4. Register with agent manifest. Update the consuming agent's manifest to reference the new tool version.
  5. Governance. Purview classification on the new Gold view; DLP policy additions for the new output shape; HITL gate design for any action tool.
  6. Deployment. CI/CD via Fabric Deployment Pipelines + Azure DevOps / GitHub Actions for the MCP server code.
  7. Documentation. Add the new tool to the client's APEX catalog with the same ten-part template.

Client-authored tools remain in the client's Fabric tenant and MCP server infrastructure. APEX framework-level tools ship with APEX updates; client-specific tools are owned by the client. Both live in the same tool catalog, invocable by agents indistinguishably.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. Tool names, Gold view names, and example payloads in this appendix are illustrative. Client-specific tool namespaces should not import APEX-internal tool names or schema identifiers without Purview classification and Independence review. The two-contract model applies: APEX framework tools are Deloitte IP; client-specific tools are client IP deployed to the client's tenant.

I.5 How E7 supports Agentic AI — deep-dive

For architects asking "how exactly does E7 enable agentic AI," the detailed answer has six pillars:

Pillar 1: Agent identity and authorisation

Entra Agent ID gives every deployed agent a durable identity with conditional access, session limits, and audit scope. Agents can authenticate to Microsoft Graph APIs, to third-party APIs via federated identity, and (through APEX's MCP layer) to Fabric Gold views as themselves — not as a shared service principal. When an agent acts, the audit trail knows which agent, with which version, in what session.

Pillar 2: Agent hosting surfaces

Copilot Studio in E7 provides the authoring environment and hosting runtime for knowledge-worker agents. For enterprise-scale or high-volume agents, E7 integrates with Azure AI Foundry as the production runtime. APEX agents are Foundry-hosted; Copilot Studio hosts the customer-facing surfaces that route queries TO Foundry agents for reasoning.

Pillar 3: Agent grounding and data access

M365 Copilot grounds on Microsoft 365 content natively. For Practice-specific data grounding (Fabric OneLake), E7's integration with Fabric enables Copilot-grounded queries over Practice semantic models. APEX-authored semantic models and APEX-authored MCP tools are what turn this platform capability into Practice-specific production value.

Pillar 4: Agent governance

Purview in E7 extends sensitivity-label propagation to AI outputs, DLP policies to prevent sensitive-data exposure in agent responses, and Communication Compliance to inspect agent interactions for policy violations. For Practice-specific classification taxonomies, APEX adds the policy content that runs within E7's Purview framework.

Pillar 5: Agent security

Defender for AI in E7 protects against prompt-injection, model-inversion, and malicious tool-call attacks. Security Copilot supports analysts investigating agent-adjacent incidents. For APEX deployments, these E7 capabilities provide the enterprise-wide security baseline on top of APEX's manifest-bound agent scope.

Pillar 6: Agent observability

Microsoft Graph telemetry captures agent invocations across the tenant. For business-outcome attribution beyond invocation counts, APEX's audit-row schema provides per-decision dollar attribution. Both telemetries live alongside; sellers explain them as complementary (E7 = "how much is the fleet running?"; APEX = "what business outcome did each run produce?").
