Appendix J

Purview Integration — Capabilities, Identity, Tier Security, Lineage, and Business Catalog

This appendix is the seller's comprehensive reference for Microsoft Purview in the context of Deloitte's agent delivery. It covers Purview's full capability surface, how Purview binds Entra identity to data authorisation for agentic workloads, the tier-level security model, data lineage, the Unified Catalog with business terms, and concrete Big Box Store Store 100 examples showing Purview in production. Sellers use this appendix in conversations with Chief Compliance Officers, Chief Privacy Officers, Chief Information Security Officers, General Counsels, and Chief Data Officers.

J.1 How to read this appendix

Purview is a Microsoft platform capability the client licenses directly from Microsoft. This appendix describes what Purview does and how Deloitte's agent delivery services use Purview — with APEX as the internal accelerator providing Practice-specific classification taxonomies, DLP policy templates, and agent-scope patterns. Clients do not buy "APEX Purview"; they license Purview from Microsoft and engage Deloitte to configure Purview for their agentic-AI workloads using Deloitte's accumulated methodology.

J.2 Purview's role in Deloitte's agent delivery

Every Deloitte agentic-AI delivery assumes Purview is load-bearing infrastructure. Without Purview, the audit row is partial, the DLP policy enforcement is absent, the lineage query for regulator inquiry is manual reconstruction, and the classification taxonomy is inconsistent across the estate. With Purview, every one of these concerns becomes a platform property — built-in, native, queryable.

Purview answers six questions a Chief Compliance Officer asks about any AI deployment:

  1. What sensitive data is in the estate? → Data Map + Classification
  2. Who can access what? → Entra integration + Purview Access Policies
  3. How does data flow through the system? → Lineage across Fabric, Foundry, Power BI, Copilot
  4. What is restricted from AI output? → DLP for AI
  5. Where are the compliance-relevant artifacts? → Compliance Manager + Unified Catalog
  6. What does the audit evidence look like? → Audit logs + classification-preserved decision trail

Deloitte's role is translating these six questions into Practice-specific implementations that pass regulatory scrutiny from day one.

J.3 Purview capability map

Ten capability areas that together form Purview's surface. Each has an APEX-delivery pattern.

J.3.1 Data Map + Unified Catalog

What it is. The inventory of the data estate with assets, schemas, classifications, lineage, and ownership. The Unified Catalog is the newer federation across Purview Data Map, Microsoft Fabric, and Power BI that presents one catalog surface to users and agents.

What Deloitte configures. Fabric Lakehouse / Warehouse / Eventhouse scanning; client SORs (Epic, Sabre, SAP, Manhattan, Plex, OSIsoft PI, Salesforce, etc.) registered with automated scan schedules; Practice-specific asset-type taxonomies mapped to Fabric objects; role-based views of the catalog per business function.

Why it matters for agents. Every MCP tool invocation cross-references Data Map metadata to determine what the agent is allowed to see. Agents without catalog-visible data cannot access it — even if the data exists in OneLake.

J.3.2 Classification & Sensitivity Labels

What it is. Automated and manual labeling of data with sensitivity categories. Purview ships ~100 out-of-box classifiers (credit card, SSN, passport, etc.) and supports custom classifiers. Sensitivity labels are the named classifications (Public, Internal, Confidential, Highly Confidential, and any custom tiers).

What Deloitte configures. Per-Practice classifier extensions — PHI classifiers for HLS, CPNI classifiers for TMT-TEL, PCI-adjacent for RC payment data, export-controlled for defense AXLE, supplier-confidential pricing for RC. Label-propagation rules through transforms. Auto-classification policies that scan Bronze and Silver continuously.

Why it matters for agents. The label on a data element determines whether an agent may read it, whether the agent's output may contain it, whether Copilot may ground on it, and whether the data appears in audit evidence packages. Classification is the foundation of every downstream Purview capability.

J.3.3 Information Protection + Data Loss Prevention (DLP)

What it is. Policies that enforce data-handling rules based on classification. Information Protection handles encryption and rights management; DLP handles output-moderation and transfer-blocking.

What Deloitte configures. DLP policies that inspect agent outputs before they leave the Foundry runtime. Policies like: "Never include cleartext SSN in a Copilot response"; "Block exports of PHI-classified data to Teams chats outside the authorized care team"; "Allow SKU data in agent output but mask supplier-confidential cost." DLP for AI specifically — the newer Purview capability that inspects agent-generated content the same way it inspects email and documents.

Why it matters for agents. An agent that has read access to a PHI-classified entity can return the entity through a tool call, but DLP inspects the agent's final response and redacts, blocks, or flags cleartext PHI that should never reach the user. The agent cannot bypass DLP.

J.3.4 Data Lineage

What it is. End-to-end provenance tracking — source system → Bronze → Silver → Gold → MCP tool → agent output → downstream consumer (Copilot, Power BI, integration).

What Deloitte configures. Lineage registration at every transform step. Fabric pipelines emit lineage automatically where supported; custom transforms register lineage explicitly. Foundry agent invocations and MCP tool calls register as lineage events. The result: any data element at any point in the pipeline can be traced to every upstream source and every downstream use.

Why it matters for agents. When a regulator asks "how did this agent conclude X," Deloitte's answer is a lineage query that returns the complete reasoning trail — source data, transforms applied, classifications carried, agent model version, tool versions invoked, HITL approval identity and timestamp, downstream effect. This is the audit row's evidential backbone.

J.3.5 Business Glossary / Business Terms

What it is. The definitional catalog of business terms — what does "Active Customer" mean in this enterprise; what's the definition of "Available Inventory"; how is "Margin" calculated? Each term has an owner, a definition, synonyms, and links to the data assets that implement it.

What Deloitte configures. Per-Practice starter glossaries — RC's glossary ships with ~200 retail terms; HLS with ~250 healthcare terms; ER with ~150 utility/energy terms. Terms are linked to APEX semantic-model entities (SKU, Store, Category, Patient, Encounter, Well, etc.). The glossary becomes the shared vocabulary across business, analytics, and agent teams.

Why it matters for agents. Agents ground on business terms. When a merchant asks "show me margin exposure on active assortments," the agent resolves "margin" and "active assortment" through the glossary before executing the query. The glossary prevents the "which margin?" ambiguity that kills analytics programs.

J.3.6 Compliance Manager

What it is. Regulatory-framework tracking with assessments, controls, and evidence management. Pre-built assessments for HIPAA, GDPR, CCPA, SOX, PCI DSS, FedRAMP, 21 CFR Part 11, and dozens more.

What Deloitte configures. Practice-relevant framework activation — HIPAA + HITECH + state privacy for HLS; SOX + FERC + NERC CIP for ER; PCI DSS + GDPR + CCPA for RC; etc. Control mapping from framework requirements to specific Purview policies, DLP rules, and classification taxonomies. Evidence-collection automation.

Why it matters for agents. A regulator inquiry about an AI deployment increasingly asks "show me your control framework and how it applies to AI workloads." Compliance Manager becomes the answer: the mapping, the evidence, the audit trail — all native.

J.3.7 Insider Risk Management

What it is. Behavioural-analytics detection for humans and workloads that deviate from expected patterns — unusual data access, exfiltration signals, policy violations, agent misbehavior.

What Deloitte configures. Insider-risk policies scoped to APEX-delivered workloads. Unusual agent behavior (e.g., an agent making ten thousand tool calls in a minute, or an agent accessing data classifications it typically doesn't touch) raises a signal to the security operations team.

Why it matters for agents. Agents are identities. Insider Risk extends to agent workloads the same behavioral analytics that monitor human users. A compromised agent surfaces as an anomalous-behavior signal before it exfiltrates data.

J.3.8 Audit

What it is. Immutable audit logs of administrative actions, data access, classification changes, policy modifications, and critically for AI — agent invocations and AI output generation.

What Deloitte configures. Retention policies aligned to regulatory requirements (7 years for HIPAA, 5 years for SOX, varying for others). Audit stream export to Sentinel for security correlation. Audit integration with APEX's decision-audit-row so business outcomes can be traced back to specific agent invocations.

Why it matters for agents. Regulator-grade evidence. Every agent decision has a Purview audit row AND an APEX business-decision audit row. The two together are the defensible evidential chain for a specific decision six months after the fact.

J.3.9 Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) for AI

What it is. Continuous monitoring of data exposure to AI — which sensitive data is reachable by which agents, which Copilot integrations touch which classifications, where does posture drift from baseline.

What Deloitte configures. Posture baselines at Wave 1 go-live. Alerts on posture drift — agent added with new tool scope, new sensitive data category classified, policy change that expands agent access. Weekly posture reports to the security operations team.

Why it matters for agents. Posture management is how sophisticated clients prove that their agent fleet remains within governance boundaries over time. It is also how Deloitte demonstrates that the post-delivery agent fleet continues to operate within the governance envelope originally designed.

J.3.10 Privileged Access Management / Just-in-Time access

What it is. Time-bounded, approval-gated access elevation for sensitive operations. Integrated with Entra Privileged Identity Management.

What Deloitte configures. JIT patterns for high-privilege agent operations — e.g., an agent needs elevated access to approve a recall action or to issue a member-notification containing PHI. Access elevates for the specific action with approval trail, then drops.

Why it matters for agents. The principle of least privilege extended to agents. Standing high-privilege agents are a risk; JIT-elevated agents perform specific actions with full audit trail.

J.4 How Purview Drives Agents with Correct Data to Correct Identities

Purview is the governance plane. Entra is the identity plane. Together they implement the rule: the right data reaches the right identity through the right surface with the right classification.

J.4.1 Entra identity + Purview scope = agent data authorisation

Every request through the APEX architecture carries an identity — a human user (via Copilot), a delegated user (an agent acting on behalf of a user), or a workload identity (an agent acting autonomously). Entra authenticates the identity and passes an access token to the MCP layer. The MCP tool cross-references the identity's effective scope with the Purview classification on the requested data. The tool returns the data allowed, redacts the classifications the identity cannot see, or denies the request with an audit log.

J.4.2 Per-agent data scope (managed identity)

Every APEX agent has a dedicated Entra Managed Identity with scoped permissions. A price-recommend agent has read scope on pricing, competitive, and demand data but no scope on customer-PII. A BOPIS substitution agent has read scope on customer preferences but no scope on pricing-strategic data. Agents cannot escalate their scope; their manifest contracts bound what they are permitted to query.

J.4.3 Per-user data scope (delegated identity)

When a Copilot Studio surface runs on behalf of a user, the surface acts as the user — inheriting the user's data scope. A junior merchant sees a narrower view than a VP Category Management; a care coordinator sees a narrower view than a chief medical officer. The delegated-identity pattern lets one agent serve multiple user roles with per-user scope enforcement via Purview.

J.4.4 HITL data-visibility and agent-view masking

When an agent prepares a HITL decision card for a human reviewer, Purview DLP inspects the card content. Data the reviewer is not authorized to see is masked or summarized rather than rendered cleartext. A junior operations lead receives a disposition card with aggregate inventory counts rather than per-line-item PII; a senior leader reviewing the same case receives the full detail.

J.4.5 Cross-agent isolation via classification

An agent in Practice A should not read data from Practice B unless explicit federation is approved. Purview enforces this at the classification layer — APEX's Practice-scoped classifications (RC-confidential, HLS-confidential, etc.) prevent cross-Practice data leaks that workspace-level RBAC alone might miss.

J.5 Tier-Level Security — The Four-Tier Model APEX Deploys

Deloitte's agent delivery uses a standard four-tier sensitivity model deployed onto Purview as the classification taxonomy. Clients can extend the model with custom tiers; the four-tier default is the reference.

J.5.1 Tier 1 — Public

Publicly shareable data. No restriction on agent access, no DLP rules, no special classification. Examples: publicly-announced product specifications, public regulatory filings, general marketing materials.

J.5.2 Tier 2 — Internal

Internal business data not for external distribution but not particularly sensitive. Classification: "Internal — Employee Access." Agent access: default for authenticated agents. DLP: block external distribution; allow all internal agent and Copilot consumption.

J.5.3 Tier 3 — Confidential (regulated and business-critical)

Data sensitive by regulation or by business consequence. Includes PII, commercial-sensitive data, trade-secret configurations, supplier-confidential pricing, CPNI. Classification: "Confidential — Role-Based Access." Agent access: role-scoped via managed identity; DLP enforces masking on agent output unless the consuming identity has explicit Tier-3 authorisation.

J.5.4 Tier 4 — Restricted (highest sensitivity)

Data requiring the strongest possible control. Includes PHI subject to HIPAA, financial-material-non-public information subject to SOX §302/§404, cryptographic keys, audit-trail data itself. Classification: "Restricted — Named-Identity Access + JIT Elevation." Agent access: explicit named-agent grants only; DLP enforces redaction in agent output unless justified business case approved in HITL gate.

J.5.5 Tier transitions and derivation rules

Derived data inherits the most restrictive tier of its inputs unless a declassification rule explicitly applies. An agent combining Tier-3 patient data with Tier-2 population data produces Tier-3 output — unless the output is a de-identified aggregate that meets declassification criteria (bucket-size minimums, k-anonymity thresholds).

J.5.6 Cross-tier flows and approval paths

Any data movement from higher tier to lower tier (e.g., Tier 3 → Tier 2 via aggregation) requires an approval rule in Purview. Deloitte's delivery configures these approvals via Compliance Manager; audit logs preserve the approval decisions.

J.5.7 Tier-breach detection

Insider Risk Management monitors for tier-breach signals — an agent accessing data above its authorized tier, a user credential accessing data at a tier not justified by role, a workload exfiltrating Tier-3 data to a Tier-1 channel. Every breach becomes a security event for investigation.

J.6 Data Lineage in Agentic AI

Lineage is where Deloitte's agent delivery differentiates most visibly from a build-your-own effort. Every Purview lineage registration answers the question "where did this come from and where did it go" for any data element.

J.6.1 Bronze → Silver → Gold lineage

Every transform step registers with Purview. A Bronze table ingested from Epic Clarity via Fabric Mirroring has lineage showing the Epic Clarity source. The Silver canonical patient entity has lineage showing the Bronze Epic tables plus Dragon-documentation, lab data, and pharmacy data it integrates. The Gold patient-360 view has lineage showing its Silver components. At each step classifications propagate; tier boundaries are enforced.

J.6.2 Gold → MCP tool → Agent → Output lineage

The agent-side lineage is where Purview extends beyond traditional data-governance tooling. When an MCP tool queries a Gold view, the lineage captures the tool, the calling agent identity, the query parameters, the result classifications, and the downstream consumption — another agent, a Copilot response, an HITL card, a Power BI visual. The complete reasoning path for any agent decision becomes queryable.

J.6.3 Regulatory-grade lineage query patterns

Four lineage query patterns APEX-delivered agents support:

  • "How did this decision get made?" — starts from the APEX audit row; walks backward through agent, tool, Gold view, Silver, Bronze, source.
  • "What happened to this specific piece of data?" — starts from a source row; walks forward through transforms, classifications, agent consumption, and downstream effects.
  • "Who accessed this data in the last 90 days?" — combines Purview audit with lineage to produce a complete access inventory.
  • "What did we do about a regulation change six months ago?" — combines Compliance Manager changelog with lineage and audit.

J.6.4 GDPR right-to-access query

A GDPR data subject requests their information. Deloitte's delivery pattern: one Purview query returns all data assets containing the subject's identifiers, the transforms they participated in, the agents that consumed them, the decisions rendered, and downstream systems where their data was exported. What historically was a 40-hour manual reconstruction across teams becomes a sub-hour query.

J.6.5 HIPAA access-log traceability

A HIPAA accounting-of-disclosures request asks who accessed a specific patient's record and why. Purview audit plus lineage returns the complete access inventory — human users, delegated agents, workload agents, and downstream integrations. The response is regulator-ready within the 60-day statutory window and typically within 24 hours.

J.7 Business Terms and the Unified Catalog

The Unified Catalog is where business, technical, and agent communities converge on shared vocabulary.

J.7.1 Business Glossary in Unified Catalog

Every business term has a name, a definition, an owner (the accountable business leader), synonyms, related terms, and links to the Purview data assets that implement it. The catalog surfaces terms through the Unified Catalog UI, through Copilot-grounded natural-language experiences, and through MCP tool calls.

J.7.2 APEX semantic-model term registration

APEX's Practice semantic models ship with starter glossaries. When Deloitte deploys SCML for a retail client, ~200 RC business terms register into the client's Purview glossary automatically — "Assortment," "Category," "Markdown," "SKU," "Store Cluster," "Inventory Position," "Demand Signal." The client extends the glossary with organization-specific terms and definitions; shared structure accelerates adoption.

J.7.3 Per-Practice business-term taxonomies

Each of the 7 Practices ships a baseline glossary:

  • RC: merchandising, supply, customer, promotional terms — ~200 starter terms
  • HLS (Payer): member, benefit, utilisation, claim terms — ~180 starter terms
  • HLS (Provider): patient, encounter, order, denial terms — ~220 starter terms
  • HLS (Life Sciences): study, subject, RWE, HCP terms — ~200 starter terms
  • ER: asset, process, grid, outage terms — ~150 starter terms
  • AXLE: item, BOM, work order, operation, quality terms — ~250 starter terms
  • TMT (MED/TEL/TEC): content, network, subscriber, product terms — ~180 starter terms
  • TH: traveler, journey, loyalty, operational terms — ~170 starter terms
  • ICE: unit, dealer, service, rental terms — ~140 starter terms

J.7.4 Business-term-to-entity mapping

Every term in the glossary links to the APEX semantic-model entity that implements it. "Active Customer" links to the CXML Customer entity with the active-status filter. "Available Inventory" links to the SCML Inventory Position entity with the available-to-promise computation. Agents consulting the glossary resolve business-term questions to precise entity queries.

J.7.5 Client glossary extensions

Clients extend the starter glossary with organization-specific terms — their definition of "active," their computation of "margin," their scoping of "territory." Extensions are client-owned IP in the client's Purview tenant; APEX starter-glossary content remains Deloitte-methodology-owned at framework level.

J.8 Big Box Store Store 100 — Purview in Production

Three events from the Store 100 narrative (§16.13) illustrate Purview in production.

J.8.1 Event 05 — FDA recall lineage trail

The FDA Class II recall on infant formula required a complete lot-to-customer trail in under 5 minutes. Purview made the sub-5-minute response possible:

  • Lineage forward from the affected lot: lot → shipments → store receivings → shelf placement → POS transactions → loyalty-identified customers
  • Classification propagation: the infant-formula lot data carries Tier-3 supplier-confidential plus Tier-4 FSMA-regulated classifications; customer data carries Tier-3 PII; the recall-notification draft carries the combined classifications
  • Audit trail: every agent action (lot-trace lookup, customer-list generation, notification draft) recorded with identity, timestamp, data classifications accessed, and downstream outputs
  • FSMA 204 evidence package: assembled automatically from Compliance Manager's FSMA 204 assessment pointing at the specific lineage records

Without Purview, the 4-minute-to-scope and 22-minute-to-quarantine would have been impossible; the regulator-facing evidence package would have been a manual reconstruction.

J.8.2 Event 07 — Shrink evidence with classification masking

The shrink pattern at register 7 required an evidence package sensitive enough to escalate to Asset Protection but restrained enough to preserve the employee's due process. Purview enabled the balance:

  • Classification: the DIM_EMPLOYEE record carried Tier-3 HR-confidential classification; the POS_VOID pattern evidence carried Tier-3 loss-prevention-sensitive classification
  • Scoped agent access: the shrink-signal agent had explicit read on the DIM_EMPLOYEE record but not a broader HR view; its output could be consumed by Asset Protection identities but not by the store manager directly (that was the design intent — protecting the investigation)
  • DLP-enforced masking: Marisol's Teams Copilot card showed the pattern signature and statistical confidence (3.1σ), not employee identifying details; the AP-routed version showed full detail
  • Audit trail: AP investigator access to the full record logged with timestamp, reason, and downstream evidence-use

Classification-aware masking let the right audience see the right view of the same underlying case.

J.8.3 Event 08 — Business-term-driven pattern detection

The plastic-fragment-in-muffin incident required recognising that three independent low-severity complaints across three stores were actually one systemic quality signal. Purview's business glossary made the cross-store pattern recognisable:

  • Shared lot business term: "Co-Manufacturer Lot" linked to the LOT_TRACE entity consistently across all 14 stores' data
  • Shared incident type term: "Foreign Object Incident (Tier 2)" normalized across stores that might otherwise have used idiosyncratic terminology
  • Cross-store query: the pattern-detection agent queried against the shared business terms, finding 2 prior low-severity complaints on the same lot in stores outside Store 100 — pattern detected

Without a shared business vocabulary across stores, the Store 100 incident would have remained a local case for weeks or months. The Unified Catalog business-term layer made cross-enterprise pattern recognition a single query.

J.9 Seller Positioning Scripts

Client asks: "How do we govern AI outputs for sensitive data?"

You say: "Your Purview deployment enforces it. Classification on your Fabric data propagates through Foundry agent outputs; DLP for AI inspects every generated response; sensitive data is redacted or blocked unless the recipient identity has authorized scope. Deloitte configures Purview with Practice-specific classification taxonomies — PHI patterns for HLS clients, CPNI patterns for telecom, PCI-adjacent patterns for retail. The governance isn't something we build into the agents; it's something the platform enforces around the agents."

Client asks: "How do we prove to a regulator that our AI is compliant?"

You say: "Purview Compliance Manager maps regulatory frameworks — HIPAA, GDPR, SOX, 21 CFR Part 11, whatever applies to your business — to the specific controls in your environment. Deloitte configures the mapping during Wave 1. When a regulator asks, you export a controls-and-evidence package from Compliance Manager that shows how each framework requirement is satisfied. The audit row traces any specific decision back to its source data and the framework controls that governed it."

Client asks: "Can an agent accidentally see data it shouldn't?"

You say: "No, by design. Every agent has an Entra managed identity with a scoped data authorisation. Purview classification determines what the agent can read; DLP determines what the agent's output can include. An agent without PHI scope cannot read PHI-classified data through MCP; even if it did, DLP would redact PHI from its output. The scope is enforced at the platform level, not trusted to the agent's own code."

Client asks: "How does business know what's in the data?"

You say: "Purview Unified Catalog with Business Glossary. Deloitte delivers a Practice-specific starter glossary — hundreds of terms relevant to your industry with definitions, owners, and links to the data assets that implement them. Business users discover data through natural language; agents resolve business-term questions to precise entity queries using the same glossary; governance team uses the glossary as the definitional source of truth."

Client asks: "What if one line of business needs isolation from another?"

You say: "Classification-scoped. Each Practice's data carries a Practice-scoped classification; cross-Practice agent access requires explicit federation approval. RC agents cannot see HLS data by accident; AXLE agents cannot see CPNI by accident. Deloitte configures the classifications and the federation rules during Wave 1 architecture."

Client asks: "What's different about Purview with Deloitte vs Purview on our own?"

You say: "Configuration accelerator. Purview is a rich platform; setting it up for agentic-AI workloads at enterprise scale is 6–12 months of engineering if you start from scratch. Deloitte's delivery brings Practice-specific classification taxonomies, DLP policy templates, compliance framework mappings, business-term starter glossaries, and the lineage-registration patterns for agent workloads. Your Purview runs on your tenant with your licensing; we configure it faster than you could configure it yourselves."

J.10 Independence Considerations

  • Purview is a Microsoft product. Client licenses directly from Microsoft. Deloitte does not quote Purview pricing or commit to Purview terms on Microsoft's behalf.
  • Deloitte configuration is services. The configuration work — classification taxonomies, DLP policies, glossary registration, lineage patterns — is Deloitte Agentic AI Delivery Services. Contracted separately from Microsoft licensing.
  • Audit-client rules still apply. At Deloitte audit clients, Purview-configuration engagements follow standard Audit Committee pre-clearance. Purview configuration is non-audit service; scope clearance required.
  • No ECIF. Microsoft-funded ECIF dollars for Purview implementation are prohibited for Deloitte. Approved funding paths only: direct client, DCIF to client, ISV Marketplace, SI teaming.
  • Language discipline. "Deloitte configures Purview" is correct; "Deloitte resells Purview" is wrong; "Deloitte's Purview product" is wrong; "Microsoft-Deloitte joint Purview offering" is wrong.
Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. Purview classification policies and DLP rules authored by Deloitte during delivery are, on the client's Purview tenant, the client's configuration. Deloitte's framework-level methodology (which classifications to create, which DLP patterns to apply, which compliance frameworks to map) remains Deloitte IP for use in the next engagement. At exit, the client keeps their configured Purview; Deloitte keeps the methodology. Two-contract model preserved.

Appendix K

Entra & Agent Identity — The Identity Plane for Agentic AI

This appendix covers Microsoft Entra's role as the identity plane for Deloitte-delivered agentic AI. Entra authenticates every human user, every agent, every MCP tool call, and every data-plane query. Without Entra's identity guarantees, Purview's classification enforcement would be unenforceable.

K.1 How to read this appendix

Entra is a Microsoft platform the client licenses directly. This appendix covers Entra capabilities in the context of Deloitte's agent-delivery services — how agents receive identity, how conditional access gates their actions, how managed identities eliminate credential sprawl, and how Entra Agent ID (emerging) elevates agents to first-class identity principals.

K.2 The four identity categories in APEX

Every action in the APEX architecture is performed by one of four identity types:

  • Human user identity — a Deloitte consultant or client employee authenticated via Entra with their named credentials.
  • Delegated identity — an agent acting on behalf of a specific human user, inheriting that user's scope for this interaction (typical for Copilot Studio agents).
  • Workload (managed) identity — an autonomous agent or service principal acting as itself, with a defined scope bound to its manifest (typical for Foundry-hosted agents invoked on events).
  • Hybrid delegated + workload — an agent that switches identity modes based on context (e.g., background processing as workload, user-facing action as delegate).

Deloitte's delivery patterns each agent into one of these categories during design. The category determines the scope model, the audit trail, and the HITL boundary.

K.3 Entra capability map

K.3.1 Core identity

Standard Entra tenant, managed identities, service principals, users, groups, guest identities. Foundation for all other capabilities.

K.3.2 Conditional Access (CA)

Rule-based access policies evaluated at every sign-in and token-acquisition event. CA policies consider: user identity, device compliance, network location, risk score, application, resource, time-of-day. APEX delivery configures CA policies specifically for AI workloads — block agent sign-in from non-approved regions, require managed-device for human access to Foundry, demand re-authentication for sensitive agent actions.

K.3.3 Identity Governance

Access reviews, entitlement management, lifecycle workflows. For APEX agent fleets, Identity Governance provides scheduled review of agent-managed-identity scopes. Every 90 days the delivery pattern requires access-review of agent permissions; expired or unused scopes revoked.

K.3.4 Privileged Identity Management (PIM)

Just-in-time elevation for high-privilege operations. Agents executing action-tools that modify downstream systems (create SOW, issue refund, approve prior auth) route through PIM for time-bounded elevation with approval trail.

K.3.5 Entra Verified ID

Cryptographic attestation of identity. For agents, emerging pattern: every agent deployment carries a Verified ID attesting to its model, version, and deployment context. Downstream systems verify agent identity before accepting tool calls.

K.3.6 Entra Agent ID (emerging)

First-class agent identity — agents treated as principals, not as service accounts. Per-agent audit, per-agent conditional access, per-agent lifecycle. Deloitte's delivery pattern positions agent fleets to adopt Entra Agent ID as it graduates from preview.

K.3.7 Entra ID Protection

Risk-based sign-in signals — unusual location, suspicious IP, credential-leak detection, behavioral anomaly. Extended to workload identities so abnormal agent behavior triggers the same risk framework as human credential compromise.

K.3.8 External ID (B2B / B2C)

Identity for partner users and customers. For APEX, relevant where client-facing Copilot Studio surfaces authenticate end-users (e.g., supplier portal, patient portal, member portal).

K.3.9 Cross-tenant access settings

Trust relationships between tenants. In multi-tenant APEX deployments (e.g., a bank with an insurance subsidiary), cross-tenant settings govern which Deloitte-delivered agents can reach which subsidiary's data.

K.4 Agent identity deep-dive

K.4.1 Managed identity per agent

Every Foundry-hosted agent runs under a dedicated Managed Identity. Identity provisioned during Wave 2 implementation; scoped to specific Fabric Gold views, Foundry endpoints, and downstream APIs the agent's manifest declares. No shared service principal; no broad-scope credentials; no credential rotation burden (managed by Azure).

K.4.2 Scope enforcement at token time

When the agent calls an MCP tool, the token carried is its managed identity. The MCP server validates the token, extracts the identity, cross-references with Purview scope rules, and returns data within authorized scope. Attempt to exceed scope returns a permission-denied error, logged to audit.

K.4.3 Conditional access for agents

CA policies on agent identities:

  • Require agent invocation from authorized Azure regions
  • Block agent sign-in outside approved hours (for scheduled-only agents)
  • Require recent managed-identity credential validation
  • Trigger step-up authentication for action-tools vs read-tools

K.4.4 Delegated identity for Copilot Studio agents

Copilot Studio surfaces user agents that act on behalf of the authenticated user. The user's delegated token authorizes the agent's actions. A junior merchandiser's delegated agent sees junior-merchandiser scope; a VP's delegated agent sees VP scope. Same agent code, different identity context.

K.4.5 Agent lifecycle management

Entra Identity Governance manages the agent-managed-identity lifecycle:

  • Provision at manifest activation during deployment
  • Rotate credential (automatic via managed identity platform)
  • Review every 90 days against current manifest
  • Retire at manifest deprecation
  • Audit every action via Entra sign-in logs + Purview audit

K.5 Tier-level security through Entra + Purview

The four-tier data security model from Appendix J executes through Entra identity + Purview classification. An agent's effective data visibility is the intersection of:

  1. Agent's Entra managed identity scopes
  2. Purview classification of the requested data
  3. Conditional Access context at the moment of query
  4. PIM elevation status (if applicable)
  5. DLP policy on the output channel

All five evaluated at each tool invocation; result cached briefly. Deny-by-default posture.

K.6 Audit and compliance

Every Entra-authenticated action writes audit events. For APEX agents:

  • Sign-in events (managed identity refresh, delegated token acquisition)
  • Tool-call events (identity, tool, parameters, result)
  • Scope-violation attempts (identity, attempted scope, denial reason)
  • Privileged-elevation events (PIM grants, reason, approver)

Feeds into Purview audit, Sentinel correlation, and APEX decision-audit-row with identity lineage.

K.7 Reference deployment — Identity design for Big Box Store Store 100

In the Store 100 illustrative narrative:

  • Marisol (store ops lead) authenticates as her named Entra identity; sees her store's data scoped to her Role-Based Access Control group
  • Agents in Store 100 scope run as dedicated managed identities — "agent-scml-cold-chain-s100", "agent-cxml-recall-s100", etc.
  • Agents are tenant-scoped — Store 100 agents cannot read Store 101 data; cross-store queries require federation-authorized identity
  • Conditional Access requires agent invocations only from the approved Azure region and only from Fabric capacity assigned to the retail practice
  • Action tools (trigger_markdown, notify_customer_recall) require PIM-elevated identity; approval routed through Copilot card to Marisol or her delegates

This design survives audit scrutiny because every action has identity provenance, every scope is minimal, and every elevation is logged.

K.8 Independence and Entra

At Deloitte-audit clients, Entra configuration is delivered by Deloitte as part of Agentic AI Delivery Services. The client licenses Entra from Microsoft. At engagement exit, the configured Entra policies remain in the client's tenant; Deloitte retains framework-level methodology.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. Never position Entra as Deloitte's product. It is a Microsoft platform capability. Deloitte's services configure Entra for agent-delivery scenarios using APEX methodology internally.

Appendix L

Azure AI Foundry — The Reasoning Plane Deep Dive

Azure AI Foundry is the intelligence plane for Deloitte's agent delivery. This appendix covers Foundry's full capability surface — model catalog, agent authoring, evaluation, monitoring, responsible-AI enforcement — and how Deloitte configures Foundry for Practice-specific agent workloads.

L.1 Foundry's role in APEX delivery

Every APEX agent runs in Foundry. Every MCP tool call reaches a Gold view whose query was authored by a Foundry agent. Every reasoning chain — single-turn decision, multi-turn planning, tool-use orchestration — executes in Foundry. Without Foundry, the agents exist as concepts but cannot run in production.

The client licenses Foundry directly from Microsoft. Deloitte's services configure and populate Foundry with:

  • Practice-specific agent definitions
  • Tool bindings to MCP servers
  • Evaluation harnesses per agent type
  • Monitoring dashboards per agent fleet
  • Responsible-AI policies per use case

L.2 Foundry capability map

L.2.1 Model catalog

Foundry's model catalog includes:

  • OpenAI models — GPT-4 class, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, o1 reasoning series, text-embedding-3
  • Anthropic — Claude family (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) on Foundry
  • Meta — Llama family
  • Mistral — Mistral Large, Small variants
  • Microsoft — Phi-4, Phi-3
  • Specialized — MedLM (healthcare), domain-tuned models
  • Open-source — curated HuggingFace models

Every APEX agent's manifest pins the model family and version. Model upgrades flow through the APEX bump-classification workflow with canary rollout.

L.2.2 Agent authoring

Two primary paths:

  • Foundry Agent Service (managed runtime) — declarative agent definitions with tool bindings, prompts, evaluation hooks
  • Custom agents (code-first) — Python or .NET with Foundry SDKs, deployed to Container Apps or Functions

Deloitte's APEX library standardises on the Foundry Agent Service for ~90% of agent patterns; custom code for the complex 10% requiring bespoke reasoning chains.

L.2.3 Prompt management

  • Versioned prompts in Foundry prompt library
  • A/B testing support
  • Prompt template variables bound to tool outputs
  • Prompt flow for multi-step chains

L.2.4 Tool use and MCP

Native MCP support in Foundry Agent Service. Each agent's manifest lists the MCP tools it can invoke; Foundry enforces the tool boundary at runtime. Tool calls typed via inputSchema; responses typed via output shape.

L.2.5 Evaluation (pre-production)

  • Groundedness — output sourced from retrieved content
  • Relevance — output addresses the query
  • Coherence — output internally consistent
  • Fluency — output readable
  • Safety — harmful content detection
  • Custom evaluators — Practice-specific (clinical accuracy for HLS, regulatory-citation correctness for Compliance agents)

L.2.6 Monitoring (production)

  • Agent invocation rate, latency, cost
  • Tool-call patterns, failure rates
  • Output evaluation scores trending
  • Drift detection vs baseline
  • Resource-consumption per agent

L.2.7 Responsible AI

Content Safety service:

  • Input filtering (prompt injection detection, jailbreak patterns)
  • Output filtering (hate, violence, sexual, self-harm, protected-material)
  • Custom blocklists and allowlists
  • Groundedness checks
  • Protected-material detection (code, text)

Foundry integrates Content Safety by default; Deloitte configures thresholds per Practice and use case.

L.2.8 Fine-tuning

Where foundation-model behavior needs customisation:

  • Few-shot prompt engineering (first line of customisation)
  • Retrieval-augmented generation (grounded on Fabric Gold)
  • Fine-tuning (when RAG insufficient; model-specific)
  • Distillation (smaller model trained from larger's outputs)

Deloitte's default: RAG over Fabric Gold. Fine-tuning reserved for high-volume narrow-domain agents where cost savings justify.

L.2.9 Multi-agent orchestration

  • Sequential — agent A output → agent B input
  • Parallel — multiple agents invoked concurrently, outputs merged
  • Hierarchical — orchestrator agent plans and dispatches to specialist agents
  • Feedback loops — agent self-critiques and re-runs until quality threshold

APEX's 47 orchestration patterns map to these primitives, with additional HITL-gate injection.

L.2.10 Cost and capacity

Foundry billing per-token for most models; per-hour for dedicated hosting. Deloitte's sizing model estimates annual Foundry cost per Practice at Wave 2 scale, enabling the CFO conversation.

L.3 Model tier strategy

Deloitte's default model-tier assignment:

Agent typeRecommended tierRationale
Triage / classificationSmall (Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini)High volume, simple decisions, cost-critical
Standard reasoningMedium (GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet)Most APEX agents
Complex reasoningLarge (o1, Claude Opus, GPT-4 frontier)Multi-step planning, 10% of catalog
EmbeddingText-embedding-3-largeRAG retrieval
Specialized clinicalMedLM or equivalentHLS-specific

Deloitte's delivery optimizes for the cheapest model that meets evaluation threshold, revisited quarterly.

L.4 Agent patterns in Foundry

L.4.1 Read-and-report

Simple pattern. Agent consumes an event, queries a Gold view via MCP tool, formats a response, returns to user surface. No HITL. Example: Store 100 morning briefing.

L.4.2 Reason-and-recommend

Agent consumes an event, queries multiple Gold views, reasons across them, produces a recommendation, routes to HITL. Example: Store 100 cold-chain dispose/save decision.

L.4.3 Plan-and-execute

Orchestrator agent plans a multi-step sequence, dispatches to specialist agents, monitors execution, handles exceptions. Example: Store 100 FDA recall workflow.

L.4.4 Monitor-and-alert

Continuous-monitoring agent consumes event streams, evaluates against pattern library, raises alerts when pattern matches. Example: sepsis early warning in hospital narrative.

L.4.5 Converse-and-gather

Copilot Studio agent interacting with a user to gather information before executing an action. Example: BOPIS substitution conversation.

L.5 Evaluation discipline

Every agent in an APEX-delivered fleet has:

  • Baseline eval at deployment — 100+ test cases scored on all quality dimensions
  • Continuous eval — sampled production invocations re-scored against expected outputs
  • Drift eval — periodic re-scoring of fixed canaries to detect model or data drift
  • A/B eval — when testing new prompts or models
  • Red-team eval — adversarial testing for safety, jailbreak resistance

L.6 Responsible AI enforcement

Content Safety policy per agent:

  • Input harm filtering
  • Output harm filtering
  • Prompt-injection shield
  • Groundedness verification (output sourced from retrieved grounds)
  • Protected-material detection
  • PII/PHI leakage prevention (integrated with Purview)

Violations log to Purview audit and Sentinel; severe violations auto-rollback agent to prior version.

L.7 Cost management

Foundry token cost is the largest ongoing Microsoft-licensing-side expense in a mature APEX deployment. Cost levers:

  • Model tier optimization (cheapest model passing eval)
  • Prompt compression
  • Response caching for deterministic queries
  • Batch inference for non-latency-sensitive agents
  • RAG optimization (retrieve less, reason over quality)

Deloitte's delivery includes quarterly cost-review cadence to tune.

L.8 Reference deployment — Big Box Store Store 100 Foundry configuration

Store 100 agent fleet runs in Foundry with:

  • ~40 agents across RC Practice
  • ~70% on GPT-4.1 / Claude Sonnet (standard tier)
  • ~20% on GPT-4o-mini / Phi-4 (small-tier for triage)
  • ~10% on o1-mini / Claude Opus (reasoning-tier for complex orchestration like recall-scope)
  • Content Safety at high-sensitivity threshold for customer-facing surfaces
  • Groundedness threshold 85%+ for action-recommending agents
  • Monthly model-tier review against cost/quality trade-off

L.9 Independence considerations

  • Foundry is a Microsoft product; client contracts Microsoft
  • Deloitte's Foundry configuration (agent definitions, evaluators, monitoring) is services work
  • Audit-client pre-clearance required for regulated-industry agent deployment
  • Language: "Deloitte configures Foundry for agent delivery" — never "Deloitte sells Foundry"

Appendix P

Regulatory Reference — What Shapes Each Practice Pursuit

This appendix is the seller's regulatory primer per Practice. Sellers do not give legal advice; they should know enough to speak intelligently when a Chief Compliance Officer raises a framework.

P.1 Retail & Consumer (RC)

  • FSMA 204 (Food Safety Modernization Act §204) — traceability requirements for high-risk food. Effective 2026. Requires lot-level trace from supplier through store to customer within specific timeframes. APEX recall-scope agents directly support compliance.
  • PCI DSS 4.0 — payment card industry data security. Applies to any RC client accepting card payments.
  • CCPA / CPRA (California) — consumer privacy. Right to access, delete, opt-out.
  • GDPR — applicable to RC clients with EU customers or operations.
  • State privacy laws — Virginia CDPA, Colorado CPA, Connecticut CTDPA, Utah UCPA, and expanding list.
  • FTC Section 5 — consumer-protection for algorithmic pricing, steering, and recommendation.

P.2 Healthcare & Life Sciences (HLS)

  • HIPAA / HITECH — PHI protection, breach notification, business-associate agreements.
  • 21 CFR Part 11 (Life Sciences) — electronic records and signatures for FDA-regulated activities.
  • FDA software-as-medical-device (SaMD) guidance — where agent outputs could be interpreted as clinical decision.
  • AI/ML-based SaMD guidance (FDA evolving) — change-control for ML models in regulated medical devices.
  • State privacy + CMIA (California Medical Information Act) — state-specific health privacy.
  • Anti-Kickback Statute + Stark Law (US) — for commercial-effectiveness agents in pharma and provider pursuits.
  • EU AI Act — high-risk AI classification for healthcare; compliance timeline extending through 2027.

P.3 Energy & Resources (ER)

  • NERC CIP (North American Electric Reliability Corporation Critical Infrastructure Protection) — cybersecurity standards for bulk power system.
  • FERC orders — ongoing FERC orders shape grid and market operations.
  • EPA regulations — air quality, methane monitoring, water.
  • State PUC rules — utility commission regulation varies by state.
  • SEC climate disclosure rules — Scope 1/2/3 emissions reporting for public companies (evolving).
  • DOE Order 140.1 — energy-sector cybersecurity.
  • PIPES Act — pipeline safety.

P.4 Industrial & Manufacturing (AXLE)

  • NHTSA regulations — automotive safety, recall processes, reporting.
  • FAA regulations — aviation manufacturing compliance.
  • DFARS + ITAR — defense manufacturing.
  • ISO 9001 / AS9100 / IATF 16949 — quality management standards.
  • EPA — emissions and environmental compliance.
  • OSHA — worker safety, particularly ergonomics in workforce-intelligence agents.
  • UFLPA (Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act) — supply-chain due diligence.
  • EU AI Act — high-risk AI classification for manufacturing-safety-critical systems.

P.5 Technology, Media & Telecom (TMT)

  • FCC regulations — telecom, broadcast, spectrum.
  • CPNI (Customer Proprietary Network Information) — telecom-specific privacy.
  • COPPA — child online privacy (media).
  • Section 230 — platform liability (media, social).
  • Network neutrality rules — evolving.
  • EU AI Act — content moderation and recommendation systems classified as high-risk.
  • DSA / DMA — EU Digital Services Act / Digital Markets Act.

P.6 Travel & Hospitality (TH)

  • DOT tarmac-rule — passenger rights on extended tarmac delays.
  • 14 CFR Part 117 — flight and duty-time limits (pilots).
  • TSA regulations — security screening, passenger data.
  • EU261 — passenger rights in EU air travel.
  • CRS rules — Computer Reservation System regulations.
  • GDPR + CCPA — passenger data.
  • Maritime regulations (cruise industry).
  • ADA — accessibility.

P.7 Industrial & Commercial Equipment (ICE)

  • EPA emissions — equipment emissions standards.
  • OSHA — safety standards for heavy equipment operation.
  • EAR / ITAR — export controls.
  • UFLPA — supply-chain due diligence.
  • Dealer-network laws — state-by-state franchise regulations.

P.8 Cross-Practice AI-specific regulation

  • EU AI Act (2024-2027 phased) — classifies AI systems by risk; high-risk AI requires specific compliance framework. Affects any client operating in EU.
  • US state AI laws — Colorado, Illinois, NYC evolving.
  • Federal AI executive orders — evolving federal posture.
  • ISO/IEC 42001 — AI management systems standard.
  • NIST AI RMF — AI risk management framework.

P.9 Regulatory-response discipline for sellers

When a client raises a regulation:

  1. Acknowledge the regulation exists and applies
  2. Note that Deloitte's delivery includes compliance design as a Wave-1 deliverable
  3. Describe the general pattern (Purview for lineage, audit row for defensibility, HITL for human accountability)
  4. Commit to specific-regulation mapping in envisioning, not in first-meeting

Never: provide definitive legal interpretation; Deloitte Legal reviews regulated-industry SOWs.

Appendix R

Managed Services & Sustain Motion — Post-Wave-2 Operations

This appendix covers the sustain phase that follows Wave 2 implementation. Managed services is where the largest long-term commercial value lives and where Deloitte's client relationship becomes durable.

R.1 What sustain means

Post-Wave-2 "go-live" is not the end. Agent fleets require ongoing operation: evaluation, retraining, drift correction, regulatory-framework-update incorporation, scope expansion, cost optimization, HITL tuning, incident response. Sustain is a multi-year commitment.

R.2 Three sustain operating models

Model A: Client-operated, Deloitte advisory

Client operates the agent fleet with their own team; Deloitte provides advisory, periodic review, major-change support. Lower ongoing fee; client owns operational maturity.

Model B: Deloitte-operated managed service

Deloitte runs agent fleet on client's Microsoft platform. Full managed operation including evaluation, tuning, scope expansion, incident response. Monthly / quarterly fee structure; SLA-backed.

Model C: Hybrid

Client operates routine; Deloitte handles exceptions, major changes, regulatory updates, scope expansions. Most common pattern at scale.

R.3 Managed-service scope dimensions

Operational:

  • Agent evaluation and monitoring
  • Drift detection and remediation
  • Incident response (agent misbehavior, performance degradation)
  • HITL-gate backlog management
  • Cost optimization

Change management:

  • Quarterly agent-library updates
  • Model-tier rebalancing
  • Prompt refinement
  • Tool-catalog extensions

Regulatory:

  • Framework-update incorporation
  • Compliance-evidence package preparation
  • Audit response
  • Regulator-simulation exercises

Strategic:

  • Quarterly business review
  • Scope-expansion planning
  • Roadmap alignment with Microsoft platform evolution
  • Cross-practice expansion opportunities

R.4 Commercial structure

Managed-service contracts typically:

  • 3-year minimum term
  • Annual fee with annual escalator
  • Includes defined scope (number of agents, number of MCP tools, number of users)
  • Scope-expansion pricing at contracted rates
  • SLA-backed with service credits on miss
  • Exit provisions (knowledge transfer, artifact retention by client)

Annual fees typically 30-40% of Wave 2 implementation envelope, varying by scope.

R.5 SLA anchors

Standard SLAs for managed services:

DimensionSLA anchor

Incident resolutionP1 within 4 hours, P2 within 24 hours

R.6 Renewal and expansion patterns

Healthy managed-service relationships:

  • 95%+ renewal at end of term
  • Typical scope expansion: 15-25% year-over-year
  • Cross-practice expansion: 30%+ of clients expand to a second Practice within 36 months
  • Deloitte's role deepens from delivery to strategic advisor

R.7 Exit and handoff

  • Artefact ownership transfer (configurations, pipelines, agents are client's)
  • APEX framework methodology remains Deloitte's (client does not own methodology)
  • Post-exit: option for periodic advisory engagement

R.8 Selling managed services

Managed services is a separate commercial conversation from Wave 1-2. Best timing: late Wave 2 (month 8-10), when delivery quality is demonstrated and the client's operational team is considering sustain options. Deliver concrete SLA proposal alongside the client's alternative (in-house operation).

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. Managed services on audit clients require pre-clearance the same as implementation. Funding-path compliance (no ECIF) applies.
