T.10.16 Using this mapping in Wave 2 scoping

The archetype cross-reference gives Wave 2 commercial envelope math concrete inputs:

  • Count orchestrations in scope → sum them; ~15–30 is typical for Wave 2
  • Map each to its archetype (using tables T.10.3 through T.10.14)
  • Archetypes shared across orchestrations reuse the specialization effort — delivery effort is per-archetype-family, not per-orchestration
  • Result: Wave 2 commercial envelope ties to archetype count × family-specialization effort + per-orchestration integration effort, not to raw orchestration count

This decomposition is what makes APEX's acceleration compound. A new client's Wave 2 doesn't re-design 150 orchestrations; it specialises 15–30 archetypes to the client's Practice semantic model. That specialization work is measured in weeks-per-archetype, not months-per-orchestration.

Using this catalog in pursuit conversations

  • CIO / architect questions about scope — point to per-schema sub-sections (T.2.1 SCML, T.3.1 Payer, etc.) as the concrete answer to "which orchestrations exist for [domain]."
  • CFO questions about Wave 2 scope — count target orchestrations × specialization effort + integration effort = Wave 2 commercial envelope math.
  • Compliance questions about governance — every orchestration in the catalog has explicit HITL pattern + classification handling + audit emission. That per-orchestration governance is the compliance story.
  • Microsoft field-team coordination — when a Microsoft seller asks "what workloads pull through" for an APEX engagement, orchestration count × Foundry consumption per orchestration = Foundry pull-through.

Appendix U

Cost Calculation — Microsoft Fabric + Agentic AI

This appendix is the seller's practical reference for sizing client investments across the two-contract model: (1) client ↔ Microsoft for platform capacity (Fabric + Azure OpenAI) and (2) client ↔ Deloitte for Agentic AI Delivery Services. Source references: Deloitte's standard Fabric licensing calculator, Azure OpenAI PTU Calculator documentation, and APEX internal delivery economics.

U.1 How to Read This Appendix

The cost of an Agentic AI program has three stacked layers:

  1. Microsoft Fabric capacity — reserved compute (F-SKU) for the data platform (Bronze / Silver / Gold medallion, OneLake storage, Power BI, real-time).
  2. Azure OpenAI + Foundry runtime — model inference (PTU or PAYGO), orchestration runtime, retrieval (AI Search), safety (Content Safety), and MCP endpoint hosting.
  3. Deloitte Agentic AI Delivery Services — Deloitte's Wave 1 / 2 / 3 services to design, build, and run agents on top of layers 1 and 2.

The client contracts layers 1 and 2 directly with Microsoft. The client contracts layer 3 with Deloitte. APEX (Deloitte's internal delivery accelerator) makes layers 1 and 2 do more per dollar — it is not priced to the client as a separate SKU.

U.2 Microsoft Fabric Cost Calculation

U.2.1 The F-SKU Capacity Model

Fabric is priced as reserved capacity units (CU) sold as F-SKUs. Clients buy compute capacity; storage (OneLake) is billed separately at ~\$0.023/GB/month.

SKUCU~PAYG \$/hr~Reserved \$/mo (1-yr, ~41% off)
F22\$0.36~\$156
F44\$0.72~\$312
F88\$1.44~\$625
F1616\$2.88~\$1,250
F3232\$5.76~\$2,500
F6464\$11.52~\$5,000 (Copilot-eligible threshold)
F128128\$23.04~\$10,000
F256256\$46.08~\$20,000
F512512\$92.16~\$40,000
F20482,048\$368.64~\$160,000

Two key inflection points:

  • F64 — minimum for Copilot in Fabric and for free Power BI Pro license passthrough to viewers.
  • F256+ — typical enterprise baseline for multi-workload platforms (warehouse + lakehouse + real-time + data science + ML).

U.2.2 The Sizing Formula (Capacity Planning Pattern)

TEXT
Required_CU = max(
    Peak_Concurrent_Workload_CU,
    Sustained_Daytime_Workload_CU × burst_factor
)

Monthly_Fabric_Cost = Required_CU × hourly_rate × 730 × (1 - reservation_discount)
                    + OneLake_GB × $0.023
                    + Mirroring_GB × mirroring_rate (free up to storage cap)
                    + Data_Egress_GB × egress_rate

Workload CU estimates (rules of thumb):

WorkloadCU range
Small Power BI dataset refresh2–4 CU
Medium semantic model (interactive users < 100)4–8 CU
Data pipeline (hourly ingest, < 100 GB)4–16 CU
Lakehouse ETL (medallion, daily)16–64 CU
Warehouse with concurrent queries32–128 CU
Real-time eventstream + KQL16–64 CU
ML training workloadsBurst 64–256 CU

U.2.3 Smoothing and Bursting

Fabric smooths CU consumption over 24 hours (background) or 5 minutes (interactive). The client can run briefly above SKU capacity so long as the rolling average fits. Right-size to the sustained P90, not the spike. This is a common source of over-provisioning by sellers unfamiliar with Fabric's smoothing window.

U.2.4 Reservation Economics

  • Pay-As-You-Go — maximum flexibility, full hourly rate, pause anytime. Right for Wave 1 pilot.
  • 1-Year Reservation — ~41% discount. Right for stable production workloads after Wave 1 proves consumption.
  • 3-Year Reservation — ~60%+ discount. Only after consumption patterns are proven through at least two quarters of production telemetry.

Seller rule: Start PAYG during Wave 1 pilot, reserve at Wave 2 baseline, extend at Wave 3 enterprise rollout. Recommending a 3-year reservation on day one is a common rookie mistake that locks the client into capacity they may not need.

U.2.5 OneLake Storage and Mirroring

  • OneLake — ~\$0.023/GB/month, billed on actual usage. Clients should plan for 3–5x the raw data size to account for Bronze + Silver + Gold copies plus Delta Lake versioning.
  • Mirroring (SQL, Cosmos, Snowflake → Fabric) — free up to the storage allowance of the F-SKU (approximately 1 TB per F64). Excess mirrored data is billed at OneLake rates.
  • Shortcuts (virtualized references to ADLS, S3, GCS) — no duplication cost; only compute on query. A powerful lever for multi-cloud clients.

U.3 Agentic AI Cost Calculation (Azure OpenAI + Foundry)

Agentic AI cost decomposes as (model inference cost) + (orchestration / Foundry runtime) + (retrieval / indexing cost) + (content safety / guardrails). Model inference is typically 70–85% of the total.

U.3.1 The Two Pricing Modes

  • Pay-As-You-Go (PAYGO) — per-token billing; right for unpredictable or low-volume workloads. No floor, no commitment.
  • Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU) — reserved per-minute throughput; right for production agents with predictable load.
  • Breakeven between the two modes is approximately 40–50% sustained utilization.

U.3.2 PTU Rates (Global Provisioned)

ModelInput TPM per PTUOutput RatioMin DeploymentIncrement
GPT-4o2,5001:1 (standard)15 PTU5 PTU
GPT-4.13,0004:1 weighted15 PTU5 PTU
GPT-5 / 5.23,400–4,7508:1 weighted15 PTU5 PTU
o-series (reasoning)lower TPM, higher latencyvaries15 PTU5 PTU

Hourly rate: \$0.0396 / PTU / hour (~\$29 / PTU / month on-demand).

  • 1-Year Reserved: 20% off (~\$23 / PTU / month).
  • 3-Year Reserved: 40% off (~\$17 / PTU / month).

Deployment-type minimums:

  • Global Provisioned — 15 PTU minimum, 5 PTU increments, cheapest per-PTU. Right for most workloads.
  • Data Zone (50/50 split) — higher rate; compliance trade-off for data-residency-sensitive clients (EU, UK, Canada).
  • Regional (100/100) — 100 PTU minimum, highest rate, strictest residency. Typical for federal, HLS PHI, and banking.

U.3.3 The PTU Sizing Formula

TEXT
Effective_Tokens_TPM = Input_TPM
                     + (Output_TPM × output_ratio_multiplier)
                     + Cached_TPM × 0       ← cached reads are FREE

PTUs_Required = Effective_Tokens_TPM / Input_TPM_per_PTU
                (rounded up to nearest increment; minimum 15 PTU on Global)

Monthly_Model_Cost = PTUs × $0.0396 × 730 × (1 - reservation_discount)

Worked example — RC store-ops agent fleet, GPT-4.1:

  • Peak load: 45,000 Input TPM + 20,000 Output TPM
  • Effective TPM = 45,000 + (20,000 × 4) = 125,000
  • PTUs needed = 125,000 / 3,000 = 41.7 → round to 45 PTU
  • Monthly (PAYG hourly) = 45 × \$0.0396 × 730 = ~\$1,300/month
  • 1-year reserved = ~\$1,040/month

U.3.4 Spillover Hybrid (PTU + PAYGO)

The canonical production pattern is deploy PTU at the sustained P50, let overflow spill to PAYGO. Typical split for an APEX agent fleet:

  • 70% PTU (baseline) + 30% PAYGO (peak bursts) — best TCO for bursty workloads.
  • Cached tokens (repeated system prompts, few-shot examples, canonical schema instructions) receive a 100% discount → steady-state effective rate drops 40–60% below list.

U.3.5 Retrieval, Safety, Foundry Runtime

ComponentRough cost (enterprise workload)

Content Safety (guardrails)\$0.75 per 1K text records
Foundry Agent runtimeincluded in Azure subscription; compute billed via underlying services
MCP endpoint hosting (APIM + Container Apps)~\$200–\$800/month per fleet
Purview scanning (sensitivity labels, classification)per-asset metering; typically \$500–\$2,500/month at enterprise scale

U.3.6 Annual Foundry Token-Spend Bands (APEX Wave Model)

U.5 APEX Acceleration Impact on Cost

APEX's internal accelerators — canonical schemas, orchestration catalog, pre-built agent templates, 47 archetypes, envelope framework — drive client cost down in three measurable ways:

  1. Token-efficiency. Canonical schemas (SCML, MERML, CXML, AXLEML) let agents retrieve via structured MCP queries instead of long unstructured prompts. Typical reduction: 30–50% fewer input tokens per call, directly reducing PTU requirement.
  2. Cache hit rate. APEX-standard system prompts and few-shot examples promote Azure OpenAI prompt caching. Steady-state cache hit rates of 40–60% are typical, which drops the effective per-token rate by the same percentage.
  3. Orchestration reuse. The pattern library (Sequential / Parallel / Hierarchical / Feedback, 47 archetypes) means fewer custom agents per outcome. Fewer deployed agents → fewer PTU floors hit → lower minimum committed capacity.

Seller-facing framing (Independence-safe):

"Client pays Microsoft for platform capacity. Deloitte's delivery services — accelerated by APEX internally — make that capacity do more, so the dollar-per-outcome on Fabric and Foundry is two-to-three times better than a greenfield build."

W.3 The 30-minute discovery agenda

For a first exploratory conversation with a C-level or VP-level sponsor. Deloitte team of 2 (lead + SME or architect); client team of 1–3.

TimeTopicLeadOutput
0–5 minIntroductions, meeting goalDeloitte leadAlignment on agenda
5–10 minClient context — what's on your board agenda for agentic AIClient speaksQualifier signal per §1.5
10–20 minDeloitte framing — 3 slides: APEX framework, reference architecture, one industry narrativeDeloitte leadArchitect credibility
20–25 minThe question we most want your input on — which decision in your operating area would you most want automated first?Client speaksLead-service hypothesis
25–30 minNext stepsBothScheduled discovery workshop OR explicit decline

Ends with one of three outcomes: discovery workshop scheduled, second exploratory meeting scheduled, or gracefully declined. A meeting that ends with "let's stay in touch" counts as declined.

W.4 The four-week discovery workshop outline

Wave 0 / Wave 1 pre-landing. Four weekly sessions, 2–3 hours each. Deloitte team of 4; client team of 6–10.

W.4.1 Week 1 — Context and pain mapping

  • Strategic-priorities review (from public disclosures + prior pursuit intelligence)
  • Persona mapping — decisions spanning personas
  • Pain articulation — three pains in client's own words, ranked
  • SOR inventory (Bronze-tier candidate list)

Output: ranked pain list, candidate service set (2–5 services).

W.4.2 Week 2 — Architecture alignment

  • Target-state reference architecture for candidate services
  • Fabric footprint (workspace design, capacity estimate)
  • Foundry footprint (PTU / PAYG for Wave 1)
  • Purview governance scope
  • Entra identity plane alignment
  • Integration inventory

Output: architecture sketch, capacity estimate, integration list.

W.4.3 Week 3 — Service selection and KPI commitment

  • Narrow candidate services from 2–5 to 1–3 for Wave 1
  • KPI baseline and Wave 1 target per service
  • HITL gate design
  • Orchestration selection (which of the 47 archetypes)
  • Success criteria

Output: service commitment, KPI targets, success criteria.

W.4.4 Week 4 — Wave 1 plan and Wave 2 roadmap

  • 4–12-week Wave 1 plan with named deliverables
  • Wave 2 roadmap outline (6–12 months)
  • Wave 3 vision (multi-year)
  • Wave 1 commercial envelope
  • Deliverables list (per §W.5)
  • SOW outline (per §W.6)

Output: Wave 1 plan, Wave 2 roadmap, draft SOW.

W.5 The Wave 1 deliverables list

  1. Current-state architecture diagram — Fabric / Foundry / Copilot / Purview / Entra layer map with client SORs.
  2. Target-state architecture diagram — same layers with Wave 2 endpoint.
  3. Service selection document — 1–3 APEX services with personas, KPIs, HITL patterns.
  4. Data-asset inventory — Bronze / Silver / Gold tier plan per service.
  5. Schema envelope declaration — canonical schemas in scope, entities materialized.
  6. Orchestration design — archetype selection + customization per service.
  7. Governance design — Purview labels, DLP policies, Entra scope, HITL inventory.
  8. Audit-row design — what each agent emits, retention per classification.
  9. Wave 2 roadmap — 6–12 months phased deliverables.
  10. Commercial envelope — Wave 2 price band, value-share options where applicable.
  11. Risk register — Independence pre-clearance, regulatory risks, technical risks.
  12. Operating-model design — client-side roles for Wave 2 co-delivery.

W.6 Wave 1 SOW outline

Each section below is a placeholder that Deloitte Commercial fills with approved language.

  1. Parties and recitals
  2. Engagement scope — "Wave 1 envisioning and landing for {{ServiceList}} on Microsoft technology platform"
  3. Deliverables — reference §W.5 list, numbered
  4. Timeline — 4–12 weeks, named weekly milestones
  5. Team — Deloitte team per §35.10.1 (individuals named at contract execution)
  6. Client obligations — data access, stakeholder availability, platform access
  7. Microsoft platform prerequisites — "Client responsible for Microsoft platform licensing and capacity independently"
  8. Commercial terms — Wave 1 fixed fee + expenses; payment schedule
  9. Wave 2 option — client option to extend, commercial envelope range declared
  10. Independence provisions — specific to Deloitte audit-client status if applicable
  11. Intellectual property — APEX IP remains Deloitte; client work product as defined
  12. Standard terms — per Deloitte MSA / engagement letter

W.7 Wave 2 SOW additions

Wave 2 SOWs add:

  • Phased deliverables across 6–12 months
  • Named milestones with exit criteria per phase
  • KPI measurement obligations (what / by whom / at what cadence)
  • Value-share schedule (if applicable) with attribution mechanism
  • Change-control process
  • Managed-services option for Wave 3

W.8 The pursuit-QR review checklist

Before submitting the SOW to the client, route through the pursuit QR:

  • [ ] Independence pre-clearance confirmed if audit client
  • [ ] Funding path identified and Independence-compliant (no ECIF direct to Deloitte)
  • [ ] Two-contract framing explicit in SOW
  • [ ] Scope / schedule / price internally consistent
  • [ ] Named team roles approved by Delivery
  • [ ] IP terms consistent with standard Deloitte IP policy
  • [ ] Regulatory obligations accurately reflected
  • [ ] KPI commitments defensible (per §C.9.10)

W.9 Common authoring mistakes

  • Vague deliverables. "Architecture guidance" is not a deliverable. "Target-state architecture diagram v1.0 delivered Week 3, signed off by client architecture lead" is.
  • Soft timeline. "Approximately 8 weeks" is unprofessional. "8 weeks from kickoff, with weekly checkpoints on Fridays" is.
  • Implicit team. Naming roles without committing to named individuals undercuts credibility.
  • Over-scoping Wave 1. Wave 1 is not for 10 services. 1–3 is right; Wave 2 grows.
  • Under-scoping KPI. "KPI improvement" is not a deliverable. "MAPE reduction of 20–35% for SKU-store-day forecast, Week 10 vs Wave 0 baseline" is.

AXLE at a glance:

Appendix Y

Comprehensive Glossary of Terms

This glossary is the comprehensive reference of terms used throughout the sellers guide. Terms are organized alphabetically. Appendix F contains a shorter quick-reference glossary for commonly-used terms; Appendix Y is the full reference including technical, commercial, regulatory, and organizational vocabulary.

Y.1 A

AAML — Assembly Analytics ML schema in the AXLE framework; covers OEE, throughput, bottleneck detection for automotive manufacturing.

Action tool — An MCP tool that invokes a state change in a downstream system (create work-order, approve engineering change, issue refund, dispatch truck). Always governed by a HITL gate.

Agent — A reasoning component built on a foundation model that uses tools, retrieved data, and orchestrated prompts to produce decisions or recommendations. APEX agents run in Azure AI Foundry.

Agent ID (Entra Agent ID) — Microsoft's emerging first-class identity primitive for agents. Agents treated as principals with conditional access, session controls, and audit scope.

Agent-safe view — A Gold data view prepared specifically for agent consumption, with classification-aware masking, identity scoping, and output signing.

Agentic AI — AI systems that use agents — LLM-backed reasoners with tool-use capability — to take multi-step actions under defined constraints.

APEX — Agent-based Platform for EXecution. Deloitte's internal delivery accelerator for agentic AI on the Microsoft platform. Never sold as a product to clients. Composed of methodology, semantic-model library, agent catalog, MCP tool library, HITL gate framework, audit-row discipline, and Wave 1/2/3 playbook.

Archetype (orchestration archetype) — One of the 47 reusable orchestration patterns in APEX's internal catalog. Practice-specific orchestrations are instantiations of archetypes, not bespoke designs. See Appendix T.

Audit row — The structured, version-pinned, tamper-evident record an APEX agent emits for every decision. Contains identity, policy version, manifest version, model version, prompt version, inputs (by content hash), tool calls (by content hash), reasoning trace reference, decision output, HITL status, and downstream effect. The unit of regulatory defensibility. See §6.10 for emission detail and §8.8 for storage and retention.

APEX Core — The shared infrastructure (manifests, runtime, tool-binding, audit row, HITL framework) that every APEX-delivered service builds upon.

APEX Wave — The delivery phases Deloitte uses: Wave 1 (Envision + Land), Wave 2 (Enable + Scale), Wave 3 (Sustain + Transform).

Attribution (audit row) — The mechanism by which every APEX agent decision traces to a measurable business outcome, enabling CFO-credible ROI conversations.

Audit row — The per-decision record that APEX writes for every agent action, containing inputs, reasoning trace, model version, tool version, HITL status, and downstream effect. Regulator-ready evidential record.

AXLE — Deloitte's Automotive eXchange Layer for Enterprise — sibling DMTSP framework to APEX, purpose-built for automotive manufacturing. 9 canonical ML schemas (AAML, QEML, PDML, SCML, WOSFML, DTML, CVML, ESML, WLML), 10 agentic orchestrations, 6 reference architecture layers, 7 MCP servers.

AXLEML — APEX's canonical semantic model for the AXLE Practice (automotive + aerospace + industrial products + discrete manufacturing). Different from the AXLE framework (narrower automotive-only).

Azure AI Foundry — Microsoft's enterprise AI platform for agents, models, and orchestration. APEX agents run here.

Azure AI Speech — Microsoft's speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and speaker identification service. Load-bearing for voice-AI contact-center scenarios.

Azure Communication Services (ACS) — Microsoft's programmable voice, SMS, email, chat, and Teams communications platform. Contact-center voice channel.

Azure Container Apps — Container hosting service used for MCP servers in APEX deployments.

Azure OpenAI — Microsoft-hosted OpenAI models (GPT-4 family, o1, embeddings). Accessible via Azure AI Foundry.

Y.2 B

Big Box Store (BBS) — Illustrative large-format retailer used in the Chapter 16 reference deployment narrative. Fictional anchor account for RC Practice examples.

Bronze layer — The raw-landing layer of the medallion architecture. Source-fidelity data with append-only semantics. Not canonicalized.

BSS (Business Support Systems) — Telecom industry term for billing, ordering, provisioning, customer-management systems. Modernisation target for TMT-TEL agentic AI.

Y.3 C

Call center — See "Contact Center."

Canonical entity — A business entity (Customer, SKU, Patient, Well, etc.) defined in an APEX semantic model with standard attributes, relationships, and classifications.

Capacity (Fabric) — Fabric is purchased in F-SKUs (F2, F4, F8, F16, F32, F64, F128, F256, F512, F1024, F2048). Capacity is a pool of CUs (Capacity Units) shared across workloads.

Case (UM Case, Service Case, Customer Incident Case) — A workflow record that aggregates related events, decisions, and actions around a specific incident or scenario.

CCX / CC-CCX — Contact-center capability codes in APEX Practice library (CC-CCX-01 Real-time Voice Assist, CC-CCX-02 Bot-First Resolution, etc.).

CDC (Change Data Capture) — Database replication mechanism that captures row-level changes in real-time. Foundation of Fabric Mirrored Database.

Classification — Purview's system for labeling data with sensitivity categories (PII, PHI, PCI, SOX-controlled, etc.). Drives downstream DLP, access control, and audit.

Commercial QR — Deloitte's Commercial Quality Review process for engagement commercials and value-share arrangements.

Compliance Manager — Purview's regulatory-framework tracking tool with assessments, controls, and evidence management.

Conditional Access (CA) — Entra's rule-based access policies evaluated at every sign-in and token-acquisition event.

Contact Center (Microsoft) — The Microsoft portfolio for customer service: Dynamics 365 Contact Center + Copilot Studio + ACS + Azure AI Speech + Foundry + Dataverse + Purview + Entra.

Copilot (Microsoft 365 Copilot) — Microsoft's user-surface AI embedded in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive.

Copilot Studio — Microsoft's environment for building custom conversational copilots grounded on enterprise data.

CPNI (Customer Proprietary Network Information) — Telecom-specific customer-data privacy regulation under FCC Section 222. Heightened Purview classification applies.

CXML — APEX Customer Experience ML canonical schema in RC Practice.

Y.4 D

Data Activator — Fabric's reflex/event-rule engine for event-driven automation on data conditions.

Data Map (Purview) — The inventory of the data estate with assets, schemas, classifications, lineage, and ownership.

Dataflow Gen2 — Fabric's managed ETL service for REST/SaaS source ingestion via Power Query (M).

Dataverse — The business-application data store underlying Dynamics 365 and Power Platform.

DCIF (Digital Cloud Investment Fund) — Approved Microsoft funding path where Microsoft allocates funds to the client who then contracts Deloitte directly. Compliant with Deloitte Independence.

DDL (Data Definition Language) — SQL statements that define database structure (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE).

Decision (agent decision) — A discrete output from an APEX agent that carries an audit row and either executes automatically (for automated patterns) or requires HITL approval.

Delegated identity — An agent acting on behalf of a specific human user, inheriting that user's data scope.

Delta Lake — The open-source Delta table format used in Fabric Lakehouse. ACID transactions, time travel, schema evolution.

Deloitte Agentic AI Delivery Services — The services Deloitte sells to clients for agentic AI on the Microsoft platform. Clients buy this; clients do not buy APEX.

DLP (Data Loss Prevention) — Purview's policy engine that enforces data-handling rules based on classification, including inspection of agent outputs.

DMTSP — Deloitte Microsoft Technology & Services Practice. Deloitte's practice dedicated to Microsoft-platform services.

DOT tarmac rule — US Department of Transportation rule limiting passenger time on aircraft tarmac during ground delays. Airline operations must detect and respond to tarmac-rule exposure.

Y.5 E

E7 (Microsoft 365 E7) — The emerging Microsoft 365 Enterprise SKU positioned as the agentic-AI-focused tier. Covered in Appendix I.

ECIF (Enterprise Customer Investment Fund) — Microsoft funding mechanism that cannot flow directly to Deloitte due to Deloitte's audit relationship with Microsoft. Approved funding paths are direct client, DCIF to client, ISV Marketplace, or SI teaming.

EHR (Electronic Health Record) — Clinical information system (Epic, Oracle Health Cerner, Meditech, etc.).

Envelope — A bounded scope in APEX terminology. Five distinct envelope types exist: (1) Commercial Envelope — money-and-time boundary of a Wave; (2) Scope Envelope — functional-scope boundary of the engagement; (3) Data Envelope — boundary around data an agent may read/write; (4) Schema Envelope — boundary around canonical entities a service depends on; (5) Trust Envelope — classification + identity + DLP boundary enforced everywhere. Envelopes nest: commercial contains scope contains data derived from schema governed by trust. See §2.2A for full deep-dive.

Envelope (Commercial) — The money-and-time boundary of a Wave engagement. Wave 1 typical $500K–$2M, Wave 2 $5–$15M, Wave 3 $8–$30M. Driven by the schema envelope beneath it.

Envelope (Data) — The boundary of what data an agent's managed identity authorizes reading and what the agent may write. Enforced at MCP tool + Purview + Entra layers.

Envelope (Schema) — The boundary around the canonical-entity subset a specific APEX service depends on. The schema envelope determines which Silver models, Gold views, MCP tools, and agents get built — and therefore determines the commercial envelope the CFO sees.

Envelope (Scope) — The functional-scope boundary of the engagement — which services, agents, MCP tools, Gold views, classifications, and KPIs are delivered. Documented in the SOW.

Envelope (Trust) — The classification + identity + DLP boundary enforced everywhere. Orthogonal to the other envelopes; intersects every one of them.

Entra ID — Microsoft's identity and access management service. The identity plane in APEX's four-plane architecture.

Eventhouse — Fabric's KQL-queryable data store for real-time events and telemetry.

Eventstream — Fabric's real-time event ingestion pipeline.

Envelope (APEX envelope framework) — See "Five envelopes."

Y.6 F

Fabric (Microsoft Fabric) — Microsoft's unified SaaS data platform. The data plane in APEX's four-plane architecture.

Five envelopes (the APEX envelope framework) — The five contractable boundaries that govern every APEX engagement: Commercial (SOW scope), Scope (services / personas / outcomes), Data (asset list + identity scopes), Schema (canonical entities in scope), and Trust (classification / DLP / HITL / audit retention). Envelopes nest: Commercial contains Scope contains Data; Data is derived from Schema; Schema is governed by Trust. See §2.2A.

Fabric Capacity — See "Capacity (Fabric)."

Fabric Deployment Pipelines — Fabric's CI/CD mechanism for promoting artifacts across dev/test/prod.

Federation (identity) — Cross-tenant or cross-system identity relationships. APEX supports federation at both Entra and agent levels.

Foundry — See "Azure AI Foundry."

FSMA 204 — Food Safety Modernization Act Section 204; US traceability requirements for high-risk food effective 2026.

FY27 — Fiscal year 2027 (mid-2026 through mid-2027 for most enterprises). Timeline reference in Appendix Q.

Y.7 G

Glossary (quick reference) — Appendix F; shorter commonly-used terms reference.

Gold layer — The serving layer of the medallion architecture. Aggregated, pre-measured, agent-consumable views derived from Silver.

Groundedness — An agent-evaluation dimension measuring whether the agent's output is sourced from retrieved grounds vs hallucinated.

Y.8 H

HIC (Human-in-Command) — The supervisory mode where humans retain strategic authority — can pause the agent fleet, redirect orchestrations, shut down agent classes, or change policy bundles — but do not monitor individual decisions. The outermost mode of the oversight spectrum. See §2.2C.

HITL (Human-in-the-Loop) — The APEX pattern where human review, approval, or intervention governs agent decisions before or after execution. Default posture for consequential / irreversible / regulator-scrutinized decisions. One of three modes in the oversight spectrum. See §2.2C.

HOTL (Human-on-the-Loop) — The supervisory mode where agents act autonomously within defined constraints and a human monitors (dashboards, exception alerts) rather than approves each action. Appropriate for routine, reversible, volumetric decisions that exceed human-approval bandwidth. One of three modes in the oversight spectrum. See §2.2C.

HLS (Healthcare & Life Sciences) — APEX Practice covering Payer (health plans), Provider (hospitals and physician groups), and Life Sciences (pharma, med-device, CROs).

Y.9 I

Identity Plane — One of APEX's four architectural planes (data / reasoning / governance / identity). Implemented on Entra.

Insider Risk Management — Purview's behavioral-analytics tool for detecting anomalous user and workload behavior.

Interaction (Customer Interaction) — A single customer touchpoint — web session, service call, in-store visit, chat. Canonical entity in CXML.

IROPs (Irregular Operations) — Airline industry term for operational disruptions (weather cancellations, mechanical, crew). Recovery is a major TH Practice use case.

ISV (Independent Software Vendor) — Software vendor who may host Microsoft solutions on Azure Marketplace. One of the approved funding paths for Deloitte DMTSP engagements.

Y.10 J

JIT (Just-in-Time access) — Time-bounded access elevation pattern governed by Entra Privileged Identity Management.

Y.11 K

KPI (Key Performance Indicator) — Metrics tracked to measure agentic-AI deployment outcomes. See Appendix S for comprehensive per-Practice KPI expectations.

KQL (Kusto Query Language) — Query language for Fabric Eventhouse and Eventhouse.

Y.12 L

Lakehouse — Fabric workload for lakehouse-pattern data (Delta tables + unstructured files).

Latency — Time from source event to agent-consumable data. Varies by integration pattern from sub-second (Eventstream) to hours (scheduled batch).

Lineage — Purview's end-to-end provenance tracking from source system through transforms to agent output and downstream consumer.

Y.13 M

Manifest — Git-versioned declarative artifact that defines an APEX service component (event manifest, orchestration manifest, agent manifest, tenant manifest).

Managed Identity — Entra identity primitive for workload-authenticated access without explicit credential management. Every APEX agent runs under a managed identity.

Markdown (merchandise) — Permanent price reduction to clear aged or overstock inventory. MERML canonical entity in RC.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) — Open standard for agent-tool interaction. APEX tools are exposed as MCP servers; agents consume them via MCP client.

Medallion architecture — The Bronze / Silver / Gold layered data architecture pattern used throughout APEX.

MERML — APEX Merchandising ML canonical schema in RC Practice.

Mirrored Database — Fabric mechanism for continuous CDC replication from source databases into OneLake as Delta tables.

Y.14 N

NPI (New Product Introduction) — Manufacturing/product-launch term. AXLE framework uses DTML (Digital Twin) for NPI simulation.

Y.15 O

OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness) — Manufacturing metric combining availability, performance, and quality. Anchor KPI for AAML and AXLE framework.

OneLake — Fabric's unified tenant-wide logical data lake.

Oversight spectrum — The three-mode framing of human oversight in APEX: HITL (checkpoint on consequential actions), HOTL (exception-based monitoring of routine actions), HIC (strategic authority over the agent fleet). Every APEX service declares which mode applies to which decision class. See §2.2C.

Orchestration — The composition of multiple agents into a governed multi-step workflow with manifest governance, HITL gate placement, classification propagation, and per-step audit-row emission. APEX has 47 reusable orchestration archetypes manifesting as ~150 Practice-specific orchestrations (see Appendix T). Distinct from data orchestration (Data Factory / Activator) and BPM workflow engines. See §6.9 for the deep-dive.

Orchestration Archetype — One of the 47 reusable patterns in APEX's internal accelerator library. Archetypes cluster into 12 families (continuous-monitor + threshold + HITL, pattern-match + multi-stakeholder response, etc.) and specialize per Practice to produce concrete orchestrations.

Orchestration Manifest — Git-versioned declarative specification of an orchestration: steps, agents, tool bindings, HITL insertion points, classification policy, audit emission, failure modes, evaluation hooks, version. The governance artifact for any multi-agent composition.

Orchestration Pattern — One of the four primitive patterns (Sequential / Parallel / Hierarchical / Feedback-Loop) or any composition thereof. See §6.9.2.

Sequential Orchestration — Primitive pattern where agent A's output feeds agent B which feeds agent C. Used for strict dependency orders (detect → classify → disposition → notify).

Parallel Orchestration — Primitive pattern where a dispatch node fans out to multiple independent agents whose outputs merge downstream. Used for concurrent independent investigations.

Hierarchical Orchestration — Primitive pattern where an orchestrator agent plans and dispatches to specialist agents, receiving outputs back. Used for complex decisions where the plan itself requires reasoning.

Feedback-Loop Orchestration — Primitive pattern where an agent produces output, an evaluator assesses, and either accepts or sends back for refinement. Used where quality thresholds matter.

OT (Operational Technology) — Industrial control systems (SCADA, DCS, PLC, historians). Common source systems in ER and AXLE.

Y.16 P

PAM (Privileged Access Management) — Entra's JIT-elevation and approval-gated access for sensitive operations.

Part II (Fabric, Foundry, Copilot, Purview) — The four Microsoft platform-pillar chapters in the sellers guide.

PCI (Payment Card Industry) — PCI DSS data security standard for payment-card data handling.

PHI (Protected Health Information) — HIPAA-protected health data. Heightened Purview classification and DLP apply.

PII (Personally Identifiable Information) — Privacy-regulated personal data under GDPR / CCPA / state privacy laws.

PIM (Privileged Identity Management) — Entra's time-bounded elevation service for high-privilege access.

Playbook — Per-Practice or per-account pursuit guidance (Part III industry chapters, Part IV account chapters).

Power BI — Microsoft's business-intelligence and semantic-model platform. Direct Lake serving is the default APEX Gold consumption path.

Practice (APEX Practice) — One of the seven APEX industry verticals: RC, HLS, ER, AXLE, TMT, TH, ICE. A Practice is not a product; it is a bundle of five reusable Deloitte internal assets — canonical schemas, agent catalog, orchestration catalog, service catalog, delivery playbook — organized per vertical to compress client time-to-value. See §1.1A.

Pre-measure — Calculated column computed during Silver → Gold transform. Embodied in Gold table columns.

Post-measure — Calculated measure computed at query time in Power BI semantic model (DAX), Warehouse view (SQL), or Eventhouse function (KQL).

Prompt injection — Attack vector where malicious input to an LLM attempts to override system instructions. Defended via Azure AI Content Safety's jailbreak shield + APEX manifest-scoped agent boundaries.

PSPS (Public Safety Power Shut-off) — Utility practice of de-energising grid segments during wildfire-risk conditions. ER Practice decision pattern.

PSS (Passenger Service System) — Airline reservation system (Sabre, Amadeus Altea, Navitaire, proprietary). TH Practice SOR.

Purview — Microsoft's governance platform. The governance plane in APEX's four-plane architecture.

Y.17 Q

QR (Quality Review) — Deloitte's internal review process. Commercial QR, Independence QR, Risk QR all apply to engagement delivery.

Y.18 R

RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) — Agent pattern where retrieved enterprise data grounds the foundation-model response. In APEX's hybrid context model (§6.12.5), RAG supports semantic search over unstructured content (docs, emails, transcripts) and is complementary to the file-first paradigm that carries agent identity and canonical schema. RAG does not carry agent identity, governance rules, or canonical entity definitions — those are file-first.

RC (Retail & Consumer) — APEX Practice covering grocery/mass retail, apparel, specialty, CPG, and related.

Recall (product recall) — Regulatory product-recall process. APEX's recall-scope agents in RC trace from affected lot to customer notification in minutes (FSMA 204-compliant).

Revenue cycle (HLS) — Hospital financial operations: admission-to-payment lifecycle, denial management, coding, collections.

RLS (Row-Level Security) — Classification-driven row-filter applied at query time in Fabric Warehouse.

Y.19 S

SCML — APEX Supply Chain Merchandising Language canonical schema in RC Practice. (Note: different from AXLE framework SCML which is Supply Chain ML for automotive.)

SDV (Software-Defined Vehicle) — Automotive architecture where vehicle functions are software-upgradable over-the-air. AXLE CVML schema supports.

Semantic model — Named set of canonical entities, attributes, and relationships. Each Practice has its semantic model(s).

Sensitivity label — Purview classification applied to data elements. Drives DLP, encryption, and access decisions.

Service (APEX service) — Productised bundle of scenario + personas + KPIs + SLOs + manifests + agents + commercial terms. Internal Deloitte shorthand; client-facing language is "Deloitte agentic-AI service."

Shortcut (OneLake shortcut) — Fabric mechanism for referencing data in place across workspaces and clouds without copying.

Silver layer — The canonical layer of the medallion architecture. Typed, cleansed, tokenized, canonical-entity-conformant data.

SOR (System of Record) — Enterprise source system (ERP, EHR, WMS, CRM, etc.) that APEX Bronze layer ingests from.

SOW (Statement of Work) — Contractual document specifying engagement scope, deliverables, timeline, and fees.

SPC (Statistical Process Control) — Quality-management technique. AXLE QEML schema supports SPC event handling.

SSO (Single Sign-On) — Identity federation pattern. Standard in enterprise Microsoft 365 deployments.

Sustain (Wave 3) — The post-Wave-2 operating phase where agentic AI deployment runs in production with continuous improvement.

Y.20 T

TCS (Tata Consultancy Services) — Major competitor to Deloitte in services delivery. See Appendix M.

TEL (TMT-TEL) — Telecom sub-segment of TMT Practice.

TEC (TMT-TEC) — Technology sub-segment of TMT Practice.

Telemetry — Sensor or event data from physical or logical sources. Foundation for ER, AXLE, ICE agent patterns.

Tenant (Microsoft tenant) — Microsoft Entra ID tenant representing a client's Microsoft identity and resource environment.

TH (Travel & Hospitality) — APEX Practice covering airlines, hotels, cruise, ground transport, and mobility services.

Tier (data classification tier) — Four-tier sensitivity model: Tier 1 Public, Tier 2 Internal, Tier 3 Confidential, Tier 4 Restricted.

TMT (Technology, Media & Telecom) — APEX Practice covering TEC, MED, and TEL sub-segments.

Tool (MCP tool) — A specific capability an agent can invoke through the MCP interface. Deloitte-delivered APEX catalog contains 165+ tools across Practices.

Two-contract model — The Independence-required commercial structure where client contracts Microsoft for platform and Deloitte for services separately.

Y.21 U

UM (Utilization Management) — Payer process for authorising healthcare services. HLS-Payer-UM is a primary APEX service.

Unified Catalog (Purview) — The federated catalog view across Purview Data Map, Microsoft Fabric, and Power BI that presents one catalog surface.

Y.22 V

Value-share — Commercial arrangement where a portion of Deloitte fees is contingent on measurable business outcomes. Applicable to select APEX services (RC shrink, RC recovery, HLS denial recovery, ICE warranty).

VoC (Voice of Customer) — Aggregate customer-feedback analytics. A contact-center capability area.

Y.23 W

Warehouse (Fabric Warehouse) — Fabric's T-SQL-native analytical warehouse. Common Gold-serving layer for agent MCP tool queries.

Warranty (WLML) — AXLE framework warranty-lifecycle ML schema.

Wave (Wave 1 / Wave 2 / Wave 3) — APEX delivery phases: Wave 1 Envision & Land (4–8 weeks envisioning + first services), Wave 2 Enable & Scale (6–15 months), Wave 3 Sustain & Transform (multi-year).

WMS (Warehouse Management System) — Operations SOR (Manhattan, Blue Yonder, SAP EWM) for warehouse inventory, receiving, pick/pack, shipping.

Workflow — A defined sequence of steps in an enterprise process that APEX agents may participate in.

Workforce (WOSFML) — AXLE framework Workforce Operations / Shift ML schema.

Y.24 X

XMLA endpoint — Power BI's API endpoint for programmatic dataset operations (refresh, partition management).

Y.25 Y, Z

Yield (hotel / airline / retail yield management) — Pricing optimization for capacity-constrained products. TH Practice use case.

Y.26 Numbers & Acronyms

21 CFR Part 11 — FDA electronic-records regulation applicable to Life Sciences.

5G slicing — Network-slicing technology in 5G deployments. TMT-TEL emerging service area.

360 (member 360, customer 360, patient 360) — Unified cross-source view of an entity. Foundation for personalisation, care management, next-best-action agents.

Independence Reminder

Independence Reminder. This glossary is internal reference material. Definitions of Deloitte-specific terminology (DMTSP, APEX, AXLE, Wave structure) should not appear in client-facing materials without Independence Office review.

Appendix AA

Runtime Addendum — Summary for Sellers (v1.5)

AA.1 Purpose of this addendum

This addendum extended the Sellers Guide with content that emerged after initial publication: the Runtime Plane (gateway, safety, evaluation, observability), the Cost envelope as the sixth commercial envelope, and the connection between the LEDGER vision and the evaluation harness. These additions do not replace prior content; they fill gaps that sophisticated architect and CIO buyers ask about directly.

Independence compliance reminder

Throughout this addendum and the sections it extends, the Deloitte–Microsoft relationship is described as "Deloitte's Microsoft practice," "DMTSP," or "Microsoft-native deployment." Never "partner," "alliance," or "strategic alliance."

AA.2 What changed in v1.5

SectionChangeWhy it was added
Chapter 5A (new)The Runtime Plane — Gateway, Safety, Evaluation, ObservabilityAnswer the four operational questions sophisticated buyers ask: cost, hallucinations, evidence of working, failure mode.
§2.2A.2 updatedFive envelopes → six envelopes (added Cost envelope)Runtime decisions burn against a FinOps boundary that wasn't explicit in the prior taxonomy.
§2.2A.3 updatedNesting now ends with "metered by Cost envelope"Cost measures what every other envelope allows; closes the economic loop.
§6.10.12 (new)Added cost_per_decision and safety_verdict fields to the typed audit rowMakes "what does it cost?" and "did we check?" queryable, not promised.
§6.12.7 (new)LEDGER → Runtime feedback loop (year-by-year superagent trajectory)Converts LEDGER from a static compliance artifact to the substrate that makes agents learn.

AA.3 Five things to remember

  1. Runtime Plane = the four operational questions answered. Gateway, Safety, Eval, Obs. One sub-plane per question.
  2. Cost is the sixth envelope. Every agent decision is bounded by six envelopes; cost is measured, not estimated.
  3. Audit row carries both cost and safety. cost_per_decision and safety_verdict on every decision.
  4. LEDGER is a learning substrate, not just a compliance log. The feedback loop closes through it. Year one instincts, year two record, year three superagent.
  5. Independence language still applies. "DMTSP," "Deloitte's Microsoft practice," or "Microsoft-native deployment." Never "partner," "alliance," or "strategic alliance."

  • §6.10.12 — Runtime Addendum audit-row extensions
  • §6.12.7 — LEDGER → Runtime feedback loop

End of addendum. For questions, contact the APEX authoring team.

Appendix AB · New 2026-05

Positioning Fabric IQ in the Commercial Narrative

Native Microsoft ontology + agentic Q&A · what it changes for the seller, what it doesn't.

What changed in May 2026

Microsoft shipped Fabric IQ — Ontology · Plan · Graph · Data Agent · Operations Agent · Power BI semantic models — as a Fabric workload. The Data Agent is GA; the rest is preview. This addendum tells the seller what to do with that fact: what it strengthens, what it commoditizes, and how to handle the inevitable "aren't you obsolete now?" question.

AB.1 The pitch shift · four positioning notes

S1 · The acceleration is now on top of Microsoft, not instead of it. Before Fabric IQ, the Deloitte pitch had to explain how APEX built the semantic + Q&A layer over OneLake. With Fabric IQ, Microsoft ships that layer natively. The Deloitte pitch becomes: "Microsoft now ships the ontology + Data Agent surface. Our acceleration is the industry-specific schema content that fills the ontology, the per-Service Data Agent topologies, the orchestration of Foundry agents over Fabric Data Agents, and the governance + audit fabric across both. We're acceleration on top — not a replacement." This is a stronger pitch, not a weaker one — it commoditizes the bits Microsoft commoditizes and concentrates Deloitte value where it always belonged.

S2 · The "101→401" answer strengthens. Matt-King-class CIOs (the "don't push us to 401 before we're at 101" objection — see Appendix C) get a stronger answer when Fabric IQ is in the picture. Why: Fabric IQ inherits Microsoft Purview governance, DLP, DSPM-for-AI, Insider Risk Management, and Audit + eDiscovery natively. The seller's foundation-readiness story moves from "we'll layer governance on top of your lake" to "your Fabric tenant comes governance-ready; we orchestrate it for your industry." Add to the objection handler in Appendix C under "data quality / foundation readiness".

S3 · Fabric-resident clients become a hot pocket. Clients already on Fabric (any F2+ capacity) inherit a much smaller engagement scope under the Fabric-IQ-led path. The commercial implication:

  • Faster Wave 1 — fewer custom MCP servers to build (the read paths collapse into Fabric Data Agent NL2X); Wave 1 envelope shrinks ~25–35% in implementation cost
  • Higher Wave 2 margin — the orchestration + industry-schema-content work is where Deloitte value concentrates; Wave 2 stays at full envelope
  • ECIF leverage — Fabric IQ adoption is a Microsoft-funded discovery moment; ECIF eligibility (see Appendix D) extends to Fabric IQ proof-of-value scoping

Fabric-resident clients are now the highest-leverage pursuits. Re-prioritize the anchor-account list (Appendix Q) to flag which 13 anchors are already on Fabric.

S4 · Objection handling · "Aren't you obsolete if Microsoft ships this?" Highly likely question from a CIO who's read the Fabric IQ launch announcement. The answer:

  • "Microsoft ships the engine. We ship the schema content — the SCML, MERML, PatientML, AXLEML, and the others — that tells Fabric IQ what your industry's nouns and verbs are. Without that, the Ontology is empty. With it, you have a productized Service catalog that other clients in your industry have already vetted."
  • "Microsoft ships the conversational surface. We ship the agent fleet that does the work — The Buyer, The Planner, The Analyst — that calls the Fabric Data Agent as one of several tools. Conversational Q&A is a single capability; agentic services are the productized outcome."
  • "Microsoft ships the deployment pipeline. We ship the governance fabric — PSG-1 through PSG-16, the LEDGER hash chain, the audit-row anchoring across Fabric pipelines and Foundry agents and custom MCP. Audit-defensibility across multiple Microsoft surfaces is a separate discipline from any single surface."

Lead with what Microsoft did ship and how Deloitte composes it. Never minimize what Microsoft shipped — the seller who sounds threatened by Fabric IQ has already lost the room.

AB.2 What stays identical in the commercial narrative

  • Two-contract Independence model — client ↔ Microsoft for platform; client ↔ Deloitte for the Service-delivery engagement. ECIF flows direct from Microsoft. Unchanged. Fabric IQ runs in the client tenant under the same structure.
  • The 38-Service catalog — still what clients buy. Fabric IQ is substrate; the Service is the contractable unit.
  • Wave 1 → Wave 2 → Wave 3 cadence — unchanged. Fabric-IQ-led pursuits move faster through Wave 1 but the wave structure stays.
  • KPI envelopes per Service — unchanged. The way the KPI is delivered changes (more Microsoft-native, less custom MCP) but the envelope is the same commitment.
  • Persona briefs in Appendix O — unchanged. Personas are industry-defined, not surface-defined.

AB.3 The Fabric IQ status pin · what's GA, what's preview

Fabric IQ itemStatusSales implication
Fabric Data AgentGASellable today. No preview disclaimer required.
DLP for Fabric Data WarehouseGASellable today as part of the governance story.
Fabric IQ workload (Ontology · Plan · Graph · Operations Agent)PREVIEWPosition as "in-flight Microsoft capability we'll adopt as it GAs"; do not commit to it as Wave-1 Service infrastructure unless the client is comfortable with preview lifecycle. Disclose preview state in SOW.
DSPM Data Risk Assessments · Insider Risk · Agent prompt/response auditPREVIEWStrong demo material; SOW-disclose preview state.

AB.4 Constraints sellers should know about

From the Fabric Data Agent doc — the limits matter for SOW scoping:

  • 5 data sources max per Data Agent — multi-domain pursuits need multi-agent topologies; price accordingly
  • 25-row × 25-column response cap — conversational analytics, not bulk extract. Set client expectations on the demo.
  • English only — non-English markets need custom MCP path or wait for Microsoft non-English support. Note in international anchor-account playbooks (Appendix Q).
  • Region affinity — Data Agent + sources share workspace capacity region. Multi-region tenants need region planning in Wave 0 discovery.
  • F2+ capacity required; Operations Agent forbids trial capacities — Day-Zero capacity sizing has a hard floor.
  • LLM not user-configurable — Microsoft picks the model. Removes a previously-negotiable variable from SOW.

AB.5 First-meeting talking points · the 60-second version

For the discovery deck (see Appendix O per-persona templates), add a slide with this language:

"Microsoft shipped Fabric IQ in May 2026 — a native semantic layer + conversational data agent in Fabric. That's good news for both of us. It means the basic plumbing we used to charge you to build is now in the platform. What we accelerate is what's specific to your industry — the schema content, the Service catalog, the agent fleet that does the work, and the governance fabric that ties Foundry, Fabric, Purview, and your existing systems together. Fabric IQ makes Wave 1 faster and Wave 2 better. We'll position the engagement to take advantage of both."
